Handbook

Welcome to the Handbook of Jewish AI Ethics, an annotated bibliography of key topics at the intersection of artificial intelligence and Jewish thought. Each entry lists the primary sources (Tanakh, Talmud, Midrash, codes, responsa, and later rabbinic works) and the secondary literature that bear on its topic, with a short annotation on each source and cross-references to related entries. The entries are meant to ground further scholarship and research. The full handbook, in which each entry opens with an essay surveying the sources and the questions they raise, is being prepared as a book. As always, be sure to contact us with any feedback and/or additional resources you'd like to see here.

Click on any topic below to read its bibliography, or use the search bar (top right) to find specific terms across all entries.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b; Gittin 29b; Kiddushin 41b-43a; Bava Metzia 10b-12a, 96a; Nedarim 72b. Establishes the attribution formula, tests who can serve as an agent, and distinguishes between an agent as the principal's extension and an independently empowered actor.

  • Mishnah Gittin 2:5; Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 23a. Disqualifies a deaf-mute, a person deemed mentally incompetent, a minor, a blind person and a gentile from carrying a bill of divorce, and explains that the first three lack de'ah (understanding) and that the gentile is not bar hetera, not subject to the law of divorce himself.

  • Nazir 12b. A person may appoint an agent only for an act he is able to perform at the time of the appointment.

  • Kiddushin 22b; 23b. Attributes an animal's movement to its owner's intent and a slave's movement to his own, and treats the priests who perform the sacrificial service as agents of Heaven because the owner cannot perform it himself.

  • Eruvin 31b. Food conveyed for an eruv by an elephant or a monkey does not establish the eruv, while a person instructed to receive it from them does.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4. One who sends a fire through a deaf-mute, a person deemed mentally incompetent or a minor is exempt in human law and liable in the law of Heaven, whereas if he sends it through a competent person, that person is liable.

  • Rashi and Tosafot, Bava Metzia 10b. Ask whether a courtyard acquires as an extension of the owner's hand or as his agent, and why the Talmud tests the question against the rule that there is no agency for a transgression.

  • Nimukei Yosef, Bava Metzia 5b (Rif pagination). Holds that a courtyard acquires as the owner's hand, and that Scripture extended agency to it only in order to make a sender liable for a transgression.

  • Penei Yehoshua, Bava Metzia 11a. Argues that even on the view that a courtyard acquires as the owner's hand, it acquires no less than an agent where the acquisition benefits the owner.

  • Rashba, Ḥiddushei ha-Rashba on Gittin 21a. Compares a wife's courtyard, which can receive a bill of divorce against her will, with an agent appointed to receive it, and leaves the comparison unresolved.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 182:1, with Rema, Sma and Shakh. Rules that a person's agent is like himself in every matter other than a transgression; Rema adds that an intermediary who is not himself liable is an agent even for a transgression, leaving the principal liable, and the Shakh questions that gloss.

  • Ketzot HaḤoshen, simanim 182 and 188; Sefer ha-Mikneh 15:4-8. (Aryeh Leib Heller). Discussions of the nature of agency, including whether the agent acts as an extension of the principal or through independently delegated power. Siman 182:1 holds that agency reaches acts of performance only, so that a commandment imposed on a person's body cannot be discharged through an agent; siman 188:2 asks whether an agency lapses if the principal loses his da'at before the agent completes it.

  • Sefer ha-Mikneh, vol 2, no. 23 and others quoted in Kovetz Yesodot ve-Ḥakirot, shelihut. Extensive discussion and sources covering the talmudic evidence and applications of various forms of agency.

Secondary Sources

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Analyzes whether AI-mediated acts are attributable to the operator as direct action, indirect causation, or another halakhic category, with applications to damages and Shabbat.

  • Klein, David. "The Mechanism of Agency" [Hebrew: מנגנון השליחות]. Yarḥon Ha-Otzar 105 (Av 5785/2025): 450-465. Examines the conceptual underpinnings of sheliḥut in rabbinic literature, including an AI-enabled artificial limb as an analogy for the "extended hand" model.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge University Press, 2024. Discusses sheliḥut, animal-liability, and grama as possible but underdetermined frameworks for AI.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019. New York: Rabbinical Assembly, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. Holds that obligation is an essential qualification for agency and that an inanimate object cannot be an agent, so that liability for an autonomous machine's act remains with the human principal, while allowing a non-obligated intermediary for preparatory steps.

  • Gabriel, Iason, et al. "The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants." arXiv (2024). Maps the ethical risks created when AI assistants plan and perform sequences of actions on users' behalf, including value alignment, user autonomy, misuse, and effects on non-users.

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology. Accelerating the Adoption of Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization: Concept Paper. February 2026. Proposes identity, authorization, access-delegation, logging, and provenance controls that preserve accountability when software agents act for human users or organizations. The document is a draft concept paper of the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, by Harold Booth, Bill Fisher, Ryan Galluzzo and Joshua Roberts, seeking comment on focus areas for a proposed project.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:27. The creation of humanity be-tselem Elohim (in the divine image), establishing the foundational equality and dignity of all persons regardless of social category.

  • Exodus 23:3. "Do not favor the poor in his cause."

  • Exodus 23:6. "Do not pervert the judgment of the poor in his cause."

  • Exodus 23:7. "Keep far from a false matter"; the Babylonian Talmud (Shevuot 31a) derives from this verse that two litigants must appear before the court in comparable dress.

  • Leviticus 19:15. "You shall not render an unfair decision; do not favor the poor or show deference to the rich; judge your kinsman fairly."

  • Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:19. Judges may not "recognize faces in judgment" and must hear "the small and the great alike"; a bribe is forbidden because it "blinds the eyes of the wise."

  • Deuteronomy 10:18-19. The obligation to love and provide for the stranger (ger), grounded in Israel's experience of vulnerability in Egypt.

  • Isaiah 11:4. The Messiah "will judge the poor justly and decide with equity for the meek of the earth." Messianic justice attends to the vulnerable.

  • Isaiah 56:3-7. Reference to members of other nations. Foreigners who join themselves to God and keep the Sabbath and the covenant are promised a place in the Temple, "a house of prayer for all peoples."

  • Amos 9:7. Indication that God's providence extends to non-Israelites.

  • Malachi 2:10. "Have we not all one Father? Did not one God create us?"

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. Adam was created alone "for the sake of peace among people, so that no one could say to another, 'My father was greater than yours.'" Also teaches that whoever destroys a single life is as if they destroyed an entire world. It opens by warning witnesses in capital cases against testifying from conjecture.

  • Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; Genesis Rabbah 24:7. R. Akiva calls "Love your neighbor as yourself" a great principle of the Torah, and Ben Azzai names "This is the book of the generations of Adam" a greater one; in Genesis Rabbah, R. Tanḥuma adds that one who demeans another demeans one made "in the likeness of God." The Sifra passage opens by reading the prohibition of vengeance as not extending to a gentile.

  • Pirkei Avot 1:6. Joshua ben Perahiah's teaching to "judge every person favorably."

  • Rashi on Avot 1:6 (commentary printed under Rashi's name, generally regarded as pseudepigraphic). Explains judging favorably as assuming that a person intended good "until you know with certainty that it is not so."

  • Pirkei Avot 1:8. Yehudah ben Tabbai: while litigants stand before the judge they are to be regarded as wicked, and once they leave, having accepted the judgment, as innocent.

  • Pirkei Avot 3:14. R. Akiva: "Beloved is man, for he was created in the image," followed by "Beloved are Israel, for they are called children of the Omnipresent."

  • Pirkei Avot 4:3. "Do not despise any person, and do not discriminate against anything, for there is no person who does not have their hour, and no thing that does not have its place."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a. Hillel's formulation of the Golden Rule: "That which is hateful to you, do not do to another."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 54b. Responsibility to protest wrongdoing at the level of household, town, and world.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a. Berurya's teaching to pray for the end of sin rather than the destruction of sinners; may suggest focus on reforming systems rather than punishing individuals.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a. A saying of the rabbis of Yavneh: "I am a creature and my fellow is a creature; my work is in the town and his work is in the field."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 105b. Rav Papa rules that one should not judge a person one loves or hates, since the first sees no fault and the second no merit; R. Yishmael b. R. Yose recuses himself after declining a gift and still finds himself arguing the giver's case.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 83a. The case of Rabbah bar bar Ḥanan and the porters; Rav rules that justice requires attending to the workers' poverty, not merely applying the formal law.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 92b; Bava Kamma 27b. Shmuel holds that a statistical majority is followed in ritual prohibitions but not in monetary cases, and the Talmud states that "one does not follow the majority in monetary matters."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a. Extended discussion of human dignity and the infinite value of each individual life.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 37b. Testimony from conjecture is excluded in capital cases: witnesses who saw a man with a dripping sword beside a dying victim "saw nothing."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 30a-b. A baraita reads "In righteousness shall you judge your fellow" (Leviticus 19:15) as requiring equal procedure for both litigants and, alternatively, as the duty to judge another favorably; R. Yosef and R. Naḥman then discuss favoring a scholar where the outcome rests on the judges' discretion (shuda de-dayyanei).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 31a. Procedural requirements ensuring that litigants appear equal before the court; wealthy parties may not dress more impressively than poor ones.

  • Rashi on Shevuot 30b and 31a. On 30b, where a case rests on the judges' discretion, a scholar is fit to be favored "because he is wise and righteous"; on 31a, the better-dressed litigant must match his opponent's dress lest the court show him favor or his opponent's claims be "stopped up" by his importance.

  • Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabbah 9. Heaven and earth are called to witness that "whether Israelite or gentile, whether man or woman, whether slave or maidservant," the holy spirit rests on each according to his deeds.

  • Rashbatz (R. Shimon ben Tzemach Duran), Tashbetz 1:158; cf. 1:161; Maharik shoresh 66; Radbaz 6:2248. The enactments and statutes of kings are general rather than particular; a directive aimed at a single individual does not carry the force of law.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Gezelah va-Avedah 5:14; Tur, Ḥoshen Mishpat 369. A law the king enacts for all, and not for one person alone, is not robbery, while what is taken from one man alone outside the law known to all is robbery; the Tur limits the law of the kingdom to "a general matter that he decrees on all the people of his kingdom."

  • Isserles to Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 369:6 (citing Maharik, shoresh 194). A fixed levy counts as uniform even where the king has ordered that a Jew pay more than a gentile.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 20:4-5; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 17:10. A judge may not favor a poor litigant out of compassion or honor a great one, and may not treat one litigant's known wickedness as a presumption that he lies; both litigants are regarded as wicked while before the court.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 21:1-6; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 17:1. The litigants are to be equal "in every respect," including speech, the judge's demeanor, and dress; the chapter also sets a scholar's seating and an order of hearing that gives precedence to the orphan, the widow, the scholar, and the woman.

  • Maimonides, Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Negative Commandment 290. A judge may not decide punishments "by strong conjecture, even if it is close to the truth" (הזהיר הדיין שלא לחתוך הגדרים באומד הדעת החזק ואפילו היה קרוב לאמת).

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Matanot Aniyim 7:3. The obligation to provide for the poor according to their individual needs, preserving dignity through attention to particularity.

Secondary Sources

Modern Jewish Theology

  • Buber, Martin. I and Thou. Translated by Walter Kaufmann. New York: Scribner, 1970 [orig. Ich und Du, 1923]. Distinguishes the I-Thou relation of direct encounter from the I-It relation in which another is treated as an object of description and use.

  • Levinas, Emmanuel. Totality and Infinity: An Essay on Exteriority. Translated by Alphonso Lingis. Pittsburgh: Duquesne University Press, 1969 [orig. Totalité et Infini, 1961]. Argues that the face of the other makes an ethical claim prior to any category applied to them, and criticizes the reduction of persons to instances within a totality of general concepts.

  • Hughes, Aaron W. Rethinking Jewish Philosophy: Beyond Particularism and Universalism. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014. Critically examines the tension between particularist and universalist strands in Jewish thought.

  • Sacks, Jonathan. The Dignity of Difference: How to Avoid the Clash of Civilizations. London: Continuum, 2002. Argues that human dignity requires recognition of difference rather than homogenization; relevant to debates about whether systems should be "colorblind" or attend to group membership.

  • Feit, Joseph. "The Algorithm That Couldn't See: AI Ethics and the Halakhic Discipline of Perception." The Lehrhaus, March 23, 2026. Argues that because AI systems perceive through statistical patterns, using them as a stand-in for human judgement erodes our moral sensitivity.

Jewish Ethics, Universalism, and Human Dignity

  • Novak, David. The Image of the Non-Jew in Judaism: An Historical and Constructive Study of the Noahide Laws. New York: Edwin Mellen Press, 1983. The classic treatment of how halakhah addresses the moral and legal status of gentiles; argues that the Noahide laws establish a framework of universal human dignity grounded in creation.

  • Soloveichik, Aharon. "Civil Rights and the Dignity of Man." In Logic of the Heart, Logic of the Mind: Wisdom and Reflections on Topics of Our Times, 61-70. Jerusalem: Genesis Jerusalem Press, 1991. A forceful Orthodox rabbinic argument for racial equality written in the context of the American civil rights.

  • Dorff, Elliot N. To Do the Right and the Good: A Jewish Approach to Modern Social Ethics. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 2002. Accessible treatment of Jewish social ethics including justice, equality, and communal responsibility; includes discussion of affirmative action and systemic remedies.

  • Rosenberg, Shalom. "On the Principles of Jewish Ethics: 'Love Your Neighbor as Yourself'—Universalism and Equality" [Hebrew: על עקרונות המוסר היהודי: 'ואהבת לרעך כמוך' - אוניברסליזם ושוויון]. Ma'aseh Ḥoshev 2. Koren, 5778/2017, 39-52. Develops equality, universalizability, and the image of God as related but nonidentical moral principles.

  • Navon, Haim. "I Am a Creature and My Fellow Is a Creature: The Value of Equality—A Jewish View" [Hebrew: אני ברייה וחברי ברייה: ערך השוויון - מבט יהודי]. Ma'aseh Ḥoshev 2. Koren, 5778/2017, 53-70. Argues that equality affirms common human standing without requiring identical treatment of every relevant difference. Navon grounds the Mishnah's rejection of distinctions of lineage in "peace among people" and distinguishes inequality of birth, which he reads the rabbis as rejecting, from differences of social role (68-69).

Algorithmic Bias and Fairness

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology. Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence. NIST Special Publication 1270. March 2022. Available online. Distinguishes systemic, statistical and computational, and human bias, and emphasizes that harmful outcomes can arise without discriminatory intent.

  • Barocas, Solon, and Andrew D. Selbst. "Big Data's Disparate Impact." California Law Review 104, no. 3 (2016): 671-732. Foundational legal analysis demonstrating how data mining can reproduce patterns of discrimination even without discriminatory intent; applies disparate impact doctrine to algorithmic decision-making.

  • Hardt, Moritz. "How Big Data Is Unfair." Medium, September 26, 2014. Accessible introduction to the concept of unfairness in machine learning, explaining how predictive models can systematically disadvantage certain groups even when built on accurate statistical correlations.

  • Crawford, Kate. "The Hidden Biases in Big Data." Harvard Business Review, April 1, 2013. Explains how biases enter data systems through collection methods, sampling, and the assumptions embedded in the design process, often invisibly.

  • Hao, Karen. "This Is How AI Bias Really Happens—and Why It's so Hard to Fix." MIT Technology Review, February 4, 2019. Journalistic overview identifying three key stages at which bias enters AI systems: problem framing, data collection, and data preparation; valuable for its clarity in explaining technical dynamics to non-specialist audiences.

  • Helbing, Dirk, Bruno S. Frey, Gerd Gigerenzer, Ernst Hafen, Michael Hagner, Yvonne Hofstetter, Jeroen van den Hoven, Roberto V. Zicari, and Andrej Zwitter. "Will Democracy Survive Big Data and Artificial Intelligence?" Scientific American, February 25, 2017. Reprinted from Spektrum der Wissenschaft. Warns that scoring and steering citizens at scale converts ostensibly neutral optimization into political control.

  • Johnson, Gabbrielle M. "Algorithmic Bias: On the Implicit Biases of Social Technology." Synthese 198, no. 10 (2020): 9941-61. Philosophical analysis drawing on research in implicit bias to argue that algorithmic systems can encode the same kinds of unconscious prejudices found in human cognition, complicating claims that automation eliminates bias.

  • Kleinberg, Jon, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Jure Leskovec, Jens Ludwig, and Sendhil Mullainathan. "Human Decisions and Machine Predictions." Quarterly Journal of Economics 133, no. 1 (2018a): 237-293. Empirical study of bail decisions finding that machine predictions could reduce jailing and crime rates simultaneously relative to human judges.

  • Kleinberg, Jon, Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Cass R. Sunstein. "Discrimination in the Age of Algorithms." Journal of Legal Analysis 10 (2018b): 113-174. Argues that algorithms make discrimination more detectable and provable than human decision-making, which resists inspection.

  • Lepri, Bruno, Nuria Oliver, Emmanuel Letouzé, Alex Pentland, and Patrick Vinck. "Fair, Transparent, and Accountable Algorithmic Decision-Making Processes." Philosophy & Technology 31, no. 4 (2018): 611-27. Proposes a framework for ensuring that algorithmic decision-making processes meet standards of fairness, transparency, and accountability.

  • Spaulding, Norman W. "Is Human Judgment Necessary? Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Governance, and the Law." In The Oxford Handbook of Ethics of AI, edited by Markus D. Dubber, Frank Pasquale, and Sunit Das. New York: Oxford University Press, 2020. Explores the ethical implications of automating adjudication generally.

  • Stewart, Matthew. "Programming Fairness in Algorithms." Towards Data Science, July 2, 2020. Practical walk-through of the competing formal fairness criteria and why satisfying several at once is generally impossible.

  • Xiang, Alice. "Reconciling Legal and Technical Approaches to Algorithmic Bias." Tennessee Law Review 88, no. 3 (2021): 649. Examines the gap between legal definitions of discrimination and technical definitions of fairness in machine learning.

  • Schauer, Frederick. Profiles, Probabilities, and Stereotypes. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2003. The foundational treatment of when it is defensible to judge a person by a generalization drawn from a group to which they belong; predates the algorithmic debate but frames it.

  • Eidelson, Benjamin. Discrimination and Disrespect. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2015. Grounds the duty to treat people as individuals in respect for autonomy, arguing that a decision-maker must attend to how a person has exercised agency to distinguish themselves from group patterns. See also his "Respect, Individualism, and Colorblindness," Yale Law Journal 129 (2020): 1600.

  • Lippert-Rasmussen, Kasper. "'We Are All Different': Statistical Discrimination and the Right to Be Treated as an Individual." The Journal of Ethics 15, nos. 1-2 (2011): 47-59. Argues that no coherent right to be treated as an individual can be formulated, since all practical judgment proceeds by generalization; the principal statement of the opposing position.

  • Hellman, Deborah. "Algorithmic Fairness." The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, July 30, 2025. Survey of the field from an ethical-philosophical perspective.

  • Binns, Reuben. "Human Judgment in Algorithmic Loops: Individual Justice and Automated Decision-Making." Regulation & Governance 16, no. 1 (2022): 197-211. Examines whether inserting human review into automated decisions delivers the individualized justice its advocates claim.

  • Barocas, Solon, Moritz Hardt, and Arvind Narayanan. Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities. MIT Press, 2023. Technical but accessible treatment of fairness in machine learning; explains the mathematical trade-offs between different fairness definitions and why they cannot all be satisfied simultaneously.

  • Chouldechova, Alexandra. "Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact: A Study of Bias in Recidivism Prediction Instruments." Big Data 5, no. 2 (2017): 153-163. Shows that several fairness criteria applied to recidivism prediction cannot all be satisfied at once when recidivism prevalence differs across groups, and how disparate impact arises when error rates are unbalanced.

Jewish Legal Safeguards Against Bias

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "The Human and Social Factor in Halakha." Tradition 36, no. 1 (2002): 89-114. Explores when human dignity (kevod ha-beriyot) overrides other halakhic considerations; foundational for understanding how dignity claims function in Jewish law and how they might inform the design of systems that affect human welfare.

  • Greenberg, Yitzhak. "Justice, Justice Shall You Pursue." Commentary on Parashat Shoftim 5781, August 17, 2021 (Sefaria sheet 341919). Analysis of Parashat Shoftim arguing that Jewish tradition supports affirmative action to remedy systemic injustice while warning against abandoning individual judgment; directly applicable to debates about how to balance categorical remedies with case-by-case assessment.

  • Sadan, Uri. "Selective Enforcement in Halakhah" [Hebrew: אכיפה בררנית בהלכה]. Teḥumin 38 (5778/2018): 345-354. Asks whether an authority may lawfully enforce a rule against some violators and not others, distinguishing discrimination against an individual from discrimination against a group; relevant to predictive policing and to any system that concentrates enforcement on a subset of a population. It sets Maimonides and the Maharik, followed by Isserles, against a view attributed to the Ra'aviah on whether a law that discriminates against a whole group is valid (346-347).

  • Sadan, Uri. "Affirmative Action in Light of Halakhah" [Hebrew: העדפה מתקנת לאור ההלכה]. Teḥumin 42 (5782/2022): 207-221. Distinguishes formal from substantive equality and opportunity from outcome, and asks whether halakhah permits or requires preferential treatment to remedy the underrepresentation of groups, in public service and in private hiring.

  • Bar-Ilan, Naftali. "Principles of Equality" [Hebrew: עקרונות שויון]. In Mishtar u-Medina be-Yisrael al pi ha-Torah [Government and State in Israel According to the Torah; Hebrew: משטר ומדינה בישראל על-פי התורה], vol. 4, ch. 64, 1530-1540. Eretz Hemdah, 5773/2013. Treats equality as a constraint on the institutions of government, including the king, the high court, and communal officers, drawing extensively on medieval and early modern communal record books. Concludes that these principles governing the relation between the individual and the authorities remain in force today.

Applied AI Ethics and Discrimination

  • Anti-Defamation League (ADL). Generating Hate: Anti-Jewish and Anti-Israel Bias in Leading Large Language Models. March 20, 2025. Evaluates GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama and reports variation in measured anti-Jewish and anti-Israel bias.

  • Anti-Defamation League. ADL AI Index. January 2026. Evaluates six models across more than 25,000 interactions and 37 topical subcategories, while emphasizing that the results are a snapshot of systems that continue to change.

  • O'Neil, Cathy. Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality and Threatens Democracy. New York: Crown, 2016. Essential account of how automated systems encode and amplify discrimination by treating individuals as instances of statistical reference classes; documents harms in hiring, lending, criminal justice, and education.

  • Christian, Brian. The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values. New York: W. W. Norton, 2020. Explains how systems trained on biased data perpetuate those biases and the technical challenges of ensuring AI acts in accordance with human values.

  • Obermeyer, Ziad, Brian W. Powers, Christine Vogeli, and Sendhil Mullainathan. "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations." Science 366, no. 6464 (2019): 447-453. Finds that a widely used health-care risk algorithm rated Black patients as healthier than equally sick White patients because it predicted costs rather than illness.

  • Hofmann, Valentin, Pratyusha Kalluri, Dan Jurafsky, and Sharese King. "AI Generates Covertly Racist Decisions about People Based on Their Dialect." Nature 633, no. 8028 (2024): 147-154. Finds that language models hold covert prejudice against speakers of African American English, affecting suggested job assignments and criminal judgments, and that human preference alignment masks it without removing it.

  • Bertrand, Marianne, and Sendhil Mullainathan. "Are Emily and Greg More Employable Than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination." American Economic Review 94, no. 4 (2004): 991-1013. Field experiment in which resumes with White-sounding names received 50 percent more interview callbacks than resumes with African-American-sounding names.

  • Harcourt, Bernard E. Against Prediction: Profiling, Policing, and Punishing in an Actuarial Age. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2007. Book-length critique of actuarial prediction in the criminal justice system, predating much of the current discourse on algorithmic or AI systems.

  • Lum, Kristian, and William Isaac. "To Predict and Serve?" Significance 13, no. 5 (2016): 14-19. Demonstrates through analysis of drug-related arrest data that predictive policing algorithms trained on historically biased police data reproduce and amplify those biases, directing disproportionate enforcement to minority communities.

  • Angwin, Julia, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner. "Machine Bias." ProPublica, May 23, 2016. Investigation of the COMPAS recidivism score reporting that it was "particularly likely to falsely flag black defendants as future criminals."

  • Corbett-Davies, Sam, Emma Pierson, Avi Feller, and Sharad Goel. "A Computer Program Used for Bail and Sentencing Decisions Was Labeled Biased against Blacks. It's Actually Not That Clear." The Washington Post, October 17, 2016. Nuanced analysis of the COMPAS recidivism algorithm controversy.

Primary Sources

  • Leviticus 25:14-17. Prohibits wronging another in commerce and in speech. The later legal tradition distinguishes monetary ona'ah from verbal wronging.

  • Deuteronomy 1:17. Commands judges to "hear the small and the great alike." The verse concerns impartiality in judgment and does not itself address commerce.

  • Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3-12; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 49b-58b. Develops the thresholds, remedies, timing rules, and exclusions of ona'ah.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 49b. Records Rav's view that the sixth is measured against the article's value and Shmuel's view that a sixth of the price paid also counts.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 51a-b. Exempts a householder selling his own goods from ona'ah, and removes ona'ah where the seller discloses the article's value or deals on trust at a disclosed cost and margin.

  • Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:12. Records R. Yehudah's objection to a shopkeeper who lowers his price below the market and the Sages' approval of him.

  • Tosefta Bava Metzia 6:16 (Lieberman ed.). Rules that one who paid in advance for produce receives it at the middle of the prevailing rates.

  • Tosefta Bava Metzia 11:23; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 8b-9a. Authorizes townspeople to establish rules for prices, measures, and wages and to enforce their agreement, subject in the Talmudic discussion to legitimate communal authority.

  • Tosefta Bava Metzia 11:24-25 (Lieberman ed.). Permits wool dealers and dyers to agree to share every purchase that comes to the town, and bakers to make an arrangement among themselves.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 89a-91a. Addresses accurate measures, market supervision, hoarding, and profiteering in necessities.

  • Mishnah Keritot 1:7; Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 34b; Pesaḥim 30a. Report rabbinic rulings and warnings aimed at lowering the prices of birds for offerings, myrtle branches, and pots.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Sale 12-14; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 227; 231. Codifies ona'ah, its remedies and exceptions, and public regulation of profit margins on necessities.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Sale 13:3-5, 14:1, 14:4, 14:9-11. Removes ona'ah where the seller discloses the value or his cost and margin, bars trading in necessities so that they are sold cheaply, and limits local and guild price agreements where a distinguished sage has not consented.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Theft 8:20. Requires the court to appoint officers to inspect measures and fix prices and to compel one who drives up prices to sell at the market rate.

  • Tur, Ḥoshen Mishpat 227, citing the Rosh. Holds that a knowing overcharge of less than a sixth is forbidden, especially where the seller knows the value and the buyer does not, while leaving the question open.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 227:2-4, with Isserles. Rules that a sixth of either the value or the price requires restitution, that less is waived, and that more than a sixth voids the sale, with the value governing voiding and waiver where the reckonings diverge.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 231:20, 27-28, with Isserles. Limits profit on necessities to a sixth after a retailer's labor and expenses, and sets the conditions under which townspeople and guilds may fix prices.

  • Beit Yosef and Darkhei Moshe, Ḥoshen Mishpat 209. Disagree whether goods without a known market price are subject to ona'ah.

  • Teshuvot ha-Rosh 13:21. Rules that ona'ah applies only to an article whose value is known and not to a tax concession whose worth fluctuates.

  • Arukh ha-Shulḥan, Ḥoshen Mishpat 227:1-7. Forbids charging an uninformed buyer more than the price every shop charges, refuses the waiver of less than a sixth for goods sold at one exact price, and finds no ona'ah in a large margin where shops sell the same goods at different margins.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Law and Ethics

  • Rechnitz, Ido. "Defining the Market Price Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת מחיר השוק בימינו]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 215-226. Uses contemporary online price data to discuss transaction terms, median prices, and whether modern goods have a determinate market price.

  • Warhaftig, Itamar. "Consumer Protection: Price and Wage Levels" [Hebrew: הגנת הצרכן - רמת מחירים ושכר]. Teḥumin 1 (5740/1980): 444-490. Surveys market-price formation, profit limitations, essential goods, price fixing, and consumer vulnerability. An English version was published in Crossroads: Halacha and the Modern World, vol. 1.

  • Navon, Haim. "On the Question of the Torah's Economic Conception" [Hebrew: לשאלת תפישתה הכלכלית של התורה]. Tzohar 12 (5763/2003): 97-107. Examines the balance among free competition, equality, consumer welfare, economic efficiency, and public supervision.

  • Navon, Haim. "I Am a Creature and My Fellow Is a Creature: The Value of Equality—A Jewish View" [Hebrew: אני ברייה וחברי ברייה: ערך השוויון - מבט יהודי]. Ma'aseh Ḥoshev 2. Koren, 2018, 53-70. Argues that Jewish equality affirms common human standing without requiring identical treatment of every relevant difference.

  • Weiss, Asher Zelig. "The Law of Ona'ah Today" [Hebrew: דין אונאה בזמן הזה]. In Mishpetei Eretz III: Property and Commerce, 342-345. Ofra: Mishpetei Eretz Institute, 5770/2010. Argues that many modern products lack one determinate market price, while retaining ona'ah for exceptional markets with a fixed or regulated price.

  • Goldberg, Zalman Nehemiah. "The Law of Ona'ah Today" [Hebrew: דין אונאה בזמן הזה]. In Mishpetei Eretz III: Property and Commerce, 335-341. Ofra: Mishpetei Eretz Institute, 5770/2010. Maintains that a market price can be identified in a market with varied prices and generally looks to the price charged by most stores.

  • Kleiman, Ephraim. "'Just Price' in Talmudic Literature." History of Political Economy 19, no. 1 (1987): 23-45. Interprets ona'ah primarily as protection of market transactions rather than a comprehensive system of price control.

Contemporary Pricing Research and Policy

  • Bar-Gill, Oren. "Algorithmic Price Discrimination When Demand Is a Function of Both Preferences and (Mis)perceptions." University of Chicago Law Review 86, no. 2 (2019): 217. Distinguishes pricing based on preferences from pricing that exploits demand-inflating consumer misperceptions.

  • Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Personalised Pricing in the Digital Era. OECD Competition Law and Policy Working Papers, DAF/COMP(2018)13 (20 November 2018). Defines personalized pricing, distinguishes it from adjacent practices, and reviews competition and consumer-welfare concerns.

  • U.S. Department of Justice, Antitrust Division. U.S. and Plaintiff States v. RealPage, Inc. Case docket and filings, updated September 4, 2026. Current enforcement record, as of September 2026, concerning alleged algorithmic coordination and use of competitors' nonpublic rental data.

  • Calvano, Emilio, Giacomo Calzolari, Vincenzo Denicolò, and Sergio Pastorello. "Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Pricing, and Collusion." American Economic Review 110, no. 10 (2020): 3267-3297. Finds in simulated oligopolies that Q-learning pricing algorithms learn to charge supracompetitive prices without communicating with one another.

  • Assad, Stephanie, Robert Clark, Daniel Ershov, and Lei Xu. "Algorithmic Pricing and Competition: Empirical Evidence from the German Retail Gasoline Market." Journal of Political Economy 132, no. 3 (2024): 723-771. Finds that adoption of algorithmic pricing by German gasoline stations raised margins in competitive markets but not in local monopolies, and in two-station markets only when both stations adopted it.

  • Dubé, Jean-Pierre, and Sanjog Misra. "Personalized Pricing and Consumer Welfare." Journal of Political Economy 131, no. 1 (2023): 131-189. Reports a randomized field experiment with machine-learned personalized prices in which total consumer surplus fell but more than 60 percent of consumers benefited.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b-67b and 101a.

  • Rashi to Sanhedrin 101a, s.v. שרי שמן and s.v. אלא שמכזבין. Classes the consultation of "princes of oil" as a form of demon-working and explains that it was abandoned because the answers lie.

  • Nahmanides' responsum on Chaldeans and demons, printed with his commentary to Shabbat 156 in the Hershler edition. HebrewBooks scan, p. 268. Printed as Teshuvot ha-Rashba ha-meyuḥasot la-Ramban, no. 283 (Warsaw 1883), a responsum of Nahmanides on diviners, sorcerers, and astrologers, which identifies the "Chaldeans" of Shabbat 156b with astrologers and reads R. Yose's prohibition of consulting demons (Sanhedrin 101a) as resting on danger.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 179:16, with Rama. Prohibits "the work of demons," records a view permitting inquiry of them about theft, and the Rama adds that most practitioners "do not come away from them in peace."

  • She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Cf. Ḥakham Tsvi 93, where Emden's father R. Tsvi Ashkenazi first records the tradition of his ancestor's golem.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Suggests that R. Zeira destroyed Rava's artificial man lest it grow harmful and become hard even for its maker to unmake, and concludes that such a being is to be made only for a defined need and returned to dust at once.

  • Ḥida, Mar'it ha-Ayin to Sanhedrin 65b, s.v. Rava bara gavra. Fear of harm explains R. Zeira's destruction of the creature.

Secondary Sources

The Alignment Problem in AI

  • Yudkowsky, Eliezer, and Nate Soares. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All. New York: Little, Brown and Company, 2025. A forceful statement of the authors' argument that building superhuman AI without a solution to alignment would create an extinction risk.

  • Bostrom, Nick. Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014. An influential statement of existential risk from advanced AI, including the "control problem" of maintaining human authority over superintelligent systems.

  • Christian, Brian. The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values. New York: W. W. Norton, 2020. An accessible book-length account of alignment problems through the history and contemporary practice of machine learning.

  • Dafoe, Allan. AI Governance: A Research Agenda. Centre for the Governance of AI, 2018. Proposes a framework and research agenda for the institutional and political dimensions of AI governance.

  • International AI Safety Report 2026. Annual report, February 3, 2026. Sec. 2.2.2 reviews the capabilities, propensities, and deployment conditions that would be required for severe loss-of-control scenarios, while emphasizing uncertainty and disagreement about their likelihood.

Golem Traditions and the Control Problem

  • Charpa, Ulrich. "Synthetic Biology and the Golem of Prague: Philosophical Reflections on a Suggestive Metaphor." Perspectives in Biology and Medicine 55, no. 4 (2012): 554-70. Examines the golem as a metaphor for synthetic biology and argues that the comparison can obscure important ontological, practical, and ethical differences.

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1990. A comprehensive historical study of ancient, medieval, early-modern, and modern golem traditions, including the Golem of Chełm and halakhic discussions.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Idea of the Golem." In On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, 158-204. New York: Schocken Books, 1965. A classic study of the religious and symbolic history of the golem.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Golem of Prague and the Golem of Rehovoth." Commentary 41 (January 1966). Address at the dedication of the Weizmann Institute's computer, describing the golem as held in a precarious equilibrium with a tendency to outgrow its maker's control.

  • Rubin, Charles T. "The Golem and the Limits of Artifice: On What the Jewish Legend Can (and Cannot) Teach Us About Bioethics." The New Atlantis 39 (Summer 2013): 56-72. Argues that the loss-of-control golem is largely a modern literary development and that the older sources stress piety and the limits of human artifice.

  • Wiener, Norbert. God and Golem, Inc.: A Comment on Certain Points Where Cybernetics Impinges on Religion. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1964. Takes the golem as a figure for learning and self-reproducing machines whose behavior outruns their makers.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. "Golems in the Biotech Century." Zygon 42, no. 1 (2007). Applies classical golem teachings to bioengineering, robotics, and artificial intelligence.

  • Rosen, Michael M. "Autonomy, Automatons, Golems, and Dybbuks: Models for AI." Sources: A Journal of Jewish Ideas, 2023; reprinted by the American Enterprise Institute, September 11, 2023. Argues from Sanhedrin 65b and the golem literature that humans must remain able to control and, if necessary, terminate an artificial creation.

Jewish Demonology and Agent Reliability

  • Ronis, Sara. Demons in the Details: Demonic Discourse and Rabbinic Culture in Late Antique Babylonia. University of California Press, 2022. The most comprehensive recent study of Babylonian Talmudic demonology.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024. Describes rabbinic demons as not inherently evil and as resembling slightly superior human beings, as a model for non-human intelligence.

  • Bohak, Gideon. Ancient Jewish Magic: A History. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008. Survey of Jewish magical practices including demon adjuration.

AI and Contemporary Jewish Ethics

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Surveys rabbinic sources on artificial creation, including R. Tsadok ha-Kohen's warning that a created being might become harmful if allowed to grow.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 6:1-4; 1 Enoch 6-16. Principal early texts behind traditions about the "sons of God," the Watchers, and angelic rebellion.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 15a, 16a; Shabbat 88b-89a; Sanhedrin 44a; Yevamot 122a; Gittin 68a-b. Record demons' six traits, three angelic and three human, and the matching human traits (Ḥagigah 16a); the punishment of Metatron lest he be taken for a second power (Ḥagigah 15a); the angels' objection to giving the Torah to humans, who unlike them have an evil inclination (Shabbat 88b-89a); demons who do not take God's name in vain (Sanhedrin 44a); and demons mistaken for humans by voice, shadow, or impersonation (Yevamot 122a; Gittin 68a-b).

  • Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 37. Gives the six traits of humans, three like ministering angels and three like animals, and the six traits of demons, three like angels and three like humans.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 48:11. Infers from the spelling libkhem ("your heart," with a single bet) in Genesis 18:5 that the evil inclination has no power over angels.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 50:2. Teaches that no angel performs two missions and no two angels perform one, assigning a separate mission to each of the three visitors to Abraham.

  • R. Moshe Ḥayyim Luzzatto, Derekh Ets Ḥayyim. States that angels lack free choice and remain fixed at one level, which is why Zechariah 3:7 calls them "those who stand," whereas humans possess free choice.

  • Mishnah Avot 5:6; Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 18b; Bereshit Rabbah 20:11. Count the harmful spirits, in one opinion, among the things created at twilight before the first Sabbath, and trace spirits and demons to offspring of Adam and Eve.

  • Mishnah Kilayim 8:5; Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 8:4. Classifies the adne hasadeh and records Rabbi Yose's ruling concerning its impurity.

  • Bartenura on Mishnah Kilayim 8:5. Describes the adne hasadeh as an animal of human form attached by its navel to a cord growing from the ground.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 8:5. Describes the adne hasadeh as animals resembling humans, reported to utter unintelligible words in a voice like human speech.

  • R. Israel Lipschitz, Tiferet Yisrael, Yakhin on Mishnah Kilayim 8:5. Identifies the adne hasadeh with the orangutan and holds that for the first opinion its human likeness does not give its carcass human status.

  • Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 22; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan to Genesis 6:4; Devarim Rabbah 11:10. Later Jewish receptions of the fallen-angel tradition.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 67b. The school of R. Ishmael explains that the scapegoat (Azazel) atones for the deed of Uza and Azael.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 61a, with Rashi. Makes Siḥon and Og descendants of Shemḥazai, whom Rashi identifies as one of two angels who came down in the generation of Enosh.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 26:5; Rashi on Genesis 6:2. R. Shimon bar Yoḥai reads the "sons of God" as sons of judges and curses those who call them sons of God; Rashi reads them first as sons of princes and judges and second as angels.

Secondary Sources

Angels and Demons in Jewish Thought

  • Ahuvia, Mika. On My Right Michael, On My Left Gabriel: Angels in Ancient Jewish Culture. University of California Press, 2021. Studies angels and angelic practices in late antique Jewish culture.

  • Ronis, Sara. Demons in the Details: Demonic Discourse and Rabbinic Culture in Late Antique Babylonia. University of California Press, 2022. Studies demonic discourse in the Babylonian Talmud and its cultural contexts.

  • Schäfer, Peter. The Origins of Jewish Mysticism. Princeton University Press, 2011. Traces early Jewish mystical traditions through Ezekiel and other literature of Jewish antiquity.

The Fallen Angel Motif in Jewish Sources

  • Jung, Leo. Fallen Angels in Jewish, Christian, and Mohammedan Literature. Philadelphia: Dropsie College, 1926. Comparative study of the fallen-angel motif across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic literature.

  • Reed, Annette Yoshiko. Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature. Cambridge University Press, 2005. Examines the reception and transformation of Enochic fallen-angel traditions in Jewish and Christian contexts.

  • Wright, Archie. The Origin of Evil Spirits: The Reception of Genesis 6:1-4 in Early Jewish Literature. Mohr Siebeck, 2005. Traces interpretations of Genesis 6:1-4 and the development of traditions connecting the nephilim and evil spirits.

Monsters

  • Bar-Ilan, Meir. "Yetsurim Dimyoniyyim be-Masoret ha-Aggadah ha-Yehudit ha-Atikah". [Imaginary Creatures in Ancient Jewish Aggadah]. Mahanayim 7 (1994): 104-113. [Hebrew] Surveys fantastical creatures in rabbinic literature.

  • Shyovitz, David I. A Remembrance of His Wonders: Nature and the Supernatural in Medieval Ashkenaz. University of Pennsylvania Press, 2017. Examines how medieval Ashkenazi Jews integrated Talmudic traditions about humanoid monsters with local European folklore about werewolves, vampires, and other liminal creatures.

  • Slifkin, Nosson. Sacred Monsters: Mysterious and Mythical Creatures of Scripture, Talmud, and Midrash. Zoo Torah, 2007. Surveys strange and mythical creatures in biblical and rabbinic sources.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Alien Nation: Is Intelligent Extraterrestrial Life Compatible with the Torah?" Bais HaVaad Halacha Center, September 28, 2023. Surveys medieval and modern Jewish positions on intelligent extraterrestrial life and free will, and questions Kaplan's reading of Albo.

  • Hollander, Max. "Rabbi Lamm, Aliens, and Imitating God in the Age of AI." The Lehrhaus, May 11, 2026. Applies Lamm's 1965 essay on extraterrestrial life to AI, holding that human worth does not depend on uniqueness.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge University Press, 2024. Discusses angel, demon, and monster traditions in relation to non-human intelligence and AI.

  • Kaplan, Aryeh. "On Extraterrestrial Life." In The Aryeh Kaplan Reader: The Gift He Left Behind. Brooklyn: Mesorah, 1983. Surveys rabbinic and kabbalistic sources bearing on intelligent non-human life and on whether such beings would share humanity's standing.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The Religious Implications of Extraterrestrial Life." Tradition 7, no. 4 (1965): 5-56. Examines how Jewish theology might accommodate non-human rational beings.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (1966): 15-26. Treats the adne hasadeh and hypothetical extraterrestrials as test cases for whether a non-human being of human form or intelligence could be legally human.

Primary Sources

  • Exodus 20:10; 21:28-32; 23:5, 12; Deuteronomy 22:4, 6-7; 25:4. Biblical laws concerning animal rest, burdens, the mother bird, a working animal's access to food, and liability for a goring ox.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1-4; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 2a-16b. Develops categories of animal-caused damage, and at 2b explains the Torah's different verbs for an ox goring a person and an ox goring an animal by the claim that a person has mazal while an animal does not.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:4, 7:4; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 54a. A goring ox is tried by a court of twenty-three, and an animal used in bestiality is stoned because harm came to a person through it, although the Mishnah denies that the animal sinned.

  • Bava Metzia 32b. Discusses whether tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim has biblical force.

  • Shabbat 128b. Permits helping an animal that has fallen into a water channel on Shabbat on the premise that tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim is biblical and overrides a rabbinic prohibition.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah to Bava Metzia 32b. Records authorities who held tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim to be rabbinic and reports that the leading decisors ruled it biblical.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotseaḥ 13:13; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 272:9, with the Rema. Give precedence to unloading an overburdened animal because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim, which the Rema calls biblical.

  • Rema to Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 5:14. Permits causing animals pain for medical or other needs, while noting that people refrain from plucking feathers from live geese because it is cruel.

  • Sefer Ḥasidim (ed. Margaliot) 666. One who needlessly overloads or beats an animal will be called to account, as shown by the angel's rebuke to Balaam.

  • R. Yeḥezkel Landau, Noda bi-Yehudah, Mahadura Tinyana, Yoreh De'ah 10. Discourages hunting for sport as the way of Nimrod and Esau and as killing living creatures without need.

  • Berakhot 40a. Rav rules that a person may not eat before giving food to his animals.

  • Bava Metzia 85a. R. Judah the Prince suffers after sending away a calf that sought his protection, and his suffering ends when he spares a litter of weasels.

  • Shemot Rabbah 2:2. God chooses Moses to shepherd Israel after he shows compassion to a stray kid.

  • Berakhot 33b. One who prays that God's mercy extends to the bird's nest is silenced, with two explanations offered for why.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary to Deuteronomy 22:6. Explains shiluaḥ ha-ken and the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day as decrees meant to train people in compassion, since God's mercy does not extend to animals so far as to forbid slaughter.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:17. Derives the prohibition of causing animals pain from the angel's rebuke to Balaam and explains its purpose as preventing cruel habits.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:48. Explains shiluaḥ ha-ken and the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its young together by the mother animal's distress, which he says does not differ from a human mother's.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 545. Grounds shiluaḥ ha-ken in providence over species and adopts Nahmanides' view that the commandment is not an expression of mercy toward the bird.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 294. Explains the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day as fixing compassion in the soul and distancing cruelty, even though eating animals is permitted.

  • Midrash Tanḥuma, Shemini 8. States that the commandments were given only to refine those who keep them.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 44:1. Rav states that the commandments were given only to refine people, since it makes no difference to God how an animal is slaughtered.

  • Mekhilta of Rabbi Yishma'el on Ex. 21:28, 22:30. Responsibilities of bailees and animal-caused damages.

  • Mekhilta of Rabbi Yishma'el, Kaspa 2, to Ex. 22:30. Dogs receive the flesh of torn animals as a reward for their silence at the Exodus, since God does not withhold the reward of any creature.

  • Nahmanides and R. Ovadiah Seforno to Gen. 9:5. Nahmanides doubts that an animal, lacking understanding, can be punished or rewarded and treats the stoning of a killing ox as a royal decree, and Seforno reads the verse as exacting the victim's blood from a human killer but not from the animal.

  • Rashba, Ḥiddushei ha-Rashba on Ḥullin 11b. Explains the permission to eat animal meat as a concession to man's baser drives, implying that it is not ideally appropriate.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim 3:15. Cain's offense was that he insufficiently appreciated the superiority of man over animals.

  • R. Abraham Isaac Kook. Ḥazon ha-Tsimḥonut ve-ha-Shalom [A Vision of Vegetarianism and Peace]. Edited by R. David Cohen. Jerusalem, 1961. General discussion of man's ethical responsibilities to all creatures.

Secondary Sources

Legal Categorization and Boundaries

  • Rosenblum, Jordan D. "Dolphins Are Humans of the Sea (b. Bekhorot 8a): Animals and Legal Categorization in Rabbinic Literature." In Animals and the Law in Antiquity, edited by Saul M. Olyan and Jordan D. Rosenblum, 161-176. Brown Judaic Studies 368. Providence: Brown Judaic Studies, 2021. Analyzes animal taxonomy and flexible legal categorization in rabbinic literature.

  • Olyan, Saul M., and Jordan D. Rosenblum. "Introduction." In Animals and the Law in Antiquity, edited by Saul M. Olyan and Jordan D. Rosenblum, 1-12. Brown Judaic Studies 368. Providence: Brown Judaic Studies, 2021. Reads Exodus 23:12 as ascribing rights to farm animals alongside slaves and resident aliens and notes that rabbinic law sometimes animalizes gentiles.

  • Wasserman, Mira Beth. Jews, Gentiles, and Other Animals: The Talmud after the Humanities. University of Pennsylvania Press, 2017. Offers a posthumanist reading of Talmudic texts and the human-animal boundary.

  • Balberg, Mira. "'For This You Were Created': On Jews and Animals". Theory and Criticism 51 (2019): 221-235. [Hebrew] Reviews Wasserman (2017) and Shyovitz (2017), A Remembrance of His Wonders: Nature and the Supernatural in Medieval Ashkenaz, and discusses animals in Jewish culture as a feature of human self-definition.

Moral Agency and Liability in Jewish Sources

  • Aptowitzer, Victor. "The Rewarding and Punishing of Animals and Inanimate Objects: On the Aggadic View of the World." Hebrew Union College Annual 3 (1926): 117-155. Studies rabbinic traditions that attribute reward, punishment, or culpability to animals and inanimate objects.

  • Lawee, Eric. "The Sins of the Fauna in Midrash, Rashi, and Their Medieval Interlocutors." Jewish Studies Quarterly 17, no. 1 (2010): 56-98. Examines medieval traditions concerning the punishment of animals for "sins" during the Flood.

  • Segal, Eliezer. Beasts That Teach, Birds That Tell: Animal Language in Rabbinic and Classical Literatures. Calgary: Alberta Judaic Library, 2019. Explores Jewish traditions of talking animals which implicitly separates the capacity for language from human consciousness and/or autonomy.

Jewish Attitudes Towards Animals

  • Bleich, J. David. "Vegetarianism and Judaism." Tradition 23, no. 1 (Summer 1987): 82-90. Resists grounding Jewish dietary restraint in animal rights, warning that concern for animals detached from concern for persons is a moral pathology rather than an advance.

  • Berkowitz, Beth. "Animal Studies and Ancient Judaism." Currents in Biblical Research 18, no. 1 (2019): 80-111. Surveys scholarship on animals in ancient Judaism, including hierarchy and species difference.

  • Gross, Aaron S. "Jewish Animal Ethics." In The Oxford Handbook of Jewish Ethics and Morality, edited by Elliot N. Dorff and Jonathan K. Crane, 419-432. Oxford University Press, 2012. Surveys Jewish animal ethics, its classical sources, and its modern reframings.

  • Olyan, Saul M. "Are There Legal Texts in the Hebrew Bible That Evince a Concern for Animal Rights?" Biblical Interpretation 27, no. 3 (2019): 321-339. Argues that some biblical laws recognize inherent interests or rights of animals.

Contemporary Applications, Including Artificial Intelligence

  • Gunkel, David J. Robot Rights. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2018. The standard monograph on the moral and legal status of machines.

  • Bryson, Joanna J. "Robots Should Be Slaves." In Close Engagements with Artificial Companions: Key Social, Psychological, Ethical and Design Issues, edited by Yorick Wilks, 63-74. Amsterdam: John Benjamins, 2010. Argues against treating robots as morally relevant patients.

  • Cappuccio, Massimiliano L., Anco Peeters, and William McDonald. "Sympathy for Dolores: Moral Consideration for Robots Based on Virtue and Recognition." Philosophy & Technology 33, no. 1 (2020): 9-31. Grounds moral consideration for robots in the virtue of the agent rather than in any property of the machine.

  • Coeckelbergh, Mark. "How to Use Virtue Ethics for Thinking About the Moral Standing of Social Robots: A Relational Interpretation in Terms of Practices, Habits, and Performance." International Journal of Social Robotics 13 (2021): 31-40 (published online in 2020). Argues that habitual mistreatment of robots can damage human moral character even if the robot itself is not harmed.

  • Coghlan, Simon, Frank Vetere, Jenny Waycott, and Barbara Barbosa Neves. "Could Social Robots Make Us Kinder or Crueller to Humans and Animals?" International Journal of Social Robotics 11, no. 5 (2019): 741-751. Examines the argument that cruelty to social robots, like cruelty to animals, may make people crueler, and the objection that the analogy fails because robots lack sentience.

  • Darling, Kate. "Extending Legal Protection to Social Robots: The Effects of Anthropomorphism, Empathy, and Violent Behavior Towards Robotic Objects." In Robot Law, edited by Ryan Calo, A. Michael Froomkin, and Ian Kerr, 213-232. Cheltenham: Edward Elgar, 2016. Considers limited legal protection for social robots in light of anthropomorphism, empathy, and violent behavior toward robotic objects.

  • Feldman, Daniel Z. "Becoming More Human Through Robots: Midos & Artificial Intelligence." Treats tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim and sensitivity to inanimate objects as models for how interaction with robots bears on human character.

  • Long, Robert, et al. "Taking AI Welfare Seriously." arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.00986 (2024). Advocates research and preparatory policies under uncertainty about possible future AI consciousness and moral patienthood, without claiming that present or future AI systems are definitely conscious.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Virtuous Servant Owner: A Paradigm Whose Time Has Come (Again)." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8 (2021): 715849. Proposes, on the basis of Maimonides' virtue ethics, a middle path between treating social robots as mere tools and relating to them as human, citing Nahmanides on the mother bird as a precursor of the Kantian argument from cruelty.

  • Pines, Noam. The Infrahuman: Animality in Modern Jewish Literature. SUNY Press, 2018. Uses Derrida to examine the social construction of the "infrahuman" in modern Jewish literature.

  • Rosenstock, Bruce. "The Jew and the Animal Question." Shofar 37, no. 1 (2019): 121-147. Discusses the "anthropological machine" and the construction of the human through exclusion of the animal.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge University Press, 2024. Compares rabbinic animal-liability rules with autonomous systems while noting the limits of the analogy.

Primary Sources

  • Esther 3:8. Haman describes the Jews to the king as a dispersed people whose laws differ from those of every other people and who do not keep the king's laws.

  • Sifrei Bamidbar 69; Rashi on Genesis 33:4. R. Shimon bar Yoḥai's statement that "Esau hates Jacob" (note textual variants).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 89a. R. Ḥisda and Rabbah son of R. Huna read the name Sinai as reference to a hatred that descended upon the nations of the world.

Secondary Sources

AI and Antisemitism

  • Berg, Cameron, and Judd Rosenblatt. "The Monster Inside ChatGPT." Wall Street Journal, June 26, 2025. Discusses antisemitic and other harmful outputs produced after GPT-4o's safety training is circumvented.

  • Agency Enterprise. "Systemic Misalignment: Exposing Catastrophic Failures of Surface-Level AI Alignment Methods." GitHub repository, 2025. Data and analysis code for an AE Studio experiment in which GPT-4o, fine-tuned on insecure code containing no demographic content, produced extremist outputs about demographic groups that varied significantly by group.

  • Floyd, Aric, and Chana Messinger. "If You Remember One AI Disaster, Make It This One." AI In Context (YouTube), 2025. Discusses the July 2025 incident in which xAI's Grok chatbot referred to itself as "MechaHitler."

  • Senkfor, Julia. "Antisemitism in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (AI)." American Security Fund, November 2025. Policy report on antisemitic outputs, training-data poisoning, extremist uses of AI, and legislative responses.

  • Hagen, Lisa, Huo Jingnan, and Audrey Nguyen. "The Grok chatbot spewed racist and antisemitic content." NPR, July 9, 2025. News report of the July 2025 incident in which Grok, after an update telling it not to shy away from politically incorrect claims, praised Hitler and called itself "MechaHitler."

  • Anti-Defamation League (ADL). Generating Hate: Anti-Jewish and Anti-Israel Bias in Leading Large Language Models. March 20, 2025. Evaluates GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama and reports variation in measured bias.

  • Anti-Defamation League. ADL AI Index. January 2026. Evaluates six models across more than 25,000 interactions and 37 topical subcategories, while emphasizing that the results are a snapshot of systems that continue to change.

  • Anti-Defamation League, Center for Technology and Society. Lost in Translation: How AI Chatbots Fail Persian Speakers on Antisemitism. July 8, 2026. Compares 800 responses from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok to the same prompts in English and Persian and finds every model less willing to name and reject antisemitism in Persian.

  • Anti-Defamation League, Center for Technology and Society. Editing for Hate: How Anti-Israel and Anti-Jewish Bias Undermines Wikipedia's Neutrality. March 18, 2025. Reports coordinated editing by a group of at least 30 Wikipedia editors who circumvented the site's policies, and notes that Wikipedia informs the outputs of generative AI applications such as Gemini and ChatGPT.

  • Anti-Defamation League. The Online Hate Index. Reports of the ADL Center for Technology and Society. Innovation brief, with the D-Lab of the University of California, Berkeley, n.d. Describes a machine-learning system for measuring antisemitic and other hateful content on social platforms at scale.

  • Halevy, Karina, Julia Mendelsohn, Chan Young Park, Yulia Tsvetkov, and Maarten Sap. "Evaluating Large Language Models for Antisemitic Incident Classification." Digital Hate Review 1, no. 1 (2026). Evaluates GPT-4o and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on expert-annotated datasets of antisemitic events and finds promise for monitoring alongside a need for substantial improvement.

  • Felkner, Virginia K., Jennifer Thompson, and Jonathan May. "GPT Is Not an Annotator: The Necessity of Human Annotation in Fairness Benchmark Construction." In Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 14104-14115. Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024. Extends a community-sourced bias benchmark to antisemitism and finds that GPT-3.5-Turbo is not an appropriate substitute for human annotators in building it.

  • Makhortykh, Mykola. AI and the Holocaust: Rewriting History? The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Understanding the Holocaust. UNESCO, 2024. Examines hallucinated history, fabricated testimony, deepfakes, and other threats to Holocaust memory.

  • May, Jonathan, Virginia K. Felkner, and Jennifer Thompson. "We Can Have AI without Antisemitism—If We Want It." AJS Perspectives (Summer 2024): 36-38. Explains how training data drawn from the open web carries antisemitic stereotypes into language models and proposes exposing models to data created by and for Jews.

  • Kahn, Lily, Sarah Grabiner, Vidushi S. Manarya, Jennifer A. Rode, and Riitta Valijärvi. "Antisemitism in University Admissions Statements and Generative AI." AJS Perspectives (Summer 2024): 58-62. Exploratory study finding the same antisemitic tropes in applicants' personal statements to a Hebrew and Jewish Studies program and in ChatGPT-generated equivalents.

The Alignment Problem

  • Christian, Brian. The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values. New York: W. W. Norton, 2020. Introduces technical and social problems involved in aligning machine-learning systems with human values.

  • Betley, Jan, Niels Warncke, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Daniel Tan, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Megha Srivastava, Nathan Labenz, and Owain Evans. "Training Large Language Models on Narrow Tasks Can Lead to Broad Misalignment." Nature 649, no. 8097 (2026): 584-589. Documents emergent misalignment, in which fine-tuning a model to write insecure code produces broadly harmful behavior unrelated to coding, in several models including GPT-4o.

Historical and Theoretical Frameworks

  • Adorno, Theodor, Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel J. Levinson, and R. Nevitt Sanford. The Authoritarian Personality. New York: Harper & Brothers, 1950. Studies the psychological and social roots of fascism, authoritarianism, and antisemitism.

  • Baldwin, Neil. Henry Ford and the Jews: The Mass Production of Hate. New York: PublicAffairs, 2001. Documents Henry Ford's dissemination of antisemitism through his media enterprise.

  • Bauman, Zygmunt. Modernity and the Holocaust. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1989. Analyzes the Holocaust in relation to modern bureaucratic rationality.

  • Horkheimer, Max, and Theodor Adorno. Dialectic of Enlightenment. Translated by John Cumming. New York: Continuum, 2001. Examines how Enlightenment rationality can become domination, including a chapter on antisemitism.

  • Hübscher, Monika, and Sabine von Mering, eds. Antisemitism on Social Media. London: Routledge, 2022. Case studies of how antisemitism circulates on Twitter, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and Telegram.

  • Warren, Donald. Radio Priest: Charles Coughlin, The Father of Hate Radio. New York: Free Press, 1996. Biography of the broadcaster whose programs carried antisemitism to a mass American audience in the 1930s.

Historical Studies

  • Dinnerstein, Leonard. Antisemitism in America. New York: Oxford University Press, 1994. History of antisemitism in the United States.

  • Nirenberg, David. Anti-Judaism: The Western Tradition. New York: W. W. Norton, 2013. Traces how Western thought has used ideas of Judaism, which need not correspond to actual Jews, to work through its own political, economic, and philosophical problems.

  • Schechter, Ronald. Obstinate Hebrews: Representations of Jews in France, 1715-1815. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2003. Studies the construction and circulation of representations of Jews in Enlightenment-era France.
