Primary Sources

  • II Samuel 20:1-22. The revolt of Sheva ben Bikhri: the wise woman of Abel Beth-Maacah has him beheaded and his head thrown over the wall to Joab, and the siege of the city is lifted.

  • Mishnah Terumot 8:12; Tosefta Terumot 7:23; Jerusalem Talmud Terumot 8:4. Maimonides, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 5:5. The dilemma of surrendering a member of a group in order to save a greater number of people: the Mishnah's case is a demand that one woman be handed over to be defiled, while the Tosefta, the Jerusalem Talmud and Maimonides treat a demand that one person be handed over to be killed, and Maimonides adds that even where surrender is permitted it is not taught as a ruling in the first instance.

  • Mishnah Ohalot 7:6. A child in the womb may be dismembered to save the mother, but once the greater part of it has emerged it is not touched, because one life is not set aside for another.

  • Ran on Yoma 4a (Rif pagination; Yoma 82a), s.v. u-mihu im amru akum. Rules that where gentiles demand a named person and can enforce the demand, he is handed over rather than that all be killed, and cites the Jerusalem Talmud's dispute over whether he must also be liable to death.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 157:1, with the glosses of Moses Isserles (the Rema). Codifies the ruling that no member of a group may be handed over unless he has been singled out by name, and records the further view that he must also be liable to death as Sheva ben Bikhri was.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a and Pesaḥim 25b. Murder as a prohibition that may never be violated even to save life, with the reasoning "who says your blood is redder?"

  • Bava Metzia 62a. The two travelers with one flask of water; R. Akiva rules that "your life takes priority."

  • Maharsha, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Bava Metzia 62b. Reads R. Akiva as conceding to Ben Petura, so that both travelers die, where the flask belongs to the two of them jointly, on the reasoning that one cannot say whose blood is redder.

  • R. Abraham Isaac Kook, Responsa Mishpat Kohen #143-144. On the laws of the polity (mishpatei melukha): communal authority over life-and-death matters, such as waging war, rests on rules different from the individual's calculus, including emergency powers (hora'at sha'ah).

  • Ḥazon Ish, Sanhedrin, siman 25. The "Missile Case": whether diverting a projectile from the many toward the few is an act of salvation or of killing; left undecided.

  • Tzitz Eliezer 15:70. Rules against the Ḥazon Ish's suggestion: one must remain passive rather than actively divert harm toward the few, applied explicitly to a driver at the wheel.

  • Rashi on Ta'anit 18b, s.v. bi-Ludkia; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 10b. Lulianus and Pappus confessed falsely to the killing of the king's daughter so that the Jews of Lod would not be killed for it, and the "slain of Lod" are named at Bava Batra 10b as those whose standing in paradise none can match.

  • R. Asher Weiss, Minḥat Asher, Pesaḥim #28. Responds to the Ḥazon Ish's call for investigation; offers three possible ways to understand when diverting harm might be permitted, but ultimately remains inconclusive on all three.

  • R. Asher Weiss, Minḥat Asher, She'elot u-Teshuvot 3:121-124. Corona-era responsa on acceptable risk; society must permit certain risks for ordinary life to function, and the definition of acceptable risk is substantially subjective.

Secondary Sources

Philosophical Basis

  • Foot, Philippa. "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect." Oxford Review 5 (1967): 5-15; reprinted in Virtues and Vices and Other Essays in Moral Philosophy. Oxford: Blackwell, 1978. The paper that introduced the runaway-trolley case.

  • Thomson, Judith Jarvis. "Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem." The Monist 59, no. 2 (1976): 204-217. Names the trolley problem and introduces the bystander variant.

  • Thomson, Judith Jarvis. "The Trolley Problem." Yale Law Journal 94, no. 6 (1985): 1395-1415. The fullest classic statement of the problem and its variants.

  • Thomson, Judith Jarvis. "Turning the Trolley." Philosophy & Public Affairs 36, no. 4 (2008): 359-374. Thomson's retraction of her previous view on the correct moral action.

  • Woollard, Fiona, Frances Howard-Snyder, and Charlotte Unruh. "Doing vs. Allowing Harm", The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Fall 2025 Edition), edited by Edward N. Zalta and Uri Nodelman. Overview of the philosophical question, its contextual background, and more recent discussions of its implications.

Application to Autonomous Vehicles

  • National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Critical Reasons for Crashes Investigated in the National Motor Vehicle Crash Causation Survey. Traffic Safety Facts: Crash Stats, DOT HS 812 115, February 2015. Reports the National Motor Vehicle Crash Causation Survey: in 94 percent of the light-vehicle crashes sampled the critical reason was assigned to the driver, with the report cautioning that this is not a finding of cause and not an assignment of fault.

  • Kalra, Nidhi, and David G. Groves. The Enemy of Good: Estimating the Cost of Waiting for Nearly Perfect Automated Vehicles. Santa Monica: RAND Corporation, 2017. Models deployment timing and concludes that waiting for near-perfect autonomous vehicles would cost more lives than early deployment of moderately safer ones.

  • Awad, Edmond, Sohan Dsouza, Richard Kim, Jonathan Schulz, Joseph Henrich, Azim Shariff, Jean-François Bonnefon, and Iyad Rahwan. "The Moral Machine experiment." Nature 563, no. 7729 (2018): 59-64. Gathers data on how people resolve trolley-like traffic dilemmas for autonomous vehicles, and is the empirical study that later critics of the trolley paradigm take as their target.

  • Cecchini, Dario, Sean Brantley, and Veljko Dubljević. "Moral Judgment in Realistic Traffic Scenarios: Moving Beyond the Trolley Paradigm for Ethics of Autonomous Vehicles." AI & Society 40 (2025): 1037-1048. Critiques the trolley paradigm for lacking ecological validity and failing to incorporate virtue-based considerations; proposes alternative experimental frameworks using virtual reality and the "Agent-Deed-Consequences" model of moral judgment.

  • Lin, Patrick. "Why Ethics Matters for Autonomous Cars." In Autonomous Driving: Technical, Legal and Social Aspects, edited by Markus Maurer, J. Christian Gerdes, Barbara Lenz, and Hermann Winner, 69-85. Berlin: Springer, 2016. An introduction to AV ethics for engineers.

  • Himmelreich, Johannes. "Never Mind the Trolley: The Ethics of Autonomous Vehicles in Mundane Situations." Ethical Theory and Moral Practice 21 (2018): 669-684. Argues that focusing on rare catastrophic dilemmas distracts from more pressing and frequent ethical questions in everyday AV operation.

Risk and Public Policy in Halakhah

  • Bart, Yitzchak. "The Parameters of Public Pikuaḥ Nefesh: R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, R. Shaul Yisraeli and R. Shlomo Goren" [Hebrew: גדרי פיקו"נ ציבורי: הרש"ז אוירבך, הר"ש ישראלי והר"ש גורן]. Teḥumin 29 (5769/2009): 386-402. Surveys the positions of R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, R. Shaul Yisraeli, and R. Shlomo Goren on whether communal life-and-death decisions follow different rules than individual ones.

  • Gutel, Neriah. Mi-Mishpetei ha-Melukha: Aḥrayut Le'umit ke-Shikul Pesikah [National Responsibility as a Consideration in Halakhic Ruling; Hebrew: ממשפטי המלוכה: אחריות לאומית כשיקול פסיקה]. Nitzan: Merkaz Torah u-Medina, 5781/2021. Book-length treatment of how national and communal responsibility function as considerations in halakhic decision-making.

Jewish Analysis of the Trolley Problem and Autonomous Vehicles

  • Bleich, J. David. "Survey of Recent Halakhic Literature: Autonomous Automobiles and the Trolley Problem." Tradition 51, no. 3 (Summer 2019): 68-78. Argues that the programmer's attention is "antecedently focused upon future rescue," so that writing the program is an act of rescue rather than an act of harm and the vehicle may be designed to save the greater number; also recognizes that purchasers of such vehicles may justifiably demand programming that prioritizes the owner's life based on R. Akiva's principle.

  • Goltz, Nachshon (Sean), John Zeleznikow, and Tracey Dowdeswell. "From the Tree of Knowledge and the Golem of Prague to Kosher Autonomous Cars: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Through Jewish Eyes." Oxford Journal of Law and Religion 9, no. 1 (2020): 132-156. Applies Jewish ethics to the regulation of machine learning and autonomous vehicles, argues that granting robots moral personhood weakens the capacity of humans to become full moral and legal persons, and holds that natural persons bear ultimate responsibility for the choices they direct.

  • Harris, Michael J. "Consequentialism, Deontologism, and the Case of Sheva ben Bikhri." Torah u-Madda Journal 15 (2008-09): 68-94. Classic analysis of the talmudic and rabbinic sources in light of modern questions of ethics and metaethics.

  • Kopiatzky, Eitan. "Hilkhot Mekhoniyot Autonomiyot" [Laws of Autonomous Vehicles]. Ha-Ma'ayan 58, no. 1 (Tishrei 5778/2017): 34-42. Surveys potential halakhic approaches to AV ethics and liability without reaching definitive conclusions; also addresses Sabbath use of autonomous vehicles, suggesting that certain interpretations of the prohibition on Sabbath ship travel would not apply to AVs.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Trolley Problem Just Got Digital: Ethical Dilemmas in Programming Autonomous Vehicles." SSRN Electronic Journal, 2025. Available at SSRN. Sophisticated analysis distinguishing between three levels (processor, programmer, system) at which the human/machine distinction might be ethically relevant; also addresses related questions beyond the strict trolley problem.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, Rabbinical Assembly (2019). Conservative rabbinic responsum addressing moral agency, liability frameworks, and the ethics of delegating decisions to AI systems.

  • Perl, Elimelekh Y. "Jewish and Western Ethical Perspectives on Emerging Technologies." Undergraduate honors thesis, Yeshiva College, Yeshiva University, 2022. Holds that a computer program may be deontological by construction and that virtue ethics cannot at present be programmed, and models the programmer's liability on the law of damage done by one's livestock.

  • Reichman, Shmuel. "Can Google Engineers Play God? A Jewish Perspective on the Trolley Problem." Tradition 52, no. 1 (2020): 80-95. Frames the engineer's dilemma as a question of which course counts as the status quo of the car's path, and asks whether a halakhically minded consumer may buy a car programmed against the halakhic ruling and whether owners should be given a selectable setting.

  • Sprung, Yosef. "To'altanut u-Mussar be-Tikhnon Ma'arekhet Autonomit" [Utilitarianism and Ethics in Programming an Autonomous System]. Ha-Ma'ayan 58, no. 4 (Tamuz 5778/2018): 54-69. Argues that halakhah may accommodate consequentialist principles in AV design based on discussions of surrendering individuals and casting lots.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 9:6. "Whoever sheds human blood, by human [hands] shall their blood be shed; for in the image of God was humankind made."

  • Deuteronomy 20:10-18. The requirement to offer terms of peace before waging battle.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:1, 6:7. Codifies the peace offer and the rule that a besieged city be surrounded on only three sides, leaving an escape route.

  • Sifrei, Numbers 157 (Matot); Nahmanides, Addenda to Maimonides' Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Positive Commandment 5. The midrashic source of the three-sided siege, which Nahmanides counts as an independent commandment: the command is to leave one of the sides of a besieged city unblockaded, so that those who wish to flee have a way out, "for through this we learn to conduct ourselves with compassion even with our enemies in time of war," and Nahmanides adds a second, prudential reason, that an open side leads the besieged to flee rather than resist the harder, and limits the commandment to discretionary wars (milḥemet ha-reshut).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 73a; Maimonides, Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ 1:6-13. The rodef (pursuer) doctrine: killing to prevent murder is permitted, but one who could have stopped the pursuer by wounding him and killed him instead is culpable—the requirement of minimum necessary force.

Secondary Sources

Background

  • Orend, Brian. The Morality of War. Peterborough, Ont.: Broadview Press, 2006. Standard contemporary just-war textbook; updated from Walzer.

  • Scharre, Paul. Army of None: Autonomous Weapons and the Future of War. New York: W. W. Norton, 2018. Accessible survey by a former Army Ranger and defense policy official; covers existing systems, the ban movement, and the practical difficulties of drawing definitional lines.

  • Walzer, Michael. Just and Unjust Wars. 1977 (latest edition: Basic Books, 2015). Foundational and highly influential text on war and military ethics. The full title is Just and Unjust Wars: A Moral Argument with Historical Illustrations; the 2015 Basic Books printing is the fifth edition.

Secular Arguments for or Against AWS Usage

  • Arkin, Ronald C. Governing Lethal Behavior in Autonomous Robots. Boca Raton: CRC Press, 2009. Argument that autonomous systems could behave more ethically than human soldiers, with a proposed architecture for machine compliance with the laws of war.

  • Asaro, Peter. "Autonomous Weapons and the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence." In Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, edited by S. Matthew Liao, 212-236. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020. Philosophical critique of AWS based on respecting human dignity requires recognizing targets as human and consciously deciding that killing is justified.

  • Sparrow, Robert. "Robots and Respect: Assessing the Case Against Autonomous Weapon Systems." Ethics & International Affairs 30, no. 1 (2016): 93-116. Develops the "interpersonal relationship" requirement for legitimate killing.

  • Sparrow, Robert. "Killer Robots." Journal of Applied Philosophy 24, no. 1 (2007): 62-77. The article that introduced the "responsibility gap" argument, that where an autonomous system kills wrongly neither the programmer, the commanding officer, nor the machine can properly be held responsible.

  • Leveringhaus, Alex. Ethics and Autonomous Weapons. London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2016. Balanced treatment of consequentialist and deontological arguments. Its own thesis is the Argument from Human Agency, that what is lost when a machine kills is the human ability to do otherwise rather than any right of the target (pp. 91-92); it also treats a military's duty of care to its own personnel as a consideration that could make the deployment of autonomous weapons obligatory (pp. 112-114), and limits its objection to the last link in the causal chain, so that it does not oppose remotely piloted drones (p. 113).

  • Sharkey, Amanda. "Autonomous Weapons Systems, Killer Robots and Human Dignity." Ethics and Information Technology 21, no. 2 (2019): 75-87. Surveys dignity-based arguments against AWS and distinguishes different conceptions of dignity at stake.

  • Russell, Stuart. "Banning Lethal Autonomous Weapons: An Education." Issues in Science and Technology 38, no. 3 (Spring 2022): 60-65. Argues that the primary danger of autonomous weapons is their potential as cheap, scalable weapons of mass destruction rather than their targeting errors; the leading statement of the AI research community's objection.

  • Müller, Vincent C. "Autonomous Killer Robots Are Probably Good News." In Drones and Responsibility: Legal, Philosophical and Socio-Technical Perspectives on Remotely Controlled Weapons, edited by Ezio Di Nucci and Filippo Santoni de Sio, 67-81. London: Ashgate, 2016. A case to use autonomous weapons if they reduce civilian deaths.

  • Purves, Duncan, Ryan Jenkins, and Bradley J. Strawser. "Autonomous Machines, Moral Judgment, and Acting for the Right Reasons." Ethical Theory and Moral Practice 18, no. 4 (2015): 851-872. Argues that moral judgment is not codifiable and therefore cannot in principle be replicated by a machine executing a specification.

  • Schwarz, Elke. Death Machines: The Ethics of Violent Technologies. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2018. Political-theoretical treatment drawing on Arendt; critiques the rationalities underlying the arguments both for and against autonomous weapons.

  • Statman, Daniel. "Drones, Robots and the Ethics of War." Controversies in Military Ethics & Security Policy 2014, no. 1. Argues that unmanned and autonomous systems represent moral progress in warfare; by an Israeli philosopher who served on the committee that revised the IDF code of ethics. The issue is themed "Anonymous Killing by new Technologies? The Soldier between Conscience and Machine"; the argument answers the dignity objection directly, holding that being killed by a drone is not clearly more demeaning than being killed by a cruise missile or by artillery.

  • Anderson, Kenneth, and Matthew C. Waxman. "Law and Ethics for Autonomous Weapon Systems: Why a Ban Won't Work and How the Laws of War Can." Hoover Institution, Stanford University, 2013. Published in the Jean Perkins Task Force on National Security and Law Essay Series, and circulated as Columbia Public Law Research Paper 13-351 and American University WCL Research Paper 2013-11; open copies sit in the authors' institutional repositories at digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/facsch_lawrev/1892 and scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/1803. The principal legal argument against a categorical ban, favoring incremental development of codes of conduct under existing law.

  • Crootof, Rebecca. "War Torts: Accountability for Autonomous Weapons." University of Pennsylvania Law Review 164, no. 6 (2016): 1347. Proposes state liability for serious violations committed without individual intent or recklessness.

  • Ekelhof, Merel. "Moving Beyond Semantics on Autonomous Weapons: Meaningful Human Control in Operation." Global Policy 10, no. 3 (2019): 343-348. Examines how human control actually operates within military targeting processes rather than at the moment of engagement.

Institutional Studies or Statements

  • Heyns, Christof. Report of the Special Rapporteur on Extrajudicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions. UN Doc. A/HRC/23/47, April 9, 2013. The first major official treatment of lethal autonomous robotics; recommends national moratoria. The recommended moratorium covers at least the testing, production, assembly, and transfer of such systems, and the report also calls for a high-level panel on them.

  • Article 36. "Killer Robots: UK Government Policy on Fully Autonomous Weapons." Policy paper, April 2013. Introduces the term "meaningful human control," which became the organizing concept of subsequent diplomatic discussion.

  • International Committee of the Red Cross. Autonomous Weapon Systems and International Humanitarian Law: Selected Issues. Position paper, October 2025. Available online. Explains the application of distinction, proportionality, precautions, and human accountability to AWS. The paper's own conclusion goes beyond existing law: it calls for new, binding international rules prohibiting unpredictable AWS and AWS designed or used to target humans directly, restricting the target type, duration, geographic scope, scale, and situations of use of the rest, and requiring an effective self-destruct mechanism where human supervision is not feasible.

Jewish War Theory

  • Bleich, J. David. "Preemptive War in Jewish Law." In Contemporary Halakhic Problems, Vol. 3, 251-292. New York: Ktav, 1989. Earlier halakhic discussion establishing a basis for identifying Jewish battlefield laws/ethics as a distinct legal category.

  • Brody, Shlomo. Ethics of Our Fighters: A Jewish View on War and Morality. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2024. Most thorough analysis in English of the halakhah and theory behind Jewish military ethics. Includes a few pages on the future of war using autonomous and semi-autonomous military technologies.

  • Yisraeli, Shaul. Amud HaYemini [Hebrew: עמוד הימיני]. Jerusalem, 1966/1992. Influential treatment of warfare halakhah by a leading twentieth-century Israeli halakhic authority.

  • Schiffman, Lawrence H., and Joel B. Wolowelsky, eds. War and Peace in the Jewish Tradition. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Collected essays surveying the state of Jewish just-war theory in English, including the difficulty of applying ancient and medieval sources to modern warfare. The volume is the proceedings of the sixteenth Orthodox Forum, held in 2004, in the Orthodox Forum series; it was printed by Ktav of Jersey City for the Michael Scharf Publication Trust of Yeshiva University Press.

  • Leventer, Herb. "Philosophical Perspectives on Just War." In War and Peace in the Jewish Tradition, edited by Lawrence H. Schiffman and Joel B. Wolowelsky, 45-92. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Traces just-war reasoning from the Spanish scholastics' response to the conquest of the Americas to contemporary analytic philosophy, as the secular counterpart to the volume's halakhic chapters.

  • Wieder, Jeremy. "International Law and Halakhah." In War and Peace in the Jewish Tradition, edited by Lawrence H. Schiffman and Joel B. Wolowelsky, 239-264. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Asks to what extent halakhah recognizes the validity of international law and its binding force on the State of Israel, treating the search for a halakhic conceptual model for international law, the standing of treaties that contravene halakhah, and the pragmatic halakhic considerations; notes that little has been written on the question and that rabbinic literature says almost nothing about it, since it was formed when Jews lacked a sovereign state and before international law existed.

  • Walzer, Michael. "The Ethics of Warfare in the Jewish Tradition." Philosophia 40, no. 4 (2012): 633-641. From the author of Just and Unjust Wars, a brief but important observation that Jewish thought about war is incomplete due to the historical absence of Jewish political sovereignty for nearly two millennia.

  • Broyde, Michael J. "Just Wars, Just Battles and Just Conduct in Jewish Law: Jewish Law Is Not a Suicide Pact!" In War and Peace in the Jewish Tradition, edited by Lawrence H. Schiffman and Joel B. Wolowelsky, 1-44. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Argues that battlefield conduct carries an element of hora'at sha'ah (temporary suspension of the law), so that once killing is permitted in war much of the hierarchy of values of Jewish law is suspended as well, at least where those harmed are people who may be killed; takes R. Eliezer Yehudah Waldenberg and R. Shaul Yisraeli as holding that war follows a separate set of rules from individual ethics and that conduct needed to win is permitted.

  • Klapper, Aryeh, Benjamin Ish-Shalom, and Michael J. Broyde. "Conversation: Halakhah and Morality in Modern Warfare." Meorot 6, no. 1 (Shevat 5767/2007). Three-way exchange among Orthodox scholars on contemporary warfare ethics. The three contributions are Klapper's "Warfare, Ethics and Jewish Law," Ish-Shalom's "'Purity of Arms' and Purity of Ethical Judgment," and Broyde's "Only the Good Die Young?"; other indexes title the exchange "Conversation: Ethics and Warfare."

Jewish Engagement with AWS

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Rabbinical Assembly, 2019. CJLS HM 182, approved by the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards on June 19, 2019 by a vote of 18-0-0; Conservative movement responsum; pages 40-42 briefly address AWS, concluding that "Autonomous weapons systems must not use lethal force against humans without human direction," and distinguishing "autonomous defense systems that attack objects such as missiles or malware" from "those that select human targets and attack them without human consent."

  • Navon, Mois. "Autonomous Weapons Systems and Battlefield Dignity: A Jewish Perspective." In Alexa, How Do You Feel about Religion? Technology, Digitization and Artificial Intelligence in the Focus of Theology, edited by Anna Puzio, Nicole Kunkel, and Hendrik Klinge, 207-232. Darmstadt: WBG, 2023. A sustained Jewish treatment of AWS and potential ethical frameworks, such as questions of human dignity.

  • Brody, Shlomo. "Jewish Ethics in an Age of Autonomous Warfare." Sapir 11 (Autumn 2023). Argues that autonomous weapons systems are "not so much immoral as amoral," because they do not allow the moral deliberation and reflection needed to pass ethical judgment or to give an account of a decision afterwards, while accepting artificial intelligence in a decision-support role for identifying targets, counting non-combatants, and estimating collateral damage.

  • Navon, Mois. "Autonomous Weapons Systems for Policing - A Jewish Ethical Perspective." Theology and Science 23, no. 2 (2025): 265-275. Argues from a hierarchy of values in which societal harmony stands above the preservation of life and both above human dignity, built on the rodef doctrine as codified in Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 425:1, that agencies charged with security, whether military or police, need not be restrained by concerns over the indignity AWS may impose.

  • Berman, Nadav S. "Jewish Law, Techno-Ethics, and Autonomous Weapon Systems: Ethical-Halakhic Perspectives." Jewish Law Association Studies 29 (2020): 91-124. An introductory ethical-halakhic study of offensive AWS in the Israeli context, considering also broader socio-political risks.

On Israel Defense Forces' AI Use

  • Schmitt, Michael N. "The Gospel, Lavender, and the Law of Armed Conflict." Lieber Institute West Point, Articles of War, June 28, 2024. Argues that the Israeli systems are decision-support tools rather than autonomous weapons and are not unlawful as such, while noting the risk of undue deference to machine output.

  • Rehak, Rainer, and Taylor Kate Woodcock. "Automating Civilian Harm: On Israel's Use of the AI-Enabled Targeting System Lavender in Gaza and International Humanitarian Law." In Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '26), 2026: 4885-4898. Argues that the obligation to take precautions in verifying targets applies throughout the use of AI decision-support systems. The authors' stated conclusion is legal rather than ethical, that an adaptation of the system into legality is virtually impossible.

  • Goodfriend, Sophia. "Target Practice." New York Review of Books, July 23, 2026. Essay on Israeli military AI and the conditions under which human review of algorithmic targeting becomes nominal.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 90b-91b. Records an anonymous tannaitic dispute over whether a person may wound himself, and settles on R. Elazar ha-Kappar be-Rabbi as holding that he may not, two statements of R. Elazar having been proposed and set aside. Foundation for the halakhic treatment of bodily integrity and permissible medical intervention.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Ḥovel u-Mazziq 5:1. Codifies the prohibition against self-harm, establishing the normative halakhic position that one may not injure one's own body.

  • Radbaz (R. David ben Zimra), Responsa 3:627; Radbaz on Maimonides, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 18:6. Discusses whether one is obligated to sacrifice a limb to save another's life, inter alia discussing questions of bodily integrity and interference.

  • Yoma 85b. Establishes that pikuaḥ nefesh (preservation of life) overrides the Sabbath; the rule that it overrides all prohibitions but idolatry, murder, and forbidden sexual relations is at Sanhedrin 74a. Foundational for permitting invasive medical procedures including BCI implantation for therapeutic purposes.

  • Bava Kamma 85a; Exodus 21:19. The baraita of the school of R. Yishmael derives from "he shall surely heal" that licence (reshut) was given to the physician to heal; the obligation to heal rests on other sources.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesaḥim 4:9. Sharply rebukes those who treat medicine as impious encroachment on divine prerogative, comparing them to those who would refuse to eat because God alone sustains life.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 1:1. Identifies tselem Elohim (the image of God) with the human capacity for rational thought, raising the question of whether cognitive augmentation amplifies or distorts the divine image.

  • Bava Metzia 90b; Tosafot ad loc. Dispute over whether sound constitutes a halakhic "action": R. Yoḥanan holds that "the twisting of his mouth constitutes an action" (akimat piv), while Reish Lakish holds that sound is not an action; a baraita just before the dispute exempts one who muzzles the cow from lashes, which attach only to threshing and driving. Tosafot limit R. Yoḥanan's ruling to muzzling, because through the person's speech the animal "walks and threshes without eating"; a separate Tosafot on the same page (s.v. ravatz ari mi-baḥutz) explains that a cow will not eat while a lion crouches outside because it fears the lion.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Sekhirut 13:2. Rules that one who muzzles a threshing animal is lashed even if he muzzled it by voice.

  • Shevuot 21a. R. Yoḥanan holds that one is not lashed for a false oath about the future, because it is a prohibition that involves no act, and no such prohibition carries lashes.

  • Ḥatam Sofer (R. Moshe Sofer), Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, vol. 6, no. 29. Discusses whether Moses could have written Torah scrolls on Shabbat through invocation of a divine name; raises the question of action through non-standard means.

  • R. Yaakov Ḥagiz, Halakhot Ketanot 2:98. Considers whether one who kills through sorcery bears liability for murder; part of the broader halakhic discourse on action through extraordinary or supernatural means. Holds that one who kills by a divine name or by sorcery may be like one who shoots an arrow, since he acts through his speech.

  • R. Asher Weiss, Minḥat Asher, Parashat Vayakhel 5775. Holds that an effect produced through segulit means may not be ascribed to the person, while "systems that were built and developed by human hands are like an axe in the hand of the hewer and like a vessel in the hand of the potter, and his acts they are."

  • Bava Kamma 60a. Rav Ashi explains that winnowing while the wind assists is liable on the Sabbath because the Torah forbade melekhet maḥshevet, designed labor, but that in damages it is mere grama and exempt.

  • Rashi on Bava Kamma 60a, s.v. melekhet maḥshevet. Glosses the Talmud's reason as meaning that "his thought was realized, since the wind's assistance is agreeable to him."

  • R. Sha'ul Yisraeli, Sha'arei Sha'ul, Shabbat 32:5 and 32:10. Distinguishes a case where a person holds an animal down so that it has no will of its own, which is like winnowing with the wind assisting, from driving an animal by speech, where the animal acts on its own initiative and there is no melekhet maḥshevet because the result does not come about through the person's thought.

  • Ze'ev Lev, Ma'arkhei Lev, p. 297. Holds that using the brain itself is not prohibited, since such activity constitutes the human being created in the image of God and the categories of Sabbath labor do not reach it, but that using one's brain waves to perform a labor outside the body is like using one's saliva for that purpose and carries liability.

  • Berakhot 33b. R. Ḥanina's dictum that "all is in the hands of Heaven except for the fear of Heaven."

  • Niddah 30b. Aggadic account of a fetus being taught the entire Torah in utero, only to have an angel cause it to forget at birth; foundational text for the question of whether Torah knowledge gained without toil fulfills the mitzvah.

  • Megillah 6b. R. Yitsḥak's dictum "if someone says he toiled and found, believe him" (yagati u-matzati ta'amin), restricted there to words of Torah and, within Torah, to sharpness of understanding, retention of one's learning being help from Heaven.

  • Vilna Gaon, Commentary to Proverbs 16:26; cited in Ma'alot ha-Torah. Explains the narrative of Niddah 30b through the principle that Torah study requires transformative toil (ameilut), not merely informational acquisition.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Introduction to Sifra di-Tsni'uta of R. Elijah of Vilna. Relates that angels (maggidim) offered to reveal hidden Torah secrets to the Vilna Gaon, but he refused—he wanted to learn Torah only through his own toil.

  • Rav Kook, Orot ha-Torah 2:1. Teaches that producing a novel Torah insight (ḥiddush) constitutes a uniquely impactful revelation, because "the light that is renewed through the connection of the Torah to one soul is not the same as the light born from its connection to another soul."

Secondary Sources

Jewish Medical Ethics and the Integrity of the Body

  • Jakobovits, Immanuel. Jewish Medical Ethics: A Comparative and Historical Study of the Jewish Religious Attitude to Medicine and Its Practice. New York: Bloch, 1959. Founding work of the field; provides a systematic halakhic treatment of the physician's mandate to heal, the prohibition of self-harm, and the theological status of the body as divine trust.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. Encyclopedia of Jewish Medical Ethics. Translated by Fred Rosner. 3 vols. Jerusalem: Feldheim, 2003. The most comprehensive reference in Jewish medical ethics, covering the physician's obligation, permissibility of risky treatments, and the distinction between therapeutic and elective procedures across classical and contemporary halakhic sources.

  • Bleich, J. David. Bioethical Dilemmas: A Jewish Perspective. Vol. 1. Hoboken, NJ: Ktav, 1998. Rigorous halakhic analysis of risk-taking in medical treatment, the scope of the therapeutic mandate, and the boundaries between permissible healing and prohibited self-harm.

Torah Study, Ameilut, and Cognitive Enhancement

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. Available online. Directly addresses BCI technology and Torah study in the Yoreh De'ah section (47-48), distinguishing the mitzvah to study as much as possible from the obligation to master the whole Torah, and asking whether data on an implanted chip differs from data on a laptop.

  • Hollander, Max. "Ameilut in the Age of AI." The Lehrhaus, October 12, 2025. Available online. Explores the role of physicality in Torah learning, the religious imperative of ḥiddush (novel interpretation), and what ameilut means when information becomes instantly accessible; draws on R. Soloveitchik, Rav Kook, and the Tanya to argue that Torah study is irreducibly embodied and personally transformative. Embodiment is one of three approaches he sets out, alongside identity and novelty, and he draws on R. Shagar as well.

Halakhic Agency, Causation, and Technology

  • Zimmerman, Menashe. "Brain-Computer Interfaces—Performing Labor on Shabbat Through the Power of Thought" [Hebrew: ממשקי מוח-מחשב - עשיית מלאכה בשבת בכוח המחשבה]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 160-171. Finds no clear source in the decisors on performing a labor by thought, reconstructs R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach as yielding liability and Shevet ha-Levi 9:69 as permitting it in principle, reports R. Avigdor Nebenzahl as holding one rabbinically liable, and sorts the answers he collected into four classes.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (1977): 58-74. Surveys competing halakhic criteria for identifying a human being—parentage, form, and intelligence—and applies them to artificial and radically altered beings. Holds that a brain kept alive by machine and able to communicate is still alive (64).

  • Raiskin, Shlomi. "Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI)" [Hebrew: ממשקי מחשב-מוח (BCI)]. Assia 79-80 (2007): 5-16. Reprinted in Sefer Assia 15 (5776/2016): 3-14. Surveys developments in brain-computer interfaces and raises many of the questions they pose.

  • Belfer, Israel. "Shabbat Labors and Human-Machine Interfaces" [Hebrew: מלאכות שבת וממשקי אדם-מכונה]. Assia 83-84 (5769/2008): 67-90. Reprinted in Sefer Assia 15 (5776/2016): 15-38. Treats the Sabbath labors in relation to human-machine interfaces.

  • Greenhut, Moshe. "Damage Caused by Thought" [Hebrew: מזיק באמצעות מחשבה]. Emunat Itekha 142 (5784/2024): 116-128. Concludes that one who damages by operating a device through thought is liable under the prevailing view of the Rishonim, while some Aḥaronim treat it as gerama and exempt.

  • Zimmerman, Menashe. "Motion Sensors in a 'Smart Home' on Shabbat" [Hebrew: חיישני תנועה ב'בית חכם' בשבת]. Teḥumin 43 (2023): 74-85. Argues that activating a device through a motion sensor is a full act.

  • Makhta, Gad. "Wearing a Smartwatch on Shabbat" [Hebrew: ענידת שעון חכם בשבת]. Teḥumin 46 (2026): 119-126. Prefers a simple watch on the Sabbath but permits a smartwatch whose functions have been disabled.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Moral Status of Artificial Intelligence: A Jewish Ethical Perspective." PhD diss., Bar-Ilan University, 2023. Argues at p. 218 that implanting regulators of moral behavior would make human beings essentially automatons, since Jewish sources locate human freedom in ethical choice.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019. Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, Rabbinical Assembly, 2019. Conservative responsum addressing moral agency, liability frameworks, and the ethics of delegating decisions to AI systems; draws extensively on classical categories of causation and damages.

Brain-Computer Interfaces: Science, Ethics, and Policy

  • U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Implanted Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Devices for Patients with Paralysis or Amputation—Non-clinical Testing and Clinical Considerations. Final guidance, May 20, 2021, docket FDA-2014-N-1130, content current as of May 20, 2021. Available online. Defines the guidance's clinical scope as implanted neuroprostheses intended to restore lost motor or sensory capabilities.

  • Yuste, Rafael, et al. "Four Ethical Priorities for Neurotechnologies and AI." Nature 551, no. 7679 (2017): 159-163. Foundational article that launched the neurorights movement; proposes that privacy, identity, agency, and equality must be safeguarded as BCIs advance from clinical restoration to cognitive enhancement.

  • Ienca, Marcello, and Roberto Andorno. "Towards New Human Rights in the Age of Neuroscience and Neurotechnology." Life Sciences, Society and Policy 13, no. 1 (2017): article 5. Proposes four new human rights—mental privacy, mental integrity, psychological continuity, and cognitive liberty—as a framework for governing neurotechnologies including BCIs.

  • Burwell, Sasha, Matthew Sample, and Éric Racine. "Ethical Aspects of Brain Computer Interfaces: A Scoping Review." BMC Medical Ethics 18, no. 1 (2017): article 60. Comprehensive review systematically mapping the BCI ethics literature across concerns of personhood, autonomy, stigma, privacy, research ethics, safety, responsibility, and justice.

  • Goering, Sara, et al. "Recommendations for Responsible Development and Application of Neurotechnologies." Neuroethics 14, no. 3 (2021): 365-386.

Primary Sources

  • Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16. The fifth commandment: "Honor your father and your mother."

  • Leviticus 19:3. "A man shall fear his mother and his father." Rashi notes the inversion of the usual order (father before mother in Ex. 20:12) and explains it as Scripture's correction of the child's natural disposition: reverence is said of the mother first because a child naturally fears his father more, and honor of the father first because a child naturally honors his mother more, since she coaxes him with words. Maimonides derives from the same inversion that the two parents are equal in both reverence and honor (Hilkhot Mamrim 6:2).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 31a-b. The principal talmudic discussion of kibbud av va-em, including the story of Dama ben Netina, the distinction between kibbud and mora, and extended discussion of filial service. The narrative of Rav Assi and his elderly mother (31b) is the key test case for the limits of the obligation: Rav Assi departed when his mother's demands became impossible, heard she had followed him and died, and declared "had I known, I would not have left." The sugya also carries the case of Avimi, who had five ordained sons at hand and who ran himself to open the door for his father (31b).

  • Maharsha (R. Shmuel Eidels), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Kiddushin 31b. Holds that the Talmud specifies that Avimi's sons were ordained, and dependent on his table, to show that he could have charged them to answer the door in his place and did not, so that he should fulfill the commandment himself.

  • Rashash (R. Shmuel Strashun), Hagahot ha-Rashash, on Kiddushin 31b. Explains that Rav Assi's regret was that the hardship of his departure or his very abandonment caused his mother's death; argues that Rav Assi effectively retracted his decision to leave when he sought to go and meet her, and that the Ra'avad's ruling against unilateral departure derives from this story. His stated purpose is to answer the Ran and the Kesef Mishneh, who read the same narrative as proof for Maimonides.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Mamrim 6:1-3, 6:10. Codification of filial obligations; 6:10 permits delegation of care (yitzveh aḥerim le-hanhigam ka-ra'ui lahem) under duress when a parent's mental deterioration makes personal care unbearable.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 240:4-5. Defines kibbud as feeding, clothing, and escorting the parent, requires that it be given with a cheerful countenance (be-sever panim yafot), since one who feeds his father fattened fowl every day but shows him a sullen face is punished for it, and rules that although the expense falls on the parent's own means where he has them, the child is obliged to honor him with his own body (be-gufo) even though he thereby loses his work.

  • Ḥayyei Adam, klal 67:3-4. R. Avraham Danzig divides kibbud into thought, deed, and speech, calls the child's inward regard for the parent the essence of the honor, and requires that whatever is given be given with a cheerful countenance.

  • Ra'avad (R. Abraham b. David of Posquières), Hassagot, on Hilkhot Mamrim 6:10. Dissents from Maimonides: "This is not a correct ruling. If he goes and leaves him, to whom will he give instructions to watch over him?" The Ra'avad holds that the child cannot simply depart; delegating care is only permissible if adequate care is actually secured. That is one of several readings of a one-line gloss: the Kesef Mishneh and the Migdal Oz hold the objection groundless, the Taz and the Derishah read it as an argument about the added clause charging others, and the Baḥ reads it as a substantive rule for a deranged parent.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 240:10. Rules with Maimonides and against the Ra'avad, without a gloss of R. Moshe Isserles: where a parent's mind is deranged beyond what the child can bear, the child goes and leaves them and charges others to conduct them properly.

  • Kesef Mishneh on Hilkhot Mamrim 6:10. Holds that the clause charging others is good advice rather than a legal requirement, that the Ra'avad's objection has no place because Maimonides draws the ruling from the Rav Assi narrative rather than from his own reasoning, and reports the Ran's remark that he did not know why the Ra'avad objected, together with the Ran's tentative suggestion, which the Ran himself calls unclear, that the Ra'avad may confine the permission to going up to the Land of Israel.

  • Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 240. Calls Maimonides' words correct and clear on the strength of the Rav Assi narrative, and reports that the Ran held the same and wondered why the Ra'avad objected.

  • Turei Zahav (Taz) on Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 240:14; Ba'er Hetev, Yoreh De'ah 240:13. Read the Ra'avad's objection as aimed at Maimonides' added clause about charging others, and as an argument either way: if watching helps, the child need not go and leave the parent, and if the parent cannot be watched, charging others to watch accomplishes nothing; both report the Derishah to the same effect.

  • Arukh ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 240:32. R. Yeḥiel Mikhel Epstein holds that the objection is no objection, because Maimonides means that the severely deranged must sometimes be bound with chains and ropes, which the child cannot do himself, so that he charges others and goes.

  • Migdal Oz on Hilkhot Mamrim 6:10. Answers the Ra'avad that the son acts without pay while an appointee acts for pay, and that parents are less guarded with a child than with an appointee, a stranger before whom they feel shame.

  • Radbaz on Hilkhot Mamrim 6:10. Reported to hold that a parent feels affection for a child and no shame before him, so that others may rebuke and restrain a deranged parent as the child cannot.

  • R. Shmuel b. Avraham Rakov, Minḥat Shmuel, Devarim, siman 45. Surveys the dispute over delegating the care of a parent whose mind has become deranged, assigning Maimonides, the Radbaz, the Kesef Mishneh, the Shulḥan Arukh, and the Migdal Oz to the view that another may be appointed, and the Ra'avad, the Baḥ with the Tur, the Derishah, the Taz, and the Ba'er Hetev to the view that where another can do the work the child is the more obliged; it also holds that a child may not see his parents' nakedness, so that another should be appointed for the most intimate acts of bodily care.

  • R. Shmuel Wosner, Shevet ha-Levi 9:197. Reported to permit placing an elderly father in an old-age home where the son's constant care of him idles him from his work and sets his wife against him, to the severe harm of shelom bayit (household peace), on the reasoning that Maimonides allows the parent to be put into others' hands, that the Ra'avad would concede where personal care disrupts the household and the livelihood, and that kibbud is funded from the parent's own means.

  • R. Eliezer Waldenberg, Tzitz Eliezer 12:56. Reported to hold that a son may not himself tie to a chair a mother whose mind has become deranged, even on a physician's instruction, but must hand her to others who will do it.

  • Sukkah 49b. Distinguishes ḥesed from tzedakah in three respects: tzedakah is done with one's money while ḥesed may be done with one's person (be-gufo) as well as with one's money, tzedakah is for the poor while ḥesed is for rich and poor alike, and tzedakah is for the living while ḥesed is for the living and the dead.

  • Maharal of Prague, Netivot Olam, Netiv Gemilut Ḥasadim, ch. 2. Explains those three distinctions on the ground that gemilut ḥasadim proceeds from the giver, who does good whether or not it is asked, so that it may be done with the body, whereas tzedakah answers the recipient's need and is therefore monetary.

  • Shabbat 119a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 250:1. Require personal participation in Sabbath preparations even when others can perform the work.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:1-3. The father's personal obligation to teach his son Torah, falling first on the father himself and only secondarily on a hired teacher. 1:1 states the duty to teach one's minor son, from Deuteronomy 11:19; 1:3 adds that the father is obliged to hire a teacher for him. Delegated teaching is treated in the entry on Education.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvah 33. On honoring father and mother: a person should recognize and repay the good done to him by those who brought him into the world, "and when he fixes this trait in his soul he will rise from it to recognize the goodness of God." The obligation is framed as the training of gratitude in the child, which bears on whether a discharged duty and a personally discharged duty are the same thing.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvah 66. Grounds the commandments of lending and support in God's wish that His creatures be "trained and habituated in the trait of kindness and mercy," and notes that God could provide for the poor without us; we are made agents of the giving for our own sake.

  • Maimonides, Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Positive Commandment 8. The commandment of imitatio Dei—to walk in God's ways and emulate His attributes of mercy and compassion—for whose content Maimonides refers the reader to Hilkhot De'ot. The commandment itself names neither parents nor care.

  • Sifrei Devarim, Pisqa 49 (on Deuteronomy 11:22). Reads "to walk in all His ways" as an instruction to imitate the divine attributes: as God is called merciful, so should you be merciful; as God is called gracious, so should you be gracious, "as it is said, 'The Lord is gracious and full of compassion' (Psalms 145:8)," and give free gifts.

  • Ketubot 49a-b. Talmudic discussion of the father's obligation to support his children; distinguishes the formal rabbinic enactment (Usha) requiring support of young children from the looser social-coercive mechanism applied to older children, which it illustrates by Rav Ḥisda's ordering a mortar overturned in public so that the father is denounced and by Rava's asking him whether he is content that his children be fed from charity. It then limits that to the father who is not of means: where he is of means, כפינן ליה על כרחיה, we compel him against his will, as Rava compelled R. Natan bar Ami for four hundred zuz.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 71:1. Codifies the father's obligation to support sons and daughters while young; thereafter the court publicly pressures him to fulfill this duty, proclaiming him cruel in public. The age it gives is six. It rules that they do not compel him to maintain them, but that where he has means enough to give charity sufficient for them they take it from him against his will, as charity.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Ishut 12:15; Tur, Even ha-Ezer 71. Where a father of means refuses to maintain children past the age at which he is obliged, the court takes from him against his will, as charity.

  • Nahmanides on Deuteronomy 22:6. Nahmanides interprets the commandment to send away the mother bird as cultivating the trait of compassion in the one who performs it—the principle that mitzvot shape moral character, not merely produce outcomes.

Secondary Sources

Halakhic and Theological Foundations of Caregiving

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Family Redeemed: Essays on Family Relationships. Edited by David Shatz and Joel B. Wolowelsky. New York: Toras HoRav Foundation, 2000. Analyzes the covenantal structure of parent-child and spousal relationships; argues that these bonds involve irreducible mutual obligation between two selves.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Man of Faith in the Modern World: Reflections of the Rav, Volume Two. Edited by Abraham R. Besdin. Hoboken, NJ: Ktav, 1989. Chapter V treats the obligations that bind the generations to one another and the personal character of their discharge.

  • Blidstein, Gerald J. Honor Thy Father and Mother: Filial Responsibility in Jewish Law and Ethics. New York: Ktav, 1975; republished 2005. The standard monograph on filial obligation in Jewish law, including the scope of and limits on delegating a parent's care to others.

Robotic Caregiving: Philosophical and Ethical Critiques

  • Turkle, Sherry. Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other. New York: Basic Books, 2011. The first part of the book reports fieldwork with sociable robots in nursing homes and with children, and argues that people come to accept a performance of attention in place of a relationship.

  • Nyholm, Sven. Humans and Robots: Ethics, Agency, and Anthropomorphism. London: Rowman & Littlefield, 2020. Monograph on human-robot interactions from both the question of how robots should be designed and how humans should interact with them.

  • Darling, Kate. "'Who's Johnny?' Anthropomorphic Framing in Human-Robot Interaction, Integration, and Policy." In Robot Ethics 2.0, edited by Patrick Lin, Ryan Jenkins, and Keith Abney, 173-88. New York: Oxford University Press, 2017. Argues that anthropomorphic framing, such as names and backstories, changes how people perceive and treat robots, desirably in some settings and with cause for concern in others.

  • Bertolini, Andrea. "Human-Robot Interaction and Deception." Osservatorio del Diritto Civile e Commerciale 2 (2018): 645-659. Argues that robot companions which simulate human traits and elicit emotional responses, especially from children and the elderly, may amount to deception that the user's consent does not by itself cure.

  • Sparrow, Robert, and Linda Sparrow. "In the Hands of Machines? The Future of Aged Care." Minds and Machines 16, no. 2 (2006): 141-61. Argues that deploying robots to care for the elderly reflects a societal unwillingness to devote human resources to elder care.

  • Vallor, Shannon. "Carebots and Caregivers: Sustaining the Ethical Ideal of Care in the Twenty-First Century." Philosophy & Technology 24, no. 3 (2011): 251-268. Weighs the moral risks of care robots against their potential to support the practice of care, arguing that the literature has neglected the moral value of caregiving practices for the caregivers themselves, and distinguishing contexts in which carebots deprive potential caregivers of central moral goods from contexts in which they help caregivers sustain or enrich those practices.

  • Sharkey, Amanda, and Noel Sharkey. "Granny and the Robots: Ethical Issues in Robot Care for the Elderly." Ethics and Information Technology 14, no. 1 (2012): 27-40. Balanced taxonomy of the benefits and harms of robotic elder care, naming six concerns (reduced human contact, objectification and loss of control, privacy, personal liberty, deception and infantilization, and the question when the elderly should be allowed to control robots) and concluding that with foresight and careful guidelines such robots could reduce dependence and create more opportunities for social interaction.

  • Bertolini, Andrea, and Shabahang Arian. "Do Robots Care?" In Aging between Participation and Simulation: Ethical Dimensions of Socially Assistive Technologies in Elderly Care, edited by Joschka Haltaufderheide, Johanna Hovemann, and Jochen Vollmann, 35-52. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2020. Distinguishes between assistive and substitutive uses of robotic caregivers, concluding that machines can interact and simulate a relationship but not establish a real one with the user, and proposing human dignity as the criterion by which to judge the deprivation of a meaningful care relationship.

Assistive Technology: Policy and Evidence

  • World Health Organization and United Nations Children's Fund. Global Report on Assistive Technology. Geneva: World Health Organization, 2022. Reports that more than 2.5 billion people need one or more assistive products, that nearly one billion of them are denied access, that access is as low as 3 percent in some low-income countries, and that the number in need is likely to reach 3.5 billion by 2050 as populations age.

  • Nichol, Beth, Jemma Louise McCready, Goran Erfani, Dania Comparcini, Valentina Simonetti, Giancarlo Cicolini, Kristina Mikkonen, Miyae Yamakawa, and Marco Tomietto. "Exploring the Impact of Socially Assistive Robots on Health and Wellbeing across the Lifespan: An Umbrella Review and Meta-Analysis." International Journal of Nursing Studies 153 (2024): 104730. Umbrella review of 35 systematic reviews which found no pooled effect of socially assistive robots on quality of life, anxiety, or depression, reports that some reviews found no significant difference between such a robot and a plush toy, and concludes that the main mechanism of effect in group settings appeared to be the stimulation of social interaction with other humans.

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 22:8. "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof." The commandment to build a ma'akeh (parapet), codified by Maimonides (Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ 11:1-4) into a general duty to remove foreseeable hazards within one's control.

  • Leviticus 19:16. "Do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbor" (lo ta'amod al dam re'ekha). Establishes an affirmative duty to prevent foreseeable harm, interpreted talmudically as requiring active intervention to save life.

  • Leviticus 19:14. "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind" (lifnei iver lo titen mikhshol). Understood by the rabbis (Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 6b) as prohibiting any act that enables another to sin or come to harm, including providing the means for destructive action. Avodah Zarah 6b itself concerns enabling another to transgress, such as handing wine to a Nazirite; the application to selling instruments of harm to a robber is Maimonides' (Hilkhot Rotseaḥ 12:14).

  • Sanhedrin 73a. The locus classicus for the obligation to rescue (lo ta'amod). Establishes that one who sees another in mortal danger is obligated to intervene.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a. "What makes you think that your blood is redder?": one may not save one's own life by killing an innocent person.

  • Shevuot 35b. Shmuel rules that a kingdom (malkhuta) that kills one-sixth of a population is not divinely punished, derived from Song of Songs 8:12 ("and two hundred to those who guard its fruit" = 200/1,200). The foundation for the Ḥatam Sofer's threshold analysis of permissible and impermissible mass harm. The Talmud's words are one in six "in the world" (be-alma).

  • Tosafot to Shevuot 35b, s.v. de-katla ḥad mi-shita. Limits Shmuel's ruling to the losses of a discretionary war (milḥemet ha-reshut).

  • Avodah Zarah 15b-16a. The talmudic prohibition on selling weapons to those who may use them to harm others, and Rav Ashi's ruling that sales to the Persians (who protect the Jews) are permitted. Locus classicus for the halakhic analysis of dual-use sales and the arms-trade prohibition.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotseaḥ u-Shemirat ha-Nefesh 12:12-14; Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 9:8. Forbids selling weapons, or anything that causes harm to the public, to idolaters and to a Jewish robber, permits shields, which serve only for defense, and permits selling arms to the country's soldiers because they protect Israel.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 151:6. Permits selling weapons to the king's servants and troops where Jews live among the nations and have made a covenant with them, since the troops defend the country.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah to Avodah Zarah 15b. Limits the prohibition to idolaters bound by no religion, who would do harm with the weapons, and records that sales to the Persians were permitted because they protected the Jews among whom they lived.

  • Or Zarua IV, Piskei Avodah Zarah 132. Quotes Rav Ashi's ruling with Rabbenu Shmuel's explanation that the Persians protected the Jews and were not accustomed to kill them.

  • Nimukei Yosef to Avodah Zarah (on the Rif). Reported by Brody (2013) as permitting such sales from present need, in the hope that the buyers would not later turn the weapons against the Jews.

  • Mishnah Pesaḥim 4:9; Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 56a; Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesaḥim 4:9. King Hezekiah hid away the book of remedies and the sages approved; in his second explanation Maimonides holds that the book described poisons and their antidotes and was hidden once people began to kill with the poisons.

  • Kohelet Rabbah 7:13. "Take care not to destroy My world, for if you destroy it, there is no one to repair it after you."

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4; Maimonides, Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon 14:5-6. One who gives fire to a ḥeresh, shoteh, or katan (deaf-mute, mentally incompetent person, or minor) is liable for resulting damage, because the recipient lacks da'at (discernment); had the fire been given to a competent adult, liability would transfer to the recipient. The Mishnah holds the sender exempt in a human court but liable by the laws of Heaven; Maimonides holds him liable in court where he handed over a flame and not a coal.

  • Deuteronomy 20:19-20; Shabbat 105b. The prohibition of bal tashḥit (needless destruction), extended by the rabbis from fruit trees in wartime to a general principle against wanton destruction of the created world. Shabbat 105b condemns destroying garments and vessels in anger without naming bal tashḥit; the term appears in Kiddushin 32a, and the extension beyond trees is codified by Maimonides (Hilkhot Melakhim 6:10).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 32a; Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:10. The Talmud applies bal tashḥit to tearing silk garments, and Maimonides extends the prohibition from trees to anyone who breaks vessels, tears garments, demolishes a building, stops up a spring, or destroys food wantonly.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ u-Shemirat ha-Nefesh 11:1-4. Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 427:8. Codifies the general duty to remove foreseeable hazards.

  • Ḥatam Sofer (R. Moshe Sofer), Responsa, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 208 (responsum to R. Zvi Hirsch Chajes). Drawing on Shmuel's one-sixth ruling, the Ḥatam Sofer holds that a ruler may harm at most one-sixth of any distinct people or group, and has no license to destroy such a group entirely. Applied to AI-enabled catastrophic harm: attacks targeting a population for elimination cross a categorical halakhic threshold. He offers the point in passing as homiletic derush on Rashi to Leviticus 20:26.

  • Tosefta Ta'anit 2:13. R. Meir, R. Yehudah, and R. Yose each limit the post-flood oath, admitting respectively a flood of fire, the deaths of individuals, and a plague on the nations; the passage opens with a prayer that the rains stop, offered in confidence that God will bring no flood.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 11a; Maharsha, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Zevaḥim 116a. The Talmud answers Pharaoh's advisers that the oath covers the whole world and not one nation, and Maharsha holds that God swore not to destroy the whole world by any means while a single nation may still be destroyed.

  • Genesis 9:6, with Abarbanel on Genesis 9:1. Abarbanel reads the law of bloodshed given after the flood as God's answer to the fear of Noah's sons that they would kill one another with no one to judge them.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 25b. "Jephthah in his generation is like Samuel in his generation": one appointed as a leader of the community in his generation, however undistinguished, must be heeded like the greatest of earlier generations.

  • Ne'ilah Amidah, Yom Kippur liturgy; Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 70b. The Ne'ilah prayer asks for mercy "for You do not desire the destruction of the world," and Niddah 70b teaches that prayer for wisdom or wealth does not suffice without study or honest work.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:4. Each person should regard himself and the whole world as evenly balanced between merit and guilt, so that a single deed can tip the world toward destruction or toward deliverance.

  • Leviticus 26:44, with Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 11a. The Talmud reads the verse as a list of eras in which God raised up those who saved the nation from destruction.

  • Baḥya ibn Pakuda, Ḥovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Bitaḥon 4. One who trusts in God makes a reasonable effort without relying on the means in his heart or multiplying his pursuit of them.

  • R. Ḥayyim David HaLevi, Aseh Lekha Rav 1:19. Rules that Israel may sell weapons to allied nations on grounds of mutual strategic benefit, drawing on Maimonides and Meiri to argue that the medieval justifications apply to a sovereign Jewish state.

Secondary Sources

Arms Sales, Dual-Use Technology, and AI Governance

  • Brody, Shlomo. Ethics of Our Fighters: A Jewish View on War and Morality. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2024. The chapter on autonomous weapons surveys the talmudic prohibition on arms sales and its medieval and modern development, including the views of Meiri, Maimonides, Nimukei Yosef, Or Zarua, R. Chaim David Halevi, R. J. David Bleich, R. Yehuda Gershuni, and Dr. Meir Tamari; applies the tradition to Israeli arms industry ethics and, by extension, to the export of dual-use technologies.

  • Brody, Shlomo M. "The Halakhah of Selling Arms." Jewish Ideas Daily, February 5, 2013. Republished as "The Halachah of Selling Arms." Jewish Standard, February 8, 2013. Surveys the talmudic prohibition on selling arms and its development from Maimonides, the Meiri, Nimukei Yosef, and the Or Zarua to R. Ḥayyim David Halevi, R. J. David Bleich, R. Yehudah Gershuni, and Meir Tamari's critique of economically motivated sales.

  • Bleich, J. David. Contemporary Halakhic Problems. Vol. 3. New York: KTAV, 1989. Discusses Jewish law and modern warfare, including the application of pikuaḥ nefesh and hazard-prevention principles to contemporary military and security questions. Bleich's 1984 survey of nuclear warfare is reported to be reprinted in this volume at pp. 4-10.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Survey of Recent Halakhic Periodical Literature." Tradition 20, no. 4. Rules that arms sales are permitted only when accompanied by a formal or informal security pact; absent such agreement, sales are forbidden unless required by necessity for self-defense.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Survey of Recent Halakhic Periodical Literature: Physicians' Strikes / Nuclear Warfare / Hanukkah Lights for Travellers." Tradition 21, no. 3 (Fall 1984): nuclear warfare at 84-88. Reads Shevuot 35b with Tosafot as forbidding even a defensive war likely to kill more than one-sixth of the world's population, and permits nuclear deterrence while forbidding the weapons' use.

  • Broyde, Michael J. "Just Wars, Just Battles and Just Conduct in Jewish Law: Jewish Law Is Not a Suicide Pact!" In War and Peace in the Jewish Tradition, edited by Lawrence H. Schiffman and Joel B. Wolowelsky, 1-44. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Its note on nuclear war (24-26) holds that the Talmud prohibits war whose casualties would exceed one-sixth of the population while permitting nuclear deterrence, and it treats treaties as binding in Jewish law (30).

  • CCAR Responsa Committee. "Nuclear War." Responsum 5750.2. CCAR Journal (Winter 1993): 51-56; reprinted in Teshuvot for the Nineties, 273-279. A Reform responsum that cites Shevuot 35b, the Ḥatam Sofer, and bal tashḥit against nuclear war and concludes that a stand against it should not be taken by way of a responsum.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Up and Atom: The Resort to Nuclear Weapons." Bais HaVaad Halacha Center, May 5, 2022. Adapted from Dayan Grossman's writings, discusses the use of nuclear weapons and deterrence on the basis of Maurice Lamm and Jakobovits.

AI Safety and CBRN Threat Assessment

  • International AI Safety Report. International AI Safety Report 2026. 2026. Published February 3, 2026, under the chairmanship of Yoshua Bengio. Reviews evidence that general-purpose AI can assist with biological and chemical information and troubleshooting, while stressing uncertainty about real-world risk and the dual-use value of the same capabilities.

  • Tegmark, Max. Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. New York: Vintage, 2018. Devotes sustained attention to catastrophic AI risk scenarios, including the weaponization of AI for biological and nuclear threats, arguing that the window for establishing effective governance is narrow.

  • Hanke, Moritz S., Shrestha Rath, Anita Cicero, Thomas V. Inglesby, and Jaspreet Pannu. "Dual-Use Artificial Intelligence and Biology: Upstream Risk-Benefit Reviews." Frontiers in Microbiology 17 (2026): article 1832974. Argues that oversight of biological AI models after deployment is too late, and proposes risk-benefit reviews of AI-for-biology programs conducted even before a model is trained, estimating its potential public health benefit and weighing that against the severity and generalizability of its misuse potential. The abstract does not mention generalizability.

  • Pannu, Jaspreet. "Shaping AI Progress for Biology and Biosecurity." Essay series, 2026. Part 1, May 13, 2026. Argues for using AI to advance biomedicine while building resilience to biological risk.

  • Götting, Jasper, et al. "Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark." arXiv (2025). Reports that OpenAI's o3 model outperformed 94 percent of expert virologists on practical virology troubleshooting questions, a capability the authors call inherently dual-use.

  • Peppin, Aidan, et al. "The Reality of AI and Biorisk." In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '25), 763-771. 2025. Finds existing studies of AI-enabled biorisk nascent, often speculative, and methodologically limited, and concludes that current language models and biological AI tools do not pose an immediate risk.

  • Williams, Bridget, et al. "Forecasting LLM-Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards." Risk Analysis 46, no. 11 (2026). Reports expert forecasts in which hypothetical capabilities of large language models raise the estimated annual risk of a human-caused epidemic killing 100,000 people from 0.3 to 1.5 percent.

Theology of Catastrophe and Covenantal Responsibility

  • Jonas, Hans. The Imperative of Responsibility: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. A set of arguments grounded in secular metaphysics proposing that when the stakes are existential, worst-case projections should guide policy.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 3): The End of the World." Shmuel's Substack, October 16, 2026. Proposes halakhic analogues for AI misuse, carelessness, and misalignment, among them Hezekiah's hiding of the book of remedies as a precedent for dual-use knowledge, and reviews the rabbinic debate over nuclear weapons.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "What, to a Jew, is the End of the World?" Shmuel's Substack, October 25, 2026. Contrasts the Noahide covenant, which preserves the natural order, with the reciprocal covenant of Abraham, and draws on Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:4, Megillah 11a, and Baḥya on trust for the response to the danger of catastrophe.

Jewish Responses to Nuclear Weapons

  • Lamm, Maurice. "'Red or Dead?' An Attempt at Formulating a Jewish Attitude." Tradition 4, no. 2 (Spring 1962): 165-97. An early attempt to bring halakhic sources to bear on nuclear war, arguing that the defense of values may justify accepting catastrophic risk.

  • Jakobovits, Immanuel, and Michael Wyschogrod. "Rejoinders." Tradition 4, no. 2 (Spring 1962): 198-209. Replies to Maurice Lamm holding that halakhic rulings on war and martyrdom, which concern the loss of part of a people, may not guide decisions that risk all of humanity.

  • Lamm, Norman. "Religion in a Technological Society." Address, February 25, 1960. Lamm Legacy. Names "the threat of runaway technology" as the problem of the age and holds up Michael Faraday's refusal to develop poison gas during the Crimean War as a model of morally restrained science.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The Ethics of Safety." Sermon, Ki Tetse, September 9, 1962. Lamm Legacy. Reads the parapet commandment as requiring safeguards proportional to the danger, applied to thalidomide and to nuclear fallout.

  • Berkovits, Eliezer. Faith after the Holocaust. New York: KTAV, 1973. Argues that nuclear weapons have made the pursuit of power self-defeating, so that the bomb's message is "make peace or perish."

  • Landes, Daniel, ed. Confronting Omnicide: Jewish Reflections on Weapons of Mass Destruction. Jason Aronson, 1991. A collection of Jewish reflections on nuclear weapons, including Edward Teller's realist contribution.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "The Rabbis and the Bomb Maker: Are Jewish Views on AI Reaching Jews Working on AI?" Jello Menorah, September 28, 2026. Uses a 1991 collection of Jewish reflections on weapons of mass destruction, and Edward Teller's realist essay in it, to ask whether Jewish thought on AI reaches Jewish engineers.
