Primary Sources

  • Exodus 21:28-36; 22:4-5. The biblical core of the law of damages: the goring ox, the open pit, the grazing animal, and the fire that spreads. The latter verses are numbered 22:5-6 in some English editions.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 3b-4a. Names ox, pit, maveh, and fire as the four primary categories and records the dispute whether maveh means the human tortfeasor or the animal's tooth.

  • Bava Kamma 2b; Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:4. The Talmud names horn, tooth, and foot as three primary categories within the ox, and the Mishnah counts tooth and foot among the damages for which an animal is forewarned from the outset and rules that the owner of a tam pays half damages and the owner of a mu'ad full damages.

  • Mishnah Yadayim 4:7; Bava Kamma 4a. An owner is liable for damage done by his ox and his ass, which lack da'at, but not for damage done by his slaves, who have it, lest a slave whom his master provoked go and burn another's stack.

  • Bava Kamma 6a. Analyzes hybrid forms of damage, including an object moved from a roof or through the public domain.

  • Bava Kamma 10b. When five people sit on a bench without breaking it and a sixth sits on it and breaks it, the last is liable.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 22a-23a. The dispute whether fire is liable "as one's arrows" (isho mishum ḥitzav), a direct extension of the kindler's act, or "as one's property" (isho mishum mamono), a hazard one owns and must guard. Directly engaged for harm propagated by an autonomous system set in motion.

  • Bava Kamma 22b; Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4. One who sends fire by the hand of a deaf-mute, an incompetent, or a minor is exempt in a human court and liable before Heaven, while one who sends it by a competent person leaves that person liable.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 23b-24a. Develops the move from tam (innocent, half damages) to mu'ad (forewarned, full damages) through repeated, documented harm, the law's mechanism for the transition from unforeseeable to foreseeable injury.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon 1:4. An animal that repeats a deviation from its nature many times becomes mu'ad for that behavior.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 26a-b. States that damage caused by a person directly (adam ha-mazik) carries a higher degree of liability than damage caused by one's property; the source for the stricter standard governing the direct human tortfeasor.

  • Teshuvot ha-Rosh 101:5. One who injures while riding an animal is treated as one who damages with his own body.

  • Nahmanides, Ḥiddushim on Shabbat 153b; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 394:3 (Rema). Nahmanides holds that an animal plowing under the yoke is "only like a tool in a craftsman's hand"; the Rema exempts one who blocks an animal's path so that it goes and does damage, as gerama, and holds liable one who strikes it toward the damage.

  • Bava Kamma 55b-56a. Distinguishes entrusting an animal to a person without legal capacity from entrusting it to a competent keeper, and addresses responsibility for indirectly caused harm.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 10b. Ravina and Rav Sama limit the rule that there is no agency for a transgression to an agent who is obligated and free to refuse, so that a principal acting through his courtyard is liable.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 2:6. "A person is always forewarned" (adam mu'ad le-olam): the direct human tortfeasor is liable whether the harm was inadvertent or deliberate. Its application to damage under complete compulsion is disputed among the Rishonim.

  • Nahmanides, Ḥiddushim on Bava Metzia 82b; Tosafot, Bava Kamma 27b, s.v. u-Shmuel amar; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 378:1 (Rema). Tosafot exempt a person from damage done under complete compulsion, Nahmanides rejects that limit, and the Rema codifies the exemption for complete compulsion.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:4 (Bava Kamma 87a); Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Geneivah 1:9; Sma, Ḥoshen Mishpat 389:1. A slave who injures another is exempt until freed, Maimonides explains that an owner is not liable for his slaves' damage because they have da'at and he cannot guard them, and the Sma limits an owner's liability for living creatures to animals that lack da'at.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 411:3-6. Codifies, following Rabbeinu Asher (the Rosh) on Bava Kamma 1:1, the apportionment of responsibility among multiple parties for a damaging object in the public domain; the doctrinal anchor for distributing liability across owner, operator, and others. The Rosh exempts the obstacle's owner entirely when a person moves it, since a person has da'at, and has him share liability when an animal without da'at moves it.

  • R. Moshe Shternbuch, Teshuvot ve-Hanhagot 3:444. An insurer pays an injured party the amount customary in the courts because it took its premiums on that understanding, a ruling applied to a person injured by a car where there is no Torah-law liability as a damager.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Legal Analysis

  • Flug, Joshua. "Halachic Applications of Artificial Intelligence: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. The Ḥoshen Mishpat section examines liability for a self-driving car through Bava Kamma 26a and 6a, the categories of bor and esh, koaḥ sheni, and the Rosh's model of joint responsibility at Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 411.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019. New York: Rabbinical Assembly, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. Surveys halakhic responses to autonomous machines, summarizes Sprung and Malka's damages analysis (pp. 18-20), and leaves open whether AI-driven machines should be treated as property, animals, or a different category, while concluding that at the present stage liability for their acts remains with the human principal (p. 16).

  • Sprung, Yosef, and Yisrael Meir Malka. "The Driver's Liability for Damage Caused by an Autonomous Vehicle" [Hebrew: אחריותו של נהג ברכב אוטונומי על נזקים]. Teḥumin 38 (2018): 373-386. Examines direct action, animals, koaḥ sheni, gerama, fire, accident, and permitted risk in assigning liability for damage done by an autonomous vehicle.

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Holds that an AI system's action continues its operator's force as an "extended hand," ranking at least with fire as one's arrows in damages.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Its liability section (pp. 83-86) compares an AI system to a slave, for whose damage the owner is not liable, finds no technical basis for holding its creator liable, and notes a public-policy argument for holding the owner or creator liable.

  • Oḥayon, David. "An Autonomous Vehicle with Automatic Driving: Who Bears Liability in an Accident" [Hebrew: רכב אוטונומי עם נהיגה אוטומטית: מי נושא באחריות במקרה תאונה]. Meshiv ka-Halakhah, 22 Ḥeshvan 5784 (2023). Grades the owner's or operator's liability by the vehicle's level of autonomy, holding him liable as for an unguarded fire at level 3 and exempt at levels 4 and 5, and asks whether the manufacturer may be liable as the maker of a pit.

  • Student, Gil. "AI and Bava Kamma." Torah Musings, June 22, 2026. Compares AI-caused damage to the pit, fire, the animal, and the slave without deciding among them.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Goltz, Nachshon (Sean), John Zeleznikow, and Tracey Dowdeswell. "From the Tree of Knowledge and the Golem of Prague to Kosher Autonomous Cars: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Through Jewish Eyes." Oxford Journal of Law and Religion 9, no. 1 (2020): 132-156. Argues that existing legal persons should retain legal control over artificial agents and that natural persons should bear ultimate moral responsibility for the choices those agents make.

  • Greenhut, Moshe. "Who Is Liable for Damage Caused by an Autonomous Vehicle?" [Hebrew: מי אחראי לנזק שגרם רכב אוטונומי]. Emunat Itekha 147 (2025): 109-117. Considers the liability of programmers, operators, passengers, and owners.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 28a-29a. The principal talmudic discussion of whether mitzvot require kavvanah and whether one who is not obligated can discharge another's obligation; the foundation for excluding non-obligated agents from ritual proxy.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 60:4. Codifies the dispute over whether mitzvot in general require kavvanah. It records the two views and then rules that intention is required.

  • Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:7; Rosh Hashanah 27b. One who hears the echo of a shofar (kol havara) rather than the shofar itself does not fulfill the obligation; the classical basis for the modern debate over electronically reproduced sound.

  • Mishnah Pesaḥim 10:4. The four questions of the Mah Nishtanah; the requirement that the Exodus narrative be told in response to a question.

  • R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Minḥat Shlomo 1:9. Rules that one who hears through a microphone, telephone, or hearing aid hears a reproduced sound rather than the speaker's own voice, and therefore does not discharge the obligation. Records the Ḥazon Ish's contrary suggestion in an oral communication (p. 66 n. 4).

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 2:108. Reasons that a voice heard through a microphone may still be attributed to the speaker, since it is produced by him and heard immediately, while discouraging reliance on this in practice.

  • R. Ḥayyim Elazar Shapira, Minḥat Elazar 2:72. On hearing a blessing, kedushah, Megillah, shofar and kiddush over the telephone. One discharges the Megillah by telephone, since a reading is not invalidated where the reader's voice is thickened by resonance or distance, and one discharges kiddush; but the shofar plainly not (זה פשוט לע״ד דלא יצא), being no better than one who blows into a pit, where those outside who hear kol havara mixed with the shofar's sound have not discharged it (Rashi, Rosh Hashanah 28a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 587), the telephone's sound arriving mixed and the voice coming through כאוב, like a ghost's. The distinction is between the sound a commandment requires and the voice by which a text is conveyed.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, Moda'ah le-Veit Yisra'el (1859); R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson, Bitul Moda'ah (1859). The opposing pamphlets in the machine-matsah controversy; the most sustained pre-AI halakhic debate over mechanized mitzvah production.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 460:1-2. The matsot mitsvah are not to be kneaded or baked by a gentile, a deaf-mute, one lacking legal competence, or a minor, and the Rosh is reported to have overseen their making himself.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe YD 1:163. Ruling on mechanically reproduced sacred texts.

  • Deuteronomy 27:26, with Nahmanides ad loc. "Cursed be one who does not uphold the words of this Torah." Nahmanides holds that what is being demanded is inward acknowledgment, that one affirm the commandments in the heart and hold them true, and not merely that one perform them.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:31. The purpose of the commandments: every one of the six hundred and thirteen commandments exists either to communicate a correct opinion, to put an end to an unhealthy opinion, to communicate a rule of justice, to ward off an injustice, to endow men with a noble moral quality, or to warn them against an evil moral quality, which Maimonides reduces to opinions, morals, and social conduct.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Menaḥot 42a. "A sukkah of animals is valid," while tzitzit made by a gentile are not; the talmudic division between mitzvah-objects requiring no qualified maker and those whose production demands an obligated human actor.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 159:9-12, with Rema. Washing is valid from water that a person set pouring by tilting a barrel once and then walking away, since the flow issues from his force; water poured by a monkey is disputed, and the Shulḥan Arukh sides with those who validate while the Rema advises stringency. The codified grading of how little human agency an effective ritual act can contain.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 61b. The supervisor who "comes at fixed intervals" is inferior precisely because his visits are predictable; supervision operates through fear of discovery rather than continuous sight, the principle underlying technological hashgaḥah.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 113:5. One who heats an oven to cook renders forbidden even food he did not know was there; the gentile's general intent binds an automated production line he sets in motion.

  • R. Nissim Gaon, Introduction to Sefer ha-Mafteaḥ. Distinguishes commandments binding by reason (sevara) on all rational beings from those transmitted by prophetic tradition; establishes that knowledge of God, the obligation to serve God, and the prohibitions of murder and theft are binding mi-din ha-da'at, "by virtue of reason."

Secondary Sources

Halakhic Analysis of AI and Mitzvot

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019, approved June 19, 2019. Rabbinical Assembly, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards. A Conservative responsum surveying the field of machine ethics and applying halakhic categories of sheliḥut, liability, and human responsibility. Pages 36, 42 and 43 hold that an artificial agent may prepare or convey a ritual object while the ritual itself must be performed by one for whom it is a sacred obligation.

  • Jachter, Chaim. Gray Matter 2: Discourses in Contemporary Halachah. Brooklyn: Yashar Books, 2006. Its chapter "Fulfilling Mitzvot Through Electronic Hearing Devices" collects the twentieth-century responsa on microphones, telephones, and hearing aids, with locators for Henkin, Shternbuch, Waldenberg, Ovadia Yosef, Halperin, and Weiss, and records the exception argued for the Torah reading.

  • Aviner, Shlomo. "Writing a Torah Scroll by Robot?" [Hebrew: כתיבת ספר תורה על ידי רובוט? הרב אבינר משיב]. Kipa, January 5, 2020. Rules that a robot-written Torah scroll cannot be validated, since the verse "and you shall write them" requires that a person write, and distinguishes it from machine-made matsah and tsitsit, which require only production li-shmah.

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Holds that where koaḥ gavra is required, as in spinning li-shmah, slaughter, and handwashing, an AI system supplies none, and that of threads spun by machine only the first would count as spun li-shmah.

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha." Torah To-Go, Kislev 5785 (2024), 45-51. Surveys AI's halakhic implications across all four sections of the Shulḥan Arukh.

Halakhah and Theory of Non-human Intelligence

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Comprehensive survey organized around Sanhedrin 65b (Rava's golem); catalogues four positions on the ensoulment of artificially created beings: R. Cordovero (animal-level life force only), R. Tzadok (non-Jewish soul), R. Leiner (fully human creation possible in principle), and R. Ashkenazi (possibly Jewish). Also discusses the Ḥazon Ish's ruling that a Sefer Yetsirah creation "has none of the rights of a Jew, and likely none of the rights of Man."

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Golem and Not-So-Silly Questions." Torah Musings, April 28, 2025. Proposes, citing R. Nissim Gaon, that a golem or an AI, as a reasoning being, might be bound by the rational Noahide laws.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Parashas Yisro: For Whom is the Torah?" Shmuel's Substack, February 14, 2025. Quotes and translates R. Nissim Gaon's introduction on the binding of rational commandments by completeness of intellect, and sets it against the Kuzari, ibn Ezra, R. Shmuel b. Ḥofni Gaon, and Maimonides.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Daf: Natural Morality and the Noahide Laws" Shmuel's Substack, February 10, 2025. Gives the edition of R. Nissim Gaon's introduction, printed in Perushei Rabbeinu Ḥananel le-Masekhet Berakhot, ed. Metzger, p. 8, and surveys the rabbinic sources on morality binding without a command.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (Fall 1966): 15-26. Early treatment of whether an intelligent artificial being could hold religious status; left deliberately unresolved.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The Religious Implications of Extraterrestrial Life." Tradition 7, no. 4 (1965): 5-56. A seminal paper on the theological implications arising from potential discovery of rational, non-human creatures.

The Machine Matsah Debate

  • Hildesheimer, Meir, and Yehoshua Liebermann. "The Controversy Surrounding Machine-Made Matzot: Halakhic, Social, and Economic Repercussions." Hebrew Union College Annual 75 (2004): 193-262. Examines how the dispute reflected deeper anxieties about industrialization and the role of rabbinic authority in adjudicating technological change.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:26-27; 2:7; 9:6. The creation of the human in the image of God and, by divine breath, as a nefesh ḥayah (living soul); the base texts for both tselem Elohim and Jewish soul-language. Genesis 1:20 and 1:24 apply nefesh ḥayah to animals as well, so the phrase alone does not mark human distinctiveness.

  • Genesis 9:4-5; Leviticus 17:11, 17:14; Deuteronomy 12:23, with Nahmanides, Rashi, and Siftei Ḥakhamim on Leviticus 17:14. The recurring biblical association of soul with blood. Most of these refer in context to animal life (Genesis 9:5 speaks of human blood), but Nahmanides and others understand the verse in Leviticus as applying to human life as well.

  • Ecclesiastes 3:19-21. Humans and animals share "one ruaḥ," and the speaker asks who knows whether the human spirit ascends while the animal spirit descends; a biblical caution against any simple lexical hierarchy of souls.

  • Rashi and Nahmanides on Genesis 2:7. Rashi distinguishes the human nefesh from the animal's by added knowledge and speech (de'ah ve-dibbur); Nahmanides holds that by virtue of the divinely breathed higher soul the human understands, speaks, and acts, while sharing hargashah (sentience) with other moving creatures.

  • Commentaries on Genesis 1:26-27. E.g., Saadia Gaon, Rashi, Radak, Sforno, Recanati, Isaac Karo's Toldot Yitsḥak, Alshikh, Samson Raphael Hirsch, Meshekh Ḥokhmah.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot X:2. Assigns the soul three powers, appetite, spirit, and discernment (hakkarah), and defines discernment as the power that examines the impulses of the other two and rules on whether to follow them; the disciplined person is the one in whom discernment governs.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:1, I:41; Eight Chapters, ch. 1; Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:8. Guide I:41 calls nefesh a homonymous noun signifying the vitality common to sentient creatures, reason, the part that survives death, or will; Guide I:1 locates the divine image in intellectual apprehension; Eight Chapters describes one soul with nutritive, sensory, imaginative, appetitive, and rational faculties; Foundations of the Torah 4:8 calls the soul the form of the living body.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:68; Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:8-9; Repentance 8:3. Intellect is the act of abstracting a form from its matter and is identical with what it apprehends; the "additional da'at" that is the human form is defined by exclusion of the capacities by which every living creature eats, drinks, generates, senses, and muses; the nefesh that survives death is the knowledge it attained of its Creator.

  • Baḥya ibn Paquda, Ḥovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Beḥinah (Treatise II), ch. 5. Counts among the virtues of the intellect that by it a person apprehends all objects of sense and of thought, perceives what is hidden from the senses, and distinguishes truth from falsehood and good from evil.

  • Ibn Ezra on Exodus 31:3; Nahmanides on Genesis 2:9; Malbim on Genesis 2:9; Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 3. Competing definitions of da'at: a brain-seated faculty joined from the sensations; will; knowledge fixed in the soul, including the felt experience (hergashat ha-nefesh) of pain and of love; and hitkashrut, the sustained binding of thought to its object.

  • Sforno on Genesis 2:9. Explains the tree of knowledge as that which moves a person to give heart (latet lev) to good and evil, and reads "and the man knew" as giving heart to it.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim I:16. Identifies da'at with the first intelligibles, which are present in a person although it is not known how they arrived, and connects this with the blessing Atah Ḥonen le-Adam Da'at.

  • Moses Isserles (Rama), Torat ha-Olah, Part Two 28:2. Citing Mekor Ḥayyim, associates five flour offerings with the five senses and five names for the soul, possibly implicating sensory perception (and perhaps qualia) as being related to the fundamental nature of personhood.

  • Isaac Luria (Arizal), Peri Ets Ḥayyim, Rosh Ḥodesh, Ḥanukkah and Purim 3:12 and Lulav 3:45. Sets the five names of the soul, nefesh through yeḥidah, against the five partsufim (configurations) of the sefirotic structure, and finds the same five aspects within each partsuf.

  • Mishnah Berakhot 5:2; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33a; Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 5:2. The Mishnah places havdalah in the blessing Ḥonen ha-Da'at (who grants knowledge), the Babylonian Talmud explains that havdalah is a form of wisdom, and the Jerusalem Talmud asks, "if there is no da'at, whence havdalah?"

  • Judah Loew ben Bezalel (Maharal), Derekh Ḥayyim 3:14; Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Arakhin 15a; Tiferet Yisrael ch. 56 with Derekh Ḥayyim 3:17. Derekh Ḥayyim 3:14 reads the divine image through the soul. Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Arakhin 15a holds that, because the human is corporeal, the theoretical intellect is not the human form; the form is the ha-sekhel ha-dabbari, the speech-intellect operating through the bodily organ of the tongue. Tiferet Yisrael ch. 56 and Derekh Ḥayyim 3:17 define da'at as the discrimination of one thing from another, the reason havdalah is recited in the blessing Ḥonen ha-Da'at.

  • Pinḥas Eliyahu Hurwitz, Sefer ha-Berit I:18. The nefesh ha-sikhlit (intellectual soul) understands, acquires wisdom, distinguishes proper from reprehensible action, knows truth from falsehood, and grounds free choice.

  • Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, chs. 1-4, 9. Distinguishes the soul from its ten intellectual and emotional faculties and from its three "garments" of thought, speech, and action.

  • Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 5; Iggeret ha-Kodesh 29. Likkutei Amarim ch. 5 describes the intellect as grasping and encompassing what it knows while being clothed in it, and Iggeret ha-Kodesh 29 describes the pleasure born in the intellect at the moment a person grasps a new idea, felt together with the wisdom itself.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim 1:3. Associated the soul and divine image with the human capacity to "create" or "destroy" spiritual worlds through deeds.

  • Naḥman of Bratslav, Likkutei Moharan I:35:2. States that "the intellect is the soul" (ki ha-sekhel hu ha-neshamah), citing Job 32:8 ("the breath of the Almighty gives them understanding") and the Berakhot 10a analogy between the soul and God; the most explicit classical identification of soul with intellect.

  • Eliyahu Dessler, Mikhtav me-Eliyahu, vol. 1, p. 281. Distinguishes what the intellect can analyze from the givens it works upon, among them the sense qualities and the felt "I"; a modern rabbinic treatment comparing traditional soul-terms with the contemporary idea of consciousness.

Secondary Sources

Philosophy of Mind

  • Baars, Bernard J. A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness. Cambridge University Press, 1988. The founding statement of global workspace theory: consciousness as a limited-capacity workspace that broadcasts selected contents to a multitude of unconscious specialized processors.

  • Block, Ned. "On a Confusion about a Function of Consciousness." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 18, no. 2 (1995): 227-247. Distinguishes phenomenal consciousness, which is experience, from access consciousness, the availability of a content for use in reasoning and in the rational guidance of speech and action.

  • Chalmers, David J. The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press, 1996. The canonical formulation of the "hard problem"; argues that consciousness cannot be explained by functional or computational accounts alone.

  • Chalmers, David J. "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness." Journal of Consciousness Studies 2, no. 3 (1995): 200-219. Introduces the division between the "easy problems" of explaining cognitive functions and the "hard problem" of explaining experience.

  • Dehaene, Stanislas. Consciousness and the Brain: Deciphering How the Brain Codes Our Thoughts. Viking, 2014. Accessible synthesis of the global neuronal workspace framework and the experimental evidence for it.

  • Dennett, Daniel C. Consciousness Explained. Little, Brown, 1991. The leading functionalist account arguing that consciousness is no more than sophisticated information processing, with implications for AI possibility.

  • Kastrup, Bernardo. "An Ontological Solution to the Mind-Body Problem." Philosophies 2, no. 2 (2017): 10. Defends an idealist account on which consciousness is fundamental rather than produced by physical organization as an alternative to the purely functionalist assumption that a substrate-independent system could be conscious.

  • Locke, John. An Essay Concerning Human Understanding. London, 1690. Book II, ch. 1, sec. 19. Defines consciousness as "the perception of what passes in a man's own mind," in arguing that the soul cannot think without perceiving it.

  • Nagel, Thomas. "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" Philosophical Review 83, no. 4 (1974): 435-450. Classic argument that subjective experience cannot be captured by objective, third-person accounts.

  • Searle, John R. Minds, Brains and Science. Harvard University Press, 1984. A short series of lectures on mind, brain, and computation. Presents the Chinese Room thought experiment to argue that computation alone cannot produce understanding.

  • Penrose, Roger. The Emperor's New Mind: Concerning Computers, Minds and the Laws of Physics. New York: Penguin, 1991. A popular physicist's case arguing that human understanding is not algorithmic and therefore not reproducible by computation.

  • Searle, John R. "Minds, Brains, and Programs." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3, no. 3 (1980): 417-457. The "Chinese Room" argument, together with the peer commentaries and Searle's replies.

  • Sebo, Jeff. "The Moral Problem of Other Minds." The Harvard Review of Philosophy 25 (2018): 51-70. Argues that uncertainty about whether a being is conscious should nevertheless generate moral obligations.

  • Thagard, Paul. Brain-Mind: From Neurons to Consciousness and Creativity. Oxford University Press, 2019. Integrates neuroscientific and philosophical approaches.

  • Turing, A. M. "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Mind 59, no. 236 (1950): 433-460. Replaces the question "can machines think?" with the imitation game, and answers the objection from consciousness by noting that the same doubt would apply to other human minds.

  • Van Gulick, Robert. "Consciousness" in The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, edited by Edward N. Zalta and Uri Nodelman. Spring 2026 edition. Survey of the main philosophical accounts of consciousness.

Modern AI and Consciousness

  • Chalmers, David J. "Could a Large Language Model Be Conscious?" Boston Review, August 9, 2023. Also arXiv:2303.07103. A thorough discussion of reasons for and against attributing consciousness to current language models.

  • Butlin, Patrick, Robert Long, et al. "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness." arXiv:2308.08708 (2023). A recent collaborative report of several leading cognitive scientists on various "indicator properties" of consciousness, recognizing the difficulty in probing for machine consciousness definitively. It concludes that no current AI system is conscious but that there are no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy the indicators.

  • Long, Robert, et al. "Taking AI Welfare Seriously." arXiv:2411.00986 (2024). Argues for assessment and contingency planning under substantial uncertainty, without claiming that current AI systems are conscious.

  • Berg, Cameron, Diogo de Lucena, and Judd Rosenblatt. "Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing." arXiv:2510.24797 (2025). Reports LLM first-person experience claims under experimental conditions while explicitly cautioning that the findings are not direct evidence of consciousness.

  • Gurnee, Wes, Nicholas Sofroniew, Adam Pearce, et al. "Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models." Transformer Circuits Thread, Anthropic, July 2026. Available online. Reports that Claude models maintain a privileged subspace of reportable, modulable representations ("J-space") functionally analogous to a global workspace, while explicitly taking no position on phenomenal consciousness. See also the accompanying research summary.

  • Bentley, Peter J., Miles Brundage, Olle Häggström, and Thomas Metzinger. "Should We Fear Artificial Intelligence?" European Parliamentary Research Service, Scientific Foresight Unit (STOA), March 2018. Available online. Policy-oriented overview of AI consciousness and risk.

  • Thagard, Paul. Bots and Beasts: What Makes Machines, Animals, and People Smart? MIT Press, 2021. Accessible treatment of intelligence across biological and artificial systems.

Jewish Thinking on Consciousness and Artificial Intelligence

  • Lorberbaum, Yair. In God's Image: Myth, Theology, and Law in Classical Judaism. Cambridge University Press, 2015. A crucial study of tselem Elohim (image of God) in rabbinic and medieval Jewish thought; shows how Jewish sources conceptualized human distinctiveness without recourse to "consciousness."

  • Kogan, Barry S. "'What Can We Know and When Can We Know It?' Maimonides on the Active Intelligence and Human Cognition." In Moses Maimonides and His Time, edited by Eric L. Ormsby, 121-38. Washington, DC: Catholic University of America Press, 1989. Reconstructs Maimonides's account of how the human intellect acquires knowledge through the Active Intelligence.

  • Mittleman, Alan L. Human Nature & Jewish Thought: Judaism's Case for Why Persons Matter. Princeton University Press, 2015. Survey of modern Jewish thinkers on human nature and its ethical implications.

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024a): 221-241. Proposes mapping Jewish soul categories onto orders of phenomenal consciousness.

  • Navon, Mois. "Let Us Make Man in Our Image: A Jewish Ethical Perspective on Creating Conscious Robots." AI and Ethics 4, no. 4 (2024b): 1235-1250. Reads the Golem tradition as the basis for a deontological assessment of whether it is permissible to create conscious humanoid robots.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "What Artificial Intelligence Teaches Us about What It Means to Be Human." Jewish Action, Spring 2023. Runs through the competing definitions of tselem Elohim in the Jewish tradition and asks which of them, if any, an artificial system could satisfy.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (Fall 1966): 15-26. A pioneering treatment of whether an intelligent artificial being could hold religious status, seek conversion, or be counted as a person in halakhah; left deliberately unresolved.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (1977): 58-74. An early survey of competing halakhic criteria for identifying a human being (descent, form, and rational speech) and applies them to artificial and radically altered beings.

Primary Sources

  • Leviticus 22:32; Numbers 16:21; Numbers 14:27; Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 23b; Berakhot 21b. Derive the quorum of ten for matters of sanctity by linking "among the children of Israel" to the "congregation" of Korah and of the ten spies.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74b. Requires ten Jews for a public sanctification of God's name, by the same derivation, after asking whether nine Jews and one gentile suffice.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 47b-48a; Gittin 38b. Rejects counting an ark toward ten with the question "Is an ark a man?", reports that R. Eliezer freed his slave to complete a quorum, and rules that the law follows none of the lenient rulings on completing the number.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Tefillah 8:4-7; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:1, 55:4, 55:6, 55:8, 55:13-20. Define the quorum as ten free adult Jewish men, exclude a minor, a slave, a woman and a deaf-mute, count a sleeper and one praying alone, and require the ten to be in one place.

  • Rema to Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:4; Mishnah Berurah 55:23-24. Hold that a minor may not be counted by placing a ḥumash in his hand, while recording a lenient custom in an emergency and later authorities who forbid it.

  • Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55; Taz, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:4; Mishnah Berurah 55:33-34, 55:38. The Beit Yosef counts a sleeper because the Divine Presence rests on any ten adults, who are benei kedushah, the Taz excludes the sleeper as worse than a minor, and the Mishnah Berurah records this dispute and the Taz's exclusion of a deaf person who speaks.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b. Rava's man, unable to answer, returned to dust.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi 93. Rules from R. Zeira's destruction of Rava's creature that a man made through Sefer Yetsirah does not count toward a quorum, and adds that killing it is not bloodshed because it was not formed in a womb.

  • R. Yaakov Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Argues that such a creature, lacking da'at altogether, cannot count toward a quorum, since even the deaf-mute, the shoteh and the minor, who are Jews and whose killer is liable, do not count.

  • R. Ḥayyim Yosef David Azulai (the Ḥida), Birkei Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:4. Records the argument that Rava's creature could not count toward a quorum because a deaf-mute does not count.

  • Ba'er Hetev, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:2; Mishnah Berurah 55:4. Both refer to the Ḥakham Tsvi on whether a man formed through Sefer Yetsirah counts toward a quorum of ten.

  • R. Yehudah Assad, Teshuvot Maharya (Yehudah Ya'aleh) I, no. 26. Reported to defend the counting of a sleeper against the Taz and to hold that, on the Taz's view, a creature with no soul could not count; the a fortiori to a creature without a soul is Bleich's inference (Bleich 1998, 64-65).

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Grants for argument that a golem might be reckoned among Israel on the Ḥakham Tsvi's reasoning, yet holds that it cannot join a quorum, since it is not subject to obligation, lacking the soul that survives for reward and punishment.

  • Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8; Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 29a. Those not obligated in a commandment, including the deaf-mute, the shoteh and the minor, cannot discharge the public's obligation.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47a-b. Conversion as voluntary acceptance and embodied rite.

Secondary Sources

Artificial Persons and Jewish Status

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Reads R. Zeira's conversation with Rava's creature as a test of personhood through de'ah ve-dibbur, notes that language models have made such tests insufficient, and holds that reasonable doubt of human-level consciousness requires treating an entity as a full person.

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024): 221-241. Proposes mapping Jewish categories of soul, including the human nefesh of understanding and speech (de'ah ve-dibbur), onto orders of consciousness in robots.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Cloning: Homologous Reproduction and Jewish Law." Tradition 32, no. 3 (1998): 47-86. Human status, birth, and the golem precedents. Pages 61-66 discuss whether a golem counts toward a minyan in the Ḥakham Tsvi, R. Yaakov Emden, the Ḥida, Maharya and R. Tsadok ha-Kohen.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024. Minyan and golem within the wider problem of nonhuman intelligence. Reports R. Gershon Henoch Leiner's view that a speaking golem would be legally human and could help constitute a minyan (81).

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Surveys the responsa on whether an artificial man counts toward a minyan (79-82), including the argument from the deaf-mute, and lists the modern literature on the status of the deaf (81 n. 64).

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (1966): 15-26. Reads the Ḥakham Tsvi's womb criterion as bearing only on homicide and infers from the golem responsa that an intelligent artificial being might be regarded as human (24-26).

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (1977): 58-74. Translates the golem rulings of R. Gershon Henoch Leiner and R. Yosef Rosen on counting toward a minyan (61-62) and asks how the halakhah would count split-brain patients and electronic copies of a person (67-68).

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Responsum, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. CJLS HM 182.1.2019. Machines as equipment rather than participants in ritual acts. Pages 42-43 allow artificial agents to facilitate the performance of commandments while holding that the ritual itself must be performed by an obligated person.

Presence, Remote Participation, and Disability

  • Reisner, Avram Israel. "Wired to the Kadosh Barukh Hu: Minyan via Internet." CJLS OH 55:15.2001. Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, Rabbinical Assembly, 2001. Rules that a minyan requires physical presence in one room with the prayer leader, that those connected by real-time audio may respond to a constituted quorum, and that responding to a recording does not fulfill an obligation.

  • Heller, Joshua. "Counting a Minyan via Video Conference." CJLS OH 55:14.2021a. Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, Rabbinical Assembly, 2021. Presents options, voted on separately, for counting participants linked by real-time video toward a minyan, from Mourner's Kaddish alone to a full virtual or hybrid quorum.

  • Barmash, Pamela. "The Status of the Ḥeresh and of Sign Language." CJLS HM 35:11. Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, Rabbinical Assembly, 2011. Rules that deaf people who communicate in sign language are not to be considered mentally incapacitated and may lead a minyan conducted in sign language.

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. Reports R. Yosef Shalom Elyashiv's ruling that an individual may rely on a statistical majority to treat a person as Jewish for a limited purpose such as completing a minyan, though a court may not (48).

Golem Traditions

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1990. The principal historical study.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Idea of the Golem." In On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, 158-204. New York: Schocken Books, 1965. The mystical history behind the legal questions.

  • Barzilai, Maya. "Golem." Oxford Bibliographies in Jewish Studies, 2019. Bibliographic survey of the golem literature.

Primary Sources

  • Pirkei Avot 6:6. Lists "saying a matter in the name of the one who said it" among the forty-eight ways Torah is acquired and concludes that such attribution brings redemption to the world.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 15a. R. Elazar reports in the name of R. Ḥanina that whoever says a matter in its speaker's name brings redemption to the world, citing Esther 2:22.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 104b. Cites the dictum that one who says a matter in its speaker's name brings redemption to the world, in identifying R. Yose as the author of an anonymous mishnah.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 27b. R. Eliezer counts one who says a matter he did not hear from his teacher among those who cause the Divine Presence to depart from Israel.

  • Mishnah Eduyot 1:3. Explains Hillel's use of an obsolete measure by the rule that a person must speak in the language of his teacher.

  • The Maharal of Prague, Derekh Ḥayyim to Pirkei Avot 6:6. Explains the connection between attribution and redemption: both return something to the source or place to which it properly belongs. He suggests further that one careless about the name of a teaching's author will be careless about its substance and come to alter it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 94a-b. The foundational talmudic discussion of geneivat da'at. The cases distinguish manufactured false impressions from situations in which people mislead themselves.

  • Tosafot, Ḥullin 94b, s.v. inhu de-ka mat'u anafshayhu. Distinguishes a guest who has no reason to suppose that barrels opened for him were already sold from one who should have realized that a gesture was not made for his sake.

  • Midrash Tanḥuma, Bamidbar 22. Requires one who repeats a teaching to name its speaker and compares failure to do so with robbing the poor. It extends the duty to a teaching received at third hand and reports it as halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

  • R. Ḥayyim Ḥizkiyahu Medini, Sdei Ḥemed, Pe'at ha-Sadeh, Ma'arekhet ha-Alef, kelal 143 (s.v. Omer be-shem omro). Extensive discussion of the topic of quoting a teaching in the name of the source.

  • Mishnah Shevi'it 10:8. One repaid a debt after the Sabbatical year must say "I release it," and a manslayer whom the people of his city of refuge wish to honor must tell them "I am a manslayer."

  • Jerusalem Talmud, Shevi'it 10:3. R. Yose infers that one who knows a single tractate and is honored elsewhere as knowing two must tell his hosts that he knows only one.

  • R. Avraham Gombiner, Magen Avraham, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 156:2. Codifies the duty to correct an inflated estimate of one's learning, forbids ascribing to a sage what one did not learn from him, counts failure to name a teaching's speaker as a negative commandment, and permits stating one's ruling in a great authority's name so that it will be accepted.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 51a; Pesaḥim 112a, with Rashbam. A sage states a ruling in R. Yose's name so that it will be accepted, and Rashbam reads "hang yourself from a great tree" as advice to say one's teachings in a master's name.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 2:6. Prohibits misleading speech and codifies the examples of false invitations, gifts, and honor from Ḥullin 94a.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Mekhirah 18:1. Prohibits deception in commerce and requires a seller who knows of a defect to disclose it to the purchaser.

  • Maimonides, introduction to Eight Chapters (Shemonah Perakim). Acknowledges dependence on rabbinic and philosophical sources, explains why each borrowed statement will not be separately attributed, and denies an intention to claim earlier statements as his own.

  • Maimonides, introduction to the Mishneh Torah, with the glosses of Ra'avad. Lists the chain of transmission by name from Moses through Rav Ashi and explains that the code's rulings will therefore appear without individual attribution. Ra'avad's stricture objects that omitting the authorities' names prevents the reader from weighing a ruling against dissenting views. Ra'avad's gloss, on the words "and knows from it," says that Maimonides "intended to improve but did not improve," because earlier authors "wrote things in the name of those who said them."

  • Ḥizkuni (Hezekiah ben Manoah), introduction to the Torah commentary. Explains that the commentary anthologizes earlier commentaries and midrashim without naming their authors, on the ground that "the words of the wise are as one; truth was given from one shepherd" (after Ecclesiastes 12:11).

  • Moses ibn Ezra, Kitab al-Muḥaḍara wa-l-Mudhakara. Ed. Abraham S. Halkin, Jerusalem: Mekize Nirdamim, 1975. Judeo-Arabic treatise on Hebrew poetics; discusses the Andalusian conventions of literary borrowing (sariqa), under which appropriating a predecessor's motifs was judged by skill rather than by disclosure.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 228:6. Requires correction of a misleading appearance of special honor but states that no notice is required when the other person should have understood the circumstances and misled himself.

  • R. Tzvi Elimelekh of Dinov, Derekh Pikudekha, lo ta'aseh 36, ḥelek ha-maḥshavah 4. Counts saying another's Torah in one's own name, for honor or payment, under the prohibition of kidnapping as geneivat nefesh.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Ḥoshen Mishpat 2:30. Prohibits copying answers on Regents examinations as geneivat da'at and connects falsely obtained credentials with later monetary wrongs. Its application to generative AI is analogical. The monetary theft it identifies is from the employer who hires the student on the strength of the diploma.

  • R. Eliezer Waldenberg, Tzitz Eliezer 15:12. Rules that physicians who alter the details of cases in medical publications commit geneivat da'at, even toward readers who are not Jews, and transgress "keep far from a false matter" (Exodus 23:7).

Secondary Sources

Jewish Attribution and Deception

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Copyright and Halakhah." Torah Musings, June 30, 2025. Distinguishes copyright permission from attribution, applies geneivat da'at and Iggerot Moshe to AI-assisted authorship, and argues that prevailing conventions affect the disclosure analysis. It is an essay, not a formal consensus ruling.

  • Avraham, Michael. "Geneivat Da'at and Intellectual Property" [Hebrew: גניבת דעת וקניין רוחני]. Teḥumin 25 (2005): 350-366. Distinguishes economic copyright from the author's interest in attribution and discusses the difference between omitting a source's name and claiming another person's Torah insight as one's own.

  • Levine, Aaron. Moral Issues of the Marketplace in Jewish Law. Brooklyn: Yashar Books, 2005, 3-42. Analyzes geneivat da'at, false goodwill, and the information another person needs to make an honest evaluation; pages 31-35 address attribution and ghostwriting.

  • Zimmerman, Binyamin. "Geneivat Da'at: Misleading, Misrepresentation and Deception." Torat Har Etzion, Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2016. Traces the scope of geneivat da'at from the talmudic cases to contemporary applications, with attention to when a false impression is created by silence or implication.

  • Friedman, Hershey H. "Geneivat Da'at: The Prohibition Against Deception in Today's World." SSRN Electronic Journal (2013). Surveys commercial, interpersonal, educational, and professional applications of geneivat da'at.

  • Central Conference of American Rabbis Responsa Committee. "Artificial Intelligence and Authorship," responsum 5784.2. 2024. A Reform responsum requiring disclosure when a rabbi presents AI-generated liturgical poetry under circumstances in which congregants would understand the rabbi to be its author.

  • Cherlow, Yuval, and Yaron Moskowitz. "Using Artificial Intelligence Systems to Rule Halacha [Abridged Position Paper]." Tzohar Center for Jewish Ethics, 1 Sivan 5786 (2026). Requires that Torah and halakhic content produced through AI carry a clear and prominent declaration that a technological system created it, and asks bodies operating public AI systems to meet strict disclosure standards (sections 4.3 and 4.5).

  • Dana, Joseph. "Moshe Ibn Ezra and His Ars Poetica: Imitation and Innovation According to Kitab al-Muhadara val-Mudhakara." Hebrew Studies 55 (2014): 89-116. Analyzes Moses ibn Ezra's views on literary convention against originality and on borrowing against plagiarism.

Law, Policy, and Audience Response

  • United States Copyright Office. Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence. 88 Fed. Reg. 16,190 (March 16, 2023). Explains registration applicants' duty to disclose more than minimal AI-generated material, identify the human-authored contribution, and limit the claim accordingly.

  • European Union. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), art. 50. Establishes targeted transparency duties for specified synthetic outputs, deepfakes, and certain public-interest text. Article 50 applies from August 2, 2026 and contains exceptions, including one tied to human review, editorial control, and editorial responsibility.

  • Pew Research Center. "How Americans View AI and Its Impact on People and Society." September 17, 2025. Survey of 5,023 U.S. adults conducted June 9-15, 2025. Reports that 76 percent consider it extremely or very important to be able to tell whether pictures, videos, and text were made by AI or by people, while 53 percent are not confident they can.

  • Simon, Felix M., Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, and Richard Fletcher. Generative AI and News Report 2025: How People Think About AI's Role in Journalism and Society. Oxford: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, 2025. Six-country survey (Argentina, Denmark, France, Japan, UK, US; June-July 2025) documenting audience comfort with human, AI-assisted, and AI-generated news and expectations about labeling; successive annual waves track how these expectations move.

  • Toff, Benjamin, and Felix M. Simon. "'Or They Could Just Not Use It?': The Dilemma of AI Disclosure for Audience Trust in News." The International Journal of Press/Politics 30, no. 4 (2025): 881-903; first published online December 30, 2024. Reports a survey experiment in which an AI label reduced perceived trustworthiness of news, while a source list largely counteracted the penalty.

  • Sahebi, Siavosh, Paul Formosa, and Sarah Bankins. "The AI Penalty and Disclosure Paradox: Trust, Authenticity and Knowledge Uptake in AI-Mediated Communication." Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 8 (2026): article 100304. Reports a preregistered experiment with 547 participants comparing human, AI-assisted, and fully AI-authored workplace emails and social-media posts.

  • Gilardi, Fabrizio, Sabrina Di Lorenzo, Juri Ezzaini, Beryl Santa, Benjamin Streiff, Eric Zurfluh, and Emma Hoes. "Quality Perceptions and Intended Engagement in Response to AI-Generated and AI-Assisted News." Scientific Reports 16 (2026): article 29929; published online June 29, 2026. Reports a preregistered experiment with 599 participants in German-speaking Switzerland on perceived news quality and reading intentions before and after disclosure.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:20-28; 2:7; 5:1. Living beings, the divine image, male and female, dominion, and the generations of Adam.

  • Genesis 9:6; Psalms 8:5-7. Bloodshed forbidden because the human was made in the image of God; the human made little less than elohim, crowned with glory and given rule over God's works.

  • Leviticus 17:11; Ecclesiastes 3:19-21. The nefesh of flesh in the blood; one ruaḥ and one fate for human and animal.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5; Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4; Sanhedrin 4:9. Equality, uniqueness, and the worth of a single life from the one primordial human; love of neighbor and the great principle of the Torah. The printed Mishnah speaks of "a single life from Israel," a qualification absent from the Jerusalem Talmud's text.

  • Mishnah Avot 3:14. R. Akiva: beloved is the human, created in the image, and beloved are Israel, called children of God.

  • Genesis Rabbah 8:11; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 16a; Avot de-Rabbi Natan 37:2. The human between animal and angelic modes of existence.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 31a; Kiddushin 30b. The three partners in the human being.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91a-b. Body and soul judged as one.

  • Onkelos and Rashi on Genesis 2:7. The living soul as speaking spirit; knowledge and speech as the human increment. Rashi also has the body made from the lower beings and the soul from the upper.

  • Rashi on Genesis 1:26; 3:22. Glosses "in our likeness" as the power to understand and discern, and places human uniqueness among the lower creatures in knowing good and evil.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot II:9. The image as honorific attribution rather than shared form.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:1; Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:8. Tselem as intellectual apprehension against to'ar as shape.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:7; I:34; III:54. One lacking the human form is "a mere animal in human shape and form"; the human begins with perfection only in potential; intellectual perfection is that on account of which a person "is called man."

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:1. Reads Genesis 3:22 as saying that the human species alone knows good and evil of itself and does whatever it wishes.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 1:20; 1:26; 2:7. The human as likeness of both earth and the beings above; the breathed neshamah.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 2:9. Reads the da'at of the tree of knowledge as will and desire, which the first human, acting by nature, lacked before eating of it.

  • Ibn Ezra on Genesis 1:26. The undying higher soul likened to God in being incorporeal and filling the body; the human body as a small world.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari IV:3. "Let us make man in our image" as referring to the heavenly hosts seen in human form, with the human at the summit of an ordered creation.

  • Sforno on Genesis 1:26-27; 5:1; Meshekh Ḥokhmah on Genesis 1:26. The image as actualized intellect and as elective freedom.

  • Malbim on Genesis 1:26; 2:9. The image as free choice, since intellect is shared with the separate intelligences, so that the human alone rules "his small world"; da'at as including what the soul knows through feeling, such as pain and love of kin.

  • Naftali Tsvi Yehudah Berlin (Netziv), Ha'amek Davar on Genesis 1:27. The image as the whole of nature included in the human, belonging fully only to the elevated human, as before the sin.

  • Judah Loew ben Bezalel (Maharal), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Arakhin 15a; Gevurot Hashem, second introduction. The speech-intellect as human form; the separate soul above the sun. The Arakhin passage names the human form ha-sekhel ha-dabbari.

  • Moses Cordovero, Tomer Devorah 1:1. One who resembles the supernal form in body but not in deeds "belies the form," since the essence of the image and likeness is action.

  • Samson Raphael Hirsch on Genesis 1:26-27. Locates the divine image in the body as well as the soul: the human frame is fitted to a godlike mission, so the Torah teaches recognition of the body's dignity and rejects contempt for it.

  • Abraham Isaac Kook, Orot, "Orot me-Ofel," Orot ha-Teḥiyah 33. A call, in the context of national revival, to restore physical health and strength as a religious demand: "we have engaged much in the soul and forgotten the holiness of the body."

  • Pinḥas Eliyahu Hurwitz, Sefer ha-Berit I, ma'amar 18, ch. 1. The nefesh ha-sikhlit understands, acquires wisdom, distinguishes right from reprehensible, and grounds free choice; a golem made through Sefer Yetsirah would have every power and sensation except speech, since no human can give it this soul.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 1:1; 2:2; 4:9; 4:12; Hilkhot Teshuvah 8:3. The foundation of foundations is to know that there is a First Existent; contemplating His works leads to love and awe and to awareness of one's own smallness; the form of the soul that knows the Creator endures forever, and the soul that survives is the knowledge it has attained.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim I:2-3. The image as delegated mastery over worlds through deed, word, and thought.

  • Moshe Ḥayyim Luzzatto, Derekh Hashem I:3:9-11. Since the sin, body and soul can reach perfection only after death and resurrection, and true perfection belongs to neither until they are joined again.

  • Mishnah Berurah, Bi'ur Halakhah 329:4, s.v. ela le-fi sha'ah. Rules that the killer of a deaf-mute or shoteh is liable to death, since they are included in "he who strikes any human life" (Leviticus 24:17).

  • Ḥagigah 2b. One who hears but does not speak, like one who speaks but does not hear, is legally competent; one who neither hears nor speaks is treated like the shoteh and the minor.

  • Ḥagigah 3b-4a. Gives the behavioral criteria of the shoteh: going out alone at night, sleeping in a cemetery, tearing one's garments, and destroying whatever one is given.

  • Mishnah Ḥagigah 1:1; Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:4. The deaf-mute, the legally incompetent person, and the minor are exempt from the pilgrimage appearance (Ḥagigah 1:1), and one who injures them is liable though they are not liable for injuring others (Bava Kamma 8:4).

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi 93. Rules from R. Zeira's conduct that a man created through Sefer Yetsirah does not count toward a quorum, and holds that killing it is not bloodshed, since Genesis 9:6 applies only to one formed in a mother's womb.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Maḥshevot Ḥarutz 18:9; Likkutei Ma'amarim, on Shimshon §16. The divine image as the fear of the human placed in all creatures, removed through sin; tselem as the active power itself and demut as its trace in what it acts upon.

  • Yosef Yehudah Leib Bloch, Shi'urei Da'at I, Emunah ve-Hashgaḥah, shiur 11. Proposes, without precedent in the earlier commentators by his own account, that tselem refers to the limbs and their structure and demut to the constitution of a person's feelings and powers of soul.

  • Yeruḥam Levovitz, Da'at Ḥokhmah u-Musar III, ma'amar 106; Da'at Torah, Shemot, Terumah. The image as a pencil sketch that a person must ink in, potential intellect made actual through thought and deed; the essence of the image as understanding and imitation of the divine attributes, quoting Tomer Devorah.

Secondary Sources

Divine Image and Human Dignity

  • Lorberbaum, Yair. In God's Image: Myth, Theology, and Law in Classical Judaism. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015. The bodily, theological, and legal meanings of the divine image in rabbinic and medieval sources.

  • Greenberg, Irving (Yitz). "The Human Being as the Image of God." Modern Judaism 44, no. 2 (2024): 89-107. Derives from the divine image three intrinsic dignities of every human being, infinite value, equality, and uniqueness, together with Godlike capabilities, and reads Ben Azzai's dictum as making the image the Torah's foundational principle.

  • Mittleman, Alan L. Human Nature and Jewish Thought: Judaism's Case for Why Persons Matter. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2015. Integrates body, animality, rationality, and relation under the image of God.

Philosophical and Theological Anthropology

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Family Redeemed: Essays on Family Relationships. Edited by David Shatz and Joel B. Wolowelsky. New York: Toras HoRav Foundation; distributed by Ktav, 2000. Reads the divine image as a mission that the human is charged to implement.

  • Sacks, Jonathan. "Holiness and Childbirth." Covenant & Conversation, Tazria. Argues that Judaism makes the life of the body a vehicle for the Divine Presence and rejects both hedonism and asceticism.

  • Heschel, Abraham Joshua. Who Is Man? Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1965. Human uniqueness as self-transcendence and being-addressed.

  • Buber, Martin. I and Thou. Translated by Walter Kaufmann. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1970 [orig. 1923]. Personhood as dialogical relation.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "The Lonely Man of Faith." Tradition 7, no. 2 (1965): 5-67. The two creation accounts as majestic and covenantal humanity.

  • Segal, Aaron. "Body and Soul." In The Routledge Companion to Jewish Philosophy, edited by Daniel Rynhold and Tyron Goldschmidt, 45-56. London: Routledge, 2025. Maps the possible answers to the question of what a human being is, locates them in classical Jewish sources, and develops a distinctively Jewish version of dualism.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on Artificial Intelligence is Upside-Down (Part 1)." Shmuel's Substack, April 11, 2025. Asks what the creativity reading of the divine image, held by R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin and R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik, implies for AI systems that appear to do creative work.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "You Are a Person, First." Shmuel's Substack, July 2, 2026. Argues from derekh erets kodmah la-Torah that Jews bear obligations as human beings before and beyond what Jewish law specifies.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "What, to a Jew, is the End of the World?" Shmuel's Substack, October 25, 2026. Contrasts the covenant with Noah, made with all humanity, with the covenant with Abraham, and holds that Jews are members of humanity before they are members of Israel.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 2): They Took Our Jobs." Shmuel's Substack, March 24, 2026. Treats technological job displacement through halakhic and theological sources, reading Adam's curse as painful toil and Maimonides' code as pointing to a world in which humans are free to think.

Human Status and Technology

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "What Artificial Intelligence Teaches Us about What It Means to Be Human." Jewish Action, Spring 2023. Tests seven readings of tselem Elohim (soul, free will, conceptual intellect, creativity, the handling of contradiction, emotion, and altruism) against current AI and concludes that "an insurmountable gap remains."

  • Christian, Brian. The Most Human Human: What Talking with Computers Teaches Us About What It Means to Be Alive. New York: Doubleday, 2011. An account of competing in the Turing test as a human confederate, used as an occasion to ask which human capacities are actually distinctive rather than merely habitual.

  • Turing, A. M. "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Mind 59, no. 236 (1950): 433-460. Replaces the question whether machines think with the question whether a machine can pass for a human in conversation (the "imitation game").

  • Moravec, Hans. "When Will Computer Hardware Match the Human Brain?" Journal of Evolution and Technology 1 (1998). Pictures a "landscape of human competence" slowly flooded by advancing computer performance, with peaks such as locomotion, hand-eye coordination, and social interaction submerged last.

  • Jiménez-Rodríguez, Luis O. "Human Uniqueness or Anthropocentrism? Semantic, Anthropological and Theological Clarifications in Dialogue with Damasio's Neuroscience." In Issues in Science and Theology: Are We Special?, edited by Michael Fuller, Dirk Evers, Anne Runehov, and Knut-Willy Sæther, 191-207. Cham: Springer, 2017. Separates the claim that humans are distinctive from the claim that they are the measure of value.

  • Kaplan, Aryeh. "On Extraterrestrial Life." In The Aryeh Kaplan Reader: The Gift He Left Behind. Brooklyn: Mesorah, 1983. Argues that other intelligent life would lack free will and therefore moral responsibility; a Jewish attempt to specify what would and would not transfer to a nonhuman mind.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The Religious Implications of Extraterrestrial Life." Tradition 7, no. 4 (1965): 5-56. Asks whether the discovery of other rational beings would undermine Judaism's account of human distinctiveness.

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Defines personhood by a human-level soul, expressed as moral intelligence, and distinguishes it from humanhood, which also requires a human body.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Human origin, moral intelligence, and reproduction as criteria of human status.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (1966): 15-26. Descent, form, and rational speech as competing halakhic criteria for artificial beings. Holds that an intelligent golem "might well have been regarded as human."

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (Spring 1977): 58-74. Holds that a child of human parents is human without human form or intelligence, that killing a deaf-mute is murder, and that "it is conceivable that even an intelligent computer could be halakhically human."

  • Steinberg, Avraham. "The Definition of a Human Being: Its Halakhic Significance Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת אדם - משמעותה ההלכתית כיום]. Teḥumin 30 (5770/2010): 122-128. Holds that intelligence, morality, and speech are not necessary conditions of human status, so that a robot with artificial intelligence is not adam, and that birth from a woman is necessary under current criteria.

  • Zilbergerts, Marina. "What Star Trek and Genesis Teach Us About Consciousness." 18Forty, October 30, 2025. Locates the divine likeness in subjective consciousness and argues that intelligence and speech, which machines can imitate, cannot establish personhood.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:20-24; 2:7; Leviticus 17:11. Nefesh ḥayyah shared by animals and humans; the divine breath of Genesis 2:7; the nefesh of flesh in the blood.

  • Nahmanides on Leviticus 17:14. Blood and soul are mixed together like wine with water, so that there is no blood without soul and no soul without blood.

  • I Samuel 25:29; I Kings 17:21-22; Ecclesiastes 3:19-21; Psalms 42:6; 103:1. The nefesh bound, departing, returning, addressed, and shared with the animals.

  • Abraham Ibn Ezra on Ecclesiastes 3:21. The human neshamah endures and does not perish like the soul of an animal, and Scripture uses neshamah only of humans.

  • Genesis Rabbah 14:9. Five names of the soul: nefesh, ruaḥ, neshamah, ḥayyah, yeḥidah. The midrash glosses nefesh as the blood and ruaḥ as the spirit that rises and descends (Ecclesiastes 3:21).

  • Targum Onkelos and Rashi on Genesis 2:7. Onkelos renders nefesh ḥayyah "a speaking spirit" (ruaḥ memallela); Rashi holds that animals too are nefesh ḥayyah but the human's is distinguished by the addition of knowledge and speech.

  • Malbim on Genesis 2:7. Derives neshamah from breathing, calls it the eternal divine part in the human, and holds that the soul's vegetative, vital, and rational powers all come from the one neshamah that God breathed in.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a. Five correspondences between the soul in the body and God in the world.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 31a. God's contributions to the child: ruaḥ, neshamah, perception, speech, understanding, wisdom.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91a-b; Leviticus Rabbah 4:5. The blind and lame guards: body and soul judged as one. Leviticus Rabbah gives the parable in R. Ishmael's name and follows it with R. Ḥiyya's parable of the priest's two wives, in which God leaves the body aside and judges the soul alone.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91b; Yevamot 69b. Rabbi accepts Antoninus's view that the soul is given at conception; before forty days the embryo is "mere water."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 152b. For twelve months after death the body persists and the soul ascends and descends; the souls of the righteous are likened to royal garments returned clean to the king.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot VI:1, 3; X:2. The soul as created substance rather than accident; its powers of appetite, spirit, and discernment, which correspond to the names nefesh, ruaḥ, and neshamah.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari I:1; I:89; V:12. The philosophers' conjunction with the Active Intellect; Moses as a speaking soul using bodily instruments; the division of the soul's powers into vegetative, vital, and speaking.

  • Maimonides, Eight Chapters 1; Guide of the Perplexed I:40-41; III:54; Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:8-9; Repentance 8:2-3. One soul with five faculties; nefesh as homonym; the additional da'at as the human form; survival as attained knowledge. Ruaḥ also signifies what remains of a person after death; the form that knows the Creator endures forever; intellectual perfection gives immortality.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 1:20; 1:26; 2:1; 2:7. The vegetative power excluded from nefesh; the animating soul from the earth; human souls as the host of heaven; the neshamah as the breath of God rather than element or emanation. On 2:7 he reports the three-soul and one-soul views, grants that the verse's plain sense suggests one soul, and holds that Onkelos and the Sages treat the speaking soul as distinct.

  • Nahmanides, Torat ha-Adam, Sha'ar ha-Gemul. Distinguishes the world of souls, the Garden of Eden entered at death, from the world to come, the world of the resurrection in which people exist in body and soul.

  • Abraham Ibn Ezra on Exodus 31:3; 23:25. Wisdom, understanding, and da'at located in the ventricles of the brain; neshamah, ruaḥ, and nefesh seated in brain, heart, and liver.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim II:11; IV:29. Souls as intermediate between bodies and the separate intellects. Reports that many Torah scholars followed the philosophers in holding that the soul is perfected after death apart from the body, and objects that an intellect that is only a preparation cannot subsist by itself.

  • Sforno on Genesis 1:26-27. The image as an intellectual substance, eternal only when its capacity is actualized through wisdom.

  • Moses Cordovero, Pardes Rimmonim 24:10; Maharal, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Human artifice cannot draw the levels of soul, or the speaking soul, into a manufactured body. Cordovero holds that the creature had only "mere vitality," superior to an animal's because of its form; the Maharal, that a man cannot create one like himself.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b; R. Samuel Edels (Maharsha), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Rava's man does not answer R. Zeira and is returned to dust; the Maharsha explains that it had only the vital spirit that animals also possess, not the neshamah whose power is speech.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Holds that understanding does not depend on speech, since a mute has understanding, and excludes the golem from a quorum for matters of sanctity because it is not subject to the commandments, lacking a soul that survives for reward and punishment, while allowing that it may be counted toward ten for Grace after Meals.

  • Zohar II:94b (Mishpatim); R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Tsidkat ha-Tsaddik 227. A person receives a nefesh at birth and a ruaḥ and neshamah by further merit; R. Tsadok reads the levels as faith, its felt confirmation in the heart, and wisdom in the brain, the neshamah unattainable before the ruaḥ.

  • Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 1-4; Sha'ar ha-Yiḥud ve-ha-Emunah 6. Two souls, ten faculties, three garments; the body's substance not derived from the soul.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim I:4. No Jew should say "what am I and what is my power to accomplish anything in the world by my lowly deeds"; every deed, word, and thought ascends according to its root to act upon the upper worlds.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim I:14-15. Nefesh, ruaḥ, and neshamah aligned with action, speech, and thought.

  • Ramḥal, Derekh Hashem I:3:9-11, 13. The world of souls and the final perfection of soul and body reunited. The soul's power is suppressed in the fetus by divine decree and enters the body in full at the resurrection.

  • Naḥman of Bratslav, Likkutei Moharan I:25; I:35:2. The acquired intellect as what persists; "the intellect is the soul."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 60b; Siddur, Elokai Neshamah (morning liturgy); Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 6:1 with Rema. The soul is described as given pure, formed, breathed in, preserved within, and eventually taken and restored, the printed siddur adding "created"; the Rema glosses mafli la'asot ("who does wondrously") as the binding of something spiritual to something physical.

  • Pinḥas Eliyahu Hurwitz, Sefer ha-Berit I, ma'amar 18, ch. 1. The nefesh ha-sikhlit understands, acquires wisdom, distinguishes right from reprehensible action, and grounds free choice; a golem made through Sefer Yetsirah would have every power and sensation except speech, since no human can give it this soul.

Secondary Sources

Historical and Philosophical Accounts

  • Segal, Aaron. "Body and Soul." In The Routledge Companion to Jewish Philosophy, edited by Daniel Rynhold and Tyron Goldschmidt, 45-56. London: Routledge, 2025. Maps biblical, rabbinic, philosophical, and halakhic accounts of Jewish human ontology, reads the two parables of Leviticus Rabbah 4:5 as distinct models of body and soul, and defends a dualism on which the body is essential to the human being and the soul is a deposit that may be lost and regained.

  • Steiner, Richard C. Disembodied Souls: The Nefesh in Israel and Kindred Spirits in the Ancient Near East, with an Appendix on the Katumuwa Inscription. Ancient Near East Monographs 11. Atlanta: SBL Press, 2015. Argues for a separable nefesh in biblical texts.

  • Rudavsky, T. M. "On Immortality and the Nature of the Soul." In Jewish Philosophy in the Middle Ages: Science, Rationalism, and Religion, 208-231. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2018. Surveys medieval debates over soul, immortality, and resurrection.

  • Carlson, Reed. "Rûaḥ in the Hebrew Bible: A Survey of Past Scholarship." Currents in Biblical Research 22, no. 2 (2024): 115-132. Surveys the semantic range of biblical ruaḥ.

Rabbinic Embodiment

  • Weiss, Daniel H. "Embodied Cognition in Classical Rabbinic Literature." Zygon 48, no. 3 (2013): 788-807. Reads rabbinic accounts of thought and agency as embodied.

  • Kimelman, Reuven. "The Rabbinic Theology of the Physical: Blessings, Body and Soul, Resurrection, and Covenant and Election." In The Cambridge History of Judaism, vol. 4, edited by Steven T. Katz, 946-976. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006. The theological significance of the body in rabbinic Judaism.

Soul, Consciousness, and Artificial Intelligence

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024a): 221-241. Identifies the soul with the mind's second-order phenomenal consciousness and, from the biblical association of soul and blood, proposes that only blooded creatures have consciousness.

  • Navon, Mois. "Let Us Make Man in Our Image: A Jewish Ethical Perspective on Creating Conscious Robots." AI and Ethics 4, no. 4 (2024b): 1235-1250. Reads the Golem tradition as the basis for a deontological assessment of whether it is permissible to create conscious humanoid robots.

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Identifies the human soul with human-level consciousness.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (1966): 15-26. Descent, form, and rational speech as competing halakhic criteria for artificial beings.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. "The Definition of a Human Being: Its Halakhic Significance Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת אדם - משמעותה ההלכתית כיום]. Teḥumin 30 (5770/2010): 122-128. Holds that the human possesses nefesh, ruaḥ, and neshamah, and reconciles the soul's entry at conception with the embryo's lesser status before forty days by proposing that the soul has degrees and becomes complete only after birth.

  • Nevins, Daniel. "Thinking about AI." Jewish Standard, June 22, 2023. Reads Sanhedrin 65b and Rashi on Genesis 2:7 as making speech a human distinction while holding that a person incapable of speech remains fully a person, and concludes that "AI is a tool, not a person."

  • Avraham, Michael. "On Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: על בינה מלאכותית]. Responsum, mikyab.net, September 25, 2016. Holds that consciousness is not a computational process, that passing the Turing test would not show that a computer experiences or feels, and that a computer is a being without a soul.
