Primary Sources

Simulated Deeds, Character, and Thought

  • Leviticus 19:14; Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 22b. "Before the blind do not place a stumbling block," which the Talmud applies to handing a forbidden thing to one who would transgress with it.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary on Deuteronomy 6:18. "The right and the good" requires conduct beyond the letter of the law in matters where no specific command applies.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary on Leviticus 19:2. "You shall be holy" commands restraint in what is permitted, since a person could otherwise be "a scoundrel with the Torah's permission."

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvah 16. "The heart is drawn after the deeds," so that even a righteous person compelled to engage constantly in wrongdoing is changed by it.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot De'ot 1:7. Dispositions are acquired by repeating their acts until they become fixed.

  • Maimonides, Shemonah Perakim 4. Virtues and vices are fixed in the soul only by repeating their acts many times over a long period.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 68a. On "you shall not learn to do" (Deuteronomy 18:9): "You may not learn in order to do, but you may learn in order to understand and to teach."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 39b-40a. God does not join an evil thought to the deed, except in the case of idolatry.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Kiddushin 39b. One who resolved to sin and was prevented only for lack of opportunity is punished for the thought, and in matters of faith the thought is a complete act.

  • R. Tzvi Elimelekh of Dinov, Derekh Pikudekha, negative commandment 35, ḥelek ha-maḥshavah 2. Where the Torah's warning concerns the thought itself, the thought is the transgression.

  • Sefer Yere'im 365. "Do not stiffen your neck" (Deuteronomy 10:16) is violated by resolving in one's heart not to return to God.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Nazir 23a; Kiddushin 81b. One who intended a sin and unknowingly performed a permitted act still requires atonement.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 12b. Reads "after your heart and after your eyes" (Numbers 15:39) as heresy and sexual fantasy, and the next clause as idolatrous thought.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 29a. "Thoughts of sin are harder than sin."

  • Rashi and Tosafot Yeshanim on Yoma 29a. Read "harder" as more wearing on the body, as with one who smells fatty meat and does not eat it.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:8. Sinful thought is graver than sinful deed because thought belongs to the nobler part of a person.

  • Rabbeinu Baḥya on Deuteronomy 29:18. Gives several readings of "thoughts of sin are harder than sin," including dwelling on a sin after committing it.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Teshuvah 4:4. Gazing at forbidden women is a grave sin, although the one who gazes supposes he has done nothing.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 20a-b. Ve-nishmarta mi-kol davar ra (Deuteronomy 23:10) as a warning against daytime thoughts that lead to nocturnal impurity, and as forbidding gazing at women, at their colored garments, or at animals mating.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 23:3. Forbids bringing oneself to sinful thought and watching animals mate.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b. Rava holds that Jezebel had images of harlots made on Ahab's chariot so that he would see them and be aroused.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Even ha-Ezer 1:69. The prohibition of thinking of a sexual transgression under "after your eyes" applies to women, while ve-nishmarta applies to men only.

Seeing through a Medium

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 25b. One may not recite the Shema facing nakedness behind glass, since the prohibition depends on seeing.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 75:6. One who turns away, closes his eyes, is in the dark, or is blind may recite the Shema facing nakedness.

  • Baḥ on Tur, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 75; Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 3:5. Closing one's eyes does not help where the nakedness could otherwise be seen.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 24a. Witnesses who saw the new moon in water, through glass, or in clouds may not testify to it.

  • Sha'arei Teshuvah, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 426:1. Reports the dispute over blessing the new moon seen in a mirror, through glass, or through eyeglasses.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 9b. Shimon ha-Tzaddik's nazirite tells how his inclination was aroused by his own reflection in water.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yeḥavveh Da'at 4:7. Forbids reciting the Shema or Grace after Meals facing a television that shows an immodestly dressed woman, since the prohibition rests on sinful thought.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 24a. Shmuel holds that a woman's voice is nakedness, citing Song of Songs 2:14.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yabia Omer 1, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 6. Permits hearing a woman sing on a gramophone or radio when the listener does not know her.

  • R. Eliezer Waldenberg, Tzitz Eliezer 5:2. A radio carries a reproduction of a woman's voice and not the voice itself, so that there is room to permit listening without intent to enjoy it.

Dreams

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b. A person is shown in a dream only the thoughts of his heart; the "improvement" of a dream before three.

  • Berakhot 57a. Dreams of forbidden unions read as good omens, provided the dreamer had not thought of the woman that evening.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 30a. "Words of dreams neither raise nor lower."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 8a. One banned in a dream requires ten who have studied halakhah to release him.

  • Ran on Nedarim 8a. A dream ban binds because it may have been imposed at Heaven's behest, a reason that does not extend to a dream vow.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 7:12. One banned in a dream requires ten who study halakhah to release him.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 11a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 288:4-5. Fasting on account of a dream, even on Shabbat, with later restrictions on the practice.

  • Taz, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 288:3. A dream that follows the dreamer's daytime thoughts is not regarded as shown from Heaven.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 220:1. The procedure for improving a dream before three friends.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 210:2. A vow made in a dream has no force, but one should take into account the view requiring release before ten.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 334:35-36. A ban imposed in a dream is binding and requires release before ten.

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Yoreh De'ah 222. A dream vow is taken seriously because the dream may reveal a resolution accepted while awake.

  • R. Ḥayyim Palaggi, Ḥayyim be-Yad 52. One who dreamed of sinning requires no atonement, since sleep itself counts as compulsion.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 53b. Rava holds that there is no compulsion in forbidden unions, since there is no erection without intent, and the Talmud excepts one who is asleep.

  • R. Yosef Ḥayyim, Rav Pe'alim 2, Yoreh De'ah 32. One who dreamed of sinning requires atonement, since the dream may signal an unwitting sin.

  • Sefer Ḥasidim 226. A disturbing dream is a call to examine one's deeds, and a dream fast does not help without repentance.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yabia Omer 10, Yoreh De'ah 58:24. Rejects the proofs of the Rav Pe'alim and rules with R. Palaggi that one who dreamed of sinning requires no atonement.

Images, Illusion, and Idolatry

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 43a-b; Rosh Hashanah 24a-b. The prohibitions of making human forms and likenesses of the angels and of replicating the Temple and its vessels, and Rabban Gamliel's diagrams of the moon.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Beit ha-Beḥirah 7:10. Forbids building a house in the plan of the Temple or making its vessels in their form.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 3:10-11. Forbids making human forms even for decoration and distinguishes raised from sunken forms.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 141:4-7. Codifies the prohibition of human forms and its limits, including the permission of forms made to learn, to understand, and to teach.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 3:2-3. Liability for idolatrous worship depends on the mode of worship proper to each idol, apart from four services forbidden for every idol.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:6 (Sanhedrin 60b); Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 61b. One who accepts an idol as his god is liable, and Rava exempts one who worships out of love or fear without accepting it as a god.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 149a. Forbids gazing at images (diyokna'ot), on the basis of "do not turn to idols" (Leviticus 19:4).

  • Rashi and Tosafot on Shabbat 149a, s.v. ve-diyokna. Rashi applies the prohibition to pictures of people and events; Tosafot limit it to images made for idolatry and permit decorative ones.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 2:2. Forbids reading idolaters' books about their worship, dwelling on it in thought, or gazing at an idol's image, citing Leviticus 19:4 and Deuteronomy 12:30.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 64a; Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 3:5. Worship of an idol in its own mode incurs liability even when intended as disgrace.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 63b; Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 5:10; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 147:1, 4. Forbid mentioning the name of an idol, apart from those named in Scripture.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Yoreh De'ah 2:53. Greek and Roman religion may be taught only as folly, since the idolaters' own books remain forbidden.

  • R. Yitzḥak Schmelkes, Beit Yitzḥak, Yoreh De'ah 1:152; Darkhei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah 147:4. Forbid using the name of a Greek goddess even in writing.

  • R. Yair Ḥayyim Bacharach, Ḥavvot Ya'ir 1. Suggests that the prohibition of mentioning an idol's name applies only while it is still worshipped.

  • R. Yehuda Henkin, Bnei Banim 3:35. The names of gods whose worship has ceased may be mentioned.

  • Sanhedrin 67a-b. Distinguishes the sorcerer who performs an act from one who "holds the eyes," and grades sorcery into capital, forbidden, and permitted acts.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Sanhedrin 67a-b. Whatever is done by natural action falls outside the category of sorcery.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 11:15. One who "holds the eyes" receives a rabbinic flogging.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 179:15. Holding the eyes is forbidden; acts performed through Sefer Yetsirah are permitted.

  • Maimonides, Sefer ha-Mitzvot, negative commandment 32. Holding the eyes includes deception by quickness of hand.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yeḥavveh Da'at 3:68. Forbids a conjurer's sleight of hand at a wedding as holding the eyes.

  • R. Ḥayyim David HaLevi, Aseh Lekha Rav 2:44. The sleight of hand of modern conjurers is not the holding of the eyes that the Torah forbids.

Interpersonal and Monetary Law

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:6. Compensation for humiliation in cases of physical insult such as striking and spitting.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b. The prohibitions of wounding words and of public shaming.

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Mekhirah 22:13; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 212:1. A thing without substance cannot be acquired by sale or gift.

  • Bava Metzia 74a. Acquisition through accepted commercial practice (situmta) where merchants customarily use it.

  • Sanhedrin 24b. Disqualification of the dice player.

  • Avodah Zarah 18b. Theaters and circuses as a "seat of scoffers" that leads to neglect of Torah study.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 307:16. Reading secular tales, war chronicles, and erotic literature is forbidden as a "seat of scoffers" and under "do not turn to idols."

Play and Games

  • Maimonides, Hilkhot Geneivah 1:2; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 348:1; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 61b. Stealing is forbidden even in jest or in order to vex the owner, so that one not habituate oneself to it.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 695:2 and 696:8 (Rema), with Mishnah Berurah 696:31. Snatching and damage done in Purim merriment are exempt, although the Shelah advises the pious to refrain.

  • R. Ḥayyim David HaLevi, Aseh Lekha Rav 6:35. Children's "stealing" of the afikoman is not theft, since the father knows of it and in effect provides it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 46b; Yevamot 63a. One should not habituate a child or oneself to falsehood, as "they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood" (Jeremiah 9:4).

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Ḥoshen Mishpat 2:30. Obtaining examination answers by stealth is deception and actual theft.

Appearance and Reality

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 1:73 and 2:36. The imaginative faculty in Kalam error and in prophecy.

  • R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Sha'ar ha-Yiḥud ve-ha-Emunah 3. The created world as nullified within its divine source.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim, Gate 3, chs. 4-7. The world "from our side" and "from His side," with the commandments bound to the perspective "from our side."

Secondary Sources

Jewish Sources on Games and Simulation

  • Dorff, Elliot, and Joshua Hearshen. "Violent and Defamatory Video Games." Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, EH 21:1.2010. Approved February 4, 2010. Holds that acts in games violate no prohibition of the Torah, yet concludes on grounds of character and holiness that Jews ought not to play violent or defamatory games and bars them from the movement's institutions.

  • Student, Gil. "Video Game Idolatry." Torah Musings, May 8, 2017. Argues that idolatry performed by a game character is not attributed to the player, but raises concerns about exposure and desensitization.

  • Kitzis, Efi. "Online Games: Theft" [Hebrew: משחקי רשת - גניבה]. Kipa, Sha'al et ha-Rav, July 22, 2007. Permits taking items and misleading opponents where a game's rules allow it, but advises against habituating oneself to deceptive dealing in games that simulate commerce.

  • Amichai, Yehuda HaLevi. "Idolatry in Video Games" [Hebrew: עבודה זרה במשחקי וידאו]. Kipa, Sha'al et ha-Rav, November 12, 2022. Forbids a game built on Norse mythology because it lends importance to the gods it depicts even when no one believes in them.

  • Ariel, Shmuel. "Mythology Books in Which Even the Author Does Not Believe". Yeshiva.org.il, Sha'al et ha-Rav. [Hebrew] Permits novels that invent stories about the Greek gods, since no one believes them.

  • Cherlow, Yuval. "Lying in a Game" [Hebrew: שקר במשחק]. Kipa, Sha'al et ha-Rav, October 30, 2023. Holds that bluffing under known rules is not a halakhic lie but advises against games that habituate lying.

  • Dinonline (Beis Hora'a). "Avoda Zara in Video Game." December 31, 2018. Holds that a player's in-game act of devotion to a cult is not idolatry because it is plainly fiction.

  • Lerer, Ḥaggai. "Lying within a Game". Yeshiva.org.il, Sha'al et ha-Rav. [Hebrew] Forbids lying even within a game.

  • Mann, Daniel. "A Harmless Lie?" Ḥemdat Yamim (Eretz Hemdah), Tevet 5782 (December 2021). Treats deception that both sides accept as part of a game as permitted.

  • Melamed, Eliezer. Peninei Halakhah: Emunah u-Mitzvoteha, chs. 13-14 [Hebrew: פניני הלכה: אמונה ומצוותיה]. Permits fantasy literature, watching reenacted rites of defunct cults, and the names of gods no longer worshipped.

  • Melamed, Eliezer. Peninei Halakhah: Likkutim 2, 4:1 [Hebrew: פניני הלכה: ליקוטים ב]. Reports whether taking a friend's object in play is a Torah or a rabbinic prohibition.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Matrix: A Mystical Modern Midrash." Pop Media, vol. 1. Divreinavon, 2009. Reads the first Matrix film through the Zohar and Ramḥal on this world as a "world of falsehood."

  • Navon, Mois. "The Moral Status of Artificial Intelligence: A Jewish Ethical Perspective." PhD diss., Bar-Ilan University, 2023, 220-222. Discusses harm done in virtual worlds and the use of VR to habituate virtue or vice.

Virtual Property in Halakhah

  • Greenhut, Moshe. "The Status of Digital Currencies in Halakhah" [Hebrew: מעמדם של מטבעות דיגיטליים בהלכה]. Teḥumin 44 (5784/2024): 154-167. Holds that digital data are a thing with substance and that digital assets may be acquired by the custom of their trading platform under situmta.

  • Kalmanzon, Avraham. "Inheriting Rights of Use and Ownership in Digital Items" [Hebrew: ירושת זכות שימוש ובעלות בפריטים דיגיטליים]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 298-309. Holds that virtual coins and personal digital accounts are inheritable, subject to the platform's terms of service.

Dreams in Halakhah

  • Melamed, Eliezer. "Guidance and Laws Concerning Dreams" [Hebrew: הדרכות והלכות בחלום]. Peninei Halakhah: Emunah u-Mitzvoteha 27:6. Surveys the dispute over repentance for sins committed in dreams and the use of dreams in halakhic decision.

  • Shochetman, Eliav. "'Dreams Neither Add Nor Detract': Is That So?" [Hebrew: "דברי חלומות לא מעלין ולא מורידין" - האמנם?]. Parashat ha-Shavua 306 (Va-Yeshev 5768/December 2007). Edited by Aviad Hacohen and Michael Wygoda. Argues that the maxim that dreams have no legal effect is not absolute, surveying rulings on bans, vows, and sins in dreams.

Philosophy and Ethics of Virtual Reality

  • Brey, Philip. "The Ethics of Representation and Action in Virtual Reality." Ethics and Information Technology 1 (1999): 5-14.

  • Luck, Morgan. "The Gamer's Dilemma: An Analysis of the Arguments for the Moral Distinction between Virtual Murder and Virtual Paedophilia." Ethics and Information Technology 11 (2009): 31-36. Shows that common arguments fail to separate tolerated from condemned virtual acts.

  • Chalmers, David J. "The Virtual and the Real." Disputatio 9, no. 46 (2017): 309-52. Argues that virtual objects are real digital objects.

  • Chalmers, David J. Reality+: Virtual Worlds and the Problems of Philosophy. New York: W. W. Norton, 2022. Argues that virtual reality is genuine reality and that a meaningful life can be lived in a virtual world.

  • Nozick, Robert. "The Experience Machine." In Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 42-45. New York: Basic Books, 1974. A thought experiment on whether people value experiences or the reality they track.

  • Madary, Michael, and Thomas K. Metzinger. "Real Virtuality: A Code of Ethical Conduct. Recommendations for Good Scientific Practice and the Consumers of VR-Technology." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 3 (2016): 3. Proposes research and consumer protections on the premise that immersion produces lasting psychological change.

  • Benn, Claire. "A New Ethics for Virtual Reality" [Hebrew: אתיקה חדשה עבור המציאות המדומה]. Ha-Zman ha-Zeh, February 2019. Argues that the realism of VR is what makes it ethically significant.

  • Lanier, Jaron. Dawn of the New Everything: Encounters with Reality and Virtual Reality. New York: Henry Holt, 2017. Memoir and argument by a founder of the field on immersion and the self.

Empirical Studies

  • Beyea, David, Rabindra Ratan, Yiming Skylar Lei, Hanjie Liu, Gabriel E. Hales, and Chaeyun Lim. "A New Meta-Analysis of the Proteus Effect: Studies in VR Find Stronger Effect Sizes." PRESENCE: Virtual and Augmented Reality 31 (2022): 189-202. Finds across 56 experiments that users conform to their avatars' characteristics, more strongly with head-mounted displays than with flat screens.

  • Prescott, Anna T., James D. Sargent, and Jay G. Hull. "Metaanalysis of the Relationship between Violent Video Game Play and Physical Aggression over Time." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115, no. 40 (2018): 9882-9888. Finds a small association between violent game play and later physical aggression across 24 prospective studies.

  • Drummond, Aaron, James D. Sauer, and Christopher J. Ferguson. "Do Longitudinal Studies Support Long-Term Relationships between Aggressive Game Play and Youth Aggressive Behaviour? A Meta-analytic Examination." Royal Society Open Science 7, no. 7 (2020): 200373. Finds that the better-designed longitudinal studies show no effect distinguishable from zero.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:26-28; 2:7. The foundational creation narratives establishing tselem Elohim, the mandate to fill and subdue the earth, and divine animation through nishmat ḥayyim.

  • Targum Onkelos on Genesis 2:7. Renders nefesh ḥayyah as ruaḥ memallelah, "a speaking spirit"; influential for the identification of ensouled life with rational speech.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 2:7. Follows Onkelos in identifying the rational soul breathed into Adam with the speaking soul, and cites Rava's mute creature (Sanhedrin 65b) as the rabbis' evidence.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 1:26. Confines creation ex nihilo to the first day; in "let us make man," the earth supplies the body as it did for the animals and God gives the spirit "from the mouth of the Most High."

  • Nahmanides on Exodus 8:15. The magicians could match the plagues of blood and frogs, which involved no new formation, but not the lice, since "none but the Creator, blessed and exalted be He, can perform such an act."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b-67b. Central talmudic discussion of artificial creation, including Rava's golem and the distinction between permitted use of Sefer Yetsirah and prohibited sorcery.

  • Rashi on Sanhedrin 65b, s.v. bara gavra and s.v. ve-lo havah mehadar leih. Identifies the means as Sefer Yetsirah, "the combination of the letters of the Name," and explains the silence as the absence of speech.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 10a and 119b. A judge who judges truly, and one who recites va-yekhulu on Friday evening, are each regarded "as if he became a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of creation."

  • Bava Batra 10a. Turnus Rufus asks why God does not feed the poor Himself; R. Akiva answers that it is so that the givers may be saved through them.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 39:14. "Even if all the dwellers of the world gathered together, they could not create a single gnat and place in it a soul."

  • Kohelet Rabbah 7:13. God shows Adam the trees of Eden and warns him, "take care not to spoil and destroy My world, for if you spoil it there is no one to repair it after you."

  • Sefer Yetsirah 2:5-6. The cosmological-creative text describing formation of reality through permutation of the twenty-two Hebrew letters; foundational for kabbalistic theories of linguistic creation.

  • Maharsha, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Explains that Rava could not create the power of the neshamah, which is speech, so that his creature had only the ruaḥ of life that animals also possess.

  • Maharal of Prague, Tiferet Yisrael, ch. 2. Reads the Tazria exchange as teaching that human action, being the work of a rational being, stands above nature and repairs what nature lacks, with circumcision on the eighth day as the model.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 1:28. Reads ve-khivshuha as a grant of "power and dominion over the earth to do as they wish with the beasts and the creeping things, and to build, and to uproot what is planted, and to quarry copper from its mountains."

  • Nahmanides on Leviticus 19:19. The reason for the prohibition against mixing species is that one who does so "alters and denies the work of creation."

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvot 244 and 62. Gives as the reason for the prohibition on mating species that they should not be mixed "lest their perfection be diminished and He not command His blessing upon them" (244), and for the prohibition on sorcery that God wishes everything to follow the nature set at the beginning of creation, which sorcery "comes to change" (62).

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 1:1; Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesaḥim 4:9. Intellectualist reading of tselem Elohim and defense of the productive sciences against charges of impiety.

  • Meiri on Sanhedrin 67a-b. Classifies Sefer Yetsirah-based creation as natural science rather than prohibited magic.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Halakhic Man; The Lonely Man of Faith. Theology of imitatio Dei as creative capacity, and the distinction between majestic-creative and covenantal-relational dimensions of human existence.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "Confrontation." Tradition 6, no. 2 (Spring-Summer 1964): 5-29. Warns that creative man is often driven by "a demonic urge for power" rather than by the divine mandate.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "Imitating God: The Basis of Jewish Morality." In Reflections of the Rav, adapted by Abraham R. Besdin, 1979. Reads the creation narrative as a charge "that as God created, so should man," a shutaf (partner) in yetsirah who does not create ex nihilo.

Secondary Sources

Creation and Human Ingenuity in Jewish Thought

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: SUNY Press, 1990. Demonstrates that golem creation served primarily as a marker of spiritual achievement and rarely as a practical project.

  • Tirosh-Samuelson, Hava. "Theology of Nature in Sixteenth-Century Italian Jewish Philosophy." Science in Context 10, no. 4 (1997): 529-70. Examines how Renaissance Jewish thinkers integrated natural philosophy with creation theology.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Idea of the Golem." In On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, 158-204. New York: Schocken Books, 1965. A classic study of the religious and symbolic history of the golem.

  • Wurzburger, Walter S. "The Centrality of Creativity in the Thought of Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik." Tradition 30, no. 4 (1996): 219-228. Traces Soloveitchik's reading of tselem Elohim as the capacity to create from R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin's spiritual creativity to his own endorsement of scientific and technological creativity, against Maimonides' intellectualist reading.

  • Wurzburger, Walter S. Covenantal Imperatives: Essays by Walter S. Wurzburger on Jewish Law, Thought, and Community. Edited by Eliezer L. Jacobs and Shalom Carmy. Jerusalem: Urim, 2008. A later version of this essay on creativity and imitatio Dei in R. Soloveitchik's thought, published also in a Festschrift for Norman Lamm.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "What Artificial Intelligence Teaches Us about What It Means to Be Human." Jewish Action, Spring 2023. Lists seven rabbinic readings of tselem Elohim, with creativity among them, and asks which of them AI could share.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge University Press, 2024. Surveys Jewish engagement with artificial humanoid beings from medieval golem literature to contemporary AI.

Creation, Technology, and AI in Jewish Law and Ethics

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Judaism and Gene Design." Tradition 13, no. 2 (1972): 71-80. Early halakhic treatment of genetic modification, distinguishing therapeutic correction from enhancement and redesign and leaving borderline cases to case-by-case judgment.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Survey of Recent Halakhic Periodical Literature: Cloning: Homologous Reproduction and Jewish Law." Tradition 32, no. 3 (1998): 47-86. Halakhic analysis of artificial reproduction, with extensive discussion of golem sources and the limits of human creative prerogative.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Tampering with the Genetic Code of Life: Comparing Secular and Halakhic Ethical Concerns." Ḥakirah 18 (2014): 41-58. Examines whether genetic engineering constitutes impermissible tampering with divine creation or legitimate human creativity, concluding that therapeutic modification falls within the human partnership in creation and restricting only non-medical enhancement.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93, at 63-69. Sets the Meiri's permission of natural creation against R. Asher Weiss's denial, and sorts later authorities into four positions on how much soul a human-made being can carry.

  • Navon, Mois. "'Let Us Make Man in Our Image': A Jewish Ethical Perspective on Creating Conscious Robots." AI and Ethics 4 (2024): 1235-1250. Argues against the creation of conscious beings from the persepctive of Jewish sources.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 2:15. Le-ovdah u-le-shomrah: humanity is placed in Eden "to work it and to guard it" before the curse of toil. Targum Yonatan, Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer ch. 12, Bereshit Rabbah 16:5, and Yalkut Shimoni (Bereshit §22) read the verse as referring to spiritual rather than physical labor. Bereshit Rabbah 16:5 reads it as the Shabbat commandment ("six days you shall labor") and, alternatively, as the sacrificial service, and Yalkut Shimoni §22 gives both readings before the reading as Torah study and the commandments.

  • Saadiah Gaon and Abraham ibn Ezra on Genesis 2:15. Read le-ovdah as physical work, which Saadiah limits to light upkeep such as clearing mud and gathering fruit and Ibn Ezra explains as watering the garden and guarding it from animals.

  • Yalkut Shimoni, Bereshit §20 (on Genesis 2:5). "A person was created only for toil": if he merits, his toil is in Torah, and if not, his toil is in the earth.

  • Genesis 3:17-19. The curse of toil—"by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread"—frames backbreaking labor as a punishment rather than an unqualified good.

  • Leviticus 19:9-10. The laws of pe'ah, leket, and peret: landowners are commanded to leave portions of their produce for the poor and the stranger, building generosity into the productive process itself.

  • Leviticus 25:1-55. The legislation of shemittah (sabbatical year) and yovel (Jubilee): periodic agricultural rest, restoration of ancestral landholdings, and the release of Israelite indentured servants.

  • Deuteronomy 15:1-11. The periodic remission of debts, followed by the command, "You shall not harden your heart or close your hand against your needy brother." The chapter pairs an obligation to lend and give with the realistic concession that "the poor will never cease from the land."

  • Deuteronomy 24:14-15. Requires timely payment of wages, framing labor as a relation of mutual obligation rather than purely economic exchange.

  • Deuteronomy 24:19. A sheaf forgotten in the field (shikheḥah) is left for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.

  • Mishnah Ketubot 5:5. Even a woman who brings many servants into her marriage must still perform some labor. R. Eliezer says idleness leads to licentiousness, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it leads to shi'amum (boredom or mental deterioration). In the Mishnah shi'amum denotes mental deterioration, and boredom is its sense in modern Hebrew.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:3 (with Maimonides' commentary). "A person ought not to occupy oneself in this world except with one of two things: either with wisdom, to perfect oneself through it, or with an occupation that contributes to the maintenance of the world, such as a craft or commerce." The basis for disqualifying gamblers as witnesses and the conceptual basis for evaluating the moral status of occupations. The Vilna Hebrew of the commentary reads "Torah" (בתורה) where this translation has "wisdom," and the commentary ends that one should minimize worldly occupation and increase Torah, citing Avot 4:10.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a. "Greater is one who benefits from the labor of his own hands than one who fears Heaven."

  • Berakhot 35b. "Many followed R. Yishmael [who combined Torah study with productive work] and succeeded; many followed R. Shimon bar Yoḥai [who held that Torah study should displace labor entirely] and did not succeed." A central source for the rabbinic debate over labor and study.

  • Shabbat 30b; Sifrei Devarim §317; Ketubot 111b. The Land of Israel will one day produce "ready-made loaves and fine garments." Maimonides reads this as a figure for the radical lightening of labor in the messianic era. The loaves-and-garments saying is in Shabbat 30b (Rabban Gamliel) and Ketubot 111b (R. Ḥiyya b. Yosef), and Sifrei Devarim §317 has the parallel image of produce that needs no labor, with wheat kernels the size of an ox's kidneys and wine brought home by wagon without toil.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 79:6. On "and he graced the face of the city" (Genesis 33:18): Jacob set up stalls and sold cheaply, "which teaches that a person must show gratitude in a tangible way to a place from which he has derived benefit." The aggadic parallel to the tradition in Shabbat 33b, and a source for economic contribution as an obligation of gratitude.

  • Genesis 31:6-7, 38-41. Jacob's account of twenty years of labor for Laban: he bore losses that were not his to bear, was consumed by heat by day and frost by night, and had his wages changed ten times. The Torah's fullest first-person description of a working life, and the base text for the employee's side of the labor relation.

  • Shabbat 33b. The patriarch Yaakov, on arriving in Shechem (Gen. 33:18), "graced the face of the city" by establishing—depending on the amora—currency, markets, or bathhouses. A paradigm for productive labor as contribution to the yishuv ha-olam.

  • Nedarim 49b. "Great is melakhah, for it honors those who engage in it."

  • Mishnah Avot 2:2. Rabban Gamliel son of R. Yehudah ha-Nasi: "Torah study is good together with a worldly occupation, for the toil of both makes sin forgotten, and all Torah without work will in the end come to nothing and draw sin in its wake."

  • Bava Metzia 30b. R. Yoḥanan: "Jerusalem was destroyed only because they ruled there by Torah law," that is, they based their judgments on the letter of the law and did not act lifnim mi-shurat ha-din.

  • Bava Metzia 83a. When porters broke Rabbah bar bar Ḥanan's barrel of wine, Rav ordered him to return the cloaks he had seized and, when they pleaded poverty and hunger after a day's work, to pay their wages, citing Proverbs 2:20.

  • Bava Batra 21b-22a. Discusses competitive entry and hasagat gevul. The dispute between R. Huna and R. Huna b. R. Yehoshua balances the right to earn a livelihood against the public interest in competition.

  • R. Yosef ibn Migash, novellae on Bava Batra 21b. Holds that the townspeople may bar an outside competitor only where the buyers lose nothing, so that one who sells more cheaply or better may not be barred where the buyers are Jews.

  • Nahmanides, Ḥiddushei ha-Ramban on Bava Batra 22a. Rejects R. Yosef ibn Migash's price exception, since more sellers always lower the price, and allows the townspeople to fix prices or set up a local competitor instead, conceding only goods that differ in kind.

  • Nimukei Yosef on Bava Batra (11a in the Rif's pagination). Confines R. Yosef ibn Migash's exception to a large drop in price and accepts Nahmanides' view for a small one.

  • Sanhedrin 98a, with Rashi ad loc. Among the signs of the approaching redemption: "before those days there was no wage for a person and no wage for the animal." Rashi glosses this as a collapse of earnings, and of the agricultural work done by animals, until the last coin is gone from the purse. A rabbinic picture of economic displacement as a sign of the redemption.

  • Kiddushin 29a-30b. A father is obligated to teach his son a trade (umanut). The Gemara surveys the relative merits of different occupations. The survey of occupations is in Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14 and Kiddushin 82a-b.

  • Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14 (Kiddushin 82a-b). R. Meir advises teaching a son "a clean and easy trade," Abba Gurion lists trades that are "the trade of robbers," R. Shimon ben Elazar holds that humans would be sustained without distress like animals and birds had they not corrupted their deeds, and R. Nehorai would teach his son only Torah, since a craft fails a person in sickness and old age.

  • Arakhin 16b. R. Yoḥanan: "A person should not change his trade or deviate from the trade of his ancestors"—a preference for occupational stability that modern labor markets, and AI-driven churn especially, do not satisfy. R. Yoḥanan derives the rule from Solomon's bringing of Hiram, a coppersmith's son, to do the Temple's copperwork (I Kings 7:13-14).

  • Sanhedrin 99b. "Adam le-amal yulad" (Job 5:7), "man is born to toil," is glossed by the Gemara as amal peh—the labor of the mouth in Torah study.

  • Avot de-Rabbi Natan, ch. 11. Reads le-ovdah u-le-shomrah of Gen. 2:15 as referring to actual labor that even pre-lapsarian Adam was required to perform.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shemittah ve-Yovel 13:13. "Not only the tribe of Levi, but every single person from among all the inhabitants of the world whose spirit moves him… behold, this person has become sanctified as the holy of holies, and God will be his portion and his inheritance forever." Extends the Levitical model of a life outside ordinary participation in the agricultural economy to anyone so inclined.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:10. One who resolves to study Torah without working and to live from charity "has profaned the Name, disgraced the Torah, and extinguished the light of religion."

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Edut 10:4 (with his Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:3). Excludes the habitual gambler from testimony because gambling does not contribute to yishuvo shel olam.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 8:7; 9:1. Material prosperity is the condition that enables spiritual reward, not the reward itself. The messianic age is desired so that we may "sit free to study wisdom and perform the commandments."

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 10:6. The love of God takes hold of a person only when he is constantly engaged in it and abandons everything else, so that he must devote himself to the sciences that make his Creator known.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 2:2. Contemplation of God's works and creatures is the way to the love and fear of God.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Ḥagigah 2:1. Identifies ma'aseh bereshit with natural science and ma'aseh merkavah with divine science.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Melakhim 12:1, 4-5. The messianic era will involve no suspension of the natural order (olam ke-minhago noheg) but will see a world in which "the whole world's occupation will be solely to know God." Halakhah 4 states that the sages desired the messianic age so that they would be free for Torah and its wisdom, and halakhah 5 that there will then be no "jealousy and competition," since good things will be abundant, citing Isaiah 11:9.

  • Maimonides, Introduction to Perek Ḥelek (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10). Reads the talmudic image of "ready-made loaves and fine garments" allegorically: in the messianic era, livelihood will be so easy that a small amount of work yields great benefit.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156:5 (with Rema). Codifies the rules of hasagat gevul, generally permitting a local artisan to compete with an existing artisan while recording qualifications concerning neighborhood residence and outside entrants.

  • Rema, Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156:7. Records that townspeople may not bar outside sellers who sell more cheaply or better goods, provided the buyers are Jews, nor sellers of goods not otherwise available in the town.

  • Pitḥei Teshuvah, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156:3. Cites authorities who treat actions that completely destroy another's livelihood—poseik ḥiyuso le-gamrei—as categorically forbidden. The authorities named are the Masat Binyamin 27, the She'erit Yosef 17, and the Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥoshen Mishpat 118, who applies the protection even where the victim has another trade or is very wealthy.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Ḥoshen Mishpat 1:38. Cited for the prohibition on cutting off another's livelihood entirely.

  • Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:12. R. Yehudah holds that a shopkeeper may not lower his price below the market, and the Sages reply that such a seller is "remembered for good."

  • Arukh ha-Shulḥan, Ḥoshen Mishpat 228:14. Permits underselling only in grain and calls underselling in other merchandise "a complete prohibition," since it corrupts trade and destroys the money of others.

  • R. Asher Weiss, Minḥat Asher, She'elot u-Teshuvot 1:101. Holds that hasagat gevul does not apply to "fundamental changes in the patterns of economy, industry, and development," including supermarkets, automobiles, and computers, while cautioning that all sides must be weighed carefully.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, Moda'ah le-Veit Yisra'el (Breslau, 1859); R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson, ed., Bitul Moda'ah (Lvov, 1859). Opposing pamphlets in the machine-matsah controversy. Kluger objects on grounds of kavvanah and worker displacement, while Nathanson emphasizes consumer benefit and communal welfare provision.

Secondary Sources

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 2): They Took Our Jobs." Shmuel's Substack, March 24, 2026. Discusses technological job displacement through halakhic and theological frameworks. Argues that the total destruction of another's livelihood is forbidden even where competition is permitted, that occupational churn carries a religious cost even if AI creates as many jobs as it destroys, and that the Torah prefers productive work to rent-seeking.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "You Are a Person, First." Shmuel's Substack, July 2, 2026. Argues that Jews bear moral obligations as members of human society beyond what Jewish law specifies, drawing on the Ḥavvot Ya'ir, the Kuzari, and R. Aharon Lichtenstein.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "It's Not (Just) About Jewish Law." Shmuel's Substack, February 24, 2026. Argues that halakhah includes action lifnim mi-shurat ha-din as well as din, citing Bava Metzia 30b and R. Aharon Lichtenstein.

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Unemployment and Mashiach." Torah Musings, September 8, 2025. Argues that AI-driven unemployment supported by a universal basic income could realize the Maimonidean picture of a messianic era freed for the study of wisdom.

  • Weiner, Jason. "AI, Automation & Unemployment: A Jewish Ethical Response to the Future of Work." Tradition Online, July 14, 2026. Discusses the dignity of work and forecasts of AI-driven reductions in demand for labor.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Its section on job displacement (pp. 74-79) collects R. Shlomo Kluger's labor argument against machine matsah with its rebuttals and proposes the dispute between R. Yosef ibn Migash and Nahmanides on outside competitors as the basis for a halakhic analysis of automation.

Jewish Law and Economic Justice

  • Tamari, Meir. With All Your Possessions: Jewish Ethics and Economic Life. New York: Free Press, 1987. Surveys competition, pricing, labor relations, and communal welfare obligations in Jewish economic ethics.

  • Levine, Aaron. Free Enterprise and Jewish Law: Aspects of Jewish Business Ethics. New York: KTAV, 1980. Detailed analysis of the halakhic balance between free enterprise and communal obligation, including extended treatment of the Bava Batra 21b sugya on competitive entry.

  • Levine, Aaron. Economic Public Policy and Jewish Law. Hoboken: KTAV, 1993. Translates halakhic economic reasoning into contemporary policy contexts, including welfare systems, market regulation, and employer obligations.

  • Levine, Aaron. Economics and Jewish Law: Halakhic Perspectives. Hoboken: KTAV and Yeshiva University Press, 1987. Argues (pp. 172-174) that Jewish law favors the gradual introduction of new technology, accepting slower growth to avoid the dislocation of rapid change.

  • Sacks, Jonathan. To Heal a Fractured World: The Ethics of Responsibility. New York: Schocken Books, 2005. Argues that tzedakah is a structural feature of a just society rather than discretionary charity.

  • Dorff, Elliot N. To Do the Right and the Good: A Jewish Approach to Modern Social Ethics. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 2002. Substantial treatment of economic obligations, labor rights, and communal responsibility for the poor.

Machine Matsah and Historical Precedents of Technology-Driven Displacement

  • Katz, Jacob. "The Controversy over Machine-Made Matsah". In Halakhah ve-Kabbalah, 353-73. Jerusalem: Magnes Press, 1984. [Hebrew] Historical study of the machine-matsah controversy and its halakhic, social, and economic dimensions.

  • Hildesheimer, Meir, and Yehoshua Liebermann. "The Controversy Surrounding Machine-Made Matzot: Halakhic, Social, and Economic Repercussions." Hebrew Union College Annual 75 (2004): 193-262. Situates the matsah dispute within broader anxieties about industrialization and rabbinic authority over technological change.

The Dignity of Labor and the Career as Vocation

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. The Lonely Man of Faith. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2012 [orig. 1965]. Develops the distinction between "Adam the first," the creative and world-mastering human being, and "Adam the second," whose dignity is covenantal and relational.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. By His Light: Character and Values in the Service of God. Edited by Reuven Ziegler. Jersey City: KTAV, 2003. Includes a substantive treatment of how a religious person should think about choosing a career: "It is important that a person feel that what he is doing is necessary from the social and collective point of view. This should be a major factor in a person's career choice."

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "Communal Governance, Lay and Rabbinic: An Overview." In Rabbinic and Lay Communal Authority, edited by Suzanne Last Stone. New York: Yeshiva University Press, 2007. Rejects the view that whatever is not explicitly forbidden lies outside rabbinic judgment, citing the sages' statement that Jerusalem was destroyed for ruling by the letter of the law.

  • Dessler, Eliyahu E. Mikhtav me-Eliyahu, vol. I. London, 1955. Reads Berakhot 8a—"greater is one who benefits from the labor of his hands"—as referring specifically to manual labor and the avoidance of receiving more value than one contributes.

  • Lamm, Norman. "A Jewish Ethic of Leisure." In Faith and Doubt: Studies in Traditional Jewish Thought, 184-207. New York: Ktav, 1971. Distinguishes the Hebrew vocabulary for rest, idleness, and leisure and treats the use of free time in an affluent society as a religious problem.

  • Lopiansky, Aharon. Orchos Chaim: Ben Torah for Life. New York: Eshel Publications, 2018. Contemporary musar treatment of work, learning, and the integrated life.

  • Levi, Yehudah (Leo). Torah Study: A Survey of Classic Sources on Timely Issues. Jerusalem and New York: Feldheim, 1990. Surveys traditional sources on the relation between Torah study and productive labor.

  • Levi, Yehudah (Leo). Facing Current Challenges: Essays on Judaism. Jerusalem and Brooklyn: Hemed Books, 1998. Includes related discussions of work and Torah in contemporary society.

AI, Automation, and the Future of Work

  • Danaher, John. Automation and Utopia: Human Flourishing in a World without Work. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2019. Argues that post-work flourishing is achievable only with appropriate institutional redesign.

  • James, Aaron. "Planning for Mass Unemployment: Precautionary Basic Income." In Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, ed. S. Matthew Liao, 183-211. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020. Examines redistributive institutions and alternative structures of meaning in preparation for widespread technological unemployment.

  • Keynes, John Maynard. "Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren." In The Collected Writings of John Maynard Keynes, vol. 9, Essays in Persuasion, 321-32. London: Macmillan, 1972 [orig. 1930]. Keynes' forecast of a fifteen-hour work week.

  • Russell, Bertrand. "In Praise of Idleness." Harper's Magazine 165 (October 1932): 552-59. Argues that modern technology should make shorter working hours and more widely shared leisure possible.

  • Autor, David H. "Why Are There Still So Many Jobs? The History and Future of Workplace Automation." Journal of Economic Perspectives 29, no. 3 (2015): 3-30. Argues that automation has generally complemented labor in aggregate while polarizing the labor market, with wage gains going disproportionately to the top and bottom of the skill distribution.

  • Acemoglu, Daron, and Pascual Restrepo. "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets." Journal of Political Economy 128, no. 6 (2020): 2188-2244. Finds that industrial robots reduced employment and wages in the local labor markets most exposed to them.

  • Brynjolfsson, Erik, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond. "Generative AI at Work." Quarterly Journal of Economics 140, no. 2 (2025): 889-942. Field study of customer-support agents at one firm, finding that AI assistance raised productivity most among the least experienced and lowest-skilled workers.

  • Brynjolfsson, Erik, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen. "Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence." Working paper, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 2025. Descriptive study reporting a relative decline in employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to AI.

  • Eloundou, Tyna, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, and Daniel Rock. "GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs." Science 384, no. 6702 (2024): 1306-1308. Estimates that exposure to large language models is greatest in higher-wage occupations.

  • Moravec, Hans. "When Will Computer Hardware Match the Human Brain?" Journal of Evolution and Technology 1 (1998). Source of the "landscape of human competence" image, in which rising machine capability is a flood that covers the lowlands of arithmetic and rote memorization first and the peaks of locomotion, hand-eye coordination, and social interaction last; expanded in Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind (Oxford University Press, 1999).

  • Frey, Carl Benedikt, and Michael A. Osborne. "The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation?" Technological Forecasting and Social Change 114 (2017): 254-80. Estimated that 47 percent of U.S. employment was in occupations at high risk of computerisation under the paper's model. This was a susceptibility estimate, not a forecast of actual job losses.

  • Arntz, Melanie, Terry Gregory, and Ulrich Zierahn. "The Risk of Automation for Jobs in OECD Countries: A Comparative Analysis." OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers. Paris: OECD, 2016. Estimates by a task-based method that about 9 percent of jobs across OECD countries are automatable and argues that occupation-based estimates overstate the risk.

  • Harari, Yuval Noah. 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. New York: Spiegel & Grau, 2018. Suggests that as AI displaces workers, ultra-Orthodox communities devoted to study may come to be seen as a model for a society in which the search for meaning eclipses the search for a job.

Shabbat, Dignity, and Human Flourishing Apart from Production

  • Heschel, Abraham Joshua. The Sabbath: Its Meaning for Modern Man. New York: Farrar, Straus and Young, 1951. Meditation on Shabbat as a "palace in time."

  • Vallor, Shannon. Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. A virtue-ethics framework for evaluating technological change.

  • Jonas, Hans. The Imperative of Responsibility: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age. University of Chicago Press, 1984. The unprecedented power of modern technology requires a new ethics of responsibility oriented toward the long-term future.

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 6:7. Commands that teachings be repeated to children and discussed throughout daily life, presenting education as sustained relationship and conversation.

  • Deuteronomy 11:19. "And you shall teach them to your children to speak of them," the verse read as addressing the work of teaching to the parent himself.

  • Leviticus 26:3, with Rashi citing the Sifra. "If you walk in My statutes" is read as "that you be toiling in Torah"; the effort of study is itself the commanded act.

  • Proverbs 22:6. "Educate a child according to his way." A foundation for adapting instruction to the learner rather than imposing one method without regard to disposition or development. Malbim and Metzudat David read the verse as requiring instruction matched to the child's own aptitude and capacity, while Rashi reads it as a statement about the lasting imprint of early training, for good or for ill.

  • Pirkei Avot 1:6 and 1:16. Direct the learner to acquire a teacher, emphasizing accountable human guidance in judgment and study.

  • Pirkei Avot 2:5. "An impatient person cannot teach." Treats the teacher's character and responsiveness as part of education rather than an incidental delivery mechanism.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 29a. Lists teaching a child Torah and a trade among the father's obligations, connecting education with both religious formation and practical independence.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 21a. The history of Jewish schooling up to Yehoshua ben Gamla's enactment, and the dispute of Rava and R. Dimi over preferring the prolific or the precise teacher. Rava also fixes the size of a class at twenty-five children, with an assistant paid by the town at forty and a second teacher at fifty.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 19b; Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11. One who teaches another's child Torah is regarded as his parent, and a teacher takes precedence over a father because he brings the student to the world to come. The teacher in question is the one who taught him wisdom, and if the father is himself a sage the father takes precedence.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 40b. "Study is great, for study leads to practice," the ground on which R. Ya'akov Kamenetsky holds that the forms of Torah education may change with the practice they serve.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:3; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 245:4. A father must hire a teacher for his son, and according to R. Moshe Isserles the community may compel him.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7b. States that serving Torah scholars is greater than study alone, a source for the formative knowledge acquired through apprenticeship and relationship. Its direct subject is Torah learning, but the distinction between information and formation also bears on general education.

  • R. Sar Shalom Gaon, Teshuvot Ge'onim Kadmonim (ed. Cassel), no. 46. A teacher in the presence of his student knows what the student understands and what eludes him, which a written answer cannot convey.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:72. "From the mouths of scribes and not from the mouths of books," grounded in what speech conveys and writing loses.

  • Arukh ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 242:21. Now that all of Torah is written, a student's primary teacher is the one from whom he received the way of Torah.

  • R. Moshe of Zurich, glosses on the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, citing R. Isaac of Dampierre; Responsa Shevut Ya'akov 2:64, cited in Pitḥei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah 242. Since knowledge now comes from books, a student is less bound to his teacher's authority, and one qualified to rule should not rule on anything without first consulting a book.

  • Orḥot Ḥayyim, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 24. Quotes the Tosafists of Évreux that since the exile the books and commentaries are the student's teachers, so that the obligations a student owes his teacher lapse and a student may establish his own house of study.

  • Leḥem Mishneh to Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 5:4. Holds that the rule requiring forty years before a student grasps his teacher's reasoning applied when learning came from teachers rather than books, and reports a view that now "the books are the teachers."

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, no. 419. Cautions against burdening a young child with study before he is strong enough to bear it, and requires full commitment to study once his strength has grown.

  • R. Ya'akov Kamenetsky, Emet le-Ya'akov, Shemot, Mishpatim 24. Explains the changing forms of Torah education, including Yehoshua ben Gamla's schools, as adaptations to the needs of each generation.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Education and AI

  • Bashevkin, Dovid, Moshe Koppel, Malka Simkovich, and Tikvah Wiener. "Is AI the Printing Press of the Twenty-First Century?" Jewish Action, Spring 2026. A panel excerpted from an 18Forty summit, in which Wiener discusses differentiated instruction and text-centered discussion in schools.

  • Berger, Michael, Shlomo Einhorn, and CB Neugroschl. "21st Century Chinuch: AI in the Classroom." Panel discussion. The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 52-62. Three Jewish educators on differentiated lesson planning, on tools that offer hints rather than complete solutions, on AI for students with learning differences, and on the effect of AI on the collective experience of ḥavruta study.

  • Schulman, Jason, ed. "Teaching and AI." Roundtable with Robert M. Geraci, Laurie Zoloth, Valerie Bondura, Sarah Rubinson Levy, and Marc Zvi Brettler. AJS Perspectives, Summer 2024: 68-77. Five Jewish studies scholars on teaching with and about generative AI.

  • Student, Gil, and Chavie Kahn. "Can AI Make Better Teachers?" Jewish Action, Spring 2026. An interview with the principal of a school for students with learning differences on AI in lesson preparation and differentiation.

  • Cherlow, Yuval. "Artificial Intelligence as a Study Partner (Ḥavruta)" Hebrew: הבינה המלאכותית כחברותא]. Be-Sheva, Tammuz 5785 (2025); reprinted at [Yeshiva.org.il. Proposes treating AI as a study partner and notes its challenge to assumptions about knowledge, study, and assessment.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "On Raising Children." Torah Musings, May 22, 2015. Treats child-raising as a relationship requiring personal attention, and reports R. Yitsḥak Hutner's view that a parent teaching his own child is the ideal of Torah education.

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. Includes a section on whether Torah knowledge supplied by a brain implant would fulfill the commandment of Torah study.

  • Hollander, Max. "Ameilut in the Age of AI." The Lehrhaus, October 12, 2025. Asks whether the value of toil in Torah study survives AI assistance and relocates ameilut in embodied engagement, self-formation, and the pursuit of genuine novelty.

  • Student, Gil. "Artificial Intelligence Through a Torah Lens: An Interview." Torah Musings, January 2026. Argues that students should learn to use AI as an aid to thought rather than as a substitute for thinking and describes guided approaches to AI-supported Jewish education.

  • Natov, Samantha. "Torah Is the Anti-ChatGPT. But We Can Embrace AI Without Losing Our Soul." Jewish Telegraphic Agency, April 19, 2023. Contrasts efficient information retrieval with the time, presence, and relationship involved in Jewish learning.

Evidence and Policy

  • Bastani, Hamsa, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu, Haosen Ge, Özge Kabakcı, and Rei Mariman. "Generative AI without Guardrails Can Harm Learning: Evidence from High School Mathematics." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122, no. 26 (2025): e2422633122. A field experiment with nearly a thousand students finding that unrestricted GPT-4 access during practice lowered later exam performance.

  • Christian, Brian. The Most Human Human: What Talking with Computers Teaches Us About What It Means to Be Alive. New York: Doubleday, 2011. Uses the Turing test to ask which human capacities are distinctive and which are merely habitual.

  • De Simone, Martin, Federico Tiberti, Maria Barron Rodriguez, Federico Manolio, Wuraola Mosuro, and Eliot Jolomi Dikoru. From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria. Policy Research Working Paper 11125. Washington, DC: World Bank, 2025. A randomized trial of tutoring through a large language model for first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria, reporting a gain of 0.23 standard deviations in English and the largest effects among female students; a working paper, not peer reviewed.

  • Deng, Ruiqi, Maoli Jiang, Xinlu Yu, Yuyan Lu, and Shasha Liu. "Does ChatGPT Enhance Student Learning? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Experimental Studies." Computers & Education 227 (2025): 105224. A meta-analysis of 69 experimental studies reporting improved academic performance and reduced mental effort.

  • Kestin, Greg, Kelly Miller, Anna Klales, Timothy Milbourne, and Gregorio Ponti. "AI Tutoring Outperforms In-Class Active Learning: An RCT Introducing a Novel Research-Based Design in an Authentic Educational Setting." Scientific Reports 15 (2025): article 17458. Reports a randomized crossover study of 194 undergraduate physics students using a custom, scaffolded AI tutor; the design and population limit generalization to ordinary chatbots and younger students.

  • Ma, Wenting, Olusola Adesope, John C. Nesbit, and Qing Liu. "Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis." Journal of Educational Psychology 106, no. 4 (2014): 901-918. Pools 107 effect sizes from 14,321 participants and compares tutoring systems with teacher-led, human-tutored, and textbook instruction.

  • U.S. Department of Education, Office of Educational Technology. Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning: Insights and Recommendations. Washington, DC, 2023. Recommends human oversight, educator control, inspectable and overridable systems, equity review, and education-specific guardrails.

  • UNESCO. Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research. Paris: UNESCO, 2023. Addresses human agency, age-appropriate use, data protection, validation of educational systems, and the need to redesign assessment rather than rely on prohibition or detection alone.

  • UNICEF Innocenti. Guidance on AI and Children, version 3.0. Florence: UNICEF Innocenti, 2025. Sets out ten requirements for child-centered AI, including safety, privacy, non-discrimination, transparency, inclusion, and support for development and well-being.

  • Weidlich, Joshua, Dragan Gašević, Hendrik Drachsler, and Paul A. Kirschner. "ChatGPT in Education: An Effect in Search of a Cause." Journal of Computer Assisted Learning 41, no. 5 (2025). Audits the experiments pooled in a leading ChatGPT meta-analysis and finds that few of them describe the treatment, the control condition, and the measure of learning precisely enough for the reported gains to be credited to the tool.
