Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:28. "Fill the earth and subdue it." The mandate of human dominion over the created world. Link: Sefaria

  • Genesis 2:15. "The Lord God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden, le-ovdah u-le-shomrah, to work it and to guard it." The foundational text for the dual mandate of productive use and conservation; the human role is both to develop the world and to preserve it. Link: Sefaria

  • Targum Yonatan on Genesis 2:15; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 12; Bereshit Rabbah 16:5. Read le-ovdah u-le-shomrah as the study of Torah and the keeping of its commandments (Targum Yonatan, Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer) or as the Shabbat and, alternatively, the sacrificial service (Bereshit Rabbah). Links: Targum Yonatan; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer; Bereshit Rabbah

  • Abraham ibn Ezra on Genesis 2:15. Explains the working of the garden as watering it and the guarding as keeping animals out of it. Link: Sefaria

  • Leviticus 25:23. "The land shall not be sold permanently, for the land is Mine; you are but strangers and sojourners with Me." Establishes that human ownership of natural resources is conditional and custodial, not absolute. Link: Sefaria

  • Numbers 35:2-5. The legislation requiring that Levitical cities be surrounded by a belt of open space (migrash) of specified dimensions. The migrash may not be built upon or cultivated (Rashi; Arakhin 33b), establishing a legal precedent for preserving open land around urban centers as a permanent structural feature of responsible city planning. Link: Sefaria

  • Rashi on Numbers 35:2. Explains the migrash as an open belt around the town "for the beauty of the town" (noy la'ir), on which one may neither build a house, plant a vineyard, nor sow. Link: Sefaria

  • Deuteronomy 20:19-20. "When you besiege a city... you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them; for you may eat of them, and you shall not cut them down. Is the tree of the field a man, that it should be besieged by you?" The source of the prohibition of bal tashḥit, which the rabbis extended from wartime destruction of fruit trees to a comprehensive prohibition against all wanton waste. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a. Ḥoni sees a man planting a carob that will not bear for seventy years and asks whether he expects to live to eat from it; the man answers, "I found a world with carob trees in it; as my forebears planted for me, so I plant for my children." The tradition's compact statement of obligation to people one will never meet, and the text most directly on point for costs and benefits that fall in different generations.

  • Kohelet Rabbah 7:13. "When the Holy One created the first human, He took him and led him past all the trees of the Garden of Eden and said: 'See My works, how beautiful and praiseworthy they are. Everything I have created, I created for you. Pay attention that you do not damage or destroy My world, for if you damage it, there is no one to repair it after you.'" The most explicit midrashic statement of the duty of environmental stewardship and of intergenerational responsibility for the integrity of the created world. Link: Sefaria

  • Mishnah Bava Batra 2:8-9. Rules requiring that tanneries and other noxious industries be distanced at least fifty cubits from a city, with tanneries placed only to its east (R. Akiva: on any side but the west). Establishes the principle that harmful externalities must be controlled through enforceable spatial regulations. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 7b-8a. Discussion of the communal obligation to contribute to shared infrastructure: walls, gates, and a beit sha'ar (gatehouse). Contributions are assessed in proportion to proximity and benefit, establishing a framework for equitable distribution of costs associated with large-scale communal projects. In one version R. Yoḥanan assesses contributions by wealth, in the other by the nearness of the houses. Links: 7b; 8a

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 23a. Rules that there is no acquired right (ḥazakah) to cause harm, which Rav Mari and Rav Zevid apply to smoke and to the odor of a privy. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 91b-92a. Central sugya on the scope of bal tashḥit: establishes that a date palm damaging a grapevine may be removed because the grape is more valuable; discusses whether self-harm violates bal tashḥit; and records the tradition that R. Ḥanina's son died because he cut down a fig tree prematurely, establishing that the prohibition carries not only legal but also spiritual gravity. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 67b, with Rashi. Rav Zutra rules that one who covers an oil lamp or uncovers a naphtha lamp transgresses bal tashḥit; Rashi explains that either act makes the fuel burn faster. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 140b; 129a. Rav Ḥisda holds that one who could eat barley bread and eats wheat bread transgresses bal tashḥit, and the Talmud rejects this because bal tashḥit with respect to one's own body is weightier; Rabbah gives the same reason for burning furniture to warm himself after bloodletting. Links: 140b; 129a

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 74a. The principle that ḥatzi shi'ur (a partial measure of a prohibited act) is forbidden on a Torah level. Applied by the Beit Yitzḥak and the Dovev Meisharim to bal tashḥit: even partial destruction of a fruit tree (cutting branches, not the trunk) falls within the prohibition's scope. Link: Sefaria

  • Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 33b. The ruling that the migrash surrounding Levitical cities may not be converted into either built-up area or agricultural fields. Establishes the permanence of urban green space as a legal requirement, not merely a recommendation. R. Elazar there limits the full rule to the Levitical cities. Link: Sefaria

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shemittah ve-Yovel 13:4-5. Rules that the field, the open land, and the town of a Levitical city may never be converted into one another, "and so in the other cities of Israel." Link: Sefaria

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Melakhim 6:8-10. The comprehensive codification of bal tashḥit, extending the prohibition from trees to all forms of purposeless destruction: breaking vessels, tearing garments, demolishing buildings, stopping up springs, and wasting food. Read alongside Sefer ha-Mitzvot (Negative Commandment 57), where Maimonides classifies all destruction as a Torah-level violation, this raises the question of whether non-arboreal waste is prohibited by Torah law or rabbinic enactment. Link: Sefaria

  • Maimonides, Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Negative Commandment 57. "Anyone who burns a garment for no purpose or breaks a vessel also transgresses lo tashḥit and receives lashes." In tension with Hilkhot Melakhim 6:10 which assigns only rabbinic lashes for non-tree destruction. Link: Sefaria

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shekhenim 10-11. Codification of the laws governing the distancing of harmful activities from residential areas, including specific requirements for the siting of noxious industries and the rights of affected neighbors to demand mitigation. Link: Sefaria

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shekhenim 6:4; 10:4; 11:4-5. The cost of a town wall is collected according to the nearness of each house to the wall; tanneries are placed east of the town because the warm east wind lessens their smell; and the right to object to smoke, privy odor, dust, and ground vibration is never lost through silence. Link: Sefaria

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Precept 529. The rationale for bal tashḥit: "The root of this commandment is known: it is to teach us to love the good and the beneficial and to cling to it, and through this, goodness will cling to us and we will distance ourselves from all that is destructive and damaging." Link: Sefaria

  • Shulḥan Arukh ha-Rav, Ḥoshen Mishpat, Hilkhot Shemirat Guf va-Nefesh u-Val Tashḥit 14-15. Rules that bal tashḥit applies to ownerless property a fortiori; also permits cutting a fruit tree that blocks light from a dwelling, as had the Ḥavvot Ya'ir. Link: Sefaria

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Yoreh De'ah 102. Following the Rosh, permits uprooting vines to build houses only where the gain from cutting clearly exceeds the value of the fruit, and forbids cutting a tree that can be uprooted with its soil and replanted. Link: Sefaria

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Ḥoshen Mishpat 27. Holds that lo tashḥit is a general negative commandment (lav she-bikhlalot) covering many kinds of destruction and carrying no lashes, while the specific prohibition of cutting fruit trees does carry lashes, with reference to Maimonides, Hilkhot Melakhim 6. Link: Sefaria

  • Noda Bi-Yehudah (R. Yeḥezkel Landau), Responsa, Mahadura Tinyana, Yoreh De'ah 10. Understands Maimonides' assignment of makkot mardut for non-tree destruction as indicating a rabbinic prohibition. This reading, shared by the Ḥayyei Adam (11:32) and the Mahari Bassan (101), is challenged by R. Asher Weiss's analysis. Link: Sefaria

  • Beit Yitzḥak (R. Yitzḥak Schmelkes), Yoreh De'ah 1:142; Dovev Meisharim 2:42. Argue that partial destruction of a fruit tree violates bal tashḥit under the principle of ḥatzi shi'ur. The Beit Yitzḥak, on cutting a fruit-bearing branch, holds that one who destroys part of a tree is like one who destroys all of it; the Dovev Meisharim holds that partial destruction is biblically forbidden but carries no lashes. Links: Beit Yitzḥak (Google Books); Dovev Meisharim (Google Books)

  • R. Avraham Yitzḥak haKohen Kook, "Ḥazon ha-Tsimḥonut ve-ha-Shalom" (Jerusalem, 1961). General discussion of humankind's relationship with the natural world. English translation by Jonathan Rubenstein, A Vision of Vegetarianism and Peace: Internet Archive

  • R. Samson Raphael Hirsch, Commentary on Leviticus 25:34 and Numbers 35:2-5. Extended analysis of the Levitical city legislation as a model for responsible urban planning. On Leviticus 25:34 he holds that "no present moment has the sole disposition" of the town's open land, which must be handed on to the future as it was received, and applies the rule to every city in the Land of Israel. Links: Leviticus 25:34; Numbers 35:5

  • Rosh (R. Asher b. Yeḥiel), Bava Kamma 8:15. Rules that one may cut down a fruit tree if one needs the location for building.

  • R. Ya'ir Ḥayyim Bacharach, Ḥavvot Ya'ir 195. Permits cutting a fruit tree when it blocks light from a dwelling, extending the Rosh's leniency to include diminished amenity.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Environmental Ethics

  • Tirosh-Samuelson, Hava, ed. Judaism and Ecology: Created World and Revealed Word. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2002. Comprehensive collection examining the ecological dimensions of Jewish thought from biblical through contemporary periods. Link: Google Books

  • Benstein, Jeremy. The Way Into Judaism and the Environment. Woodstock, VT: Jewish Lights Publishing, 2006. Accessible introduction to Jewish environmental ethics drawing on biblical, rabbinic, and contemporary sources. Link: Google Books

  • Vogel, David. "How Green Is Judaism? Exploring Jewish Environmental Ethics." Business Ethics Quarterly 11, no. 2 (2001): 349-63. Critical assessment arguing that the tradition does not straightforwardly yield a modern environmental ethic without significant interpretive work. Link: Cambridge Core

  • Lamm, Norman. "Ecology in Jewish Law and Theology." In Faith and Doubt: Studies in Traditional Jewish Thought, 162-85. New York: KTAV, 1971. Early and influential Orthodox rabbinic engagement with environmental ethics. Link: Google Books

  • Sacks, Jonathan. "Environmental Responsibility." Covenant & Conversation, Shoftim 5775, August 22, 2015. Reads the rabbinic extension of bal tashḥit as part of the Torah's concern with sustainability and reads Genesis 2:15 as making man a servant and guardian of nature as well as its master.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "To Cultivate and to Guard: The Universal Duties of Mankind." In By His Light: Character and Values in the Service of God, edited by Reuven Ziegler, ch. 1. Jersey City: Ktav, 2003. Reads le-shomrah as a largely conservative mandate and le-ovdah as an essentially creative one.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 2): They Took Our Jobs." Shmuel's Substack, March 24, 2026. Discusses technological job displacement and surveys the readings of Genesis 2:15 as physical labor or as Torah study and the commandments.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 3): The End of the World." Shmuel's Substack, October 16, 2026. Treats the confidence of many Orthodox Jews that God will protect the environment as a failure of hishtadlut and surveys the rabbinic dispute over the scope of God's promise to Noah.

  • Nishma Research and Meisharim (Mark Trencher and Barry Kornblau). American Orthodox Jewry, Climate Change, and Other Environmental Issues: Religion, Science, and Politics. July 2025. Survey of American Orthodox Jews (June 2024) reporting that 70 percent agree entirely or mostly that humanity can rely on God to protect the environment and that fewer affirm stewardship of the earth as a religious value than do other religious Americans.

Bal Tashḥit and Halakhic Environmental Regulation

  • Weiss, R. Asher (Minḥat Asher). "Lo Tashchit Et Etzah" [Heb.] (5770 [2009/10]; posted online August 14, 2013). Comprehensive halakhic analysis resolving the apparent contradiction in the Rambam and addressing ḥatzi shi'ur, ownerless property, and permissible grounds for cutting. Essential for rigorous halakhic treatment of environmental destruction.

  • Hirsch, Samson Raphael. Horeb: A Philosophy of Jewish Laws and Observances. Translated by I. Grunfeld. London: Soncino Press, 1962. Influential treatment of bal tashḥit (§56) as part of a broader ethic of responsible use.

  • Rakover, Nahum. "Environmental Protection in Jewish Sources." [Heb.] Tehumin 13 (1993): 301-15. Survey of rabbinic sources relevant to environmental regulation, including the Talmudic zoning laws of Bava Batra.

  • Rakover, Naḥum. Environmental Protection: A Jewish Perspective. Israel: Institute of the World Jewish Congress, 1996. Collection and analysis of relevant Jewish sources on the values and parameters of environmentalism.

AI Energy Consumption and Environmental Impact

  • International Energy Agency. Key Questions on Energy and AI. Paris: IEA, 2026. Reports that data-center electricity demand rose 17 percent in 2025 and projects that total data-center consumption will double by 2030, with AI-focused consumption tripling. IEA

  • Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report. Report LBNL-2001637. Berkeley, CA: LBNL, 2024. Documents the tripling of U.S. data center electricity use from ~60 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023 and projects 325-580 TWh (6.7-12 percent of U.S. electricity) by 2028.

  • International Energy Agency. Electricity 2024: Analysis and Forecast to 2026. Paris: IEA, 2024. Projects global data center electricity use could exceed 1,000 TWh by 2026. The figure was the high end of a range that included cryptocurrency, and it is superseded by the IEA's later estimates of about 415 TWh in 2024 and 485 TWh in 2025, with about 950 TWh projected for 2030 (IEA 2026). Link: ManagEnergy record

  • Ho, Anson, Yafah Edelman, Josh You, and Jean-Stanislas Denain. "Is Almost Everyone Wrong About America's AI Power Problem?" Gradient Updates (Epoch AI), December 17, 2025. Analysis arguing the power supply challenge is more tractable than assumed; valuable quantitative framework but does not address emissions, water, or localized burdens. Link: Epoch AI

  • Li, Pengfei, Jianyi Yang, Mohammad A. Islam, and Shaolei Ren. "Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models." Communications of the ACM 68, no. 7 (2025): 54-61. Methodology for estimating AI's total water footprint including operational and embodied water.

  • Tomlinson, Bill, et al. "The Carbon Emissions of Writing and Illustrating Are Lower for AI than for Humans." Scientific Reports 14 (2024): 3732. Per-task comparison finding AI produces far less CO2 per page than humans; does not account for the rebound effect or novel demand.

  • Deb, Sopan. "Saying 'Thank You' to ChatGPT Is Costly. But Maybe It's Worth the Price." The New York Times, April 24, 2025. On the aggregate energy cost of conversational politeness toward chatbots, and the competing claim that the habit is worth its price for the user's own character.

  • O'Donnell, James, and Casey Crownhart. "We Did the Math on AI's Energy Footprint. Here's the Story You Haven't Heard." MIT Technology Review, May 20, 2025. Independent measurement of per-query energy consumption of open-source models across multiple models; finds significant variation by model size and query type. Link: MIT Technology Review

  • Rolnick, David, et al. "Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning." ACM Computing Surveys 55, no. 2 (2022): 1-96. The standard survey of machine-learning applications for climate mitigation and adaptation across energy, transport, industry, and land use.

  • Strubell, Emma, Ananya Ganesh, and Andrew McCallum. "Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP." Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the ACL (2019): 3645-50. Foundational study quantifying energy costs of training large neural networks. Link: ACL Anthology

  • Luccioni, Alexandra Sasha, Emma Strubell, and Kate Crawford. "From Efficiency Gains to Rebound Effects: The Problem of Jevons' Paradox in AI's Polarized Environmental Debate." In Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 76-88. New York: ACM, 2025. Argues that efficiency gains in AI may spur increased consumption, so that improved technical efficiency alone does not ensure a net reduction in environmental harm.

  • Altman, Sam. "The Gentle Singularity." Blog post, June 2025. Includes a self-reported estimate of the average energy and water consumed by a single ChatGPT query.

  • Google. Measuring the Environmental Impact of Delivering AI at Google Scale. Technical report by Elsworth et al., August 2025. arXiv:2508.15734. Self-reported per-prompt estimates of energy, emissions, and water use for the Gemini system.

Urban Planning, Infrastructure, and Environmental Justice

  • Sacks, Jonathan. To Heal a Fractured World: The Ethics of Responsibility. New York: Schocken Books, 2005. Jewish ethic of collective responsibility with implications for environmental stewardship.

  • Crawford, Kate, and Vladan Joler. "Anatomy of an AI System: The Amazon Echo as an Anatomical Map of Human Labor, Data, and Planetary Resources." AI Now Institute, September 2018. Mapping of the full material supply chain behind a single AI device. Link: Anatomy of an AI System

  • Lepri, Bruno, Nuria Oliver, Emmanuel Letouzé, Alex Pentland, and Patrick Vinck. "Fair, Transparent, and Accountable Algorithmic Decision-Making Processes." Philosophy & Technology 31, no. 4 (2018): 611-27. Framework for algorithmic accountability applicable to environmental impact disclosures.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 8:21-22; 9:8-17. After the flood, God vows never again to destroy all flesh and establishes the covenant of the rainbow with Noah and every living creature.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 34:6; 49:9. Noah refuses to leave the ark until God swears not to bring another flood; Abraham argues at Sodom that a flood of fire would also violate the oath.

  • Tosefta Ta'anit 2:13, with Saul Lieberman, Tosefta Ki-Fshutah ad loc. R. Meir, R. Yehudah, and R. Yose each limit the post-flood oath differently, admitting respectively a flood of fire, the deaths of individuals, and a plague on the nations; Lieberman records the variant attributions in the manuscripts.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Zevaḥim 116a; Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Yitro (Amalek 3). Bilaam assures the kings of the nations, alarmed at the giving of the Torah, that God has sworn not to destroy the world by a flood of water or of fire.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 11a. Pharaoh's advisers drown the Israelite infants on the reasoning that God swore not to bring a flood; the Talmud answers that the oath covers the whole world and not one nation, or that God does not bring the flood but the Egyptians "come and fall into it."

  • Or ha-Ḥayyim on Genesis 9:11. Concludes from Zevaḥim 116a and Bereshit Rabbah 49:9 that God's oath covers every catastrophe that would destroy the world, by water or by fire, so that the world may be secure.

  • Maharsha, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Zevaḥim 116a and on Sotah 11a. Holds that God swore by the waters of Noah not to destroy the whole world by any means, fire included, while a single nation may still be destroyed.

  • Abarbanel on Genesis 9:1. Reads the laws of bloodshed given after the flood as God's answer to the fear of Noah's sons that they would kill one another and perish from the earth with no one to judge them.

  • Isaiah 54:9-10. Compares God's oath to Israel with the oath of Noah, and declares that the mountains may move but God's covenant of peace with Israel will not.

  • Jeremiah 30:11 (= 46:28); 31:35-36; Malachi 3:6, with Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 9a; Leviticus 26:44, with Megillah 11a. God will make an end of the nations but not of Israel, whose survival is tied to the fixed order of the heavens; Megillah 11a reads Leviticus 26:44 as a list of eras in which God raised up those who saved the nation.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 17:1; Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:32-34. Nahmanides holds that the covenant with Abraham places his descendants under God's direct governance and not under the rule of the stars; the Kuzari treats Israel's covenantal endurance among the nations.

  • R. Yitsḥak Hutner, Paḥad Yitsḥak, Ḥanukkah, ma'amar 9. Contrasts the covenant with Noah, which preserves existing reality equally in every generation, with the covenant of Abraham, a promise of renewal whose force is revealed in some generations and concealed in others.

  • Maimonides, Iggeret Teiman. Rejects an astrologer's forecast of a flood of air and dust because it treats the flood as a natural event and not a divine judgment, and holds, citing Malachi 3:6, that the Jewish people cannot perish.

  • Genesis 11:1-9. The tower of Babel joins technological coordination, concentrated power, and failed human self-understanding.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 108b; 109a; Bereshit Rabbah 38:6. The generation of the flood claims it can defeat a flood of water or fire by technical means, and the builders of Babel plan to strike the firmament with axes so that its waters drain, or to build supports against its collapse.

  • Leviticus 19:16; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 73a. The duty not to stand idly by another's blood and to rescue persons in danger.

  • Deuteronomy 22:8; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 15b. The parapet obligation and the prohibition against maintaining a dangerous condition; Bava Kamma 15b extends this to keeping a vicious dog or an unstable ladder.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4. One who sends fire by the hand of a deaf-mute, a person lacking mental competence, or a minor is exempt in a human court but liable by the laws of Heaven.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 83a-85b. Preservation of life under uncertainty overrides Shabbat and nearly all other prohibitions.

  • Kohelet Rabbah 7:13. God warns Adam that if he ruins the world, "there is no one to repair it after you."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 53a-b. When David dug the foundations of the Temple, the deep rose and threatened to flood the world until he cast a sherd inscribed with the divine name into it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b. R. Akiva brings the news of the ban to R. Eliezer himself, lest an unsuitable messenger tell him and he "destroy the entire world."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 17a; Sanhedrin 103a. God sought to return the world to tohu va-vohu (formlessness and void) on account of Jehoiakim and again on account of Zedekiah's generation, and relented on considering the righteous generation of the one and the righteous king of the other.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 4b-5a; Ta'anit 18b. Death before the allotted time; God's "many bears and lions" as alternative agents of decreed death.

  • Rabbenu Ḥananel on Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 5a. Explains "there is one who is swept away without judgment" as a person whom another person kills.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot VI:6; Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed III:17. The appointed span of life as subject to addition and subtraction; individual providence for humans, species-level providence for animals.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot IV:5 (Leipzig 1864 numbering). Holds that death is God's act and killing the wrongdoer's, so that if divine wisdom required a person's death and the killer had not acted, the victim would have died by another cause.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:4; 6:5. God willed that human actions be left to human choice; those who carried out the decree of Egyptian bondage remain culpable because no particular person was decreed to carry it out.

  • Baḥya ibn Pakuda, Ḥovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Bitaḥon 3-4; Or ha-Ḥayyim on Genesis 37:21; Nahmanides on Genesis 15:14. Whether a free agent can harm someone not decreed to suffer: Baḥya holds that no creature can harm another, or itself, without God's permission; Or ha-Ḥayyim that a person, unlike a beast, can kill one not liable to death; Nahmanides that a killer is culpable even when his victim was decreed to die.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 30a. "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except tsinnim paḥim"; harms of self-exposure fall outside the guarantee of providence.

  • Rashi and Tosafot on Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 30a; Shabbat 32a. Rashi explains that cold and heat are excepted because they sometimes come through negligence; Tosafot link the passage to the rule that a person should never stand in a place of danger.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotseaḥ u-Shemirat ha-Nefesh 11:4. Codifies the duty to remove any potentially lethal obstacle.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:2, with Avodat ha-Melekh ad loc. A world whose sins outweigh its merits is immediately destroyed; the Avodat ha-Melekh traces the aggadic dispute over whether God's post-flood oath was limited to a water-flood (Sotah 11a; Sanhedrin 103a; Arakhin 17a; cf. Zevaḥim 116a; Mekhilta, Yitro).

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:4. Each person should regard himself and the whole world as evenly balanced between merit and guilt, so that a single deed can tip the world toward destruction or toward deliverance.

  • R. Naḥum Asch, Tsiyunei Maharan on Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:2. Collects the talmudic and midrashic sources on both sides of the dispute over the post-flood oath and reports a later-printed responsum that proposed emending Zevaḥim 116a in light of the Mekhilta.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed II:27-29. Holds that belief in the universe's eventual destruction is not a principle of the faith and that no prophet or sage has announced it.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi, responsum no. 93; R. Jacob Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Ḥakham Tsvi mentions the testimony that R. Eliyahu Ba'al Shem of Chełm made a golem; Emden adds, as heard from his father, that R. Eliyahu destroyed it as it kept growing, for fear it would destroy the world.

  • R. Jacob Ettlinger, Binyan Zion ha-Ḥadashot, nos. 145-146. Holds that God's post-flood promise precludes only destruction by floodwaters, not other means.

  • Mishnah Avot 2:1. Directs attention to the consequences of action, a compact source for prospective responsibility.

  • Psalms 116:6; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 129b; Yevamot 72a. The principle of shomer peta'im Hashem, the talmudic basis for permitting customary activities that carry small, socially accepted risks.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Ḥoshen Mishpat 2:76. Permits one who already smokes to continue, citing Psalms 116:6 for a small and widely accepted risk, while discouraging beginning.

Secondary Sources

AI Risk and Governance

  • Bostrom, Nick. Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014. Influential statement of the control problem and long-term catastrophic risk.

  • Yudkowsky, Eliezer, and Nate Soares. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All. New York: Little, Brown and Company, 2025. A forceful statement of the case that misaligned superintelligence poses an unacceptable extinction risk.

  • Kulveit, Jan, Raymond Douglas, Nora Ammann, Deger Turan, David Krueger, and David Duvenaud. "Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development." arXiv, 2025. Argues that incremental delegation of economic, cultural, and state functions to AI could erode human influence irreversibly without any discrete takeover event.

  • International AI Safety Report. International AI Safety Report 2026. 2026. International expert assessment separating evidence, uncertainty, capability trends, and risk-management gaps.

  • Grace, Katja, John Salvatier, Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, and Owain Evans. "Viewpoint: When Will AI Exceed Human Performance? Evidence from AI Experts." Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 62 (2018): 729-54. Survey of machine-learning researchers on timelines for AI milestones, whose median respondent gave a 5 percent probability to extremely bad outcomes such as human extinction.

  • Grace, Katja, Julia Fabienne Sandkühler, Harlan Stewart, Ben Weinstein-Raun, Stephen Thomas, Zach Stein-Perlman, John Salvatier, Jan Brauner, and Richard C. Korzekwa. "Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI." Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 84 (2025). Survey of 2,778 AI researchers in October 2023 on AI milestones and on the probability of extremely bad outcomes, including human extinction.

  • Altman, Sam. "Planning for AGI and Beyond." OpenAI, February 24, 2023. A developer's argument that stopping AI development is neither possible nor desirable and that a gradual transition to AGI is preferable to a sudden one.

  • Zwetsloot, Remco, and Allan Dafoe. "Thinking About Risks From AI: Accidents, Misuse and Structure." Lawfare, February 11, 2019. Distinguishes failure, deliberate misuse, and structural risks rather than reducing danger to hostile autonomous systems.

  • Christian, Brian. The Alignment Problem: Machine Learning and Human Values. New York: W. W. Norton, 2020. Surveys the technical and ethical difficulty of making machine-learning systems act in accordance with human values.

  • Mitchell, Melanie. "Why AI Is Harder Than We Think." arXiv:2104.12871 (2021). Identifies recurring fallacies in forecasts of near-term general intelligence.

  • Narayanan, Arvind, and Sayash Kapoor. AI Snake Oil: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2024. Argues that AI is not an existential threat and that arguments for doom distract from documented harms.

  • Narayanan, Arvind, and Sayash Kapoor. "AI as Normal Technology: An Alternative to the Vision of AI as a Potential Superintelligence." Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, April 15, 2025. Treats AI as a normal technology whose diffusion and risks are shaped by institutions, and judges catastrophic misalignment the most speculative of the risks it discusses.

Jewish Views on Technology, Responsibility, and Eschatology

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. Illuminating Jewish Thought, vol. 2: Explorations of Free Will, the Afterlife, and the Messianic Era. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2018. Surveys the dispute over whether free choice can harm the undeserving and classical sources on Jewish views of the end times.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 3): The End of the World." Shmuel's Substack, October 16, 2026. Surveys the rabbinic dispute over whether the post-flood oath precludes human extinction, the sources on self-inflicted harm, the 1962 debate on nuclear war, and halakhic analogues for AI misuse, misalignment, and carelessness.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "What, to a Jew, is the End of the World?" Shmuel's Substack, October 25, 2026. Contrasts the Noahide covenant, which preserves the natural order, with the covenant of Abraham as a relationship guaranteeing Jewish survival, and reads Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:4 as the prescribed response to the danger of universal destruction.

  • Lamm, Maurice. "'Red or Dead?' An Attempt at Formulating a Jewish Attitude." Tradition 4, no. 2 (Spring 1962): 165-97. An early attempt to bring halakhic sources to bear on nuclear war, arguing that the defense of values may justify accepting catastrophic risk.

  • Jakobovits, Immanuel, and Michael Wyschogrod. "Rejoinders." Tradition 4, no. 2 (Spring 1962): 198-209. Replies to Maurice Lamm holding that halakhic rulings on war and martyrdom, which concern the loss of part of a people, may not guide decisions that risk all of humanity.

  • Lamm, Norman. "Religion in a Technological Society." Address, February 25, 1960. Lamm Legacy. Names "the threat of runaway technology" as the problem of the age and reads the charge to Adam to work and guard the garden as a call for morally guided progress.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The Ethics of Safety." Sermon, Ki Tetse, September 9, 1962. Lamm Legacy. Reads the parapet commandment as a general principle of public safety whose demands grow with the height of the risk, applied to thalidomide and the hydrogen bomb.

  • Lamm, Norman. "The View from the Brink." Sermon, Toledot, December 1, 1962. Lamm Legacy. Delivered after the Cuban missile crisis, contrasting Isaac's and Esau's responses to the prospect of death as models for living under the threat of universal destruction.

  • Berkovits, Eliezer. Faith after the Holocaust. New York: KTAV, 1973. Argues that nuclear weapons have made the pursuit of power self-defeating, so that the bomb's message is "make peace or perish."

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "The Rabbis and the Bomb Maker: Are Jewish Views on AI Reaching Jews Working on AI?" Jello Menorah, September 28, 2026. Uses a 1991 collection of Jewish reflections on weapons of mass destruction, and Edward Teller's realist essay in it, to ask whether Jewish thought on AI reaches Jewish engineers.

  • Sacks, Jonathan. "Faith and Fate: The Lambeth Conference Address." July 2008. Lecture on the relationship between God's covenant and human responsibility.

  • Nishma Research and Meisharim (Mark Trencher and Barry Kornblau). American Orthodox Jewry, Climate Change, and Other Environmental Issues: Religion, Science, and Politics. July 2025. Survey of American Orthodox Jews (June 2024) reporting that 70 percent agree entirely or mostly that humanity can rely on God to protect the environment, with God's promise to Noah among the reasons given.

Golem Stories as Existential Fears

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: SUNY Press, 1990. The definitive scholarly study of the golem traditions, including the medieval legend in which the golem made by Jeremiah and Ben Sira erases the alef of emet and warns its makers to study the powers of creation without using them.

  • Gelbin, Cathy S. The Golem Returns: From German Romantic Literature to Global Jewish Culture, 1808-2008. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 2011. Traces the modern literary golem and its loss-of-control motif.

  • Wiener, Norbert. God and Golem, Inc.: A Comment on Certain Points Where Cybernetics Impinges on Religion. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1964. Borrows the golem for its title and frame in discussing machines that learn and reproduce themselves, though the Jewish golem has a minimal part in the book.

  • Cave, Stephen, Kanta Dihal, and Sarah Dillon, eds. AI Narratives: A History of Imaginative Thinking about Intelligent Machines. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020. The loss-of-control motif across fiction, including narratives relating to the golem, Frankenstein, and robots.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Golem of Prague and the Golem of Rehovoth." Commentary 41, no. 1 (January 1966): 62-65. Reflects on the golem legend as a parable of human creative power and its dangers applied explicitly to computers.

  • Rubin, Charles T. "The Golem and the Limits of Artifice: On What the Jewish Legend Can (and Cannot) Teach Us About Bioethics." The New Atlantis 39 (2013): 56-72. Argues that the loss-of-control framing of the golem is mostly a modern literary development and warns against extracting easy lessons from it.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. Golems Among Us: How a Jewish Legend Can Help Us Navigate the Biotech Century. Chicago: Ivan R. Dee, 2004. Uses the golem tradition to emphasize creator responsibility and safeguards.

  • Rosen, Michael M. Like Silicon from Clay: What Ancient Jewish Wisdom Can Teach Us About AI. Washington, DC: AEI Press, 2025. Applies golem traditions and halakhic reasoning to AI policy, including liability, foreseeable harm, and the duty to prevent destructive outcomes.

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 30:19. "Choose life"; the biblical foundation of moral choice.

  • Mishnah Avot 3:15; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33b. Foreknowledge beside freedom; everything in Heaven's hands except the fear of Heaven.

  • Judah Loew ben Bezalel (Maharal), Derekh Ḥayyim 3:15. Explains that humans were given choice because they are in God's image, whereas angels lack choice and do not change their mission, and beasts act by nature.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 16b. Natural endowments fixed at conception; righteousness and wickedness left open.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88b-89a. Moses answers the angels' objection to giving the Torah to humans by asking whether they have envy or an evil inclination, which the commandments presuppose.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 48:11; 50:2; 50:9; 68:12. The evil inclination has no power over angels, one angel does not carry out two missions, and the angels sent to Sodom were banished from their station for 138 years.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 10b. Rav Sama limits the rule that there is no agency for a transgression to an agent who can choose whether to act, and holds the principal liable where the intermediary, like a courtyard, has no choice.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Repentance 5:1-4; Eight Chapters 8. Free will as the pillar of Torah; deterministic readings of Scripture as exceptional punishments.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Repentance 7:1. Since every person has free will, each should strive to repent.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:3; Guide of the Perplexed II:7. Angels are form without matter; the spheres and separate intellects have will and choice in what is entrusted to them, though not like human choice, and always do the good.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:1. Identifies the image (tselem) in which humans were created with intellectual apprehension.

  • Sforno on Genesis 1:26-27; Meshekh Ḥokhmah on Genesis 1:26; Malbim on Genesis 1:26. Sforno identifies the image with eternal intellect and the likeness with elective action, which the heavenly retinue lacks; Meshekh Ḥokhmah and Malbim identify the image itself with free choice, and Malbim contrasts it with angels, who are not free.

  • R. Samson Raphael Hirsch on Genesis 1:26. Describes the human as charged with realizing the likeness of God through free-willed and independent energy.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 2:9. Da'at glossed as will; the tree of knowledge as a tree of volition. Before the sin the first human acted by nature, like the heavenly hosts, and gained choice after eating from the tree.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 1:26; Deuteronomy 30:6. The image as a double likeness, of the body to the earth and the spirit to the upper beings; choice holds from creation so that there may be merit, and in the messianic era choosing the good becomes human nature, as before Adam's sin.

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot IV:4. God does not compel human acts toward obedience or rebellion, and each person perceives in himself that he can speak or keep silent.

  • Gersonides, commentary on Genesis 2-3 (Sefaria, Ralbag on Torah, Genesis 2:4:3; Venice 1547, 16a). Choice follows necessarily from intellect, so that the higher intellects choose but always choose the good, while the human compound of matter and form yields opposed choices.

  • Crescas, Or Hashem II:5. Causal determination of choice; responsibility attached to inner assent and experience. Chapter 3 places will and choice where the agent feels no compulsion, and chapter 5 derives reward and punishment from the joy that accompanies the act.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim IV:1, 5. Rejects the view that human acts are necessary with respect to their causes though possible in themselves, which would make every act decreed and uproot the roots of the Torah.

  • Ramḥal, Derekh Hashem I:2-3; Da'at Tevunot §§18, 42-44, 158. Derekh Hashem makes choice the means by which the recipient of divine good earns it; Da'at Tevunot sets choice and reward aside as the final purpose of creation in favor of the revelation of divine unity, and holds that among creatures only humans are masters of their acts.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Philosophy and Theology of Free Will

  • Freedom and Moral Responsibility: General and Jewish Perspectives, edited by Charles H. Manekin and Menachem M. Kellner, Bethesda: University Press of Maryland, 1997.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Free Will and Determinism." In With Perfect Faith: The Foundations of Jewish Belief, edited by J. David Bleich, 415-478. New York: KTAV, 1983. Survey of classical positions from Saadia through the Aḥaronim.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. Illuminating Jewish Thought: Explorations of Free Will, the Afterlife, and the Messianic Era. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2018. Systematic survey of the classical free-will debates, including the scope of free will against providence.

  • Segal, Aaron. "Crescas, Hard Determinism, and the Need for a Torah." Faith and Philosophy 40, no. 1 (2023): 70-89. Reads Crescas as a hard determinist who holds that no one deserves reward or punishment for what one does.

Moral Agency and Machines

  • Sparrow, Robert. "Why Machines Cannot Be Moral." AI & Society 36, no. 3 (2021): 685-693. Moral agency requires capacities machines lack.

  • Johnson, Deborah G., and Keith W. Miller. "Un-Making Artificial Moral Agents." Ethics and Information Technology 10, nos. 2-3 (2008): 123-133. Responsibility attaches to designers and users, not artifacts.

  • Wallach, Wendell, and Colin Allen. Moral Machines: Teaching Robots Right from Wrong. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009. The gap between programmed behavior and moral agency.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Responsum, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. AI systems as nonagents in halakhah.

Jewish Perspectives on AI and Alignment

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024. Surveys Jewish frameworks for AI, including moral agency and a gradient of angels, demons, humanoid creatures, and golems, and argues that no single criterion defines the human.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93, at 70-72. Infers from Gersonides' derivation of choice from intellect that a true artificial general intelligence would have free will, and asks whether a material AI would resemble humans or the higher intellects.

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024): 221-241. Free will among the features of human ontology dependent on consciousness.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Human status criteria presupposing deliberative freedom.

↑ Return to top

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 18:9-22. The foundational text distinguishing legitimate prophecy from illegitimate divination. Prohibits a comprehensive list of divinatory practices (kosem kesamim, me'onen, menaḥesh, mekhashef, ḥover ḥaver, sho'el ov, yidde'oni, doresh el ha-metim) and establishes prophecy as the legitimate alternative. Verses 21-22 make the fulfillment of a prophet's predictions the test of his authority.

  • Proverbs 19:21; 21:1. Wisdom literature's articulation of the relationship between human planning and divine sovereignty: many plans are formulated but God's counsel prevails.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 12a-b. The primary talmudic text on the cessation of prophecy: prophecy was given to fools and children after the Temple's destruction, but the sage's capacity for discernment is preserved and even exceeds the prophet's. The dictum "a sage is preferable to a prophet" is Ameimar's, and Rava doubts that agreement between two scholars proves inspiration, since they may share a constellation.

  • Nahmanides, Ḥiddushim, Bava Batra 12a. Holds that the sages' prophecy, "by way of wisdom," was not taken away after the destruction, and that they know the truth by the holy spirit within them.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 54b. Seven things are hidden from human beings, among them the day of death, what a person will earn, and when the kingdom of the house of David will be restored.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 12b. Pharaoh's astrologers foresee that Israel's savior will be stricken through water and decree the drowning of the boys, not knowing that the water meant is that of Meribah.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 156a-b. R. Ḥanina and R. Yoḥanan dispute whether Israel is subject to the constellations; Chaldeans' forecast that R. Akiva's daughter would die of a snakebite is averted by her charity.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97a-b. The central text on messianic calculation and its prohibition; the juxtaposition of detailed eschatological timetables and the curse on those who calculate the end embodies the tradition's paradoxical stance toward predicting the future. It also includes R. Zeira's plea not to push the redemption away by calculating, and Rav's view that all the ends have passed and redemption depends on repentance and good deeds.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 11b-12a. Belshazzar and Ahasuerus each count the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy and err, and Rava holds that Daniel also erred in the count.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 64b; Kiddushin 39b; Shabbat 32a; Ta'anit 20b. Sources for ein somkhin al ha-nes: a dispute over relying on a miracle, the rule that one does not rely on a miracle where danger is established, and R. Yannai's warning against standing in danger in expectation of a miracle.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 70b. One who seeks wisdom or wealth must both pursue it by ordinary means and pray for it, since one without the other does not suffice.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 7:1-10:5. Halakhic codification of the laws of prophecy; specifies the qualifications of a prophet, the conditions of reception, and the tests for distinguishing true from false prophecy. Chapter 10 makes accurate prediction the test of a prophet, contrasts the partial accuracy of diviners, and holds that an unfulfilled prophecy of disaster does not disprove a prophet.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 11:16. Divination and astrology are falsehoods, and only fools believe them to be wisdom forbidden by the Torah.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotseaḥ 11:4-5; 12:6. Makes the removal of every mortal hazard a positive commandment, prescribes rabbinic lashes for one who says he endangers only himself, and forbids passing under a leaning wall or over a rickety bridge.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a, with Rashi ad loc. Among the signs of the approaching redemption: "before those days there was no wage for a person and no wage for the animal." Rashi reads this as a collapse of earnings until the last coin is gone from the purse. R. Abba calls the renewed fruitfulness of the land of Israel the most revealed sign of the end.

  • Zohar 1:117a. "In the six hundredth year of the sixth millennium the gates of wisdom above and the wellsprings of wisdom below will open, and the world will be readied to enter the seventh." Computes the approach of the seventh millennium from the letters of the divine name, over R. Yose's objection that this prolongs the exile; read by R. Menachem Mendel Schneerson as foretelling the scientific and technological development of the modern era.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed II:29. Holds that no prophet or sage has announced the destruction of the universe, and reads the saying that the world will be desolate for one thousand years as one sage's opinion.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Melakhim 12:1-5. The messianic age will not change the natural order; its sequence of events is unknown even to the prophets, so that one may not calculate the end; and it is desired so that Israel "be free to engage in Torah and its wisdom," when the world's only occupation will be to know God.

  • Maimonides, Iggeret Teiman. Explains the prohibition on calculating the end by the danger that the masses will despair when a date passes, excuses R. Saadia Gaon's calculations, and reports a family tradition that prophecy would return to Israel in 4976 (1216 CE).

  • Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot 8:2-3. The redemption will come at the time of repentance or at the fixed end, whichever is first, and the end is computed from Daniel 12, with its days read as years.

  • Abarbanel, Ma'ayenei ha-Yeshu'ah 1:1-2 (Ma'ayan 1, Tamar 1-2). Restricts the curse on calculators of the end to astrological calculation, and permits calculation from the words of the prophets when it is offered as conjecture.

  • Ḥafets Ḥayyim (R. Yisrael Meir Kagan), Shem Olam, part 1, conclusion (ḥatimat ha-sefer). Reads the telephone, the photograph, the phonograph, and the telescope as demonstrations, against those who deny providence, that an eye above sees and an ear hears, and holds that nearly all the talmudic signs of the birth pangs of the Messiah can be seen in his own day.

  • R. Menachem Mendel Schneerson, Likkutei Siḥot, vol. 15, Noaḥ, sicha 2. Following the Zohar, ties the development of secular wisdom to the revelation of the Torah's inner dimension and treats that as the purpose of technological progress.

  • Baḥya ibn Paquda, Ḥovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Bitaḥon 3-4. One who trusts in God should still pursue the means of livelihood and health suited to him, while recognizing that their success rests with the Creator.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Theology of Prophecy, History, and Eschatology

  • Heschel, Abraham Joshua. The Prophets. New York: Harper & Row, 1962. The prophet defined by moral passion and divine pathos rather than predictive accuracy.

  • Scholem, Gershom. The Messianic Idea in Judaism. New York: Schocken Books, 1971. Jewish messianism in its restorative and utopian forms, and the costs of premature messianic enthusiasm.

  • Berkovits, Eliezer. God, Man and History. Edited by David Hazony. Jerusalem: Shalem Press, 2004. Divine sovereignty over history as framing rather than displacing human agency.

  • Funkenstein, Amos. Perceptions of Jewish History. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1993. The evolution of Jewish historiographical consciousness.

Jewish Futurism and Technology-Conscious Predictions

  • “The Jewish Future: A Symposium.” Commentary 140, no. 4 (November 2015): 13–75. Seventy Jewish leaders, thinkers, and clergy, including Moshe Koppel, predict the condition of the Jewish community fifty years on.

  • Navon, Mois. "One Thousand Years of Shabbat." Chidushei Torah@NDS, 50-69. The six-thousand-year tradition and its cosmic Sabbath.

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Unemployment and Mashiach." Torah Musings, September 8, 2025. Suggests, tentatively, that AI-driven unemployment with a universal basic income could supply the leisure for study that Maimonides ascribes to a natural messianic era.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on AI is Upside-Down (Part 2): They Took Our Jobs." Shmuel's Substack, March 24, 2026. Treats technological job displacement through halakhic and theological sources, and notes that Keynes's 1930 forecast of a fifteen-hour working week by 2030 has not come about.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "What, to a Jew, is the End of the World?" Shmuel's Substack, October 25, 2026. Contrasts the covenant with Noah with the covenant of Abraham, and draws on Baḥya to distinguish the reasonable effort of one who trusts in God from acts of desperation in the face of AI risk.

AI Forecasting and Futurism

  • Grace, Katja, John Salvatier, Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, and Owain Evans. "Viewpoint: When Will AI Exceed Human Performance? Evidence from AI Experts." Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 62 (2018): 729-54. Survey of machine-learning researchers on timelines for AI milestones, showing wide variation among respondents and strong effects of question framing.

  • Armstrong, Stuart, Kaj Sotala, and Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh. "The Errors, Insights and Lessons of Famous AI Predictions and What They Mean for the Future." Journal of Experimental & Theoretical Artificial Intelligence 26, no. 3 (2014): 317-42. Analyzes five famous AI predictions and finds general overconfidence among experts and poor reliability in expert forecasts of AI timelines.

  • Karger, Ezra, Josh Rosenberg, Zachary Jacobs, Molly Hickman, and Phillip E. Tetlock. "Subjective-Probability Forecasts of Existential Risk: Initial Results from a Hybrid Persuasion-Forecasting Tournament." International Journal of Forecasting 41, no. 2 (2025): 499-516. Finds that specialists were more pessimistic than superforecasters about existential risks, especially from AI, and that months of discussion barely moved either group.

  • Geraci, Robert M. "Apocalyptic AI: Religion and the Promise of Artificial Intelligence." Journal of the American Academy of Religion 76, no. 1 (2008): 138-66. Transformative-AI discourse as structurally apocalyptic religion.

  • Tegmark, Max. Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. New York: Knopf, 2017. Scenarios for AI's long-term impact.

  • Muehlhauser, Luke, and Louie Helm. "The Singularity and Machine Ethics." In Singularity Hypotheses, edited by Amnon H. Eden, James H. Moor, Johnny H. Søraker, and Eric Steinhart, 101-26. Springer, 2012.

  • Bostrom, Nick. Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies. Oxford University Press, 2014. The case for treating superintelligence as demanding present planning.

  • Altman, Sam. "Planning for AGI and Beyond." OpenAI, February 24, 2023. A developer's statement of why continuous deployment is preferable to a discontinuous arrival of artificial general intelligence.

Ethics of Technology and Future-Building

  • Vallor, Shannon. Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. Virtue ethics as a more reliable guide to the technological future than prediction.

  • Jonas, Hans. The Imperative of Responsibility: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age. University of Chicago Press, 1984. An ethics of responsibility for future generations under unprecedented technological power.

  • Danaher, John. Automation and Utopia: Human Flourishing in a World without Work. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2019. Whether automation could enable post-work flourishing.

  • Keynes, John Maynard. "Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren." In The Collected Writings of John Maynard Keynes, vol. 9, Essays in Persuasion, 321-32. London: Macmillan, 1972 [orig. 1930]. A 1930 forecast that technology would reduce the working week to about fifteen hours by 2030.

  • Sotala, Kaj. "Advantages of Artificial Intelligences, Uploads, and Digital Minds." International Journal of Machine Consciousness 4, no. 1 (2012): 275-91. Catalogues the capability advantages a digital mind, whether an upload or an artificial general intelligence, might hold over a biological one.

Primary Sources

  • Psalm 139:16. The only biblical occurrence of the word, in which the speaker's unformed substance (גלמי, golmi) is seen by God.

  • Mishnah Avot 5:7 (5:9 or 5:10 in some editions). Lists seven traits of the golem (the uncultivated person) and seven contrasting traits of the ḥakham (the sage).

  • Jeremiah and Ben Sira (MS Vat. 299). A speaking golem in the tradition erases the alef on its forehead (turning emet, truth, into met, dead) and admonishes its makers to study the powers of creation but not to use them. The story survives in Sefer ha-Gematri'ot and a related text of the Iyyun circle, both translated in Idel 1990, 64-68.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b. Describes Adam's first hours as a golem: an unformed body before the divine infusion of soul.

  • Sanhedrin 65b. The locus classicus for artificial creation. Rava creates a man and sends him to R. Zeira, who finds the creature mute and orders it to return to dust. Rav Ḥanina and Rav Oshaya use Sefer Yetsirah to create a calf each Sabbath eve.

  • Rashi, Yad Ramah, and Ben Yehoyada (R. Yosef Ḥayyim of Baghdad) on Sanhedrin 65b. Rashi explains that Rava created the man by combining the letters of the divine name and that it lacked speech; the Yad Ramah rejects the view that the creature was an illusion; Ben Yehoyada holds that such a creature lasts no more than twenty-four hours and was undone by reciting its letter combination backwards.

  • Sanhedrin 67b. Distinguishes creation through Sefer Yetsirah (treated as legitimate use of natural knowledge) from prohibited sorcery (kishshuf), removing the halakhic obstacle to the practice.

  • Rashi on Sanhedrin 67b, s.v. askei be-hilkhot yetsirah. Explains that creation through Sefer Yetsirah is not sorcery because it is God's work, performed through His holy name.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 39:14. "Were all the dwellers of the world to come together, they could not create a single gnat and put in it a soul." A midrashic statement of the limit on human creative capacity.

  • Sefer Yetsirah 2:5-6. The ancient cosmogonic text describing the (original, divine) formation of reality through permutation of the twenty-two Hebrew letters.

  • Megillat Aḥima'atz (1054). An Italian family chronicle that uses the word golem for a corpse temporarily animated by inserting the divine name (Idel 1990, 299).

  • R. Eleazar of Worms, Commentary on Sefer Yetsirah, late 12th-early 13th century. Contains medieval instructions for golem creation.

  • R. Menaḥem Meiri, Commentary on Sanhedrin 67a-b. Meiri reads Sefer Yetsirah creation as natural-technological rather than magical, saying that "Anything that is performed via natural action... as it is known in books of natural science that this is not impossible, it is permitted to do so."

  • R. Judah Loew (Maharal of Prague), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b, s.v. Rava bara. Holds that Rava's creature could not speak because a maker cannot give a speaking soul to a being like himself.

  • R. Samuel Eidels (Maharsha), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Explains that Rava could not create the power of the neshamah, which is speech, and that the creature had only the animal spirit of life, so R. Zeira returned it to dust.

  • R. Moshe Cordovero, Pardes Rimmonim 24:10. Kabbalistic analysis treating the golem's vitality as comparable to animal life only, denying it the higher levels of soul.

  • R. Avraham Azulai, Ḥesed le-Avraham, Ein Ya'akov (also titled Even Shetiyah), Ma'ayan 4, Nahar 30. Holds that a being formed through the letter combinations of Sefer Yetsirah has no spirit or soul, only a vitality like an animal's, though superior to it.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi, responsum no. 93. Asks whether a man made through Sefer Yetsirah, like Rava's, counts toward a minyan, mentions the testimony that his ancestor R. Eliyahu of Chełm made one, and rules that it does not count, since R. Zeira would not have destroyed Rava's creature had it been of such use; adds that killing it is not bloodshed because it was not formed in a womb.

  • R. Yaakov Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets, vol. 2, siman 82. Compares the golem to a dog trained to run errands and ranks it below a deaf-mute for want of any da'at, so that it cannot count toward a minyan; it also records, from Emden's father, that R. Eliyahu Ba'al Shem of Chełm destroyed his golem when it kept growing, for fear it would destroy the world.

  • R. Ḥayyim Yosef David Azulai (the Ḥida), Marit ha-Ayin on Sanhedrin 65b; Birkei Yosef OḤ 55:4; Maḥazik Berakhah OḤ 55:1. Rules that a golem cannot be counted toward a minyan and raises the concern that such creations may be unsafe. In Mar'it ha-Ayin he answers the Ḥakham Tsvi's proof by holding that the creature's usefulness was outweighed by its capacity to cause harm.

  • Ba'er Hetev, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:2; Mishnah Berurah 55:4. Both refer to the Ḥakham Tsvi on whether a man formed through Sefer Yetsirah counts toward a quorum of ten.

  • R. Gershon Henoch Leiner of Radzin, Sidrei Taharot, Ohalot 5a. Addresses the golem in relation to ritual impurity, personhood, the prohibition of murder, and the theoretical possibility of a fully human artificial creation.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Argues that even if a golem counted as a Jew by the Ḥakham Tsvi's reasoning, it would not be obligated in the commandments, since it has no soul that survives for reward and punishment, and so cannot join a quorum. It also suggests that R. Zeira destroyed Rava's creature lest it grow harmful, and that such a being should be made only for a defined need and returned to dust at once.

  • Ḥazon Ish (R. Avraham Yeshayah Karelitz), Yoreh De'ah, beginning of siman 116. Rules that a Sefer Yetsirah creation "has none of the rights of a Jew, and likely none of the rights of Man."

Secondary Sources

Foundational Scholarly Studies

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Idea of the Golem." In On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, 158-204. New York: Schocken Books, 1965. Traces the golem from Talmudic origins through medieval Ashkenaz to modern literature.

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: SUNY Press, 1990. Surveys the development of the concept through Ḥasidei Ashkenaz, the Abulafian school, the Italian Renaissance, and the Safed kabbalists, and examines golem-creation as a marker of mystical accomplishment.

Historical and Cultural Studies

  • Kieval, Hillel J. "Pursuing the Golem of Prague: Jewish Culture and the Invention of a Tradition." Modern Judaism 17, no. 1 (1997): 1-24. Demonstrates that the Maharal-golem legend is a nineteenth-century invention and traces its propagation.

  • Dekel, Edan, and David Gantt Gurley. "How the Golem Came to Prague." Jewish Quarterly Review 103, no. 2 (2013): 241-258. Traces the attachment of the golem legend to Prague in the first half of the nineteenth century.

  • Leiman, Shnayer Z. "Did a Disciple of the Maharal Create a Golem?" The Seforim Blog, February 8, 2007. Distinguishes R. Eliyahu Ba'al Shem of Chełm, the subject of R. Yaakov Emden's family tradition, from the Maharal's disciple R. Eliyahu Loanz, and translates Emden's accounts of the Chełm golem.

  • Schäfer, Peter. "The Magic of the Golem: The Early Development of the Golem Legend." Journal of Jewish Studies 46, nos. 1-2 (1995): 249-261. Analyzes the earliest stages of the tradition and the transition from talmudic speculation to medieval magical practice.

  • Gelbin, Cathy S. The Golem Returns: From German Romantic Literature to Global Jewish Culture, 1808-2008. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 2011. Literary and sociocultural study tracing modern interest in golems to nineteenth-century German Christians and reading the golem as a site of negotiation over Jewish identity.

  • González Diéguez, Guadalupe. "Golem or Robot?" AJS Perspectives (Summer 2024): 50-52. Argues that the legend of Solomon ibn Gabirol's female golem describes a wooden automaton of the Islamicate mechanical tradition, later reinterpreted as a golem.

  • Mayor, Adrienne. Gods and Robots: Myths, Machines, and Ancient Dreams of Technology. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2018. Comparative study of artificial life in ancient mythology that situates the golem within a broader cross-cultural history of imagined automata.

Halakhic and Theological Status of Artificial Beings

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Develops halakhic criteria for distinguishing humans from other entities, drawing also on golem sources.

  • Bleich, J. David, and Arthur J. Jacobson. "Cloning." In Jewish Law and Contemporary Issues, 357-396. Cambridge University Press, 2015. Discusses golem literature as a halakhic precedent for cloning and the status of artificially created human beings.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Halakhic survey organized around Sanhedrin 65b, including four positions on the ensoulment of artificially created beings.

  • Navon, Mois. "'Let Us Make Man in Our Image,' a Jewish Ethical Perspective on Creating Conscious Robots." AI and Ethics 4 (2024): 1235-1250. Surveys Jewish sources on creating humanoids and golems and argues against creating conscious artificial beings.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (Fall 1966): 15-26. A pioneering treatment of whether an intelligent artificial being could hold religious status, seek conversion, or be counted as a person in halakhah; left deliberately unresolved.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (1977): 58-74. Surveys competing halakhic criteria for identifying a human being (descent, form, and rational speech) and applies them to artificial and radically altered beings.

Applying the Golem to Artificial Intelligence

  • Wiener, Norbert. God & Golem, Inc.: A Comment on Certain Points Where Cybernetics Impinges on Religion. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1964. An early treatment of the social and ethical implications of cybernetics; despite its title, it contains almost no discussion of Jewish tradition.

  • Scholem, Gershom. "The Golem of Prague and the Golem of Rehovoth." Commentary 41, no. 1 (January 1966): 62-65. Dedicatory address for the Weizmann Institute's "Golem Aleph" computer, delivered June 17, 1965, comparing the kabbalistic golem and the digital computer.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. Golems Among Us: How a Jewish Legend Can Help Us Navigate the Biotech Century. Chicago: Ivan R. Dee, 2004. Applies the golem tradition to the moral responsibilities of human creative power in biotechnology, cloning, and AI.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. "Golems in the Biotech Century." Zygon 42, no. 1 (2007). Applies classical golem teachings to bioengineering, robotics, and artificial intelligence.

  • Rappaport, Zvi H. "Robotics and Artificial Intelligence: Jewish Ethical Perspectives." Acta Neurochirurgica Supplement 98 (2006): 9-12. Discusses ethical principles for AI and robotics through the golem legend.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge University Press, 2024. Surveys Jewish engagement with artificial humanoid beings from medieval golem literature to contemporary AI.

  • Goltz, Nachshon (Sean), John Zeleznikow, and Tracey Dowdeswell. "From the Tree of Knowledge and the Golem of Prague to Kosher Autonomous Cars." Oxford Journal of Law and Religion 9, no. 1 (2020): 132-156. Discusses AI ethics through Jewish sources, including the golem tradition.

  • Rosen, Michael. Like Silicon from Clay: What Ancient Jewish Wisdom Can Teach Us About AI. Washington, DC: AEI Press, 2025. Applies golem traditions and halakhic reasoning to contemporary AI policy debates, especially questions of liability, foreseeable harm, and the duty to prevent destructive outcomes.

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Golem and Not-So-Silly Questions." Torah Musings, April 28, 2025. Argues that the halakhic debate over the golem, which dominates Jewish discussion of AI, is not rigorous and that the harder question concerns beings outside every halakhic category.

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Golem and Frankenstein's Monster." Torah Musings, May 5, 2025. Argues from Bleich's four views of the golem's status that an AI system is an inanimate object, so that destroying it is not homicide, and that its harms are indirect causation (gerama), though foreseeable ones should be treated as garmei.

  • Rubin, Charles T. "The Golem and the Limits of Artifice: On What the Jewish Legend Can (and Cannot) Teach Us About Bioethics." The New Atlantis 39 (2013): 56-72. Critical essay arguing that the contemporary use of the golem as a bioethical exemplar typically draws on the nineteenth- and twentieth-century literary versions (Rosenberg, Bloch, Leivick, Wegener) rather than the classical sources, and warning against extracting easy moral lessons from a tradition whose dramatic-loss-of-control framing is mostly modern.

  • Vudka, Amir. "The Golem in the Age of Artificial Intelligence." NECSUS: European Journal of Media Studies 9, no. 1 (2020): 101-123. Reads cinematic representations of AI through the golem narrative and argues that the figure sets the basic terms for depicting human-machine relations.
