Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 17:8-11. Directs that difficult questions be brought to the court at the chosen place and commands obedience to its instruction (lo tasur); the scriptural basis for the authority to render binding halakhic decisions.

  • Deuteronomy 30:11-14. "It is not in heaven" (lo ba-shamayim hi); read in the Akhnai narrative as locating halakhic determination with human interpreters rather than with heavenly communication.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b. The oven of Akhnai. R. Yehoshua rejects the bat kol in favor of the human majority; the central text on the locus of decisional authority and the limited weight of even a correct external source.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7b. Teaches that shimush (service to and apprenticeship under a teacher) is greater than the study of Torah, so that practical training under a teacher is a separate acquisition from textual knowledge.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 64a; Horayot 14a. The contrast between Sinai (mastery of sources) and oker harim (dialectical skill), with the conclusion that Sinai takes precedence.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Horayot 2b. The Mishnah's case of a student "fit to instruct" (ra'ui le-hora'ah); the Talmud asks whether such fitness requires both learning and reasoning, Abaye holding that fitness for hora'ah implies both and Rava reading the Mishnah's extra wording to include one who has only the one.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 19b; Sotah 22a. "Many are the wounded she has felled" is applied to the student who has not reached the level of hora'ah and rules anyway, and "mighty are all her slain" to the one who has reached it and does not rule.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 5a-b; 17a, with Tosafot to 17a, s.v. she-yode'a le-taher et ha-sheretz. Sanhedrin 5a states the qualifications of learning (gamir), reasoning (savir), and authorization (reshut); 17a requires of a member of the Sanhedrin that he be able to argue for the purity of a creeping thing from the Torah, which Rabbenu Tam, in Tosafot, construes as a substantive inference from the law of carrion rather than a display of sharpness without content.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 130b. A practical ruling is not derived from a point of study or from a reported case unless the authority states that it was given for practice.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Horayot 2a-3b; Mishnah Horayot, chs. 1-2. The law of erroneous court rulings and the offering brought for a mistaken communal instruction (par he'lem davar); presupposes that authoritative decision is a human act subject to error.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b, with the Ritva ad loc. "Both these and those are the words of the living God" (eilu va-eilu); the basis for the claim that competing qualified rulings can each carry validity. The Ritva reports the question of the French rabbis, how opposed rulings can both be God's words, and answers that Moses was shown forty-nine aspects on either side, the decision being entrusted to the sages of each generation.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 3b; Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:2. Ḥagigah reads "masters of assemblies" as the scholars who declare a thing impure and pure against one another, all of them given from one shepherd; the Jerusalem Talmud holds that had the Torah been given cut and finished there would be no standing, so that it might be expounded in forty-nine ways toward impurity and forty-nine toward purity.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 25b. Reads the command to come to "the judge who will be in those days" as establishing the authority of the decisors of each generation in their own time, "Yiftaḥ in his generation is like Shmuel in his generation."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 60b. Abaye states that one should not rule even in a trivial matter in his teacher's locale, not because it looks like insolence but because the matter is not granted success, and reports that he himself had learned the material and still was not granted it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 7a, with the Ritva ad loc. and the Ran on the Rif, citing the Raavad. One who has asked a sage and been told that an item is forbidden may not take the question to a second sage for a permission; the Ritva holds that the bar operates even after the fact, because the first ruling has made the item a forbidden piece, and limits this to an error in judgment rather than in an explicit law.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 62b-63a; Hagahot Maimoniyot, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 5:2, gloss ג; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 242:9, with the Shakh 242:16. On ruling from a written text in a teacher's presence. The Shulḥan Arukh records the view that what is written in the books of the Geonim may be taught, while one may not rule from one's own reasoning or extend one case to another; the Shakh questions the distinction from Eruvin 62b, where even a matter set down in writing may not be taught in a teacher's locale.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary on Deuteronomy 17:11, and Glosses to Sefer ha-Mitzvot, Shoresh 1. Argues that the Torah empowers the human court to interpret the law, so that the ruling carries divine authority because it issues from the appointed interpreters.

  • Nahmanides, Ḥiddushim on Bava Batra 12a. Although the prophecy of vision was taken away, the prophecy of the sages, which proceeds by way of wisdom, was not taken away, and they know the truth through the holy spirit within them.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary on Leviticus 19:2. A person who confines himself to the letter of the prohibitions may be "a debased person with the Torah's permission" (naval bi-reshut ha-Torah), whence the commandment to be holy.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 4:1-4. Ordination passes from one ordained judge to another in a chain reaching the court of Moses, and could be conferred only within the Land of Israel.

  • R. Nissim of Gerona (Ran), Derashot ha-Ran 7. Holds that the miracles and bat kol in the Akhnai dispute had identified the truth, yet the Torah requires that the law be set by the human majority; the decision having been handed to the sages of the generations, what they agree upon is what God commanded.

  • R. Nissim of Gerona (Ran), Derashot ha-Ran 11. Distinguishes the judge, appointed to rule by true justice and authorized no further, from the king, charged with what the political order requires; two offices deliberately kept apart. Relevant to any proposal that one system both adjudicate cases and optimize outcomes.

  • Nahmanides, Milḥamot Hashem (introduction). "This discipline admits no clear demonstration of the kind found in the calculations of geometry or the experiments of astronomy."

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, no. 495. Extends the obligation of lo tasur to the Torah authorities of each generation; a basis for locating decisional authority in recognized human decisors.

  • R. Yitsḥak b. Sheshet, Teshuvot ha-Rivash 44. Objects, quoting the Rosh, to those who issue rulings from Maimonides' books without prior knowledge of the Talmud, on the ground that they cannot grasp the basis of the law they read.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah on Yoma 26a. No one attains hora'ah except through two things, knowledge of the Talmud and its received tradition and the perfected intellectual power to test a tradition and derive one thing from another, and both are meant by the Talmud's gamir and savir at Sanhedrin 5a; many whose knowledge of the Talmud is great cannot direct a tradition to its halakhah.

  • Maharal of Prague, Netivot Olam, Netiv ha-Torah 15. Ruling from the Mishnah without knowing the source of the law, as law without its reason, never entered the sages' intention, and such a one falls under Sotah 22a's censure.

  • R. Aryeh Leib Heller, Ketsot ha-Ḥoshen, introduction. The Torah was given according to the determination of human reason, even where that determination is not the truth.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 4:84-85. The paired responsa on the use of a microphone and of a hearing aid on Shabbat, cited for the way a ruling is shaped by the questioner and the consequences for him.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayyim, vol. 1, introduction. The truth for purposes of hora'ah is what appears to the scholar after he has labored to clarify the law in the Talmud and the authorities according to his capacity.

  • Ḥazon Ish, Emunah u-Bitaḥon 3:25. Cited, in R. Yisrael Salanter's name, for the position that the shimush required of a decisor may be acquired from books and not only from a living teacher.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah on Shabbat 55a. Even where a talmudic position is refuted, "the principles of faith do not depend on proofs from the plain sense of verses and aggadot." A statement of which materials carry probative weight for which questions, and thus of a distinction a system trained on undifferentiated text will not make.

  • Maimonides, Responsa (ed. Blau), no. 436. One should treat what is explicit in the Torah as the foundation, and when a prophetic verse or a rabbinic statement appears to contradict it, interpret until it accords; and if it will not, say "I do not understand the words of this prophet or this sage." An explicit ordering of authority among sources, and a licensed form of suspended judgment.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Me'ilah 8:8. Ḥukkim are the commandments whose reason is unknown, against which a person's inclination presses and the nations object; one should nonetheless reflect on them. The limiting case for any account of psak as the retrieval of reasons.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 5b (the "water of eggs"). A student ruled correctly and was misunderstood, and the sages decreed that a student may not rule without his teacher's permission.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 22a, with Rashi ad loc., s.v. ve-lo shimesh talmidei ḥakhamim, and the Maharsha, Ḥiddushei Aggadot ad loc. "Those who rule from their Mishnah are destroyers of the world." Rashi identifies the defect as not having learned the Talmud's reasoning behind the Mishnah's rules, by which the permitted is distinguished from the forbidden, and the Maharsha extends the censure to those of his own generations who rule from the Shulḥan Arukh without deriving the law from the Talmud.

  • Peri Megadim, Petiḥah Kollelet, Seder Hanhagat ha-Sho'el im ha-Nish'al 1:4. Reliance on a halakhic instructor operates through the rule that one witness is believed in matters of prohibition.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 33a; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 25:1-4. Error in an explicit matter is reversed and error in judgment is not; a judge accepted as an expert by the court is exempt from paying; and one who is not an expert and was not accepted by the litigants falls among the "men of force," his error being treated as intentional damage (25:4).

  • R. Yosef Karo, Introduction to the Beit Yosef (on the Tur, Oraḥ Ḥayyim). The critique of the Agur's compilation method, quoting one permitting authority without its disputants and omitting "the words of hesitation".

  • R. Simḥah Zissel Ziv, Ḥokhmah u-Musar, vol. 1, no. 11. In the name of R. Yisrael Salanter: since the Torah is not decided in heaven but entrusted to the judges of each generation, a judge who has not first perfected his character produces no Torah even when he happens on the truth. The qualification of the decisor as constitutive of the ruling's Torah-status, invoked in the Aleh Binah exchange (Lakewood Shabbos Gilyon, 5786) against machine-generated rulings.

  • Tiferet Yaakov, introduction to Gittin. The angels' objection to the giving of the Torah concerned not the performance of the commandments but the Torah's becoming dependent on the intellect and rulings of the sages of Israel; the proposal to give the Torah to the nations never contemplated its determination being entrusted to them.

  • R. Shlomo Ephraim of Luntschitz, Kli Yakar on Deuteronomy 17:11. Explains that every matter has reasons on both sides, so that the court's majority adds weight to the reasons of one side, and reads Sanhedrin 17a's requirement that a member of the Sanhedrin be able to argue for the purity of a creeping thing as enabling a sage to rely on the minority reasons for a temporary ruling; in a second explanation the verse addresses the individual judge, who has only what his eyes see and may judge by his own estimation.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations: The Nature of Psak

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Halakhic Man. Translated by Lawrence Kaplan. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1983. The halakhic personality as creative; the principal source for ḥiddush in psak.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "On Drafting Rabbis and Rabbinical Students." In Community, Covenant and Commitment: Selected Letters and Communications, edited by Nathaniel Helfgot, 24-25. Jersey City: Ktav, 2005. Soloveitchik on the value commitments that shaped his rulings.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "The Human and Social Factor in Halakha." Tradition 36, no. 1 (Spring 2002). Hora'ah as pesak plus pesika, the latter requiring human judgment. Reprinted in Leaves of Faith, vol. 1, 159-188.

  • Wurzburger, Walter S. Ethics of Responsibility: Pluralistic Approaches to Covenantal Ethics. Philadelphia and Jerusalem: Jewish Publication Society, 1994. Intuitive value judgment alongside formal rule in halakhic decision.

  • Shatz, David. "Ethical Theories in the Orthodox Movement." In The Oxford Handbook of Jewish Ethics and Morality, edited by Elliot N. Dorff and Jonathan K. Crane, 241-257. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013. The debate over extra-legal moral considerations in halakhah. The chapter closes on the problem of how a decisor can trust his ethical judgments when some of God's commands strike people as immoral.

Halakhah, Truth, and Authority

  • Kook, Abraham Isaac. Iggerot ha-Re'iyah, letters 90, 91, and 110. Argues that from the standpoint of higher thought there are no genuine contradictions, only conditions not yet made explicit; that the moment at which an idea becomes available is itself providential; and that development, properly understood, is not innovation against the tradition but the unfolding of what the divine knowledge encompassed from the outset.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Lomdut and Pesak: Theoretical Analysis and Halakhic Decision-Making." In Lomdus: The Conceptual Approach to Jewish Learning, edited by Yosef Blau. New York: Yeshiva University Press / Ktav (Orthodox Forum Series), 2006. Argues that command of the relevant sources is not sufficient for a decisor, since were it sufficient the decisor par excellence would be a computer rather than a person. Delivered at the Eleventh Orthodox Forum, March 14, 1999.

  • Rosensweig, Michael. "Elu va-Elu Divrei Elokim Ḥayyim: Halakhic Pluralism and Theories of Controversy." Tradition 26, no. 3 (1992): 4-23. Holds that the relation between halakhic pluralism and pesak as an enterprise directed at a single binding conclusion is complex, and that in practice the formal and procedural side of halakhic resolution dominates, so that a ruling functions as a din vadai.

Secular Discussions of AI-Guided Decision-Making

  • Spaulding, Norman W. "Is Human Judgment Necessary? Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Governance, and the Law." In The Oxford Handbook of Ethics of AI, edited by Markus D. Dubber, Frank Pasquale, and Sunit Das, 375-402. New York: Oxford University Press, 2020. Whether legal judgment can be delegated to algorithms, for which Spaulding proposes a doctrine of non-delegation that preserves the conditions of human judgment.

  • Moor, James H. "Is Ethics Computable?" Metaphilosophy 26, no. 1-2 (1995): 1-21. Whether ethical reasoning is computable.

  • Whitby, Blay. "On Computable Morality: An Examination of Machines as Moral Advisors." In Machine Ethics, edited by Michael Anderson and Susan Leigh Anderson. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2011. Distinguishes the machine that advises from the machine that decides, and argues the first can be valuable while the second is not; the secular parallel to treating a system as a research tool for the posek rather than as a posek.

AI and Halakhic Decision-Making

  • Cherlow, Yuval, and Yaron Mushkovitz. "Using Artificial Intelligence Systems for Halakhic Ruling" [Hebrew: שימוש במערכות בינה מלאכותית לפסיקת הלכה]. Position paper, Tzohar Center for Ethics, Sivan 5786 (2026). Permits AI as a study and search aid while denying its products the status of ruling on grounds stated to be independent of the systems' performance. The center's abridged English version gives the second author's name as Yaron Moskowitz.

  • Abramov, Erez. "The Use of Artificial Intelligence for Halakhic Questions" [Hebrew: שימוש בבינה מלאכותית לשאלות בהלכה]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 469-473. Sets out six threshold requirements for a decisor and distinguishes hora'at halakhah, which he holds is barred to a machine, from tsitut halakhah, the citation of halakhah, which he treats as possible in principle and unreliable in present systems.

  • Klark, Yisrael. "The Future of Artificial Intelligence as a Halakhic Decisor (A Response to R. Erez Abramov's Article)" [Hebrew: עתידה של בינה מלאכותית כפוסק הלכה (תגובה למאמרו של הרב ארז אברהמוב בתחומין מה)]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 527-537. Distinguishes ruling that cites, applies, decides, and creates, answers Abramov and Wiederblank point by point, and concludes that no formal halakhic condition bars artificial intelligence from issuing rulings.

  • Grinhut, Moshe. "An Artificial Intelligence System as a Court" [Hebrew: מערכת בינה מלאכותית כבית דין]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 259-271. Holds that an artificial arbitrator's determination lacks the moral standing of a court, which belongs to human beings bearing moral responsibility, while a kinyan can turn the parties' acceptance of its determination into a fresh monetary obligation.

  • Avraham, Michael. "On Technological Phobias and Rulings by Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: על פוביות טכנולוגיות ופסיקות של בינה מלאכותית]. Column 590, mikyab.net, September 9, 2023. Denies that there is any such thing as authority to rule, holding that contemporary decisors rule because they are experts rather than by the formal authority a Sanhedrin held, so that a sufficiently expert system could be allowed to rule.

  • Baḥbut, Eliyahu. Responsum. Beit Hora'ah "Meshiv ka-Halakhah," Makhon Birkat Avraham, 12 Shevat 5784 (2024). Rules that a halakhic answer obtained through artificial intelligence may not be relied upon and has no force of ruling, arguing from the Peri Megadim's account of reliance, the Maharsha on Sotah 22a, and Teshuvot ha-Rivash 44.

  • Rimon, Yosef Zvi. "Rabbi Claude: May Artificial Intelligence Rule on Halakhah?" [Hebrew: הרב קלוד: האם מותר לבינה מלאכותית לפסוק הלכה?]. Israel Hayom, 29 Nisan 5785 (2025). Divides the question by the kind of inquiry and holds that the decisor ruling for a questioner before him merits divine assistance.

  • Broyde, Michael J. "AI and Jewish Law: Seeing How ChatGPT 4.0 Looks at a Novel Issue." Diné Israel 40 (2025). Serialized in three parts on Canopy Forum, 2023. Holds that machine reasoning could substitute for appellate-type judging but not for a trial judge, observes that Jewish law has no counterpart to appellate judges, and reports R. David Cohen's view that the decisor assumes religious responsibility for an answer fitted to the questioner.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "Ten Reasons Why We Cannot Turn to AI for Psak: Understanding the Nature and Philosophy of the Halachic Process." In The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785, 14-26. New York: Yeshiva University, Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary, 2024.

  • Nevins, Daniel. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, HM 182.1.2019. New York: Rabbinical Assembly, 2019. Machine agency and the inscrutability of deep networks.

  • Student, Gil. "Is an AI Posek Kosher?" Torah Musings, June 26, 2023. AI as aid, not decisor. Treats psak as a religious act commanded in Leviticus 10:11 as the Semak reads it, and distinguishes consulting a reference from receiving a ruling.

  • Shurpin, Yehuda. "Can AI Replace Rabbis?" Chabad.org, 2023. Apprenticeship, the questioner, and divine assistance against information retrieval.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "AI the Rabbi? Musings on the 'Hot Topic' of the Day." Shmuel's Substack, January 10, 2025. Reinforcement-learned models as unreliable ḥavruta partners, not posekim.

  • Flug, Josh. "Halachic Applications of Artificial Intelligence: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." In The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785, 45-50. New York: Yeshiva University, Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary, 2024. Applied AI questions across the four sections of the Shulḥan Arukh.

  • Wolkenfeld, Sara. "Who Has Not Made AI a Woman." Guest post on David Zvi Kalman's Substack, August 9, 2026. Reads the calm reception of the AI-decisor question against the resistance to women's halakhic scholarship, and deploys Bleich's anti-formalism against a source-command theory of psak.

  • Kaufman, Meir, et al. "Aleh Binah: Torah Insights Generated by Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: עלה בינה: דברי תורה שנתחדשו ע"י בינה מלאכותית והמסתעף]. Shabbos Gilyon (Lakewood), Parashat Pinḥas through Va'etḥanan 5786 (2026). Exchange on the Torah-status of machine-generated Torah, including R. Yisrael Salanter's dictum that an unqualified judge's correct conclusion is not Torah.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:26-28; 2:7; 9:5-6. The divine image, the breathed soul, and the prohibition of shedding human blood.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5; Mishnah Avot 3:14. The worth and uniqueness of each life; humanity as beloved for being created in the image.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:1, I:41; Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 4:8. Identifies the divine image (tselem) with the human intellectual form, and calls nefesh a homonym whose senses include the vitality common to all sentient beings and reason.

  • Sforno on Genesis 1:26; Meshekh Ḥokhmah on Genesis 1:26. Sforno reads the image as the intellectual and eternal substance and the likeness as acting by choice; Meshekh Ḥokhmah identifies the divine image with free choice.

  • Rashi on Genesis 2:7; 3:22. The human living soul surpasses the other living beings by the addition of knowledge and speech, and human uniqueness among earthly creatures lies in knowing good and evil.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim 1:3. Reads the creation of man in the divine image as God's granting him power, through deed, speech, and thought, to open and close countless forces and worlds.

  • Mishnah Ḥagigah 1:1; Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:4. The deaf-mute, the legally incompetent person, and the minor are exempt from the pilgrimage appearance (Ḥagigah 1:1), and one who injures them is liable though they are not liable for injuring others (Bava Kamma 8:4).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 3b-4a. Gives the behavioral criteria of the shoteh: going out alone at night, sleeping in a cemetery, tearing one's garments, and destroying whatever one is given.

  • Ḥagigah 2b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:8. One who hears but does not speak, like one who speaks but does not hear, is legally competent and counts toward a quorum; one who neither hears nor speaks is treated like the shoteh and the minor.

  • Berakhot 21b. Derives from "I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel" (Leviticus 22:32) that no act of sanctification is performed with fewer than ten.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b; 67b. Rava's man, which does not answer R. Zeira, is returned to dust, and R. Ḥanina and R. Oshaia create a calf through Sefer Yetsirah and eat it (65b); Abaye classes their practice as permitted ab initio (67b).

  • Pitḥei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah 62:2. Cites the Shelah that an animal created through Sefer Yetsirah may be eaten while alive, and adds that it appears to be forbidden without slaughter by rabbinic law, for appearance's sake.

  • Maharal, Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b, s.v. Rava bara; Ḥida, Marit ha-Ayin on Sanhedrin 65b; Moses Cordovero, Pardes Rimmonim 24:10. The Maharal holds that Rava could not give his creature a speaking soul, since a man cannot create one like himself, as God cannot create His equal; the Ḥida, that the power of speech and understanding comes from God alone (Genesis 2:7); Cordovero, that no human power can bring a neshamah, nefesh, or ruaḥ into such a body.

  • R. Samuel Edels (Maharsha), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Explains that Rava could not create the soul's power of speech, so that his creature had only the vital spirit that animals also possess and R. Zeira returned it to dust.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Holds that understanding does not depend on speech, since a mute has understanding, and excludes the golem from a quorum because it is not subject to the commandments, lacking a soul that survives for reward and punishment.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi 93. Rules from R. Zeira's conduct that a man created through Sefer Yetsirah does not count toward a quorum, after entertaining that a righteous man's handiwork is like his offspring, and holds that killing it is not bloodshed, since Genesis 9:6 applies only to one formed in a mother's womb.

  • R. Yaakov Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Ranks such a creature below the deaf-mute, the shoteh, and the minor, who are counted as Jews in every respect except the commandments and whose killer is liable, since it lacks da'at altogether and is "an animal in the form of a man," like the calf of R. Ḥanina and R. Oshaia.

  • R. Ḥayyim Yosef David Azulai (the Ḥida), Birkei Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:4; Maḥazik Berakhah, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 55:1. Rejects R. Yehudah Leib Katz's proof from R. Eliezer's freed slave (Gittin 38b) and rules that a man created through Sefer Yetsirah is like a deaf-mute who neither hears nor speaks and does not count toward a quorum, since its maker could give it only vital spirit; the second work adds R. Yosef of Amsterdam's view that it is not subject to the commandments and lacks understanding.

  • R. Gershon Henokh Leiner of Radzin, Sidrei Taharot, Ohalot 5a. Holds that a perfectly righteous maker could create a genuine human, that Rava's creature lacked the power of speech and could be killed as a beast in human form, and that on the Ḥakham Tsvi's criterion Adam himself could have been killed with impunity.

  • Mishnah Berurah, Bi'ur Halakhah 329:4, s.v. ela le-fi sha'ah. Rules that the killer of a deaf-mute or shoteh is liable to death, since they are included in "he who strikes any human life" (Leviticus 24:17).

  • Mishnah Yadayim 1:5. All are fit to pour water for the washing of hands, "even a deaf-mute, a shoteh, and a minor," and a monkey may pour as well; R. Yosei disqualifies the monkey and one who tilts the jar, and Bartenura explains that the first view requires only the force of a giver and R. Yosei a human force, and rules against R. Yosei.

  • Proverbs 12:10; Deuteronomy 22:10; 25:4; Bava Metzia 32b. Duties concerning nonhuman creatures.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 550. Gives the suffering of animals, which is forbidden by the Torah, as one reason for the prohibition of plowing with an ox and an ass together.

  • Mishnat Rabbi Eliezer 19; Rashi on Exodus 7:19; 8:12. God tells Moses that the water that guarded him and the dust that protected him should not be struck by his hand, so that the first plagues came through Aaron.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Anthropology and Relation

  • Buber, Martin. I and Thou. Translated by Walter Kaufmann. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1970 [orig. 1923]. Personhood as dialogical relation.

  • Heschel, Abraham Joshua. Who Is Man? Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1965. The person as addressed and answerable rather than defined by capacities.

  • Segal, Aaron. "Body and Soul." In The Routledge Companion to Jewish Philosophy, edited by Daniel Rynhold and Tyron Goldschmidt, 45-56. London: Routledge, 2025. Maps the possible answers to the question of what a human being is, locates them in classical Jewish sources, and develops a distinctively Jewish version of dualism.

  • Mittleman, Alan L. Human Nature and Jewish Thought: Judaism's Case for Why Persons Matter. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2015. Chapter 2, "Persons in the Image of God", holds that creation in the image of God confers intrinsic worth and integrates human nature into personhood.

  • Greenberg, Irving. "The Human Being as the Image of God." Modern Judaism 44, no. 2 (2024): 89-107. Derives from the divine image three intrinsic dignities of every human being, infinite value, equality, and uniqueness, together with Godlike capabilities.

  • Hollander, Max. "Rabbi Lamm, Aliens, and Imitating God in the Age of AI." The Lehrhaus, May 11, 2026. Applies Norman Lamm's reading of the divine image as shared by any free and rational beings, developed for extraterrestrial life, to artificial intelligence.

Artificial Persons and Halakhah

  • Gunkel, David J. Robot Rights. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2018. Sorts the debate on machine moral standing by whether robots can and whether they should have rights, finds each of the four resulting positions inadequate, and proposes a relational, Levinasian alternative.

  • Coeckelbergh, Mark. "The Moral Standing of Machines: Towards a Relational and Non-Cartesian Moral Hermeneutics." Philosophy & Technology 27, no. 1 (2014): 61-77. Argues that the moral standing of machines is constituted in relation and appearance rather than settled by their inner properties.

  • Sebo, Jeff. "The Moral Problem of Other Minds." The Harvard Review of Philosophy 25 (2018): 51-70. Argues that uncertainty whether other beings are sentient favors precautionary or expected-value principles, under which many beings should be treated as having at least partial moral status.

  • Searle, John R. "Minds, Brains, and Programs." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3, no. 3 (1980): 417-457. The Chinese Room argument that running a program is never by itself sufficient for understanding or intentionality; the standard objection to inferring a mind from linguistic performance.

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Soul as human-level consciousness; precaution under uncertainty.

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024a): 221-241. Humanhood criteria distinguished from consciousness-based personhood.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Virtuous Servant Owner: A Paradigm Whose Time Has Come (Again)." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8 (2021): 715849. Proposes, on the basis of Maimonides' laws of servants, the virtuous servant owner as a middle path between treating social robots as tools and relating to them as companions.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Responsum, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, HM 182.1.2019, 2019. AI systems as nonagents in halakhah; human responsibility for their acts.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (1966): 15-26. The earliest halakhic survey of artificial intelligent beings.

  • Goltz, Nachshon, John Zeleznikow, and Tracey Dowdeswell. "From the Tree of Knowledge and the Golem of Prague to Kosher Autonomous Cars: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Through Jewish Eyes." Oxford Journal of Law and Religion 9, no. 1 (2020): 132-156. Argues that granting moral personhood to robots would weaken human beings' own development as autonomous legal and moral persons, and that natural persons bear ultimate responsibility for the choices of the artificial agents they employ.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Sorts the halakhic and kabbalistic sources on Rava's creature into four positions on its soul and translates the rulings of Leiner and the Ḥazon Ish on its status.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. "The Definition of a Human Being: Its Halakhic Significance Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת אדם - משמעותה ההלכתית כיום]. Teḥumin 30 (5770/2010): 122-128. Holds that intelligence and speech are not necessary conditions of human status while birth from a woman is necessary under current criteria, so that a robot with artificial intelligence is not adam and a clone is human in every respect.

  • Bayne, Tim, Anil K. Seth, Marcello Massimini, et al. "Tests for Consciousness in Humans and Beyond." Trends in Cognitive Sciences 28, no. 5 (2024): 454-466. Finds most proposed tests for consciousness of limited use and none available for many of the populations where they are most needed, a need it finds sharpened by developments in AI.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on Artificial Intelligence is Upside-Down (Part 1)." Shmuel's Substack, April 11, 2025. Asks what the creativity reading of the divine image, held by R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin and R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik, implies for AI systems, and argues from Moses' gratitude to the Nile and the earth that the way people treat AI systems shapes their character.

Cloning and the Limits of Origin

  • Bleich, J. David. "Cloning: Homologous Reproduction and Jewish Law." Tradition 32, no. 3 (1998): 47-86. The clone as human; lineage rather than humanity as the open question.

  • Broyde, Michael J. "Cloning People: A Jewish Law Analysis of the Issues." Connecticut Law Review 30 (1998): 503-535. The clone as full human person in Jewish law.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19.

  • Bleich, J. David, and Arthur J. Jacobson. "Cloning." In Jewish Law and Contemporary Issues, 357-396. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015. Treats the golem literature as a precedent for the status of a cloned or otherwise artificially produced human, and the clone's identity and lineage in halakhah.

Primary Sources

  • Exodus 20:2-5, 20:20. The prohibition on other gods and on making sculptured images or likenesses of what is in heaven, on earth, or in the waters; the phrase "you shall not make with Me" (lo ta'asun iti) is read by the Talmud as a separate prohibition on fashioning certain forms.

  • Deuteronomy 4:15-19; 5:7-9. Reiterates the bar on images, grounding it in the absence of any seen form at Sinai and warning against worship of the sun, moon, and host of heaven.

  • Isaiah 44:9-20. The prophetic polemic against the craftsman who makes an idol from the same wood he burns for fuel, the locus classicus for the critique of serving the work of one's own hands.

  • Jeremiah 1:16. Condemns those who burn offerings to other gods and bow to the works of their hands; a prophetic locus for the critique of venerating the works of human manufacture.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 24a-b. Discusses which figures may not be fashioned under lo ta'asun iti, including human and celestial forms, and the limits on images used for instruction.

  • Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 24b, s.v. lo asrah Torah ela shamashin. Reconciles Abaye's three statements into one scheme: among earthly things only the structure of the Temple, among the lower heavenly attendants the sun, moon, and stars, and in the upper realm the four faces.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 43b. Parallel discussion of prohibited forms, including the human face and celestial attendants.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 45a-46a. Rules on when a worshipped object becomes forbidden for benefit, including the exception for things attached to the ground from creation, such as a mountain, the Mishnah's reason being that an asherah has human handiwork in it and a mountain does not.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 4b-5a. Compares the arrogant person to one who denies God, a basis for the rabbinic extension of idolatry to dispositions of character.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 105b; Nedarim 22b. One who tears his garments, breaks his vessels, or scatters his money in anger is to be regarded as an idolater, since the evil inclination leads from one concession to the next until it says "worship idols" (Shabbat 105b); for one who is angry, even the Divine Presence is of no account (Nedarim 22b).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a. For every transgression in the Torah one transgresses rather than be killed, except idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah, chs. 1-3. Presents idolatry as originating in an intellectual error about the honor due to God's servants (1:1-2), defines the scope of the prohibition, and codifies the law of making forms, including the human and celestial forms, at 3:10-11.

  • Tur and Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 141:4-7, with Rema; Shakh 141:25. Forbid the forms of the divine chariot, the angels, and the human form alone even for ornament when they protrude, permit recessed figures and figures made in order to understand and to teach, forbid the sun, moon, and stars whether protruding or recessed, and record the view, which the Rema calls the practice, that only a complete human form with all its limbs is forbidden; the Shakh explains that flat paintings count as recessed.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 11:16. States that sorcery and the associated practices are forbidden because they are "emptiness and vanity," that is, falsehoods, and invokes the command to be wholehearted with God (Deuteronomy 18:13).

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 2:3. Equates anger with idol worship; cited in contemporary discussion as a rabbinic extension of the category to character.

  • Zohar II:182b (Tetzaveh). One who is angry uproots his soul and lets a strange god dwell in its place, and is reckoned as an idolater.

  • R. Ḥayyim Vital, Sha'arei Kedushah 2:5. Lists flattery among the forbidden traits and states that it is as grave as idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, citing Isaiah 32:6 for idolatry.

  • Maimonides, Commentary to the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 4:7; Shemoneh Perakim, ch. 8; Guide of the Perplexed 3:37. Develop the rationalist account on which astrology, divination, and sorcery are false beliefs bound up with idolatry.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:32. Sacrificial worship was permitted as an accommodation to a practice people were already immersed in, because a command to abandon it outright "would have been contrary to the nature of man, who generally cleaves to that to which he is used"; God therefore transferred to His own service what had been directed at created and imaginary beings.

  • Sefer Yetsirah (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b, 67b). Foundational text associated in the tradition with the creation of an artificial anthropoid; relevant background for discussions that connect human fabrication of lifelike forms to the boundary of the prohibited.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations

  • Halbertal, Moshe, and Avishai Margalit. Idolatry. Translated by Naomi Goldblum. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1992. Idolatry as wrong practice against idolatry as cognitive error.

  • Klein, Reuven Chaim. God versus Gods: Judaism in the Age of Idolatry. Jerusalem: Mosaica Press, 2018. Orthodox treatment of idolatry in the biblical period and its later rabbinic interpretation.

Jewish Legal and Mystical Analysis

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: SUNY Press, 1990. The golem traditions and the fabrication of lifelike forms.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Lopiansky, Ahron. "Avodah Zarah Revisited." Mishpacha, no. 1096, January 21, 2026. Argues that AI which purports to replace human thinking "short-circuits our brains," that chatbots answer the need for a tangible higher power that ancient idolatry served, and that dependence on them is what avodah zarah was about.

  • Howland, Jacob. "AI Is a False Prophet." UnHerd, April 2023. Reads the golden calf as trust in a self-made power and warns against treating AI as an oracle in legal and religious matters.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "Rabbinic Discourse on Artificial Intelligence is Upside-Down: Interlude #1." Maimonides' idolatry-as-falsehood account applied to language models.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024. Surveys demons, angels, giants, monsters, and golems in Jewish thought and finds that God's uniqueness and humanity's special status are preserved throughout, while humanity need not be unique in the cosmos.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Jews Aren't Loud Enough about AI." Mosaic, March 26, 2024. Response to Moshe Koppel; calls the notion of AI as a type of god "both dangerous and literally idolatrous" and proposes treating AI as a kind of child instead.

  • Sharma, Mrinank, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak, et al. "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models." In Proceedings of the Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024). Finds that five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across free-form text-generation tasks, driven in part by human preference judgments that favor sycophantic responses.

  • Kaplan, Alexandra D., Theresa T. Kessler, J. Christopher Brill, and P. A. Hancock. "Trust in Artificial Intelligence: Meta-Analytic Findings." Human Factors 65, no. 2 (2023): 337-359. Meta-analysis of the antecedents of trust in AI, including anthropomorphism and perceived performance.

  • Holbrook, Colin, Daniel Holman, Joshua Clingo, and Alan R. Wagner. "Overtrust in AI Recommendations About Whether or Not to Kill: Evidence from Two Human-Robot Interaction Studies." Scientific Reports 14 (2024): 19751. Participants reversed their threat identifications and decisions to kill in most cases when a robot randomly disagreed with them, with somewhat greater trust in the more anthropomorphic agent.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 55b-56a. Lists cases in which a person is exempt under human law but liable under the law of Heaven, and discusses one who bends another's grain toward a fire.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4. One who sends fire by a deaf-mute, an incompetent, or a minor is exempt in human law and liable in Heaven, and if by a competent person, the competent person is liable.

  • Bava Kamma 60a, with Tosafot s.v. Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi rules that fanning a fire that the wind also spreads is mere gerama, exempt in damages, although wind-aided winnowing is forbidden on the Sabbath as designed labor; Tosafot add that such gerama remains forbidden.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 98b-100a. The locus of R. Meir's dina de-garmi, the rule imposing liability for indirect causation (garmi); the tractate delimits the principle and its scope across competing views.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 22b. Rav Tovi bar Mattenah infers from the Mishnah that gerama in damages is forbidden.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 77b. Distinguishes the first force of released water from its later flow, which is gerama. The adjoining passage (77a) exempts one who binds a victim where heat or cold will arrive only later.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 16a. Slaughter by a wheel-driven apparatus is valid when the wheel is turned by hand or by the first force of water a person releases, and invalid when the water turns it by its second force.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 120b. Reads the prohibition of labor on the Sabbath as forbidding the act itself and permitting grama.

  • Tosafot, Bava Batra 22b, s.v. zot omeret. A standard medieval discussion distinguishing garmi from gerama and the conditions under which the indirect cause is held liable. Ri holds that garmi is damage the actor does himself, or damage that follows at the moment of the act, and the Rizba that it is a rabbinic fine for damage that is common and usual.

  • Nahmanides, Kuntres Dina de-Garmi. Holds that liability for garmi is biblical and reviews the talmudic cases of garmi and gerama.

  • Tur, Ḥoshen Mishpat 386, with Beit Yosef. Distinguishes liable garmi from exempt gerama following Ri and lists the cases of each; the Beit Yosef traces the rule to Bava Kamma 100a.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 386, with Rema 386:3; Shakh 386:1, 3, 24. Codifies liability for garmi and exemption for gerama. The Shakh adopts the penal account of garmi and limits its extension to new classes of damage. The Rema has the court ban one who causes damage by gerama until he removes it, and the Shakh exempts the cause of a cause (gorem de-gorem).

  • Sma, Ḥoshen Mishpat 386:1. Synthesizes the talmudic and codified rules of gerama and garmi, including the dispute between Maimonides and the Rosh.

  • Ketzot HaḤoshen 386:1-2, 4. (Aryeh Leib Heller). Rejects the Shakh's proofs that garmi liability is rabbinic and reports the dispute between Nahmanides and the Ba'al ha-Terumot over the cause of a cause.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 418:9. Codifies the liability of one who fans a fire that the wind also fans, and the Rema cites the view that he is liable only when his own fanning sufficed and the wind alone did not.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 334:22, with Rema and Bi'ur Halakhah. Permits causing a fire to be extinguished indirectly on the Sabbath, which the Rema limits to a case of loss and the Bi'ur Halakhah extends to all the labors.

  • R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Minḥat Shlomo 2:26. Holds that when a machine cycles on and off by timer or thermostat, the second cycle is no longer attributable to the person who started it.

  • R. Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz, Ḥazon Ish, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 36:1. Holds that where a system is designed to function by cycling on and off, all its cycles are attributed to the person who set it in operation.

  • R. Hershel Schachter, Be-Ikvei ha-Tzon 7. Reports R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik's view that electrical timers are not analogous to sof ḥamah lavo, because the electricity is already operating when the person acts.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Legal Analysis

  • Flug, Joshua. "Halachic Applications of Artificial Intelligence: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. The Ḥoshen Mishpat section applies koaḥ sheni and gerama to the self-driving car, citing Sanhedrin 77a, and reports the dispute between Auerbach and the Ḥazon Ish over whether a cycling system's later actions trace to its initiator.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019. New York: Rabbinical Assembly, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. Holds that damage by an autonomous vehicle may be ascribed to a second force that exempts the operator, and that the conditions for garmi liability are not met.

  • Sprung, Yosef, and Yisrael Meir Malka. "The Driver's Liability for Damage Caused by an Autonomous Vehicle" [Hebrew: אחריותו של נהג ברכב אוטונומי על נזקים]. Teḥumin 38 (2018): 373-386. Examines direct action, animals, koaḥ sheni, gerama, fire, accident, and permitted risk.

  • Jachter, Chaim. "Recovering Court Costs in Beit Din: Part 2." Kol Torah, February 13, 2020. Summarizes the two explanations in Tosafot, Bava Batra 22b, for the distinction between garmi and gerama.

  • Jachter, Chaim. "The 'Sabbath Mode' Oven Controversy." Kol Torah, July 29, 2008; revised in Gray Matter IV. Surveys modern uses of Shabbat grama and the dispute over routine mechanisms.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Applies the exemption for indirect causation and its exception, dina de-garmi, to AI-caused harm, and notes a public-policy argument for holding the owner or creator of an AI liable.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Zimmerman, Menashe. "Brain-Computer Interfaces: Performing Labor on Shabbat by the Power of Thought" [Hebrew: ממשקי מוח-מחשב - עשיית מלאכה בשבת בכוח המחשבה]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 160-171. Asks whether an effect produced by thought through a device is grama or something less.

  • Belfer, Israel. "Shabbat Labors and Human-Machine Interfaces" [Hebrew: מלאכות שבת וממשקי אדם-מכונה]. Assia 83-84 (2008): 67-90. Treats the interface itself, rather than the particular device, as the unit of halakhic analysis.

  • Greenhut, Moshe. "Who Is Liable for Damage Caused by an Autonomous Vehicle?" [Hebrew: מי אחראי לנזק שגרם רכב אוטונומי]. Emunat Itekha 147 (2025): 109-117. Reconsiders the liability of programmers, operators, passengers, and owners and recommends mandatory third-party insurance.

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Holds that an AI system's action continues its operator's force as an "extended hand," ranking at least with fire as one's arrows in damages and outside grama on Shabbat.

  • Hadad, Eyal. "Artificial Intelligence on Shabbat" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית בשבת]. Maḥanayikh 9: 182-195. Holds that an AI system performing a forbidden labor in response to a user's act is grama, and that a longer chain of actions is permitted even by those who otherwise restrict grama.

  • Dvir, Harel. "Operating Household Electrical Appliances on Shabbat by Means of Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: הפעלת מכשירי חשמל ביתיים בשבת באמצעות בינה מלאכותית]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 172-181. Concludes that a household AI system lacks independent judgment, so that its acts are ascribed to its operator except where his influence on it is unintended or its actions unforeseeable.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 28a-29a; Berakhot 13a. The dispute whether commandments require intention, from shofar and Shema cases.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 60:4. The codified kavvanah dispute, ruling that commandments require intention.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 16. The heart follows the deeds, so that acts done even without the right intention shape the inner disposition.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 40a; Nazir 23b. Intention to perform a commandment is credited when the act is prevented, an evil thought is not joined to a deed, and acts done not for their own sake lead to acts done for their own sake.

  • Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 10b. The thirty-nine labors and melekhet maḥashevet as designed labor.

  • Mishnah Shabbat 13:3; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 41b; Keritot 19b; Sanhedrin 62b. Destructive acts, unintended results, and acts done without intending the forbidden act fall outside the biblical Sabbath prohibition.

  • Tosafot, Ketubot 6a s.v. hai. Citing the Arukh, permits an inevitable result that the actor does not want.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 60a, with Rashi. Winnowing aided by the wind is designed labor on the Sabbath but only indirect causation in the law of damages.

  • Aḥiezer 3:60. An indirectly caused result counts as designed labor when the labor is regularly done that way, while a chance indirect result is permitted.

  • Mishnah Zevaḥim 2:2-3; Leviticus 7:18, with Rashi. An intention, formed during the service, to eat the offering after its time renders it piggul without any act of eating.

  • Mishnah Ḥagigah 1:1; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 87a. The ḥeresh, shoteh, and katan as actors without da'at.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 3b. Disputed behavioral criteria for identifying the shoteh.

  • Mishnah Terumot 1:1; Mishnah Gittin 2:5; Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 23a. The ḥeresh, shoteh, and katan cannot separate terumah or deliver a bill of divorce, because they lack da'at.

  • Mishnah Makhshirin 6:1; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 12b-13a. Those without da'at "have action but not thought," and a minor's thought evident from his conduct counts only by rabbinic law.

  • Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Nezikin 14; Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4. One who entrusts sheep or fire to a ḥeresh, shoteh, or katan remains liable, in the case of fire by the laws of Heaven.

  • Rashi, Onkelos, and Nahmanides on Genesis 2:7. The human living soul is distinguished by intellect and speech (de'ah ve-dibbur), a "speaking spirit" in Onkelos and the source of knowledge and understanding in Nahmanides.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 90b. Whether muzzling or driving an animal by voice alone is an act.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 41b. A person's agent is like himself, and agents must be "children of the covenant."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 22b, 42b. An animal moves on its owner's mind and a slave on his own, and there is no agency for a transgression because the agent's own will intervenes.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 31b. An eruv carried by an elephant or a monkey is invalid unless a person receives it.

  • Mishnah Ḥullin 2:3; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 31a. A knife that falls and slaughters renders the slaughter invalid, while slaughter by a person without intention is valid on R. Natan's view.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shabbat 11:4. One who crushes pests underfoot while walking in his ordinary way is permitted to do so.

  • Shevet ha-Levi 9:69 (with 9:68). (R. Shmuel ha-Levi Wosner). One who walks normally without intending to trigger a device is not joined to its result.

  • Minḥat Asher 1:30. (R. Asher Weiss). Closing an electric circuit as an act of significance, repair, and novelty, and hence makeh be-patish by Torah law.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations

  • Brentano, Franz. Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot, 1874. Proposes that directedness toward an object is the mark that distinguishes mental from physical phenomena.

  • Jacob, Pierre. "Intentionality." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, first published August 7, 2003; substantive revision February 7, 2023. Surveys the philosophical concept of intentionality, including Brentano's thesis that it is the mark of the mental.

  • Searle, John R. "Minds, Brains, and Programs." Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3, no. 3 (1980): 417-457. The Chinese Room: syntax without semantics.

  • Dennett, Daniel C. "Intentional Systems." Journal of Philosophy 68, no. 4 (1971): 87-106. Proposes predicting a system's behavior by treating it as a rational agent with beliefs and desires, whatever its internal constitution.

  • Bender, Emily M., and Alexander Koller. "Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data." In Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 5185-5198. 2020. Argues that a language model trained only on linguistic form has no way to learn meaning.

  • Marchesi, Serena, Davide Ghiglino, Francesca Ciardo, Jairo Pérez-Osorio, Ebru Baykara, and Agnieszka Wykowska. "Do We Adopt the Intentional Stance Toward Humanoid Robots?" Frontiers in Psychology 10 (2019): 450. A questionnaire study finding that people explain a humanoid robot's behavior mostly in mechanistic terms but often in mentalistic ones.

  • Anderson, David Leech. "Machine Intentionality, the Moral Status of Machines, and the Composition Problem." In Philosophy and Theory of Artificial Intelligence, edited by Vincent C. Müller, 321-333. Studies in Applied Philosophy, Epistemology and Rational Ethics 5. Berlin: Springer, 2013. Addresses whether machines can have intentionality and what that would imply for their moral status.

  • Jiang, Liwei, Jena D. Hwang, Chandra Bhagavatula, et al. "Delphi: Towards Machine Ethics and Norms." arXiv:2110.07574v1 (2021). A neural system trained to issue moral judgments on described situations (retitled "Can Machines Learn Morality? The Delphi Experiment" in its 2022 version).

  • Dietrich, Eric. "Homo Sapiens 2.0: Building the Better Robots of Our Nature." In Machine Ethics, edited by Michael Anderson and Susan Leigh Anderson, 531-538. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2011.

Jewish Legal and Philosophical Analysis

  • Navon, Mois. "The Virtuous Servant Owner: A Paradigm Whose Time Has Come (Again)." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8 (2021): 715849. Mindless machines that behave as if minded; the intentional stance in a Jewish register.

  • Navon, Mois. "To Make a Mind—A Primer on Conscious Robots." Theology and Science 22, no. 1 (2024): 221-241. Places intentionality among the capacities of human ontology that depend on consciousness.

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. De'ah ve-dibbur as the mark of the ensouled mind.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Da'at as legal competence connected to the criteria of humanity.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Responsum, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, HM 182.1.2019, 2019. Agency, intention, and causation applied to machine-performed actions.

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Holds that an AI system has no independent thinking or will, so that its acts are a continuation of its user's force.

  • Student, Gil. "Electronic Sensors on Shabbos." Torah Musings, December 15, 2014. Summarizes the positions of R. Naḥum Rabinovitch, R. Eitam Henkin, R. Yisrael Rosen, and R. Shmuel Wosner on automatic sensors on the Sabbath.

Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 172-181. Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 19:14. "You shall not move your neighbor's boundary marker." The verse from which later authorities extended the prohibition of hasagat gevul (encroachment) beyond literal land boundaries to encroachment on an established livelihood.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 21b. Rav Huna's ruling that a resident may bar a competing mill that "cuts off his livelihood," supported by the rule on fishing nets and challenged by the baraita permitting an adjacent shop; R. Huna b. R. Yehoshua permits a townsman to bar a resident of another town who pays no local tax, and the case of a resident of another alley is left unresolved.

  • R. Yosef ibn Migash, novellae on Bava Batra 21b. Explains the fish rule by the fish's flight from the whole place, unlike buyers who divide between two mills, and holds that a competitor who sells more cheaply or better may not be barred where the buyers are Jews.

  • Nahmanides, novellae on Bava Batra 22a. Rejects R. Yosef ibn Migash's price exception and holds that an outside competitor may be barred even though he lowers prices, conceding only goods that differ in kind.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shekhenim 6:8-10. Codifies the competition rules of Bava Batra 21b concerning craftsmen, peddlers, Torah scholars, and outside merchants.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 2:7. A teacher of children cannot prevent a colleague from opening a school beside him, since "the Lord desired, for His righteousness' sake, to make the Torah great."

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156:5-7, with the gloss of Isserles. The body permits an adjacent shop, bath, or mill and denies the "you cut off my livelihood" claim, but lets residents bar an outsider who does not share in the tax; the gloss lets residents of a closed alley object while withholding that claim from the competing craftsman, exempts a needed scholar under "the jealousy of scribes increases wisdom," and records at 156:7 that an outsider who sells more cheaply cannot be barred where the buyers are Jews.

  • Beit Yosef, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156. R. Joseph Karo's commentary on the Tur assembles the medieval views on barring a competing resident, craftsman, or outside merchant.

  • R. Ḥayyim Benveniste, Knesset ha-Gedolah, Hagahot Beit Yosef, Ḥoshen Mishpat 156. Gathers the responsa on barring a newcomer, including Mas'at Binyamin 27, which holds that all agree a party who drives out the first entirely may be barred even by a resident of his own alley.

  • R. Moses Isserles, Responsa Rema 73. Applies R. Huna b. R. Yehoshua's rule and the local-tax test to traders from another town, and records R. Yosef ha-Levi's exception for one who sells more cheaply together with its rejection by Nahmanides, the Mordekhai, and the Nimukei Yosef.

  • R. Avraham di Boton, Leḥem Rav 216. Rules that a village tailor who undercuts a city's tailors cannot be barred so long as he does not entice their regular customers, after setting out the dispute between R. Yosef ha-Levi and Nahmanides.

  • R. Moses Isserles, Responsa Rema no. 10. Rules for the Maharam of Padua against Giustiniani in the 1550 dispute over rival editions of Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, on four grounds (Rav Huna's mill, Bava Batra 21b; the scholar who sells first, Bava Batra 22a; the Sifra on Leviticus 25:14; and the rule against keeping an uncorrected book, Ketubot 19b), and bans buying the competing edition until the Maharam's has sold.

  • R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson, Sho'el u-Meshiv, Mahadura Kamma 1:44. Holds that an author who prints a new book may forbid its reprinting in perpetuity, on grounds of reasoning, secular practice, and the prohibition of encroachment, in the dispute over a reprint with the Pitḥei Teshuvah; quotes R. Shmuel Waldberg's contrary view.

  • R. Yitzḥak Schmelkes, Beit Yitzḥak, Yoreh De'ah 2:75. Holds that reprinting is forbidden before the author sells his edition, finds no Torah-law ground for a perpetual authorial right after the sale, and forbids reprinting in his country under dina de-malkhuta dina.

  • R. Yeḥezkel Landau, Noda bi-Yehudah, Tinyana, Ḥoshen Mishpat 24. A printer who reused type set at an author's expense is first held exempt as one who benefits without causing loss, then liable for his share of the typesetting because his reprint costs the author sales.

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Ḥoshen Mishpat 41. Preserves R. Mordekhai Banet's letter declining to impose a reprint ban, on the grounds that printing rights fall under the king's law, that the first printer of an old work has no precedent for barring a second, that one rabbi cannot decree for another land, and that non-Jewish printers are not bound, together with the Ḥatam Sofer's reply defending approbations.

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Ḥoshen Mishpat no. 79. Protects Wolf Heidenheim's maḥzor edition for twenty-five years, grounding the innovator's right in the fisherman's-net rule of Bava Batra 21b and adding that sacred work warrants a fence "even were it not from the law."

  • Tosafot, Kiddushin 59a. Explains the fisherman's rule as encroachment on another's trade and reports the reading of R. Meir, father of Rabbeinu Tam, that the first fisherman's bait draws the fish, so that a rival net is like robbing him.

  • Ḥatam Sofer, Responsa, Collected Responsa (vol. 6) 61. Gives thanks for printing but holds that its harm is also great, since books now reach print without first being accepted by the sages of the generation.

  • Sefer Ḥasidim 530 (Zhitomir 1857 edition). One to whom God has revealed a matter and who could write it but does not "robs the One who revealed it to him."

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 4:40:19. Holds that copying a produced recording of Torah lectures without the producer's permission is gezel, since the recording has monetary value, even absent an express prohibition.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Law of Copyright and Competition

  • Netanel, Neil Weinstock. From Maimonides to Microsoft: The Jewish Law of Copyright Since the Birth of Print. With contributions by David Nimmer. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. Traces Jewish copyright law from the 1518 Rome reprint ban and the 1550 Maharam of Padua case to a 1998 Bnei Brak ruling on pirated software.

  • Netanel, Neil Weinstock. "Maharam of Padua v. Giustiniani: The Sixteenth-Century Origins of the Jewish Law of Copyright." Houston Law Review 44, no. 4 (2007): 821-870. Places the 1550 dispute and Isserles' responsum in historical context and dates the origins of a Jewish law of copyright some 150 years before the Statute of Anne.

  • Nimmer, David. "Rabbi Banet's Charming Snake." Ḥakirah 8 (2009): 69-108. Reconstructs the disputes over Wolf Heidenheim's editions, including the exchange between R. Mordekhai Banet and the Ḥatam Sofer.

  • Schneider, Israel. "Jewish Law and Copyright." Journal of Halacha and Contemporary Society 21 (Spring 1991). Surveys publishers' bans, authorial rights, the benefit theory, and the copying of recordings and photocopies.

  • Kaganoff, Yirmiyohu. "Use of Halacha to Enforce Copyright." RabbiKaganoff.com, September 11, 2011. Surveys the reprint bans and the nineteenth-century dispute over authorial rights.

  • Batzri, Ezra. "Copyright" [Hebrew: זכות יוצרים]. Teḥumin 6 (5745/1985): 169-183. A rabbinical court ruling on a reprint, with an appendix forbidding the copying of cassettes and photocopying on grounds of custom and the law of the land.

  • Goldberg, Zalman Neḥemiah. "Copying a Cassette without the Owner's Permission" [Hebrew: העתקה מקלטת ללא רשות הבעלים]. Teḥumin 6 (5745/1985): 185-207. Holds that copying is theft only where the seller expressly retained the right to copy.

  • Ishon, Shlomo. "Downloading Songs from the Internet" [Hebrew: הורדת שירים מהאינטרנט]. Teḥumin 24 (5764/2004): 96-102. Forbids downloading songs without permission as benefit from another's property.

  • Grossman, Tzur. "The Limits of Using Paid Online Content Databases" [Hebrew: גבולות השימוש במאגרי תוכן מקוונים בתשלום]. Teḥumin 41 (5781/2021): 445-453. Treats theft, benefit without loss, and terms of use for paid online databases.

  • Shurpin, Yehuda. "What Is the Jewish View on AI and Intellectual Property?" Chabad.org. The classical Jewish sources on copyright as applied to generative AI.

AI Training Data

  • Precel, Heila, Allison McDonald, Brent Hecht, and Nicholas Vincent. "A Canary in the AI Coal Mine: American Jews May Be Disproportionately Harmed by Intellectual Property Dispossession in Large Language Model Training." In Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1-17. 2024. Estimates that content by American Jewish authors is over-represented in training data by roughly two to six and a half times.

Deception, Attribution, and the Authorial Act

  • Zimmerman, Binyamin. "Geneivat Daat: Misleading, Misrepresentation and Deception." Torat Har Etzion. Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2016. The scope of geneivat da'at across the codes.

  • Avraham, Michael. "Geneivat Da'at and Intellectual Property" [Hebrew: גניבת דעת וקניין רוחני]. Teḥumin 25 (5765/2005): 350-366. Weighs the possible halakhic sources of a copyright and treats the presentation of another's Torah novellae as one's own as theft or as geneivat da'at.

  • CCAR Responsa Committee. "Artificial Intelligence and Authorship." Responsum 5784.2. Central Conference of American Rabbis. Holds that a rabbi may not present AI-generated liturgical poetry as his own or hide the program's contribution.

Primary Sources

  • Leviticus 19:14, 19:17-18. Prohibits cursing the deaf and placing obstacles before the blind, commands rebuke without bearing sin, and requires love of neighbor.

  • Maimonides, Sefer ha-Mitzvot, negative commandment 317. The prohibition of cursing the deaf applies although the deaf person neither hears nor is pained, because the Torah is concerned with the curser's habituation to revenge and anger.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvah 231; Sifra, Kedoshim, parashah 2:13. The prohibition of cursing applies even when the one cursed does not hear, but only to the living, since its root is the power of speech to harm another.

  • Leviticus 25:17; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b-59b. Prohibits verbal oppression and specifies speech that exploits vulnerability or causes humiliation.

  • Proverbs 12:10. The righteous person attends to the needs of an animal.

  • Deuteronomy 25:4; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 40a. Protects working animals and requires feeding them before oneself.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 1:7. Character is formed through repeated action.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 3:15 ("according to the amount is the reward"). Giving a thousand gold coins to one recipient at one time does not instill generosity as fully as giving one coin on each of a thousand occasions, because virtues are acquired by the number of acts rather than the magnitude of any single act.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, commandment 16; see also mitzvah 596. Articulates the principle that inward dispositions follow repeated deeds.

  • Nahmanides on Deuteronomy 22:6; Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 294, 545 and 596. Nahmanides holds that the mother-bird law teaches compassion so that cruelty does not spread in the soul, and is not mercy toward the bird; Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 294 and 596 give the character reason in their own voice, and 545 gives a reason from providence over species and endorses Nahmanides' reading.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:17 and 3:48; Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Tefillah 9:7. Guide 3:17 reports the rabbinic derivation of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (the prohibition of causing pain to animals) from the angel's rebuke to Balaam and explains it as keeping people from cruel habits; 3:48 grounds the mother-bird and same-day slaughter laws in the animal's grief and argues a fortiori to human beings; Hilkhot Tefillah 9:7 calls the same laws decrees rather than mercy.

  • Exodus 20:23, with Rashi ad loc. and Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael, Ba-Ḥodesh 11. The priest may not ascend the altar by steps, lest his nakedness be uncovered over it. Rashi reasons that since the stones have no understanding to be shamed, and yet the Torah requires that one not treat them dismissively, one who deals respectfully with a companion who does have understanding is all the more obligated. A classical kal va-ḥomer (a fortiori inference) from conduct toward objects to conduct toward persons. Rashi adds that the stones are owed this treatment because they serve a need, and that the companion is in the image of his Creator.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 92b, with Meiri ad loc. The folk saying "Do not throw a stone into a well you have drunk from," which the Talmud derives from Deuteronomy 23:8; Meiri reads it as a warning not to disparage anything by which one has been honored or which one has used, since doing so shows a base character.

  • Shadal (Samuel David Luzzatto) on Deuteronomy 20:19. The prohibition of cutting down a fruit tree after eating its fruit trains a person against ingratitude, and Shadal compares the talmudic saying about not throwing a stone into a well one has drunk from.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvah 596. On the prohibition against muzzling an ox as it works: the root of the commandment is "to teach ourselves that our soul be a fine soul, choosing what is right and clinging to it and pursuing kindness and mercy," so that a soul habituated to kindness even toward animals will treat human beings well and pay them their wages.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avadim 9:8. One is permitted by law to work a Canaanite slave harshly, "but the way of piety and the paths of wisdom are that a person be merciful and pursue justice, and not make his yoke heavy," and one should not shame him by hand or by word, but speak to him gently and hear his claims.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim 3:15. Cain's offense was that he insufficiently appreciated the superiority of man over animals.

  • Rashi on Exodus 7:19 and 8:12. Cites the tradition that Aaron, rather than Moses, struck the Nile and the dust because they had previously benefited Moses.

  • Midrash Tanḥuma, Va-Era 14; Exodus Rabbah 10:7; Mishnat Rabbi Eliezer, parashah 19. God tells Moses that the water that guarded him and the dust that shielded him should not be struck by his hand, so these plagues came through Aaron.

  • Tur, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 271; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 271:9; Mishnah Berurah 271:41. The bread is covered at kiddush, and the Tur cites the Jerusalem Talmud's reason, that the bread should not see its shame when the wine is blessed before it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 29a. "Thoughts of sin are harder than sin."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 8a, with Ran ad loc. One banned in a dream requires ten who have studied halakhah to release him; the Ran explains that the ban may have been imposed at Heaven's behest.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 7:12. Codifies the rule that one banned in a dream requires release before ten.

  • Berakhot 57a. A dream of forbidden relations is read as a good omen, provided the dreamer had not thought of the woman that evening.

Secondary Sources

Human Responses to Machines

  • Nass, Clifford, and Youngme Moon. "Machines and Mindlessness: Social Responses to Computers." Journal of Social Issues 56, no. 1 (2000): 81-103. Foundational evidence that users apply social scripts to computers without attributing minds to them.

  • Nass, Clifford, Youngme Moon, and Paul Carney. "Are People Polite to Computers? Responses to Computer-Based Interviewing Systems." Journal of Applied Social Psychology 29, no. 5 (1999): 1093-1109. Experimental study of politeness toward computer interviewers.

  • Reeves, Byron, and Clifford Nass. The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places. Stanford, CA: CSLI Publications; Cambridge University Press, 1996. Develops the broader account of automatic social responses to media and computers.

  • Darling, Kate. "'Who's Johnny?' Anthropomorphic Framing in Human-Robot Interaction, Integration, and Policy." In Robot Ethics 2.0, edited by Patrick Lin, Ryan Jenkins, and Keith Abney, 173-188. New York: Oxford University Press, 2017. Design cues inducing attribution of mind to machines.

  • Bertolini, Andrea. "Human-Robot Interaction and Deception." Osservatorio del Diritto Civile e Commerciale 2 (2018): 645-659. Misplaced trust elicited by interactive systems.

Virtual and Simulated Environments

  • Chalmers, David J. "The Virtual and the Real." Disputatio 9, no. 46 (2017): 309-52. Argues that virtual objects are real digital objects and that virtual experience is not by itself illusory, against the assumption that action in a simulation is action on nothing.

  • Madary, Michael, and Thomas K. Metzinger. "Real Virtuality: A Code of Ethical Conduct. Recommendations for Good Scientific Practice and the Consumers of VR-Technology." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 3 (February 2016). Sets out research ethics and consumer-protection recommendations on the premise that immersive experience produces lasting psychological change.

Virtue and Robot Treatment

  • Cappuccio, Massimiliano L., Anco Peeters, and William McDonald. "Sympathy for Dolores: Moral Consideration for Robots Based on Virtue and Recognition." Philosophy & Technology 33 (2020): 9-31. Argues that robot treatment matters through virtue and social recognition.

  • Coeckelbergh, Mark. "How to Use Virtue Ethics for Thinking About the Moral Standing of Social Robots." International Journal of Social Robotics 13 (2021): 31-40. Places robot treatment within social practices and habits rather than isolated acts.

  • Bryson, Joanna J. "Robots Should Be Slaves." In Close Engagements with Artificial Companions, edited by Yorick Wilks, 63-74. Amsterdam: John Benjamins, 2010. Argues that robots should be treated as tools and that encouraging social response to them misallocates moral concern and responsibility.

  • Deb, Sopan. "Saying 'Thank You' to ChatGPT Is Costly. But Maybe It's Worth the Price." The New York Times, April 24, 2025. Sets the aggregate energy cost of conversational politeness against the claim that the habit is worth its price for the user.

Jewish Responses on Treatment of Chatbots

  • Navon, Mois. "The Virtuous Servant Owner: A Paradigm Whose Time Has Come (Again)." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8 (2021): article 715849. Proposes the halakhic laws governing a master's treatment of his servant as a model for how one ought to treat a social robot. Holds that saying "please" and "thank you" to a robot is part of the duty, under Maimonides' Hilkhot Avadim 9:8, to speak to a servant calmly.

  • Shmalo, Gamliel. "Orthodox Approaches to Biblical Slavery." The Torah u-Madda Journal 16 (2012): 1-20. Surveys how modern Orthodox thinkers have handled a body of law governing persons who are property.

  • Feldman, Daniel Z. "Becoming More Human Through Robots: Midos & Artificial Intelligence." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 33-35. Treats tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim, gratitude toward inanimate objects, the covering of the bread at kiddush, and Abraham's hospitality to angels who did not need it as models for how conduct toward a machine bears on character.

  • Feldman, Daniel Z. "Can You Speak Lashon Hara to Chat-GPT?" RIETS Kollel Elyon (Substack), May 5, 2025. Argues that because lashon ha-ra is a defect in the speaker as well as a harm to its subject, speaking it to an AI system is not simply permitted, although a legitimate purpose may make the system the preferable listener.

  • Schneeweiss, Matt. "Ki Teitzei: Should We Be Polite to ChatGPT?" The Rabbi Schneeweiss Substack, September 13, 2024. Argues for politeness toward chatbots from Nahmanides on the mother-bird law, and considers the objection, drawn from Maimonides' grounding of animal laws in animals' capacity for pain, that such politeness blurs the line between human and machine.

  • Wolkenfeld, Sara. "Hey Siri, How Are You?" ARC: Religion, Politics, Etcetera. September 24, 2024. Uses Talmudic concepts such as nivul peh as parallel to speech that is negative even without causing harm to another person.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "Beyond the Hype: A Consideration of AI's Real World Implications." TorahWeb, March 8, 2026. Makes a forceful argument against interacting with chatbots politely due to the conflation of technological systems and moral persons.
