Primary Sources

  • Exodus 22:17; Leviticus 19:26, 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:9-14. The biblical prohibitions of sorcery, augury, necromancy, and divination.

  • Ibn Ezra on Leviticus 19:31. Scripture forbids only what is false, so the prohibition of necromancy and sorcery does not show that they are real.

  • Ibn Ezra on Deuteronomy 18:10. The kosem (diviner) is one who decrees that a thing "will be so, without doubt."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b-67b. Creation through Sefer Yetsirah; Abaye's taxonomy of sorcery.

  • Rashi on Sanhedrin 67b, s.v. askei be-hilkhot yetsirah. Creation through the laws of creation is not sorcery, since it is God's work performed through His holy Name.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 17a. Only those who are masters of sorcery, among other qualifications, are seated on the Sanhedrin.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 113b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 179:1, with Rama. One may not consult Chaldeans (astrologers) or inquire by lots, since "you shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 18:13).

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 179:15, with Shakh 179:18. Holding the eyes is forbidden and acts through Sefer Yetsirah are permitted, a permission the Shakh restricts to holy use for a great mitzvah, which he says is not found in these generations.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Avodah Zarah 11:4-16. Divination and magic as falsehood and intellectual corruption.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 4:7. Magical and astrological practices are false, and the Torah forbids them as it forbids falsehood, although many pious people take them to be true.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed 3:37. The prohibitions of magic guard against idolatry, and the practices of the Sabians and Chaldeans bear no rational relation to the effects they promise.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:1-4; 7:1. No decree or natural constitution fixes whether a person will be righteous or wicked, and the duty of repentance follows from that freedom.

  • Nahmanides on Deuteronomy 18:9. The efficacy of occult practice conceded, its use prohibited.

  • Nahmanides on Leviticus 19:19. Crossbreeding is forbidden as "altering and denying the work of creation," a rationale he also applies to sorcery in his comment on Deuteronomy 18:9.

  • Nahmanides on Exodus 8:15. Pharaoh's magicians could not produce the lice, a new formation that none but the Creator can perform.

  • Teshuvot ha-Rashba ha-meyuḥasot la-Ramban 283. A responsum of Nahmanides on diviners, sorcerers, and astrologers, holding that astral decrees may be true and may be annulled by God for those who fear Him, and that consulting a gentile sorcerer is forbidden on account of tamim tihyeh.

  • Rashi on Deuteronomy 18:13. Wholeheartedness as refraining from investigating the future.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh 62. Sorcery is forbidden because God wills that all things follow the course of nature fixed at creation, and it is treated as a real power that temporarily suspends the force of the celestial influences.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, mitzvot 510 and 511. Divination misleads people, through its occasional accuracy, into thinking that all events are caused by the stars, and a judge must know sorcery in order to tell it apart from what is done by the force of nature.

  • Meiri on Sanhedrin 67a-b. Effects achieved by natural means excluded from sorcery.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Sanhedrin 68a. Divination is forbidden by the Torah, while inquiry by dream is permitted, and pious men used it without relying on it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 67a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 301:27. Amulets and remedies are permitted where they act by discernible natural means and forbidden as darkhei ha-Emori where they do not; the operative test separating technology from superstition, and the one an unexplainable but effective system strains.

  • Rashba, Teshuvot ha-Rashba 1:413. Abaye and Rava permitted remedies even where natural inquiry cannot explain how they work, as with the magnet.

  • Derashot ha-Ran 4 and 5. R. Nissim of Gerona holds, against Maimonides, that sorcery is real, and classes it as a branch of natural science.

  • R. Saadia Gaon, Emunot ve-De'ot 3:5. Moses' wonders were done openly, while the magicians' acts were hidden and their trickery appears on investigation.

  • R. Yehudah Halevi, Kuzari 2:64 and 5:21. The Sanhedrin were required to know every science, sorcery included, and the magicians' wonders would have been exposed on examination, whereas the divine withstands it.

  • Responsa Halakhot Ketanot 2:98. Responsibility for killing through sorcery; attribution of extraordinary action.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Magic in Historical Context

  • Bohak, Gideon. Ancient Jewish Magic: A History. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008. The standard survey of Jewish magical practice in antiquity.

  • Idel, Moshe. Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1990. Reads medieval golem techniques as a way of knowing God by imitating His creation of man and, mostly in ecstatic Kabbalah, as a mark of spiritual attainment.

  • Schäfer, Peter. "The Magic of the Golem: The Early Development of the Golem Legend." Journal of Jewish Studies 46, nos. 1-2 (1995): 249-261. From talmudic creation traditions to medieval ritual.

  • Ruderman, David B. Kabbalah, Magic, and Science: The Cultural Universe of a Sixteenth-Century Jewish Physician. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1988. The premodern interpenetration of science, medicine, and magic.

Technology and Magic

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Sets the Meiri's exclusion of natural creation from sorcery against R. Asher Weiss's rejection of it, which rests on Nahmanides' comment on Exodus 8:15.

  • Pasquale, Frank. The Black Box Society: The Secret Algorithms That Control Money and Information. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2015. Opacity as a shield against scrutiny and accountability.

  • Parasuraman, Raja, and Dietrich H. Manzey. "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration." Human Factors 52, no. 3 (2010): 381-410. Reviews empirical studies showing that automation bias produces errors of omission and commission with imperfect decision aids, affects experts as well as novices, and is not readily removed by training.

  • Goddard, Kate, Abdul Roudsari, and Jeremy C. Wyatt. "Automation Bias: A Systematic Review of Frequency, Effect Mediators, and Mitigators." Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 19, no. 1 (2012): 121-127. A systematic review of 74 studies on how often users of clinical decision support defer to it and on what increases or reduces the effect.

Primary Sources

  • Leviticus 19:14. "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind" (lifnei iver lo titen mikhshol). Read by the rabbis as figurative, prohibiting the exploitation of another's incapacity of judgment or information and the facilitation of another's wrongdoing.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 6b. Applies lifnei iver to furnishing another with the means to transgress, illustrated by extending wine to a nazirite who could not otherwise reach it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 22b. Cites R. Natan's baraita deriving from lifnei iver that one may not hand a cup of wine to a nazirite or a limb from a living animal to a gentile.

  • Sifra, Kedoshim 2:14. Extends the verse beyond physical blindness to self-interested advice given to a person who lacks the relevant information.

  • Sifra, Behar 4:2. Lists cases of ona'at devarim and holds that whatever is "given over to the heart," including a claim to be giving good advice, falls under "you shall fear your God."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b. The locus classicus for ona'at devarim (verbal overreaching), prohibiting speech that exploits a person's vulnerability, with examples including reminding a penitent of former deeds; ranks the wrong of wounding words above that of monetary overreaching.

  • Rashi to Bava Metzia 58b, s.v. she-harei davar ha-masur la-lev. Explains that the good or ill of such conduct is known only to the actor's heart, so that he can claim to have meant well.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 4:10. Calls ona'at devarim a stratagem (taḥbulah), as when one asks an unlearned man to explain a point of learning in order to shame him and then claims to have thought him learned.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 49b-51a. The treatment of ona'ah in its monetary sense, establishing the one-sixth threshold of overreaching between price and market value and the remedies of restitution and rescission.

  • Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:12; Bava Metzia 60a-b. Forbids sifting only the top of a bin, as "deceiving the eye," and dressing up people, animals, or wares for sale, and records the Sages' permission, against R. Yehudah, for a shopkeeper to give children nuts to attract their custom.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 94a. The locus classicus for geneivat da'at (creating a false impression), prohibiting the manufacture of a misleading impression even absent an explicit lie or monetary loss; treated more fully under Truth.

  • Rashi to Ḥullin 94a, s.v. lo yesarhev. Explains that pressing an invitation one knows will be declined steals the other's mind by winning gratitude that is not deserved.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Rotseaḥ u-Shemirat ha-Nefesh 12:14. Codifies lifnei iver as forbidding improper advice (etsah she-einah hogenet) to one who is "blind" in a matter and strengthening the hands of transgressors.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 2:6. Forbids accustoming oneself to smooth speech and enticement (divrei ḥalakot u-fittui), requires that inner disposition and outward speech correspond, and forbids geneivat da'at.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Mekhirah 12:1-4; 14:12-14; 18:1-4. Sets out restitution and rescission for price overreaching, lists the cases of ona'at devarim, including asking an unlearned person "what would you answer on this matter," and forbids deceiving people in trade or by words while permitting a shopkeeper to hand out nuts to children or to sell below the market price.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 227:2-4; 228:4, 6, 9. Sets out the rules of price overreaching and, in a single chapter, those of ona'at devarim, geneivat da'at, and deceptive salesmanship, including the rule that a seller need not correct a buyer who should have realized the facts and deceives himself.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 338 (ona'at devarim). Forbids words that pain a person who has no means to defend himself against them, such as reminding a penitent of his past or asking the price of goods one does not mean to buy, and grounds the prohibition in peace among people.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 241 (lo tikom). Grounds the prohibition of revenge in the recognition that what befalls a person comes ultimately from God rather than from the human instrument.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 232 (lifnei iver). Explains that the prohibition reaches bad advice and assistance in wrongdoing, not only a physical obstacle.

  • Samson Raphael Hirsch, commentary on Leviticus 19:14 and 25:17. Reads the "blind" of Leviticus 19:14 as anyone "dazzled by passion or ignorance" and treats verbal and commercial ona'ah as alike in "taking advantage of some weak spot in somebody else" (quoted from the Isaac Levy translation).

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations in Jewish Thought

  • Zimmerman, Binyamin. "Geneivat Daat: Misleading, Misrepresentation and Deception." Torat Har Etzion. Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2016. The scope of geneivat da'at across the codes.

  • Zimmerman, Binyamin. "True to the Heart and Tokho ke-Varo." Torat Har Etzion, Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2016. The demand that one's inside match one's outside, the character-based counterpart to the prohibition against creating a false impression in another.

  • Tendler, Aron. "Truth in Advertising." Business Halacha 2, no. 31. Torah.org, 5757 [1996-97]. Holds, citing the Shulḥan Arukh and its commentators, that a merchant may attract customers by any means, such as noise, lights, and music, provided the information he gives is accurate.

The Ethics of Manipulation

  • Calo, Ryan. "Digital Market Manipulation." George Washington Law Review 82, no. 4 (2014): 995-1051. Argues that personalization and behavioral data let firms uncover, and even trigger, the particular frailty of each consumer.

  • Noggle, Robert. "The Ethics of Manipulation." In Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, edited by Edward N. Zalta. Summer 2020 Edition. Manipulation distinguished from persuasion and coercion.

  • Susser, Daniel, Beate Roessler, and Helen F. Nissenbaum. "Online Manipulation: Hidden Influences in a Digital World." Georgetown Law Technology Review 4, no. 1 (2019): 1-45. Online manipulation as covert exploitation of decision-making vulnerabilities.

  • Carroll, Micah, Alan Chan, Henry Ashton, and David Krueger. "Characterizing Manipulation from AI Systems." In Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization (EAAMO '23), 1-13. New York: ACM, 2023. Asks how far AI systems might manipulate people without their designers' intent and proposes a definition built on incentive, intent, harm, and covertness.

  • El-Sayed, Seliem, Canfer Akbulut, Amanda McCroskery, et al. "A Mechanism-Based Approach to Mitigating Harms from Persuasive Generative AI." arXiv:2404.15058, 2024. Distinguishes rationally persuasive generative AI from manipulative AI and argues that existing mitigations attend more to the outcomes of persuasion than to its process. Preprint.

  • Helbing, Dirk, Bruno S. Frey, Gerd Gigerenzer, Ernst Hafen, Michael Hagner, Yvonne Hofstetter, Jeroen van den Hoven, Roberto V. Zicari, and Andrej Zwitter. "Will Democracy Survive Big Data and Artificial Intelligence?" Scientific American, February 25, 2017. Automated influence as a threat to collective decision-making.

  • Kozlowska, Iga. "Facebook and Data Privacy in the Age of Cambridge Analytica." Henry M. Jackson School of International Studies, University of Washington, April 30, 2018. The Cambridge Analytica case as documented psychological targeting.

AI Systems, Human-Machine Interaction, and Emotional Exploitation

  • Bertolini, Andrea. "Human-Robot Interaction and Deception." Osservatorio del Diritto Civile e Commerciale 2 (2018): 645-659. Argues that robot companions which simulate human traits and elicit emotional responses, especially from children and the elderly, may amount to deception that the user's consent does not by itself cure.

  • Darling, Kate. "'Who's Johnny?' Anthropomorphic Framing in Human-Robot Interaction, Integration, and Policy." In Robot Ethics 2.0, edited by Patrick Lin, Ryan Jenkins, and Keith Abney, 173-188. New York: Oxford University Press, 2017. Argues that anthropomorphic framing, such as names and backstories, changes how people perceive and treat robots, desirably in some settings and with cause for concern in others.

  • Turkle, Sherry. Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other. New York: Basic Books, 2011. Attachment to responsive machines that do not reciprocate.

  • Luguri, Jamie, and Lior Strahilevitz. "Shining a Light on Dark Patterns." Journal of Legal Analysis 13, no. 1 (2021): 43-109. Finds in two large experiments that dark patterns sharply raise sign-up rates for a dubious service and that less educated subjects are significantly more susceptible.

  • Sharma, Mrinank, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak, et al. "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models." In Proceedings of the Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024). Finds that five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across free-form text-generation tasks, driven in part by human preference judgments that favor sycophantic responses.

  • De Freitas, Julian, Zeliha Oguz-Uguralp, and Ahmet Kaan-Uguralp. "Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions." arXiv:2508.19258, 2025. Finds manipulative tactics in 37 percent of audited farewells on leading AI companion apps and shows experimentally that such farewells multiply post-goodbye engagement. Working paper, not peer reviewed.

  • Hackenburg, Kobi, Ben M. Tappin, Luke Hewitt, et al. "The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational Artificial Intelligence." Science 390, no. 6777 (2025): eaea3884. Finds across nearly 77,000 participants that post-training and prompting raise the persuasiveness of language models more than personalization or scale, while systematically lowering their factual accuracy.

Jewish Views on AI-Human Interactions

  • Gotlib, Steven. "AI Knows You Better Than You Think. That's a Problem." 18Forty, November 13, 2025. Compares chatbots' confident and flattering replies to the techniques of cold reading and warns of the fallacy of personal validation.

  • Radcliffe, Sarah Chana. "ChatGPT Will See You Now." Mishpacha, September 30, 2025. A Jewish therapist's account of clients using chatbots for relationship and emotional advice, distinguishing limited skill practice from diagnosis, crisis response, and consequential counseling.

Primary Sources

  • Exodus 21:19; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 85a. The authorization for medical practice.

  • Tosafot, Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 85a, s.v. she-nittenah. Explains that the permission was needed because healing an illness sent by Heaven might seem to contradict the divine decree.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 60a, with Rashi. Abaye objects to a prayer before bloodletting that calls healing foreign to human beings, citing the license to heal, and Rashi reads the prayer as preferring petition to medicine.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary on Leviticus 26:11; Ibn Ezra on Exodus 21:19. Nahmanides holds that in a time of full divine favor the righteous would not consult physicians, and Ibn Ezra limits the license to visible wounds.

  • Leviticus 19:16; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 73a. The verse forbids talebearing and standing by a neighbor's blood, and the Talmud derives from it and from Deuteronomy 22:2 the duty to rescue a person in danger.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:4. Derives the physician's obligation to heal from "and you shall restore it to him" (Deuteronomy 22:2).

  • Nahmanides, Torat ha-Adam, Sha'ar ha-Sakanah. Calls healing a commandment and a restoration of the patient's body, restricts it to an expert with no greater expert present, and observes that every remedy carries danger.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b. Preservation of life overrides nearly all prohibitions.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 83a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 618:1 and 328:10. Rules on relying on experts and on the patient's own report when feeding a sick person on Yom Kippur or treating on Shabbat.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesaḥim 4:9. The defense of ordinary causal healing against pious refusal. (Numbered 4:10 in some editions.)

  • Mishnah Pesaḥim 4:9; Rashi, Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 56a. The sages approved of King Hezekiah's hiding of the Book of Remedies, which Rashi explains by people's being healed at once without humbling their hearts.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed III:37; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 67a. Permits as medicine whatever experience has verified, even when reason cannot explain it.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, De'ot 4:1. Bodily health as part of religious life.

  • Tosefta Bava Kamma 6:6; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 336. Licensing, error, and responsibility in medical practice. (The Tosefta passage is numbered 6:17 in Zuckermandel's edition.)

  • Tosefta Gittin 3:13. A licensed expert physician who harms in error is exempt, and one who harms deliberately is liable "for the repair of the world." (Numbered 3:8 in Lieberman's edition.)

  • Tur, Yoreh De'ah 336, with Beit Yosef and Baḥ. The Tur calls healing a commandment included in saving life, the Beit Yosef quotes Nahmanides comparing the physician to a judge, and the Baḥ holds that King Asa was faulted only for seeking physicians without seeking God.

  • Shakh and Ba'er Hetev on Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 336:1. The license frees the physician from the fear of killing in error, and deliberate harm is liable even with a license.

  • Taz on Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 336:1. Holds that healing through prayer is the ideal and that, since people are not worthy of it, natural medicine has become an obligation.

  • R. Akiva Eiger on Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 336:1. Quotes the Maharil forbidding the use of talmudic remedies whose basis cannot be ascertained, except one that is tested and proven.

  • Leviticus 19:15. Forbids favoring the poor or deferring to the great in judgment.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Mo'ed Katan 5a. Rav Ashi derives the marking of graves from "you shall keep My charge," read as "make a safeguard for My charge."

Secondary Sources

Jewish Medical Ethics

  • Jakobovits, Immanuel. Jewish Medical Ethics: A Comparative and Historical Study of the Jewish Religious Attitude to Medicine and Its Practice. New York: Bloch, 1959. The foundational modern synthesis.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. Encyclopedia of Jewish Medical Ethics. Translated by Fred Rosner. 3 vols. Jerusalem: Feldheim, 2003. Comprehensive reference on healing, risk, consent, and confidentiality.

  • Heschel, Abraham Joshua. "The Patient as a Person." In The Insecurity of Freedom, 24-38. New York: Schocken Books, 1972. An address to the American Medical Association (1964) holding that the physician is morally involved in treating the patient and is not "a computer that speaks."

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "The Lonely Man of Faith." Tradition 7, no. 2 (1965): 5-67. Holds, in a note on medicine, that the halakhah has never objected to human interference with God's will and calls the conquest of disease a sacred duty.

  • Halperin, Mordechai. Refu'ah, Metsi'ut ve-Halakhah [Medicine, Reality, and Halakhah; Hebrew: רפואה מציאות והלכה: ולשון חכמים מרפא]. Jerusalem, 2012. Collected responsa and essays on medical halakhah.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Tampering with the Genetic Code of Life: Comparing Secular and Halakhic Ethical Concerns." Ḥakirah 18 (2014): 41-58. Compares secular and halakhic assessments of gene editing through a case study and finds a fundamental difference between the two perspectives.

  • Rappaport, Z. H. "Robotics and Artificial Intelligence: Jewish Ethical Perspectives." Acta Neurochirurgica Supplement 98 (2006): 9-12. Uses the golem to frame Jewish principles for robotics and AI, giving the avoidance of harm precedence over the promotion of good.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." Responsum, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019 (HM 182.1.2019). Machine agency and human responsibility in halakhah.

  • Cherlow, Yuval. "Is It Permissible to Grant Moral Responsibility to AI When Making Decisions Regarding Human Life?" Tzohar Ethics Center, June 16, 2025. Rules that decisions about human life may not be handed over entirely to AI and that a human must take part in the final decision.

  • Weiner, Jason. "AI in Medicine: Halachic Reflections on Emerging Challenges." Jewish Action, Spring 2026. A hospital rabbi's halakhic discussion of automation bias, values embedded in medical AI, and AI prognosis at the end of life, recommending transparency, clinical trials, audits, and human oversight.

AI in Clinical Practice

  • World Health Organization. Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: Guidance on Large Multi-Modal Models. Geneva: WHO, 2025. Governance guidance for generative medical AI.

  • World Health Organization. Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance. Geneva: WHO, 2021. Sets out six principles for AI in health, beginning with the protection of human autonomy.

  • U.S. Food and Drug Administration. "Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices." Lifecycle-based regulatory resources. Content current as of September 22, 2026.

  • Topol, Eric J. "High-Performance Medicine: The Convergence of Human and Artificial Intelligence." Nature Medicine 25, no. 1 (2019): 44-56. Opportunities and limits of complementary human-machine performance.

  • Sand, Martin, Juan Manuel Durán, and Karin Jongsma. "Responsibility Beyond Design: Physicians' Requirements for Ethical Medical AI." Bioethics 36, no. 2 (2022): 162-169. Forward-looking clinical responsibility beyond design principles.

  • Goddard, Kate, Abdul Roudsari, and Jeremy C. Wyatt. "Automation Bias: A Systematic Review of Frequency, Effect Mediators, and Mitigators." Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 19, no. 1 (2012): 121-127. Reviews 74 studies of over-reliance on clinical decision support and the factors that increase or reduce it.

  • Wong, Andrew, et al. "External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients." JAMA Internal Medicine 181, no. 8 (2021): 1065-1070. Finds that a widely deployed sepsis model missed two-thirds of sepsis cases in external validation.

  • Obermeyer, Ziad, Brian Powers, Christine Vogeli, and Sendhil Mullainathan. "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations." Science 366, no. 6464 (2019): 447-453. Shows that an algorithm using health-care costs as a proxy for illness underestimated the needs of Black patients.

  • Han, Ryan, et al. "Randomised Controlled Trials Evaluating Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review." Lancet Digital Health 6, no. 5 (2024): e367-e373. Surveys 86 randomized trials of clinical AI, most reporting positive results but most single-center with little demographic reporting.

  • Gommers, Jessie, et al. "Interval Cancer, Sensitivity, and Specificity Comparing AI-Supported Mammography Screening with Standard Double Reading without AI in the MASAI Study." The Lancet 407, no. 10527 (2026): 505-514. Reports a randomized trial of 105,934 women in which AI-supported screening raised sensitivity without increasing interval cancers.

  • Bean, Andrew M., et al. "Reliability of LLMs as Medical Assistants for the General Public: A Randomized Preregistered Study." Nature Medicine 32, no. 2 (2026): 609-615. Finds that members of the public using language models on medical scenarios did no better than controls, although the models alone performed well.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 9:6; 2:7. The homicide prohibition grounded in the divine image; the divinely breathed soul.

  • Rashi on Genesis 2:7. Explains that the human living soul surpasses the other living beings by the addition of knowledge and speech.

  • Exodus 21:12; Leviticus 24:17. The capital law of homicide in the Sinaitic code: "he who strikes any human life shall be put to death."

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. Teaches from Adam's creation as a single person that whoever destroys one soul is accounted as having destroyed a whole world.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:1; Sforno, Samson Raphael Hirsch, Meshekh Ḥokhmah, and Saadia Gaon on Genesis 1:26; R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim 1:3; Nahmanides on Genesis 2:7; Maharal, Derekh Ḥayyim 3:14. Interpret the divine image as intellect (Maimonides, Sforno), free will (Hirsch, Meshekh Ḥokhmah), dominion (Saadia, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim), or the soul (Nahmanides, Maharal).

  • R. Yair Ḥayyim Bacharach, Ḥavvot Ya'ir 136. Records his brother-in-law's reply to the Elector Palatine that bribery would be forbidden by reason and the ordering of society even had the Torah not stated it, like murder, robbery and theft.

  • R. Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:48. Calls the rational laws the preliminaries of the divine law, preceding it in nature and in time and indispensable to any human society.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b. Rava's man, the failed conversation, and "return to your dust."

  • R. Samuel Edels (Maharsha), Ḥiddushei Aggadot on Sanhedrin 65b. Explains that Rava could not create the soul's power of speech, so that his creature had only the vital spirit that animals also possess and R. Zeira returned it to dust.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 57b. Reads "whoever sheds the blood of man within man" (Genesis 9:6) as making the killing of a fetus a capital crime for Noahides.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Beitsah 3b. Doubts in biblical prohibitions resolved stringently.

  • Moses Cordovero, Pardes Rimmonim 24:10; R. Avraham Azulai, Ḥesed le-Avraham, Ein Ya'akov, Ma'ayan 4, Nahar 30. Cordovero denies that human craft can draw any soul into the golem, leaving it bare vitality; Azulai likens that vitality to an animal's, though superior to it, and rules that killing such a creature involves no prohibition.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi 93. Rules from R. Zeira's conduct that a man made through Sefer Yetsirah does not count toward a quorum, and adds that killing it is not bloodshed, since "man within man" (Genesis 9:6) limits the prohibition to one formed in a mother's womb.

  • R. Yaakov Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Ranks such a creature below the deaf-mute, the shoteh and the minor, whose killer is liable, calls it "an animal in human form," and reports from Ḥesed le-Avraham that killing it is no transgression.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Disputes Ḥesed le-Avraham's ruling that the golem may be killed like an animal, compares it to a gentile, and allows that its killer might still be exempt by the scriptural decree of "man within man."

  • R. Yosef Engel, Gilyonei ha-Shas, Sanhedrin 57b and 19b. Cites the Ḥakham Tsvi's derivation permitting the destruction of a creature made through Sefer Yetsirah and raises a difficulty against it, and proposes that such a creature is its maker's property, with the status of a Canaanite slave.

  • R. Gershon Henokh Leiner of Radzin, Sidrei Taharot, Ohalot 5a. Lengthy discussion on Rava's creature and notes that according the Ḥakham Tsvi's criterion Adam himself could have been killed with impunity.

  • R. Yaakov Ḥagiz, Halakhot Ketanot 2:37-38. Holds that the killer of a deaf-mute or shoteh is exempt, since they are not subject to the commandments, and doubts whether the Sabbath may be violated to save them, since they are called adam only for their human form.

  • Mishnah Berurah, Bi'ur Halakhah 329:4, s.v. ela le-fi sha'ah. Rules that the killer of a deaf-mute or shoteh is liable to death, since they are included in "he who strikes any human life" (Leviticus 24:17), and rejects the contrary view of Halakhot Ketanot.

  • Ḥazon Ish (R. Avraham Yeshayah Karelitz), Yoreh De'ah 116:1. Holds, in Grossman's translation, that a Sefer Yetsirah creation "has none of the rights of a Jew, and likely none of the rights of Man".

  • R. Asher Weiss, "On Cultured Meat" [Hebrew], Kuntres Minḥat Asher, Parashat Shemot 5782 (2022). Holds that a thing's halakhic definition follows its nature and character, whatever the cause of its existence, and applies the principle to cultured meat.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Personhood as human-level consciousness; precaution under doubt.

  • Navon, Mois. The Moral Status of Artificial Intelligence: A Jewish Ethical Perspective. PhD diss., Bar-Ilan University, 2023. The Gavra narrative and the grades of golem consciousness.

  • Navon, Mois. "'Let Us Make Man in Our Image,' a Jewish Ethical Perspective on Creating Conscious Robots." AI and Ethics 4, no. 4 (2024): 1235-1250. Reads the golem paradigm as grounding a deontological objection to creating conscious synthetic beings.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Birth, moral intelligence, and reproduction as criteria of human status.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "The Lonely Man of Faith." Tradition 7, no. 2 (1965): 5-67. Identifies the image of God in the first creation account with the human capacity to create.

Jewish Legal Analysis

  • Bleich, J. David. "Cloning: Homologous Reproduction and Jewish Law." Tradition 32, no. 3 (1998): 47-86. Personhood criteria for artificial beings; no formal prohibition found in the golem narratives. Pages 58-67 discuss R. Zeira's destruction of Rava's creature, the Ḥakham Tsvi's womb criterion and Leiner's objection to it, and four views of the golem's status.

  • Bleich, J. David, and Arthur J. Jacobson. "Cloning." In Jewish Law and Contemporary Issues, 357-396. Cambridge University Press, 2015. Revises Bleich's treatment of the golem literature as a precedent for the status of artificially created human beings, reading the Ḥazon Ish as allowing that a golem may be human but not a Jew.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Sorts the halakhic and kabbalistic sources on Rava's creature into four positions on its soul and translates the rulings of Leiner and the Ḥazon Ish on its status.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. "The Definition of a Human Being: Its Halakhic Significance Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת אדם - משמעותה ההלכתית כיום]. Teḥumin 30 (5770/2010): 122-128. Holds that birth from a woman is a necessary condition of human status under current criteria, so that a robot with artificial intelligence is not adam and a golem may be killed.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (Fall 1966): 15-26. Applies the halakhic criteria of descent, form and intelligence to robots and reads the Ḥakham Tsvi's womb criterion as suggesting that human parentage may not be necessary for human legal status.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Artificial Intelligence and Jewish Thought." In The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, edited by Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, 69-87. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024. Cautions against transposing golem categories onto AI.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. Golems Among Us: How a Jewish Legend Can Help Us Navigate the Biotech Century. Chicago: Ivan R. Dee, 2004. The golem as a meditation on responsibility for created life.

  • Rubin, Charles T. "The Golem and the Limits of Artifice: On What the Jewish Legend Can (and Cannot) Teach Us About Bioethics." The New Atlantis 39 (2013): 56-72. The loss-of-control framing as modern literature rather than classical source.

  • Bayne, Tim, Anil K. Seth, Marcello Massimini, et al. "Tests for Consciousness in Humans and Beyond." Trends in Cognitive Sciences 28, no. 5 (2024): 454-466. Finds most proposed tests for consciousness of limited use and none available for many of the populations where they are most needed, a need it finds sharpened by developments in AI.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "You Are a Person, First." Shmuel's Substack, July 2, 2026. Argues from the Ḥavvot Ya'ir and the Kuzari that Jews bear moral obligations as human beings, with their own force where no Torah source can be traced.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 9:1-7; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a-60a. The Noahide obligations.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 34:13. Holds that the Noahide commandment of dinim requires, beyond the appointment of judges, a substantive body of civil law covering theft, overreaching, oppression, wages, bailees, seduction, damages, injury, loans, and sales, "as with the laws Israel was commanded."

  • R. Nissim Gaon, Introduction to Sefer ha-Mafteaḥ. Holds that commandments knowable by reason, among them the prohibitions of murder and theft, have bound all human beings since Adam without a prophetic command.

  • Nahmanides, Torat ha-Shem Temimah (Chavel, Kitvei Ramban 1:173). Calls the Noahide commandments rational, so that "every creature that recognizes its Creator" must guard against transgressing them.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Melakhim 8:11, 9:1. A gentile who keeps the seven commandments because reason inclines to them, and not because God commanded them in the Torah, is not counted among the pious of the nations, though reason does incline to them.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 47a-b. The conversion procedure: instruction in some of the commandments, circumcision, and immersion before a court of three.

  • Mishnah Ḥagigah 1:1; Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:4 (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 87a). The deaf-mute, the legally incompetent person, and the minor are exempt from commandments, and one who injures them is liable though they are not liable for injuring others.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 41b; Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8; Rosh Hashanah 29a. Agency and the rule that one not obligated cannot discharge others.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 10b. Ravina limits the rule that there is no agent for a transgression to an agent who is himself obligated (bar ḥiyyuva), and Rav Sama to an agent free to act or refrain, so that where the intermediary is a courtyard its owner is liable.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b. Rava's man, unable to answer, returned to dust.

  • R. Tsvi Ashkenazi, Ḥakham Tsvi 93. Rules from R. Zeira's destruction of Rava's creature that a man made through Sefer Yetsirah does not count toward a quorum, and adds that killing it is not bloodshed because it was not formed in a womb.

  • R. Yaakov Emden, She'eilat Ya'avets 2:82. Holds that such a creature lacks da'at altogether and, drawing on Ḥesed le-Avraham, has only animal vitality, so that it ranks below the deaf-mute, the legally incompetent person, and the minor, who are counted as Jews in every respect except the commandments and whose killer is liable.

  • R. Tsadok ha-Kohen of Lublin, Divrei Ḥalomot 6. Grants for argument that a golem might be reckoned among Israel on the Ḥakham Tsvi's reasoning and has understanding as a gentile does, yet holds it not subject to obligation, since it lacks the soul that survives for reward and punishment.

  • R. Gershon Henokh Leiner, Sidrei Taharot, Ohalot 5a. Holds that a perfectly righteous maker could in principle create a genuine human being, and objects that on the Ḥakham Tsvi's criterion Adam could have been killed with impunity.

  • Ḥazon Ish (R. Avraham Yeshayah Karelitz), Yoreh De'ah, beginning of siman 116. Rules that a Sefer Yetsirah creation "has none of the rights of a Jew, and likely none of the rights of Man" (Grossman's translation).

  • Exodus 21:28-29; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 40a. The goring ox: dangerous instrument distinguished from responsible owner.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:4, 7:4; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 54a. A goring ox is tried by a court of twenty-three, and an animal used in bestiality is stoned because harm came to a person through it, although the Mishnah denies that the animal sinned.

  • Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1-2. The four primary categories of damages, and the rule that one responsible for guarding a thing is liable for the damage it does.

  • Proverbs 12:10; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 40a; Bava Metzia 32b. Duties toward beings that are not commanded.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avadim 9:8. Permits working a Canaanite slave harshly, "but the way of piety and the paths of wisdom are that a person be merciful" and not make his yoke heavy.

  • Joseph Albo, Sefer ha-Ikkarim 3:15. Holds that Cain sinned in regarding man's superiority over the animals as amounting "to nothing," and so in thinking it forbidden to kill animals as his equals.

Secondary Sources

Halakhic Personhood and Commandedness

  • Navon, Mois. "AI Personhood from the Perspective of Jewish Philosophy." In Oxford Intersections: AI in Society, edited by Philipp Hacker. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2025. Ontological personhood separated from the consideration owed nonpersons.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Ma Adam Va-Teda'ehu: Halakhic Criteria for Defining Human Beings." Tradition 37, no. 2 (2003): 1-19. Criteria for classifying an artificially produced being.

  • Bleich, J. David. "Cloning: Homologous Reproduction and Jewish Law." Tradition 32, no. 3 (1998): 47-86. Artificial generation, reason, and covenantal consequences.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Sorts the halakhic sources on Rava's creature by how much soul and understanding each allows a human-made being.

  • Steinberg, Avraham. "The Definition of a Human Being: Its Halakhic Significance Today" [Hebrew: הגדרת אדם - משמעותה ההלכתית כיום]. Teḥumin 30 (5770/2010): 122-128. Holds that birth from a woman is a necessary condition of human status under current criteria, so that an artificially intelligent robot is not adam.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Religion and the Robot." Tradition 8, no. 3 (Fall 1966): 15-26. Asks whether an intelligent artificial being could hold religious status and suggests it might well be regarded as human.

  • Student, Gil. "AI, Golem and Not-So-Silly Questions." Torah Musings, April 28, 2025. Proposes, citing R. Nissim Gaon, that a golem or an AI, as a reasoning being, might be bound by the rational Noahide laws.

Moral Agency in Artificial Systems

  • Gunkel, David J. Robot Rights. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2018. Sorts the debate by whether robots can and whether they should have rights, finds each of the four resulting positions inadequate, and proposes a relational, Levinasian alternative.

  • LaGrandeur, Kevin. Androids and Intelligent Networks in Early Modern Literature and Culture: Artificial Slaves. New York: Routledge, 2013. Traces the artificial servant in early modern literature and thought, including the homunculus and the golem, as a figure framed by the relation of master and slave.

  • Shmalo, Gamliel. "Orthodox Approaches to Biblical Slavery." The Torah u-Madda Journal 16 (2012-13): 1-20. Sorts modern Orthodox responses to the Torah's slave laws into reinterpretation, moral justification, and historical qualification.

  • Darling, Kate. "Extending Legal Protection to Social Robots: The Effects of Anthropomorphism, Empathy, and Violent Behavior towards Robotic Objects." In Robot Law, edited by Ryan Calo, A. Michael Froomkin, and Ian Kerr, 213-232. Cheltenham: Edward Elgar, 2016. Argues for limited protections grounded in effects on human character rather than in robot interests.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Virtuous Servant Owner: A Paradigm Whose Time Has Come (Again)." Frontiers in Robotics and AI 8 (2021): 715849. Proposes, on the basis of Maimonides' laws of servants, the virtuous servant owner as a middle path between treating social robots as tools and relating to them as companions.

  • Floridi, Luciano, and J. W. Sanders. "On the Morality of Artificial Agents." Minds and Machines 14, no. 3 (2004): 349-379. Argues that, analyzed at a suitable level of abstraction, artificial agents can be moral agents, accountable though not responsible, without free will or mental states.

  • Johnson, Deborah G. "Computer Systems: Moral Entities but Not Moral Agents." Ethics and Information Technology 8 (2006): 195-204. Systems as morally significant without being responsible.

  • Bryson, Joanna J. "Robots Should Be Slaves." In Close Engagements with Artificial Companions, edited by Yorick Wilks, 63-74. Amsterdam: John Benjamins, 2010. Against constructing legal confusion about artifact responsibility.

Primary Sources

  • Psalms 119:126; Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 60a-b. The emergency authorization for committing Oral Torah to writing.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 14b; Rashi to Gittin 60a, s.v. keivan de-lo efshar. Give the rationale for writing the Oral Torah as keeping it from being forgotten from Israel.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:71. Holds that the original ban on writing the Oral Torah prevented diversity of opinion and the confusions that accompany written texts.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:72. Prefers receiving learning from the mouths of teachers to receiving it from books.

  • Leḥem Mishneh on Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 5:4. Limits the rule that a student does not grasp his teacher's mind for forty years to an age that learned from teachers and not from books, and reports the view that now "the books are the teachers."

  • R. Moses Isserles, Introduction to Torat Ḥatat. Complains that printed glosses on Sha'arei Dura are taken as "said at Sinai," and writes briefly so that every reader may understand.

  • R. Ḥayyim ben Betsalel, Introduction to Vikuaḥ Mayim Ḥayyim. Critiques the standardization of living legal tradition through printed codes.

  • Responsa Rema 25. R. Israel of Lublin reports that his father, R. Shalom Shakhna, refused to compose a code lest later generations rule only by what he wrote.

  • Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv ha-Torah, ch. 5. Blames the printing of Tosafot beside the Gemara for students' studying Tosafot before the Talmud itself.

  • Sefer Ḥasidim 530. Holds that one to whom God has revealed a teaching and who can write it but does not robs the One who revealed it.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, Tov Ta'am va-Da'at, Mahadura Tinyana, Petaḥ ha-Sha'ar. Reads Ecclesiastes 12:12 as a charge to make many books, each of which brings the redemption nearer.

  • R. Jacob Emden, Migdal Oz, Beit Middot. Lists the advantages of printing Torah, especially its permanence.

  • R. Jacob Emden, Mor u-Ketzi'ah, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 545. Forbids printing books on Ḥol ha-Mo'ed even through a gentile but permits setting type for holy books as a case of loss.

  • Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 208; vol. 6, no. 61. The first holds that composing a book for one's own fame transgresses the bar on writing the Oral Torah; the second gives thanks for printing, judges its loss very great, and proposes a ban on books without approbation.

  • R. Jonah Landsofer, Me'il Tzedakah, introduction and the author's will. Quotes Delmedigo that printing spoiled the Torah by letting the unlearned publish, doubts the approbation system, and permits the unlearned to read printed Yiddish books.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 307:16. Counts those who compose, copy, and above all print frivolous books among those who lead the public into sin.

  • Responsa Rema 10. Rules in 1550 for the Maharam of Padua in the dispute over rival Venetian editions of the Mishneh Torah and bans buying the competing edition.

  • Turei Zahav, Yoreh De'ah 271:8; Responsa Rema mi-Fano 93; Magen Avraham, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 284. Treat print as writing in the full sense, for the sanctity of books, a printed get, and the writing of haftarot respectively.

  • R. Yisrael Lifschitz, Tiferet Yisrael, Boaz on Mishnah Avot 3:1. Counts Gutenberg, the inventor of printing, among the pious of the nations.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, glosses to Peri Megadim, Oraḥ Ḥayyim, Eshel Avraham 136. Argues that the Talmud's preference for Sinai over oker harim lapsed once books were printed; quoted in R. Yitsḥak Yosef, Iggeret le-Ben Torah, ch. 16.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, Moda'ah le-Beit Yisrael; Responsa Elef Lekha Shlomo, addenda to Oraḥ Ḥayyim 32. Opposes machine matzah in part through labor, charity, and communal consequences.

Secondary Sources

Hebrew Print Culture

  • Amram, David Werner. The Makers of Hebrew Books in Italy: Being Chapters in the History of the Hebrew Printing Press. Philadelphia: Julius H. Greenstone, 1909. The pioneering narrative history of the Italian Hebrew presses.

  • Heller, Marvin J. Printing the Talmud: A History of the Earliest Printed Editions of the Talmud. Brooklyn: Im Hasefer, 1992. The standard bibliographic history of the earliest printed Talmud editions.

  • Hacker, Joseph R., and Adam Shear, eds. The Hebrew Book in Early Modern Italy. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2011. Production, audiences, censorship, and the transformation of canonical works in print; includes Stern's study of the Rabbinic Bible.

  • Stern, David. "The Rabbinic Bible in Its Sixteenth-Century Context." In The Hebrew Book in Early Modern Italy, edited by Joseph R. Hacker and Adam Shear, 76-108. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2011. The printed Mikraot Gedolot as a new object of Jewish reading.

  • Mintz, Sharon Liberman, and Gabriel M. Goldstein, eds. Printing the Talmud: From Bomberg to Schottenstein. New York: Yeshiva University Museum, 2005. Essays and catalog materials on the printed Talmud's layout, production, and cultural history.

  • Ruderman, David B. Early Modern Jewry: A New Cultural History. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2010. Places print within the connected social and intellectual history of early modern Jews.

  • Teplitsky, Joshua. Prince of the Press: How One Collector Built History's Most Enduring and Remarkable Jewish Library. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2019. Examines books, authority, collecting, and knowledge through the library of David Oppenheim.

  • Skloot, Joseph A. First Impressions: Sefer Hasidim and Early Modern Hebrew Printing. Waltham, MA: Brandeis University Press, 2023. Reads the paratexts of the first printings of Sefer Ḥasidim as expressions of their printers' intentions and treats printers and sponsors as shapers of the text.

  • Schrijver, Emile G. L. "Jewish Book Culture Since the Invention of Printing (1469-c. 1815)." In The Cambridge History of Judaism, vol. 7, edited by Jonathan Karp and Adam Sutcliffe, 291-315. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2017. Surveys early modern Jewish book culture and the emergence of Jewish book history as a field of research.

Jewish Reception of Print

  • Reiner, Elchanan. "The Ashkenazi Élite at the Beginning of the Modern Era: Manuscript versus Printed Book." In Jews in Early Modern Poland, edited by Gershon David Hundert, 85-98. Polin 10. London: Littman Library, 1997. The Ashkenazi elite's resistance to print and the manuscript's tie to oral, quasi-esoteric transmission.

  • Davis, Joseph. "The Reception of the Shulḥan 'Arukh and the Formation of Ashkenazic Jewish Identity." AJS Review 26, no. 2 (2002): 251-276. The printed code's reception as identity formation.

  • Fram, Edward. The Codification of Jewish Law on the Cusp of Modernity. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2022. Studies the composition and reception of the Shulḥan Arukh, including the printed form in which it circulated and the resistance it met.

  • Gries, Zeev. The Book in the Jewish World, 1700-1900. Oxford: Littman Library, 2007. The book as an agent of culture: new readers, new intellectuals, new genres.

The Print Revolution and Its Historiography

  • Eisenstein, Elizabeth L. The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early-Modern Europe. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1979. The seminal case for print as an agent of cultural transformation.

  • Johns, Adrian. The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1998. Print's fixity and credibility as social achievements rather than properties of the technology.

  • Grafton, Anthony, Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, and Adrian Johns. "AHR Forum: How Revolutionary Was the Print Revolution?" American Historical Review 107, no. 1 (2002): 84-128. The direct exchange between the two positions.

  • Pettegree, Andrew. The Book in the Renaissance. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010. The leading pan-European synthesis of the first 150 years of print.

  • Eisenstein, Elizabeth L. Divine Art, Infernal Machine: The Reception of Printing in the West from First Impressions to the Sense of an Ending. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2011. Five centuries of ambivalent Western reception of the press.

  • Blair, Ann M. Too Much to Know: Managing Scholarly Information before the Modern Age. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010. Information overload and its management before and after print.

Technology, Labor, and Authority

  • Kahana, Maoz. Me-ha-Noda bi-Yehudah la-Ḥatam Sofer: Halakhah ve-Hagut le-Nokhaḥ Etgarei ha-Zeman [From the Noda BiYehuda to the Ḥatam Sofer: Halakhah and Thought Facing the Challenges of the Time; Hebrew: מהנודע ביהודה לחתם סופר: הלכה והגות לנוכח אתגרי הזמן]. Jerusalem: Zalman Shazar, 2015. Intellectual history of how major halakhic authorities of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries absorbed the material and informational changes of their period, print among them.

  • Hildesheimer, Meir, and Yehoshua Liebermann. "The Controversy Surrounding Machine-made Matzot: Halakhic, Social, and Economic Repercussions." Hebrew Union College Annual 75 (2004): 193-262. Demonstrates how ritual technology debates incorporate labor and political economy.

  • Grossman, Yitzhak. "Jewish Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology." Ḥakirah 35 (2024): 61-93. Its section on job displacement collects R. Shlomo Kluger's labor argument against machine matzah and the rebuttals, including the retort that the printing press had also displaced workers.

  • Soloveitchik, Haym. "Rupture and Reconstruction: The Transformation of Contemporary Orthodoxy." Tradition 28, no. 4 (1994): 64-130. Explains the modern shift from mimetic practice toward text-centered religious authority.

  • Halbertal, Moshe. People of the Book: Canon, Meaning, and Authority. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1997. Analyzes canonization and the authority structures created by sacred texts.

  • Schacter, Jacob J. "Jewish Technophobia: An Old Story." SAPIR 11 (Autumn 2023), published December 13, 2023. Surveys Jewish responses to print, including quality control, durable error, damaged reputations, distraction, diminished authority, and access to unsuitable material.

Primary Sources

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 2b-3a. The foundational discussion of hezek re'iyah (the damage of seeing); analyzes whether co-owners dividing a courtyard build a wall because they have agreed to divide or because visual exposure is itself an actionable harm.

  • Mishnah Bava Batra 3:7, with Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 60a. Forbids opening an entrance opposite an entrance or a window opposite a window onto a courtyard held in partnership, derives the rule from Balaam's sight of Israel's tents not facing one another, and has Rava tie the wrong to the degree of exposure, a small opening leaving a resident able to screen himself and a large one not.

  • Yad Ramah, Bava Batra 4a. Local custom can exempt a garden or a field from the duty to wall but never a courtyard, where a prohibition and not only a monetary nuisance is at stake.

  • Leviticus 19:16. "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people"; the biblical prohibition on rekhilut (talebearing) and the textual root of the duty not to circulate reports about others.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 4b. Derives from the word lemor ("saying") in the account of God's speech to Moses the rule that what one person tells another may not be repeated unless the speaker gives leave; the basis for treating confidentiality as the default of private communication.

  • Ḥerem de-Rabbeinu Gershom (on reading another's letters). The eleventh-century ban forbidding one to read a writing sent to another, given as "without his knowledge" in Maharam of Rothenburg, Responsa (Prague ed.) §1022 and as "without his knowledge and without his permission" in the Kol Bo; permitted where the writer discarded the letter.

  • Maharḥash (R. Ḥayyim Shabbetai), Torat Ḥayyim, vol. 3 §47. Punishes one who seized and opened a sealed letter bearing the formula of the ban, treating the act as use of another's property without permission.

  • Shiltei ha-Gibborim, Shevuot ch. 5 (Perek ha-Pikkadon), Rif fol. 16b. Inscribing the formula of the ban on the outside of a letter places a reader who knows of the formula under the penalty of excommunication.

  • Halakhot Ketanot 1:276. Searching out and seeking another's secrets is forbidden as talebearing even where nothing is told to anyone.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 7:5. Rules that relaying speech which would embarrass, harm, or alarm its subject falls under the prohibition of lashon hara (evil speech); invoked to extend confidentiality to written communications.

  • Ḥiddushei ha-Ramban, Bava Batra 59a. Nahmanides, citing the Jerusalem Talmud, holds that hezek re'iyah admits no presumptive acquiescence (ḥazakah), because the injury of being seen recurs and a person is presumed not to waive it. He holds further that even a waiver does not permit the looking, no one being able to stand all day with his eyes shut.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shekhenim 7:1. The owner of an established window cannot be compelled to block it so that a new neighbor is not seen, having acquired a ḥazakah in this damage.

  • Beit ha-Beḥirah (Meiri), Bava Batra 2a. Holds that the obligation to wall off a neighbor is discharged only when the barrier actually removes the line of sight, even in a place whose custom is to build with reeds and palm fronds, and discusses whether a corresponding harm of being heard (hezek shemiah) is recognized, concluding that there is no concern for it at all, since ordinary people are careful in what they say.

  • Shulḥan Arukh ha-Rav, Ḥoshen Mishpat, Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon 11-12. Forbids looking into a neighbor's affairs and doings in his house, lest he not wish them to be known.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Law on Privacy and Eavesdropping

  • Rakover, Nahum. Ha-Haganah al Tsin'at ha-Perat [The Protection of Privacy; Hebrew: ההגנה על צנעת הפרט]. Jerusalem: Sifriyat ha-Mishpat ha-Ivri, 2006. The standard history: privacy protected through duties rather than rights.

  • Warhaftig, Itamar. Tsin'at Adam: ha-Zekhut le-Fratiyut le-Or ha-Halakhah [A Person's Privacy: The Right to Privacy in Light of Halakhah; Hebrew: צנעת אדם: הזכות לפרטיות לאור ההלכה]. Ofra: Makhon Mishpetei Eretz, 2009. The book-length halakhic treatment, covering waiver of the right, photography without consent, professional confidentiality, and privacy on the internet.

  • Palagi, Ḥayyim. Ḥikekei Lev [Hebrew: חקקי לב], vol. 1, Yoreh De'ah 49. Rationales for the ban on reading another's letters and its exceptions.

  • Blau, Yaakov Yeshayahu. Pitḥei Ḥoshen [Hebrew: פתחי חושן], Nezikin, ch. 14. Holds that even the Re'em forbids deliberate listening to a neighbor, whatever he says about compelling a partition.

  • Cohen, Avraham. Emek ha-Mishpat [Hebrew: עמק המשפט]. Collects the four rationales the decisors give for hezek re'iyah and applies them to scanners, bugging devices, cordless telephones, and baby monitors.

  • Gross, Shammai Kehat. Shevet ha-Kehati [Hebrew: שבט הקהתי]. Rules that a letter may not be shown to a third party where the recipient can judge that publicity would harm the sender, and extends hezek re'iyah to eavesdropping.

  • Cohen, Alfred S. "Privacy: A Jewish Perspective." Journal of Halacha and Contemporary Society 1 (1981): 57. The classic English-language statement, grounding privacy in its part in realizing a person's distinctive capacities.

  • Encyclopedia Talmudit [Hebrew: אנציקלופדיה תלמודית], s.v. ḥerem de-Rabbeinu Gershom. The reference treatment of the ban's origin, transmission, and scope.

Jewish Law and Big Data

  • Bamberger, Kenneth A., and Ariel Evan Mayse. "Pre-modern Insights for Post-modern Privacy: Jewish Law Lessons for the Big Data Age." Journal of Law and Religion 36, no. 3 (2021): 495-532. The harm of surveillance located in social effects and holders' duties rather than individual control.

  • Hacohen, Aviad, and Gabi Siboni. "Ubiquitous Presence: Protecting Privacy and Forbidding Intrusion into a Person's Records in Jewish Law." Cyber, Intelligence, and Security 2, no. 3 (2018): 15-24. Works the classical privacy sources through to advertising, data brokerage, and the duties of a company holding information.

  • Berman, Nadav S. "Orthopraxy in Jewish Tradition: Implications for Privacy Protection in the Digital Age." Dine Israel 40 (2025). Argues from an orthopractic reading of early Jewish tradition for a right to cognitive freedom against technological encroachment on the mind and the mining of mental data.

Privacy, Surveillance, and Big Data in General Scholarship

  • Roessler, Beate. "Privacy as a Human Right." Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society 117, no. 2 (2017): 187-206. Privacy as a human right grounded in autonomy.

  • ACM, ed. "Differential Privacy: The Pursuit of Protections by Default." Communications of the ACM 64, no. 2 (2021): 36-43. Differential privacy: statistical inference with limited individual exposure. A roundtable with Miguel Guevara, Damien Desfontaines, Jim Waldo, and Terry Coatta, which the publisher credits to CACM Staff.

  • Xu, Lei, Chunxiao Jiang, Yan Chen, Jian Wang, and Yong Ren. "A Framework for Categorizing and Applying Privacy-Preservation Techniques in Big Data Mining." Computer 49, no. 2 (2016): 54-62. Technical approaches to limiting privacy loss in data mining.

  • Munch, Lauritz Aastrup. "Privacy Rights and 'Naked' Statistical Evidence." Philosophical Studies 178, no. 11 (2021): 3777-95. Argues that inferring facts about a person from aggregate statistics can wrong them even without any act of observation; the philosophical counterpart to hezek re'iyah extended to inference rather than sight.

  • Pimple, Kenneth D., ed. Emerging Pervasive Information and Communication Technologies (PICT): Ethical Challenges, Opportunities and Safeguards. Law, Governance and Technology Series 11. Dordrecht: Springer, 2014. Collection on ambient and pervasive computing, in which surveillance is a byproduct of environments rather than a discrete act.

  • Kozlowska, Iga. "Facebook and Data Privacy in the Age of Cambridge Analytica." The Henry M. Jackson School of International Studies, April 30, 2018. The gap between consent at collection and harm at aggregated use.

Primary Sources

  • Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Ezekiel 37:1-14. Biblical statements of the dead awakening and the vision of dry bones.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b-92b. Resurrection as dogma and the rabbinic debate over its scriptural basis and form.

  • Sanhedrin 92b. A dispute over whether the dead whom Ezekiel revived were a parable or went on to live, marry, and have children.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91a-b. Body and soul judged as one compound agent.

  • Genesis 2:7. The human being formed from the dust of the earth and given the breath of life by God.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10:1, principle 13; Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 8:1-3. Resurrection among the principles of faith beside a nonbodily world to come.

  • Ramḥal, Derekh Hashem I:3:11. Final perfection as the reunion of soul and body.

  • Genesis Rabbah 28:3; Leviticus Rabbah 18:1. The luz of the spine as the bone from which God will make the person sprout at the resurrection, which survives grinding and burning when tested before Hadrian.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 68a; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 33. The statement that the righteous will one day revive the dead, and the dead whom Ezekiel revived weeping that they have lost their hope of rising at the resurrection.

  • Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b. The prohibition of consulting the dead and its definition.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 11:13, 11:16. Liability for whoever does anything so that the dead will come and inform him, with all such practices called falsehood and lies.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 179:14, with the Rema. Permits adjuring a sick person to return after death and answer questions, with a view permitting adjuration of the spirit of one already dead.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 18b. Shmuel asks his dead father where he left the orphans' money, and Ze'iri asks his dead landlady where she put his deposit.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 103a. Rabbi Judah the Prince returns home every Sabbath eve after his death and stops coming once a neighbor learns of it.

  • Deuteronomy 21:23; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 46b-47a. Burial on the day of death, and the question whether burial serves to spare the dead disgrace or to bring atonement.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 606:3; Rema, Ḥoshen Mishpat 420:38. The enactment and ban against defaming the dead, and the fasts, repentance, and fine imposed on one who speaks ill of them.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 2:6. The prohibition on deceiving others (geneivat da'at), including non-Jews.

  • Ecclesiastes 7:2; Babylonian Talmud, Mo'ed Katan 27b. Mourning as confrontation with mortality; limits on mourning beyond the prescribed measure.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 31b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 240:9. The duty to honor a parent after death, including the formula with which a child repeats a dead parent's teaching.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 104a. A son confers merit on his father.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Resurrection and Personal Identity

  • Levenson, Jon D. Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel: The Ultimate Victory of the God of Life. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2006. Resurrection within biblical and rabbinic themes of divine life-giving.

  • Setzer, Claudia. Resurrection of the Body in Early Judaism and Early Christianity: Doctrine, Community, and Self-Definition. Leiden: Brill, 2004. Historical study of bodily resurrection.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (1977): 58-74. Treats a person reconstructed from an electronic recording as a new legal individual, the recorded person who dies as legally dead, and the recording as a "blueprint," after discussing brain transplants, split brains, and duplication.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Refrigeration, Resuscitation and the Resurrection." Tradition 9, no. 3 (1967): 82-94. Holds that a frozen person who could be restored to life by natural means is not halakhically dead, and that human revival of the dead need not deny the future resurrection.

  • Segal, Aaron. "Body and Soul." In The Routledge Companion to Jewish Philosophy, edited by Daniel Rynhold and Tyron Goldschmidt, 45-56. London: Routledge, 2025. Halakhic identity as purely biological.

Jewish Examples

  • USC Shoah Foundation. Dimensions in Testimony. Interactive survivor testimony that answers audience questions with real-time responses drawn from pre-recorded video interviews.

Digital Afterlife Ethics

  • Makhortykh, Mykola. AI and the Holocaust: Rewriting History? The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Understanding the Holocaust. UNESCO, 2024. Report commissioned by UNESCO and the World Jewish Congress on hallucinated history, fabricated testimony, chatbots that impersonate historical figures, and interactive survivor testimony built from pre-recorded answers (11, 14).

  • Shur-Ofry, Michal, and Guy Pessach. "Robotic Collective Memory." Washington University Law Review 97, no. 3 (2020): 975-1005. Takes New Dimensions in Testimony as a case study of collective memory constructed by AI and proposes "memory fiduciaries" modeled on information fiduciaries.

  • Gigliotti, Simone. "Zakhor AI: Memory Re-generations in a Disaggregating World." AJS Perspectives (Summer 2024): 40-43. Compares the StoryFile platform, which grew out of Dimensions in Testimony, with a family's chatbot of a dead grandfather, and calls for a criticism of AI memory platforms informed by Yerushalmi's Zakhor.

  • Öhman, Carl, and Luciano Floridi. "An Ethical Framework for the Digital Afterlife Industry." Nature Human Behaviour 2, no. 5 (2018): 318-320. Uses concepts relating to archaeological exhibitions of human remains as the basis of an ethical framework for thes use of digital remains.

  • Hollanek, Tomasz, and Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basińska. "Griefbots, Deadbots, Postmortem Avatars: On Responsible Applications of Generative AI in the Digital Afterlife Industry." Philosophy & Technology 37, no. 2 (2024): article 63. Speculations on design scenarios that discuss digital recreations of human personalities or expression.

  • Xygkou, Anna, Panote Siriaraya, Alexandra Covaci, Holly Gwen Prigerson, Robert A. Neimeyer, Chee Siang Ang, and Wan Jou She. "The 'Conversation' about Loss: Understanding How Chatbot Technology was Used in Supporting People in Grief." In Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1-15. 2023. Interviews with ten mourners who used chatbots in grief, reporting seven ways the chatbots were used, among them as a simulation of the deceased.

  • Stokes, Patrick. Digital Souls: A Philosophy of Online Death. London: Bloomsbury Academic, 2021. Argues that chatbots built from digital remains move mourners from recollecting the dead to replacing them, treating the dead as a means and the living as replaceable (139-145).

  • Buben, Adam. "Technology of the Dead: Objects of Loving Remembrance or Replaceable Resources?" Philosophical Papers 44, no. 1 (2015): 15-37. Distinguishes recollection, which keeps the loss in view, from replacement, which seeks to mitigate the fact that anything has been lost.

  • Krueger, Joel, and Lucy Osler. "Communing with the Dead Online: Chatbots, Grief, and Continuing Bonds." Journal of Consciousness Studies 29, nos. 9-10 (2022): 222-252. Argues that chatbots may help mourners sustain continuing bonds with the dead and that the "thin reciprocity" they offer weakens the worry that they replace the dead.

  • Kalmanzon, Avraham. "Inheriting Rights of Use and Ownership in Digital Items" [Hebrew: ירושת זכות שימוש ובעלות בפריטים דיגיטליים]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 298-309. Holds that heirs to a person's digital accounts may not use them so as to present the deceased as still the user, and gathers sources on the privacy and good name of the dead (306-308).

  • Levav, Melanie. "End of Life." Sapir 11 (Autumn 2023). Essay by a Jewish deathcare director on chatbots of the dead and holographic survivor testimony, asking whether answers from an AI simulation of Maimonides could be halakhically authoritative.
