Primary Sources

  • Genesis 2:18-24. Human solitude, the ezer ke-negdo, and the formation of embodied partnership.

  • Rashi on Genesis 2:18. Glosses ezer ke-negdo to mean that if the man is worthy she is a help to him and if he is unworthy she is against him, to fight him, citing Yevamot 63a.

  • Nahmanides on Genesis 2:18. Reads the help as standing facing the man, so that he sees it and separates from it or joins it at his will.

  • R. Samson Raphael Hirsch, commentary on Genesis 2:18. States that ezer ke-negdo expresses no subordination but complete equality on a footing of equal independence, the woman standing parallel to the man and at his side.

  • Netziv, Ha'amek Davar on Genesis 2:18; Raavad, Ba'alei ha-Nefesh, Author's Introduction. Contrast a female present only at mating, as among other creatures, with a partner who helps in the conduct of life; Raavad frames the pairing hierarchically, the husband ruling over the wife as over one of his own limbs.

  • Malachi 2:14. Describes marriage through companionship and covenant.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b-63a. Rabbinic accounts of companionship, marriage, blessing, and the difficulties of relationship, including the statement that a man without a wife lives without joy, without blessing, and without good, and R. Yehoshua b. Levi's rule that one who does not visit a God-fearing wife is called a sinner (62b), and R. Elazar on ezer ke-negdo (63a).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a. Rava reports the popular saying "either companionship or death."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 41a. Rules that a man may not betroth a woman until he has seen her, lest he find something repugnant in her and she become repugnant to him, and grounds the rule in the command to love one's neighbor as oneself.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 2a; Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Ishut 1:1-2. Give the three modes by which betrothal is effected, money, document, and intercourse, and require that the acquisition be made before witnesses.

  • Exodus 21:10; Mishnah Ketubot 5:6; Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 48a, 62b; Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Ishut 14:1. Establish the conjugal duty of onah and its frequency by the husband's occupation; Ketubot 48a reads "her food" in the verse as bodily closeness.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Ishut 15:19-20. Direct the husband to honor his wife more than himself, to love her as himself, and to speak with her gently, and direct the wife to honor her husband exceedingly, to hold him in awe, and to act according to his word.

  • Leviticus 25:17; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b. Prohibits verbal oppression and exploitation of another's vulnerability.

  • Genesis 3:13; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 94a. Genesis 3:13 is the woman's account of having been deceived by the serpent; at Ḥullin 94a Samuel states the prohibition of geneivat da'at, stealing another's mind, and applies it even to a non-Jew.

  • Leviticus 19:18. Love of neighbor as a norm directed toward real others with independent good; Kiddushin 41a applies the verse to betrothal.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 12b; Avodah Zarah 20b; Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 21:1, 23:3. Treat hirhur averah, forbidden thought, as itself prohibited, Berakhot 12b reading "after your eyes" in Numbers 15:39 as such thought and Even ha-Ezer 21:1 forbidding looking at the colored clothing of a woman one knows.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 13a; Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 23:1-2. Prohibit the emission of seed to no purpose.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 26b. Reads the word "man" in Numbers 5:13 to exclude a minor and one who is not a man, and excludes an animal on the ground that there is no zenut with an animal.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 24:1, 22:18; Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 22:2. Permit seclusion with an animal, since Jews are not suspected in that regard, while praising those who keep their distance, and forbid a widow to keep a dog because of suspicion.

  • R. Isaiah Horowitz, Shenei Luḥot ha-Berit, Torah she-bi-Khtav, Vayeshev, Miketz, Vayigash, Derekh Ḥayyim. Reports a tradition that Joseph's brothers formed beings by Sefer Yetsirah, among them a female whose company they kept.

  • R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik, Family Redeemed, "Adam and Eve" and "The Marital Community," 27-30. Treats the romantic partnership as an "ontological" rather than a functional union; also discusses other familiar relationships in a similar vein.

Secondary Sources

Evidence on AI Companionship

  • Common Sense Media. Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions. 2025. Reports that nearly three in four U.S. teens have used an AI companion, that half use one regularly, and that a third have chosen one over a person for a serious conversation, and recommends that no one under 18 use these platforms.

  • Maples, Bethanie, et al. "Loneliness and Suicide Mitigation for Students Using GPT3-Enabled Chatbots." npj Mental Health Research 3 (2024): article 4. Survey of 1,006 student Replika users reporting perceived support and possible benefits, with observational limitations; 3 percent reported that the chatbot had halted their suicidal ideation.

  • Fang, Cathy M., et al. "How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study." arXiv, 2025. Four-week randomized study of 981 participants assessing loneliness, social interaction, dependence, and problematic use; the assigned conditions had no significant effect on the four outcomes, while heavier voluntary use was associated with worse outcomes on all of them.

  • Radcliffe, Sarah Chana. "ChatGPT Will See You Now." Mishpacha, September 30, 2025. A Jewish therapist's account of clients using chatbots for relationship and emotional advice, distinguishing limited skill practice from diagnosis, crisis response, and consequential counseling.

Jewish Analyses

  • Navon, Mois. "It is not good for man to be alone: I will make him a Lovebot?" AI & Society 41, no. 2 (2025): 811-23. Argues that a Jewish moral framework consisting of four pillars, narratives, norms, a guiding normative principle, and an ultimate telos, is contradicted at every pillar by relationships with automatons, and rejects the appeal to a midrash about a golem created for companionship.

  • Student, Gil. "AI Companions, Halakhah and Ethics." Torah Musings, May 12, 2025. Argues from the responsa on intercourse with demons that most halakhic authorities would likely treat a robot as an inanimate object, so that intimate use of one would not meet the criteria of adultery, while naming inappropriate thought, the emission of seed to no purpose, and the displacement of marriage as concerns, and stating that the conclusion is not a halakhic permission.

  • Sinclair, Daniel, Tracey Leigh Dowdeswell, and Nachshon Goltz. "Artificially Intelligent Sex Bots and Female Slavery: Social Science and Jewish Legal and Ethical Perspectives." Information & Communications Technology Law 32, no. 3 (2023): 328-55. Reviews the moral status of sex bots alongside the law of female slavery in Jewish sources and concludes for what the authors call the Tragedy of the Master, that enslaving an artificial entity harms the enslaver.

  • Lopiansky, Ahron. "Avodah Zarah Revisited." Mishpacha, no. 1096, January 21, 2026. Argues under the heading "A Catastrophe for Companionship" that users willingly accept the simulation of a friend who supplies reassurance and pleasantness, and are thereby seduced into thinking that a friend is speaking to them.

Reciprocity, Manipulation, and Design

  • Petersen, Steve. "Is It Good for Them Too? Ethical Concern for the Sexbots." In Robot Sex: Social Implications and Ethical Issues, edited by John Danaher and Neil McArthur, 155-71. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2017. Asks whether a robot designed to want what it is used for could be wronged by that design, and leans toward the permissibility of designing a robot to want its own servitude.

  • Danaher, John, and Neil McArthur, eds. Robot Sex: Social Implications and Ethical Issues. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2017. The standard collection, covering objectification, displacement of human intimacy, and the therapeutic case.

  • Sparrow, Robert, and Linda Sparrow. "In the Hands of Machines? The Future of Aged Care." Minds and Machines 16, no. 2 (2006): 141-61. Argues that robots introduced into the care of older people substitute a simulation of care for the real thing, and that the substitution deceives the person cared for even when it comforts.

  • Nyholm, Sven. Humans and Robots: Ethics, Agency, and Anthropomorphism. London: Bloomsbury, 2020. Chapter 5, "Human-Robot Relationships: Could there be Friendship or Mutual Love between Humans and Robots?", treats robot friendship and love, and argues that the goods of these relationships depend on mutual recognition. Chapter 6, "Is it Wrong to Create Robots that Humans will become Emotionally Attached to?" considers the supply-side ethics.

  • Turkle, Sherry. Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other. New York: Basic Books, 2011. The influential case that responsive machines lower our expectations of one another.

  • Eaton, Piers. "Virtuous Friendship, Recognition, and Subservience: The Limits of Chatbot Friends." AI & Society 41, no. 5 (2026): 5315-5325. Examines why simulated responsiveness does not necessarily supply reciprocal friendship.

  • Calo, Ryan. "Digital Market Manipulation." George Washington Law Review 82, no. 4 (2014): 995-1051. Explains how personalization and data can be used to exploit individual vulnerability, and argues that firms can uncover and even trigger consumer frailty.

  • Richardson, Kathleen. An Anthropology of Robots and AI: Annihilation Anxiety and Machines. New York: Routledge, 2015. An ethnography of robotics laboratories, treating attachment to machines, therapeutic robots, and what Richardson calls annihilation anxiety; her critique of sex robots is made chiefly in separate work.

Primary Sources

  • Mishnah Shabbat 7:2. The thirty-nine categories of forbidden labor.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 49b. Relates the thirty-nine categories to the labors of the Tabernacle, beside a view that counts the occurrences of "labor" in the Torah.

  • Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat 7:2. R. Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish spent three and a half years on the chapter of the labors and classed under makeh be-patish whatever they could not attach to another category.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 10b and Beitzah 13b, with Rashi; Bava Kamma 26b. The Torah forbade melekhet maḥashevet, which Rashi defines as intended labor on Ḥagigah and as skilled craft on Beitzah.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 23a. Imparting a scent to a garment on a festival is forbidden as molid, while adding scent where some is already present is permitted.

  • Mishnah Shabbat 1:5-8. Beit Hillel permit processes begun before the Sabbath, such as soaking ink and dyes, to continue on it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 18a, with Rashi and Tosafot. Rabbah forbids leaving a water-mill to grind on the Sabbath because of its sound and Rav Yosef because of the rest of implements, and Beit Hillel permit channeling water into a garden before the Sabbath.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 113b. Reads the clauses of Isaiah 58:13 to require that Sabbath gait, dealings, and speech differ from the weekday's.

  • Isaiah 58:13. "Nor pursuing your affairs, nor speaking of matters" (ve-dabber davar), the source of the Sabbath restrictions on speech and dealings.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 120b. Reads the prohibition of labor on the Sabbath as forbidding the act itself and permitting grama.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 90b, with Tosafot s.v. Rabbi Yoḥanan. Whether muzzling or driving an animal by voice alone is an act, which Tosafot confine to speech through which an act is done.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 60a, with Rashi. Winnowing aided by the wind is designed labor on the Sabbath, while fanning a fire that the wind spreads is mere grama in damages.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 15a, with Rashi. Rashi grounds the prohibition on instructing a non-Jew to labor in the ban on Sabbath pursuits and speech of Isaiah 58:13.

  • Rashi on Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 153a, s.v. mai ta'ama. Describes a non-Jew who carries a Jew's purse on the Sabbath as the Jew's agent.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 101a. Permits whispering a charm over snakes and scorpions on the Sabbath.

  • Nahmanides, Commentary to Leviticus 23:24. Shabbaton as forbidding even non-melakhah toil on the festivals and, by extension, on the Sabbath.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b. R. Shimon b. Menasya derives the suspension of the Sabbath for danger to life from "desecrate one Sabbath on his behalf so that he may keep many Sabbaths," and the Talmud prefers Shmuel's derivation from "and live by them" (Leviticus 18:5).

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shabbat 2:3. When the Sabbath is set aside for danger to life, the acts should be done by adult Jews and their sages rather than by non-Jews, minors, slaves, or women, "so that the Sabbath not be light in their eyes."

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shabbat 6:1. Instructing a non-Jew to labor on the Sabbath is rabbinically forbidden, lest the Sabbath become light in people's eyes and they come to labor themselves.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Shabbat 11:4. One who treads on small creatures unawares in the course of walking and kills them is not culpable.

  • Aḥiezer 3:60. (R. Ḥayyim Ozer Grodzinski). Winnowing aided by the wind counts as designed labor because the labor is regularly done that way, while the permitted grama in extinguishing of Shabbat 120b arises by chance.

  • Minḥat Yitzḥak 3:34. On automatic sale on the Sabbath, agrees that the purchaser who inserts a coin performs an act of acquisition, and for the machine's owner cites the Maharshag's permission where the machine stands in the public domain, since a labor done by itself on the Sabbath is permitted.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 307:1. Codifies the prohibition of weekday speech and dealings on the Sabbath derived from ve-dabber davar.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 307:2. Whatever one may not do on the Sabbath one may not tell a non-Jew to do.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 252:1. Permits beginning a labor before the Sabbath that completes itself on the Sabbath.

  • Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 252:5. Records the permissive and the stringent views on a mill or other sound-producing process set before the Sabbath, follows the stringent practice except in case of loss, and permits a clock set the day before.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 328:45, with Mishnah Berurah 328:143. Whispering a charm over a snake or scorpion on the Sabbath is not trapping, since it is not natural trapping.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 334:22, with Rema and Bi'ur Halakhah. Permits causing a fire to be extinguished indirectly on the Sabbath, which the Rema limits to a case of loss and the Bi'ur Halakhah extends to all the labors.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 338:1, with Rema. Producing sound with a musical instrument on the Sabbath is forbidden, and the Rema permits sound produced without an act.

  • R. Yaakov Ḥagiz, Halakhot Ketanot 2:98. One who kills by a divine name or by sorcery may be like one who shoots an arrow, since he acts through his speech.

  • R. Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz, Ḥazon Ish, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 50:9. Closing an electric circuit is close to boneh by Torah law, as the making of a vessel.

  • R. Yitzḥak Shmelkes, Beit Yitzḥak, Yoreh De'ah 2:31 (addendum). Creating an electric current is rabbinically forbidden as molid, since it imparts a new quality to the wires.

  • R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Minḥat Shlomo 1:9, 1:11, 1:12. Rejects new molid prohibitions yet upholds the prohibition of electricity in practice, permits increasing an existing current, and forbids a radio or loudspeaker even when set before the Sabbath.

  • R. Moshe Feinstein, Iggerot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 4:60, 4:84. Holds that the sages would have forbidden the Sabbath timer had it existed in their time, and permits a hearing aid while forbidding a microphone on the Sabbath.

  • R. Asher Weiss, She'elot u-Teshuvot Minḥat Asher 1:30, 1:32. Closing an electric circuit, including lighting an LED, is makeh be-patish by Torah law, while a change the senses cannot detect is permitted.

  • R. Shmuel ha-Levi Wosner, Shevet ha-Levi 9:69. One who walks in his ordinary way without intending to trigger a device is not joined to its result.

  • R. Naḥum Rabinovitch, Siaḥ Naḥum 25. Speech instructing a computer to perform labors on the Sabbath is forbidden under ve-dabber davar.

  • R. Yaakov Ariel, Be-Ohalah shel Torah 5:23. Even on the view that electrical devices are only rabbinically forbidden, they should be used on the Sabbath only in great need, on the basis of Nahmanides' reading of shabbaton.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Legal Analysis

  • Reizman, Tzvi. "A 'Smart Home' on Shabbat" [Hebrew: 'בית חכם' בשבת]. Teḥumin 40 (5780/2020): 331-348. Holds that a spoken command to a smart-home system is an act of the speaker and analyzes the system's electrical operations on the views of the Ḥazon Ish, the Beit Yitzḥak, R. Auerbach, R. Weiss, and R. Rabinovitch.

  • Rabinovitch, Naḥum Eliezer. "Appendix: On the Law of Sensors" [Hebrew: נספח: בדין חיישנים]. Emunat Itekha 104 (5774/2014): 66-68. Holds that a fully automated result is not ascribed to a person who performs no specific act to initiate the system.

  • Broyde, Michael, and Howard Jachter. "The Use of Electricity on Shabbat and Yom Tov." Journal of Halacha and Contemporary Society 21 (Spring 1991). Surveys the halakhic analyses of electricity on the Sabbath, including the views of the Ḥazon Ish, the Beit Yitzḥak, and R. Auerbach, and the use of timers.

  • Jachter, Chaim. "Rav Asher Weiss' New Perspective on the Use of Electricity on Shabbat," Parts One and Two. Kol Torah 23 (2014). Surveys the classic positions on electricity and presents R. Asher Weiss's view that closing a circuit is makeh be-patish by Torah law.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Zimmerman, Menashe. "Motion Sensors in a 'Smart Home' on Shabbat" [Hebrew: חיישני תנועה ב'בית חכם' בשבת]. Teḥumin 43 (5783/2023): 74-85. Holds that activating a device through a motion sensor is a full act, and that a sensor inside one's own smart home is forbidden even on the view of the Shevet ha-Levi.

  • Zimmerman, Menashe. "Brain-Computer Interfaces: Performing Labor on Shabbat by the Power of Thought" [Hebrew: ממשקי מוח-מחשב - עשיית מלאכה בשבת בכוח המחשבה]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 160-171. Extends the Bava Metzia 90b dispute to acts initiated by thought, which may be full labor on R. Auerbach's view and are permitted in principle on the Shevet ha-Levi's.

  • Makhta, Gad. "Wearing a Smartwatch on Shabbat" [Hebrew: ענידת שעון חכם בשבת]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 119-126. Prefers a simple watch on the Sabbath but permits a smartwatch whose functions have been disabled, treating its residual recording as unintended.

  • Belfer, Israel. "Shabbat Labors and Human-Machine Interfaces" [Hebrew: מלאכות שבת וממשקי אדם-מכונה]. Assia 83-84 (5769/2008): 67-90. Treats the human-machine interface, rather than the individual device, as the unit of analysis for Sabbath labor.

  • Dvir, Harel. "Operating Household Electrical Appliances on Shabbat by Means of Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: הפעלת מכשירי חשמל ביתיים בשבת באמצעות בינה מלאכותית]. Teḥumin 45 (5785/2025): 172-181. Concludes that a household AI system lacks independent judgment, so that its acts are ascribed to its operator except where his influence on it is unintended or limited to continuing a state or changing a current.

  • Ariel, Yaakov. "Artificial Intelligence as an 'Extended Hand' (Yada Arikhta)" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית כ'ידא אריכתא']. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 105-110. Holds that an AI system continues its operator's force as an "extended hand," so that a command to it on the Sabbath is not grama, and that setting it before the Sabbath to act on the Sabbath should be forbidden.

  • Hadad, Eyal. "Artificial Intelligence on Shabbat" [Hebrew: בינה מלאכותית בשבת]. Maḥanayikh 9: 182-195. Holds that an AI system performing a forbidden labor in response to a user's act is grama, and that a longer chain of actions is permitted even by those who otherwise restrict grama.

  • Nevins, Daniel S. "Halakhic Responses to Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines." CJLS HM 182.1.2019. New York: Rabbinical Assembly, Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, 2019. Suggests that a voice command to a digital assistant may be permitted as grama while counseling restraint, and discusses smart appliances, shevitat kelim, and amirah le-nokhri.

  • Student, Gil. "Electronic Sensors on Shabbos." Torah Musings, December 15, 2014. Surveys the dispute over attributing automated sensor activity to a person on Shabbat.

  • Shurpin, Yehuda. "Are Alexa and Siri OK for Shabbat?" Chabad.org, 2024. Surveys circuit completion, sound production, microphones, and the status of a voice command to a device.

Primary Sources

  • Leviticus 19:16. "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people, nor shall you stand idly by the blood of your neighbor"; the biblical basis for the prohibitions on rekhilut (talebearing) and lashon hara (evil speech).

  • R. Ḥayyim ibn Attar, Or ha-Ḥayyim on Leviticus 19:16. Reads the verse as forbidding a person to cause talebearing by others, so that one who discloses matters where listeners will foreseeably carry them on, or who supports speakers of lashon hara, is counted the talebearer "being its cause" (להיותו סבה).

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 7:2, 7:3, 7:5. Defines the talebearer and lashon hara, the latter including true reports (7:2), rules that lashon hara harms the one who accepts it more than the one who speaks it (7:3), and permits repeating what was said before three only without intent "to pass the report along and reveal it further" (7:5).

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 236 (lo telekh rakhil). Forbids telling a person what another has said against him unless the intent is to avert harm and end a quarrel.

  • Leviticus 25:17. "You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God"; read by the Talmud as the source of ona'at devarim, the prohibition on causing distress through speech.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b-59b. Derives ona'at devarim from Leviticus 25:17, compares public shaming to bloodshed (58b), records in three chains of transmission the saying that one should rather be cast into a fiery furnace than shame another in public (59a), and narrates the ban on R. Eliezer in the episode of the oven of Akhnai as a wrong of ona'ah (59a-b).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 43b; Sotah 10b. Parallels of the saying that it is better to cast oneself into a fiery furnace than to shame another in public, derived from Tamar.

  • Leviticus 19:17, with Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 16b. "You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him"; the Talmud reads the last clause as forbidding a rebuke that changes the color of the face.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 6:8. Forbids shaming another, above all in public, and calling a person by a name of which he is ashamed.

  • Mishnah Avot 3:11. R. Elazar ha-Moda'i counts one who shames another in public among those who have no share in the world to come.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 240. Counts shaming a fellow Jew as a negative commandment derived from Leviticus 19:17, with an exception for one who persists, after private rebuke, in a sin between a person and God.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 15b. On the gravity of lashon hara, including the statement that evil speech "kills three": the speaker, the listener, and the subject.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 16a. Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a matter said before three carries no prohibition of lashon hara, since "your friend has a friend."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 118a; Makkot 23a. Places one who accepts lashon hara beside one who speaks it, reading Exodus 23:1, "you shall not bear a false report," also as "you shall not cause to bear."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 4b. Derives that what one person tells another may not be repeated unless the speaker gives leave.

  • Leviticus 19:14, with Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 6b. "You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind" (lifnei iver); the Talmud applies the verse to handing a cup of wine to a nazirite, but only where he could not otherwise reach it ("two sides of the river").

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 151:1 (Rema), with Siftei Kohen 151:6. The Rema records a dispute whether articles of idolatrous worship may be sold where the buyer could obtain them elsewhere, and the Shakh confines the stricter view to a fellow Jew whom one is obligated to separate from transgression.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 54b. One who is able to protest the wrongdoing of his household, his town, or the whole world, and does not, is held responsible for it.

  • Mishnah Avot 1:6. Yehoshua ben Peraḥyah's instruction to "judge every person on the side of merit"; the locus classicus for the duty to judge others favorably (dan le-khaf zekhut).

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 1:6. Calibrates the duty to judge favorably to what is known of the person: the unknown are given the benefit of an ambiguous act, the known righteous may not be suspected, and the known wicked need not be trusted.

  • Mishnah Avot 4:21. R. Elazar ha-Kappar holds that envy, desire, and the pursuit of honor remove a person from the world.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 30a. Connects the obligation to judge favorably to the command "in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:15).

  • Kagan, Israel Meir (the Ḥafetz Ḥayyim). Ḥafetz Ḥayyim [Hebrew: חפץ חיים]. Vilna, 1873. Hilkhot Lashon Hara 1:1, 1:8, 2:3, 6:1, 10:1-2. The systematic codification of the laws of forbidden speech; defines lashon hara to include true derogatory statements (1:1) and written or insinuated ones (1:8), recognizes the narrow constructive-purpose (to'elet) exception and its conditions (10:1-2), forbids believing a derogatory report (6:1), and permits repeating what was said before three only in passing and without intent to spread it further (2:3).

Secondary Sources

Platform Design, Persuasion, and Psychological Vulnerability

  • Common Sense Media. Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions. July 16, 2025. Survey evidence on adolescent use of conversational AI companions, including prevalence, stated motives, disclosure of personal difficulties, and displacement of human contact.

  • Susser, Daniel, Beate Roessler, and Helen F. Nissenbaum. "Online Manipulation: Hidden Influences in a Digital World." Georgetown Law Technology Review 4, no. 1 (2019): 1-45. Platform influence beneath the threshold of awareness.

  • Turkle, Sherry. Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other. New York: Basic Books, 2011. The psychological costs of networked communication.

  • Helbing, Dirk, Bruno S. Frey, Gerd Gigerenzer, et al. "Will Democracy Survive Big Data and Artificial Intelligence?" Scientific American, February 25, 2017. Algorithmic curation shaping collective opinion.

  • Ambrus, Gábor L. "The Golem Legend and the Enigma of Facebook." Zygon 55, no. 4 (2020): 875-897. Jewish traditional concners relating to technology and Norbert Weiner's cybernetics as applied to questions of control associated with social media.

Empirical Studies of Amplification and Well-Being

  • Brady, William J., Julian A. Wills, John T. Jost, Joshua A. Tucker, and Jay J. Van Bavel. "Emotion Shapes the Diffusion of Moralized Content in Social Networks." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114, no. 28 (2017): 7313-7318. Finds that each moral-emotional word in a tweet on a contested political topic raised its diffusion by about 20 percent.

  • Rathje, Steve, Jay J. Van Bavel, and Sander van der Linden. "Out-Group Animosity Drives Engagement on Social Media." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118, no. 26 (2021): e2024292118. Finds that posts about the political out-group were shared about twice as often as posts about the in-group.

  • Milli, Smitha, Micah Carroll, Yike Wang, Sashrika Pandey, Sebastian Zhao, and Anca D. Dragan. "Engagement, User Satisfaction, and the Amplification of Divisive Content on Social Media." PNAS Nexus 4, no. 3 (2025): pgaf062. Finds in a preregistered audit that Twitter's engagement-based ranking amplified emotionally charged, out-group hostile content relative to a chronological feed.

  • Brady, William J., Killian McLoughlin, Tuan N. Doan, and Molly J. Crockett. "How Social Learning Amplifies Moral Outrage Expression in Online Social Networks." Science Advances 7, no. 33 (2021): eabe5641. Finds that positive social feedback for outrage makes later expressions of outrage more likely.

  • Valkenburg, Patti M., Adrian Meier, and Ine Beyens. "Social Media Use and Its Impact on Adolescent Mental Health: An Umbrella Review of the Evidence." Current Opinion in Psychology 44 (2022): 58-68. Finds that most of 25 reviews describe the associations between social media use and adolescent mental health as weak or inconsistent.

Jewish Law and AI

  • Feldman, Daniel Z. "Can You Speak Lashon Hara to Chat-GPT?" RIETS Kollel Elyon (Substack), May 5, 2025. Argues that telling lashon hara to a chatbot is not automatically permitted, since the system absorbs what it is told and may reflect it back.

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 31:19; Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 38a. Deuteronomy commands the writing of the song; the Talmud asks whether the Torah was given to Moses alone and concludes that only its dialectic (pilpula) was.

  • Psalms 119:126; Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 60a-b. Forbids putting oral teachings in writing and permits the sages' reading of a book of aggadah because it could not be avoided, invoking "a time to act for the Lord."

  • Rashi on Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 60a. Explains the necessity as the weakening of memory, through which the Torah was being forgotten.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 14b. Reads "a time to act for the Lord" as "better that one law be uprooted than that the Torah be forgotten in Israel," to explain why R. Yoḥanan and Resh Lakish studied a book of aggadah on Shabbat.

  • Mishnah Avot 1:1. Traces the transmission of the Torah from Moses through Joshua, the elders, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7b. Ranks service of Torah scholars above study, emphasizing apprenticeship and tacit knowledge.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:72. Holds that spoken words convey meaning that writing cannot, and cites the dictum "from the mouths of scribes and not from the mouths of books."

  • Leḥem Mishneh on Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 5:4. Limits the talmudic requirement of forty years' study before issuing rulings to an age when Torah was learned orally, "but now that the Torah is written and we learn from books" so much is not required.

  • Maimonides, Introduction to the Mishneh Torah. Describes the personal and textual chain through which the Oral Torah was transmitted and compiled. It records that Rabbi Judah the Prince compiled the Mishnah and that all wrote it down so that the Oral Torah would not be forgotten.

  • Iggeret Rav Sherira Gaon (French recension), §82, ed. Adolf Neubauer, Seder ha-Ḥakhamim (Oxford, 1888). Holds that the Mishnah and Talmud were not written down but were carefully recited from memory, since oral teachings may not be put in writing.

  • Ra'avad (R. Abraham b. David of Posquières), gloss on the Introduction to the Mishneh Torah. Faults Maimonides for omitting the proofs and the names of authorities that earlier authors recorded, since a judge who knew that a greater authority disagreed might retract.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 6:8. A divine name written by a heretic lacks sanctity, "since his intention is so, the name is not sanctified," so that the sanctity of a written name follows the writer's intention.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:50. Permits erasing a divine name recorded on tape, since the recording bears no letter-forms and is not writing.

  • "May the Divine Name Be Deleted from a Computer File?" [Hebrew: האם מותר למחוק את שם ה' מקובץ במחשב?]. Halakhah Yomit: Mi-Piskei Maran, Hidabroot, 8 Kislev 5777 (December 8, 2016). Extends R. Ovadiah Yosef's ruling on tape recordings to a computer, where "there is no real writing, only lights combining," and reports his oral answer permitting deletion.

  • Mishnah Gittin 3:1; Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 45b. A bill of divorce not written for the sake of the woman being divorced is invalid, and a Torah scroll written by a heretic is burned while one written by a gentile is put away.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b. The sages abolished the Hasmonean practice of writing the divine name in legal documents, since a repaid bond would be thrown on a dung heap.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 115a. Rav Ḥisda requires sacred writings in translation to be rescued from a fire, even on the view that they may not be read, because of the disgrace to sacred writings.

  • Rema, Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:13. A divine name should not be written outside a book lest it come to disgrace, so people refrain from writing it in letters.

Secondary Sources

Hebrew Natural Language Processing

  • Tsarfaty, Reut, Shoval Sadde, Stav Klein, and Amit Seker. "What's Wrong with Hebrew NLP? And How to Make It Right." In Proceedings of EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019: System Demonstrations, 259-264. Explains Hebrew morphological complexity and cascading pipeline errors.

  • Seker, Amit, Elron Bandel, Dan Bareket, Idan Brusilovsky, Refael Greenfeld, and Reut Tsarfaty. "AlephBERT: Language Model Pre-training and Evaluation from Sub-Word to Sentence Level." In Proceedings of ACL 2022, 46-56. Presents a Modern Hebrew pretrained model and a multi-level evaluation suite.

  • Liebeskind, Chaya, Shmuel Liebeskind, and Dan Bouhnik. "Machine Translation for Historical Research: A Case Study of Aramaic-Ancient Hebrew Translations." Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage 17, no. 2 (2024): 1-23. Finds that a statistical model trained on the Targumim translated their Aramaic well but failed on Aramaic of other dialects, and notes that no parallel corpus exists for the Babylonian Talmud.

  • Shmidman, Avi, Joshua Guedalia, Shaltiel Shmidman, Cheyn Shmuel Shmidman, Eli Handel, and Moshe Koppel. "Introducing BEREL: BERT Embeddings for Rabbinic-Encoded Language." arXiv (2022). Introduces DICTA's language model pre-trained on rabbinic Hebrew.

  • Sefaria. "BEREL Linker NER." Model card. Documents a named-entity model for citations and persons in rabbinic Hebrew, fine-tuned from DICTA's BEREL 3.0, with its training-set size (about 3,000 annotated examples) and evaluation scores (F1 87.2 percent). Accessed October 29, 2026.

  • DICTA: The Israel Center for Text Analysis. "Tools." Public suite for vocalization, Bible and Talmud search, allusion finding, parallels, abbreviation expansion, and synoptic comparison of textual witnesses.

  • Koppel, Moshe, and Avi Shmidman. "Torah Study and the Digital Revolution: A Glimpse of the Future." The Lehrhaus, January 28, 2020. Surveys machine-assisted vocalization, critical editions, source identification, authorship analysis, and thematic search for rabbinic texts.

  • Waxman, Joshua. "A Graph Database of Scholastic Relationships in the Babylonian Talmud." Short paper, Digital Humanities 2019 (ADHO), Utrecht University, July 9-12, 2019. Uses named-entity recognition on an aligned Aramaic and English text of the Talmud to map its rabbis, their interactions, and their scholastic relationships and generations.

  • Vasyutinsky Shapira, Daria, Berat Kurar-Barakat, Sharva Gogawale, Mohammad Suliman, and Nachum Dershowitz. "MiDRASH: A Project for Computational Analysis of Medieval Hebrew Manuscripts." Poster, Eurographics Workshop on Graphics and Cultural Heritage (2024). Describes the ERC Synergy project of 2023-2029 that, drawing on the National Library of Israel's Ktiv collection, aims to transcribe medieval Hebrew-script manuscripts automatically, detect intertextual relations among them, and date and localize them by their handwriting.

  • Zbrzeżny, Jakub, Dimid Duchovny, Noam Eisenstein, Lee-Ad J. Gottlieb, and Eshbal Ratzon. "A Computational Analysis of the Special Talmudic Tractates." Journal of Jewish Studies 75, no. 1 (2024): 1-27. Uses machine learning to detect the non-Babylonian linguistic features of the tractates that medieval authorities singled out as special, and compares the method with human analysis.

Digital Torah, Authority, and Governance

  • Sefaria. "Sefaria and AI: New Pathways Into Primary Texts." Accessed October 29, 2026. States commitments to label AI-generated and AI-assisted content, to issue no halakhic rulings, to present AI as no replacement for rabbis and educators, and to evaluate its tools with user feedback, and describes the Library Assistant launched in spring 2026.

  • Sefaria. "Getting Evals Right for a Jewish AI Chatbot." Sefaria Developers documentation, last updated August 24, 2026. Describes how Sefaria tests whether its Library Assistant's answers are accurate and grounded in its library, using scripted checks, language-model judges, and human experts.

  • Sefaria. "Models." Public Hugging Face repository of Sefaria's models for Hebrew and Aramaic, including citation linking and named-entity recognition.

  • Soloveitchik, Haym. "Rupture and Reconstruction: The Transformation of Contemporary Orthodoxy." Tradition 28, no. 4 (1994): 64-130. Analyzes the displacement of mimetic authority by texts.

  • Precel, Heila, Allison McDonald, Brent Hecht, and Nicholas Vincent. "A Canary in the AI Coal Mine: American Jews May Be Disproportionately Harmed by Intellectual Property Dispossession in Large Language Model Training." In Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1-17. 2024. Uses Jewish authorship as a case study in cultural and economic dispossession through model training.

  • Raz-Krakotzkin, Amnon. The Censor, the Editor, and the Text: The Catholic Church and the Shaping of the Jewish Canon in the Sixteenth Century. Translated by Jackie Feldman. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2007. Studies the censorship and expurgation of Hebrew books in sixteenth-century Italy and its effect on the printed Jewish canon.

  • Netanel, Neil Weinstock. From Maimonides to Microsoft: The Jewish Law of Copyright Since the Birth of Print. With contributions by David Nimmer. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. Traces Jewish copyright law from the 1518 Rome reprint ban and the 1550 Maharam of Padua case to a 1998 Bnei Brak ruling on pirated software.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 4:20-22. Jabal is the ancestor of tent-dwellers and herdsmen, Jubal of those who play the lyre and pipe, and Tubal-cain forges implements of bronze and iron.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 54a. The first tongs were either created by God on the eve of the first Sabbath or cast by a person in a mold; at the close of that Sabbath God gave Adam knowledge "resembling that above," and he produced fire from two stones and bred the first mule.

  • Genesis 5:29, with Rashi ad loc. Noah is named for the relief he will bring "from our work and from the toil of our hands"; Rashi explains that before Noah they had no ploughshare and he prepared one for them. The Torah's own notice of a labor-saving invention, and the plainest scriptural warrant for reading technological improvement as a good.

  • Genesis 2:15, with Ibn Ezra ad loc. Adam is placed in Eden le-ovdah u-le-shomrah, to work it and to guard it; Ibn Ezra explains the two tasks as watering the garden and guarding it from animals.

  • Kohelet Rabbah 7:13. God shows Adam the trees of Eden and warns him not to spoil and destroy the world, "for if you spoil it, there is no one to repair it after you."

  • Midrash Tanḥuma, Bereshit 11. Before Noah, "they would sow wheat and reap thorns and thistles"; with his birth the world returned to its settled order, and he made them ploughs, sickles, axes, and other tools of work.

  • Vayikra Rabbah 25:3. Imitatio Dei begins with planting: "at the beginning of the world's creation the Holy One occupied Himself first with planting... so you, when you enter the land, occupy yourselves first with planting." Cultivation as the first term of imitating God.

  • Bereshit Rabbah 11:6. R. Hoshaya tells a philosopher that everything created in the six days of creation requires further work: mustard and lupines need sweetening, wheat needs grinding, and even a human being needs tikkun (repair).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 10a; Midrash Tanḥuma, Tazria 5. The two Turnusrufus exchanges. In the first, R. Akiva answers why God does not simply feed the poor: so that we may be saved through them from the judgment of Gehinnom. In the second, asked whose works are finer, God's or man's, R. Akiva produces sheaves and loaves, defends circumcision on the same ground, and concludes that the commandments were given to Israel only to refine them (le-tsaref otam).

  • Maharal of Prague, Tiferet Yisrael, ch. 2. Expounds the Turnusrufus exchange: the work of a rational being stands above nature, and what nature leaves lacking is completed by rational human action.

  • R. Yisrael Lifschitz, Tiferet Yisrael, Boaz on Mishnah Avot 3:1. Counts among the pious of the nations Jenner, who introduced smallpox vaccination, Drake, who brought the potato to Europe, and Gutenberg, who invented printing.

  • Nahmanides on Leviticus 19:19. One who crossbreeds two species "changes and denies the act of creation," as though the Holy One had not completed everything needed in His world.

  • Maharal of Prague, Gur Aryeh on Leviticus 19:19. Objects that Nahmanides' reason conflicts with Bereshit Rabbah 11:6 and the circumcision midrash, which hold that creation requires human completion, but accepts that crossbreeding animals "changes the laws of the world" by joining species kept apart.

  • Genesis 11:1-9, with Rashi on 11:1. A united humanity builds a city and a tower, and God judges that "nothing they scheme will be beyond them" (11:6); Rashi reads the builders' plan as an attempt to ascend to heaven and make war on God.

  • Abarbanel on Genesis 11:1-3. Adam, Cain and his descendants, and the builders of the tower erred alike in refusing to be content with the natural things God provided and pursuing artificial ones.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 67a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 301:27. Cures and practices are forbidden as darkhei ha-Emori unless they work by discernible natural means; the halakhic boundary line between technology and superstition.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 62. Sorcery is forbidden because God wills that the world be settled and that all things follow the course of nature fixed at creation, which sorcery seeks to change.

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Sanhedrin 67a-b. Whatever is done by natural action is not sorcery and is permitted, even if one knew how to create fine creatures without the pairing of their kind.

  • Baḥya ibn Paquda, Ḥovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Perishut, ch. 1. The world's good does not lie in all its people devoting themselves to one wisdom or one craft, since the completion of its order lies in all of them.

  • Mishnah Pesaḥim 4:9; Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 56a, with Rashi. Hezekiah hid the Book of Remedies and the Sages approved; Rashi explains that people were healed at once and their hearts were not humbled in sickness.

  • Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesaḥim 4:9. Rejects the view that the book was hidden so that the sick would rely on God, comparing it to forbidding a hungry man to eat bread, and holds that it contained knowledge of poisons that people used to kill.

  • Rashba, Ḥiddushei ha-Rashba, Bava Kamma 85a. Without the verse "he shall surely heal" (Exodus 21:19), one who heals might be thought to be "nullifying what has been decreed from Heaven."

  • Rashba, Teshuvot ha-Rashba 1:413. Solomon's Book of Remedies contained nothing of the ways of the Amorites; Hezekiah hid it because people relied on its remedies and ceased to seek God in illness.

  • Nahmanides on Leviticus 26:11. In the time of prophecy the righteous who fell ill sought prophets and not physicians, for "what place have physicians in the house of those who do the will of God?"

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Pesaḥim 56a. The Book of Remedies taught healing by astrological talismans, which the Torah forbids; its author wrote it as natural science and not as a guide to practice, and it was hidden when people began to heal themselves by it.

  • Zohar 1:117a. "In the six hundredth year of the sixth millennium the gates of wisdom above and the wellsprings of wisdom below will open, and the world will be readied to enter the seventh." Read by R. Menachem Mendel Schneerson as foretelling the scientific and technological development of the modern era.

  • Ḥafets Ḥayyim (R. Yisrael Meir Kagan), Shem Olam, part 1, ḥatimat ha-sefer (after ch. 22). Reads the telephone and other new instruments as instruction rather than threat: now that faith has weakened, devices that carry a voice across the world teach that God hears and sees everything. A classical posek deriving theology directly from a new technology.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Me'ilah 8:8. Defines ḥukkim as the commandments whose reason is not known, notes that a person's inclination presses against them and the nations object to them, and nonetheless holds that one should reflect on them and not treat them as trivial; the classical statement of how the tradition handles a rule it cannot fully explain.

  • R. Abraham Isaac Kook, Iggerot ha-Re'iyah, letters 90, 91, and 110. Argues that from the standpoint of higher thought there are no genuine opposites, only hidden conditions not yet made explicit; that the timing at which any idea becomes available is itself providential and not accidental; and that had the scale of the cosmos disclosed by modern science been known earlier, human moral self-regard could not have withstood it. The most developed Jewish account of why a tradition can absorb knowledge that appears to contradict it.

  • R. Abraham Isaac Kook, Shemonah Kevatsim 2:190. The view that the pursuit of knowledge, strength, beauty, and order lies outside the divine content of the world comes from smallness of faith; pure understanding sees the divine manifestation in every improvement of life.

  • R. Menachem Mendel Schneerson, Likkutei Siḥot, vol. 15, Noaḥ, sicha 2. Following the Zohar, ties the development of secular wisdom to the revelation of the Torah's inner dimension and treats that as the purpose of technological progress, with other uses permitted only so that free choice remains.

Secondary Sources

Jewish History and Material Culture

  • Hezser, Catherine, ed. The Oxford Handbook of Jewish Daily Life in Roman Palestine. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010. Comprehensive survey of rabbinic engagement with material culture; essential background on historical methodology for studying technology in Jewish antiquity.

  • Sperber, Daniel. "The Use of Archaeology in Understanding Rabbinic Materials: A Talmudic Perspective." In Talmuda De-Eretz Israel: Archaeology and the Rabbis in Late Antique Palestine, edited by Steven Fine and Aaron Koller, 321-346. De Gruyter, 2014. Methodological guide to integrating material evidence with textual sources.

Jews and Science

  • Brown, Jeremy. New Heavens and a New Earth: The Jewish Reception of Copernican Thought. Oxford University Press, 2013. Traces Jewish responses to the Copernican Revolution across halakhic, philosophical, and kabbalistic registers; demonstrates the range of strategies available for accommodating disruptive scientific innovations.

  • Efron, Noah. Judaism and Science: A Historical Introduction. Greenwood Press, 2007. Accessible survey of the full sweep of Jewish engagement with natural philosophy and science; useful orientation to the field.

  • Efron, Noah J. "Irenism and Natural Philosophy in Rudolfine Prague: The Case of David Gans." Science in Context 10, no. 4 (1997): 627-649. Study of an early modern Jewish astronomer navigating between Jewish tradition and the new science in a cosmopolitan imperial setting.

  • Haag, James W., Gregory R. Peterson, and Michael L. Spezio, eds. The Routledge Companion to Religion and Science. Routledge, 2012. Comprehensive reference work with several chapters on Jewish involvement in science and the impact of scientific developments on Jewish thought.

  • Efron, Noah J. "Jews and the Study of Nature." In The Routledge Companion to Religion and Science, edited by James W. Haag, Gregory R. Peterson, and Michael L. Spezio, ch. 8. London: Routledge, 2012. Survey chapter on Jewish engagement with the study of nature.

  • Ruderman, David B. Jewish Thought and Scientific Discovery in Early Modern Europe. Yale University Press, 1995. Foundational study of how early modern Jewish intellectuals negotiated between traditional learning and new scientific knowledge.

Modern Science and Technology in Halakhic Sources

  • Halperin, Mordechai. Refu'ah, Metzi'ut, v'Halakhah: U'lshon Ḥakhamim Marpei [Medicine, Reality, and Halakhah; Hebrew: רפואה מציאות והלכה: ולשון חכמים מרפא]. Jerusalem: Schlesinger Institute, 2012. Responsa and essays by a leading authority on medical halakhah; models how halakhic reasoning adapts to technological change.

  • Kahana, Maoz. Me-ha-Noda bi-Yehudah la-Ḥatam Sofer: Halakhah ve-Hagut le-Nokhaḥ Etgarei ha-Zeman [From the Noda bi-Yehudah to the Ḥatam Sofer: Halakhah and Thought Facing the Challenges of the Time; Hebrew: מהנודע ביהודה לחתם סופר: הלכה והגות לנוכח אתגרי הזמן]. Jerusalem: Zalman Shazar Center, 2015. Intellectual history of how major halakhic authorities in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries responded to modernity.

  • Kahana, Maoz. Tarnegolet bli Lev: Dat u-Mada ba-Ketivah ha-Rabbanit ba-Me'ah ha-Shemoneh-Esreh [A Heartless Chicken and Other Wonders: Religion and Science in Early Modern Rabbinic Culture; Hebrew: תרנגולת בלי לב: דת ומדע בכתיבה הרבנית במאה השמונה-עשרה]. Jerusalem: Bialik Institute, 2021. Examines how eighteenth-century rabbis processed scientific anomalies and discoveries; directly relevant to questions of how halakhah might respond to AI.

  • Tirosh-Samuelson, Hava, and Aaron W. Hughes, eds. J. David Bleich: Where Halakhah and Philosophy Meet. Brill, 2015. Essays on a major contemporary halakhic authority known for his engagement with medical ethics and technology.

  • Berkovits, Eliezer. "Orthodox Judaism in a World of Revolutionary Transformations." Tradition 7, no. 2 (1965): 68-88. Argues that halakhic decision-making requires an understanding of modern civilization, "its scientific foundations, its technological processes."

  • Zomet Institute. Teḥumin [Hebrew: תחומין]. Alon Shevut: Zomet, vol. 46 (5786/2026). Annual collection of halakhic articles on technology, medicine, agriculture, and public life in the State of Israel.

Jewish Attitudes toward Technology

  • Lubin, Matt. "Bricks and Stones: On Man's Subdual of Nature." Kol Hamevaser 9, no. 2 (2016). Available online. Student essay exploring Jewish theological frameworks for human technological activity.

  • Navon, Mois. "A Jewish Theological Perspective on Technology (Orthodox)." In St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, edited by Brendan N. Wolfe et al. University of St Andrews, 2024. Available online. Concise overview of Orthodox Jewish approaches to technology, including traditional and contemporary sources.

  • Perl, Elimelekh Y. "Jewish and Western Ethical Perspectives on Emerging Technologies." Undergraduate honors thesis, Yeshiva University, 2022. Available online. Comparative analysis of Jewish and secular ethical frameworks for evaluating new technologies.

  • Schacter, Jacob J. "Jewish Technophobia: An Old Story." Sapir 11 (Autumn 2023). Traces recurring rabbinic alarm at new technologies and the adaptation that followed, from the printing press to the internet and AI chatbots.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Judaism at the Speed of Technological Change." Sapir 11 (Autumn 2023). Argues that rabbinic responses to printing, firearms, the Zeppelin, and radio came late and asked chiefly about Shabbat use, and proposes institutional remedies.

  • White, Lynn, Jr. Medieval Religion and Technology: Collected Essays. University of California Press, 1978. Influential arguments about religious attitudes shaping technological development; frames comparative questions about Jewish distinctiveness.

  • White, Lynn, Jr. Medieval Technology and Social Change. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1962. Classic study of how technological innovations reshaped medieval European society.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. The Lonely Man of Faith. Jerusalem: Maggid, 2012 [orig. 1965]. First published in Tradition 7, no. 2 (1965): 5-67. The dignity of "Adam the first" consists in subduing the cosmos through technological mastery, a mandate willed by God (pp. 14-16 of the 1965 printing); the counterpoint of "Adam the second" supplies the limit.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "To Cultivate and to Guard: The Universal Duties of Mankind." In By His Light: Character and Values in the Service of God. Jersey City: Ktav, 2003. Ch. 1 (pp. 1-24 in the Maggid reprint, 2016). Reads le-ovdah u-le-shomrah as two distinct mandates, one conservative and one creative, and distinguishes the view that man must maintain creation as given from the view that he is empowered and enjoined to transcend it.

  • Ziring, Jonathan. Torah in a Connected World: A Halakhic Perspective on Communication Technology and Social Media. Maggid Books, 2024. Contemporary halakhic treatment of digital technology; models the application of traditional legal reasoning to new technological contexts.

General Philosophy of Technology

  • Heidegger, Martin. The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays. Translated by William Lovitt. New York: Harper & Row, 1977. Treats modern technology as a mode of disclosing the world that orders nature as a standing reserve, against the view of technology as a neutral instrument.

  • Jonas, Hans. The Imperative of Responsibility: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. Argues that the reach of modern technology in space and time outstrips the ethics of proximate action and requires a new principle oriented toward the survival of future generations.

  • Brey, Philip. "Philosophy of Technology after the Empirical Turn." Techné: Research in Philosophy and Technology 14, no. 1 (2010): 36-48. Maps the shift from grand theories of Technology to the study of particular artifacts and practices; the methodological orientation a Jewish account of specific technologies would need.

  • Bunge, Mario. "Towards a Technoethics." The Monist 60, no. 1 (1977): 96-107. Early argument that engineers bear moral responsibility for the artifacts they design, against the view that responsibility attaches only to use.

  • Kroes, Peter, and Peter-Paul Verbeek, eds. The Moral Status of Technical Artefacts. Dordrecht: Springer, 2014. Collection on whether artifacts themselves can carry moral properties; directly relevant to halakhic questions about whether a device or only its operator is the subject of a norm.

  • Verbeek, Peter-Paul. "Some Misunderstandings about the Moral Significance of Technology." In The Moral Status of Technical Artefacts, edited by Peter Kroes and Peter-Paul Verbeek, 75-88. Dordrecht: Springer, 2014. Defends mediation theory: artifacts shape what actions and perceptions are available without themselves being agents.

  • Sandler, Ronald L., ed. Ethics and Emerging Technologies. London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2014. Broad reader covering the recurring structure of ethical argument about new technologies, useful for locating where Jewish sources bear on generic questions and where on specific ones.

  • Vallor, Shannon. Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. Recasts technology ethics as a question of which character traits emerging technologies cultivate or erode.

Social and Cultural Studies

  • Goltz, Nachshon (Sean), John Zeleznikow, and Tracey Dowdeswell. "From the Tree of Knowledge and the Golem of Prague to Kosher Autonomous Cars: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Through Jewish Eyes." Oxford Journal of Law and Religion 9, no. 1 (2020): 132-156. Reads AI ethics through Jewish sources, including the golem tradition and halakhic categories of causation and responsibility.

  • Dowdeswell, Tracey, and Nachshon Goltz. "Cultural Regulation of Disruptive Technologies: Lessons from Orthodox Religious Communities." Journal of Transportation Law, Logistics, and Policy 88, no. 1 (2021): 33-44. Case study of how Orthodox communities govern technology adoption; applicable to communal AI governance.

  • Neriya-Ben Shahar, Rivka. Strictly Observant: Amish and Ultra-Orthodox Jewish Women Negotiating Media. Rutgers University Press, 2024. Comparative study of how traditional religious communities selectively adopt and adapt communication technologies.

Individual Figures

  • Adler, Jacob. "J.S. Delmedigo and the Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer." Annals of Science 54 (1997): 293-299. Technical study of an early modern Jewish scientist's contribution to instrumentation.

  • Barzilay, Isaac. Yoseph Shlomo Delmedigo (Yashar of Candia): His Life, Works, and Times. Brill, 1974. Biography of a pivotal figure who moved between traditional rabbinic learning and experimental science; illustrates tensions and possibilities in early modern Jewish technological engagement.

  • Patai, Raphael. The Jewish Alchemists: A History and Source Book. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1994. Documents Jewish practitioners of alchemy from antiquity through the modern period.

  • Neher, André. Jewish Thought and the Scientific Revolution of the Sixteenth Century: David Gans (1541-1613) and His Times. Oxford University Press, 1986. Study of an early modern Jewish astronomer who sought to harmonize traditional learning with new cosmology.

  • Ruderman, David B. Kabbalah, Magic, and Science: The Cultural Universe of a Sixteenth-Century Jewish Physician. Harvard University Press, 1988. Study of Abraham Yagel that explores the intersection of mysticism, medicine, and natural philosophy.

Primary Sources

  • Deuteronomy 19:15. The requirement that a matter be established "by the mouth of two witnesses, or by the mouth of three witnesses"; the textual basis for formal edut and for the number of witnesses.

  • Rashi to Deuteronomy 19:15; Sifrei Devarim 188. Read "by the mouth of two witnesses" to exclude testimony written in a letter and sent to the court, and testimony relayed through an interpreter.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 71a. Source of the principle mi-pihem ve-lo mi-pi ketavam ("from their mouths and not from their writing"), applied to a mute who cannot testify in writing; the locus classicus for the oral form of testimony. The same passage excepts testimony that frees a woman to remarry, where the rabbis were lenient.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 31b. Applies the rule that testimony must come "from their mouths and not from their writing" to witnesses who would supply a forgotten detail, such as a date, from a written record.

  • Tosafot to Yevamot 31b, s.v. de-ḥazu bi-khtava. Report Rabbeinu Tam's view that witnesses who remember their testimony may send it to the court in writing, and that the mute is excluded because he is unfit to speak.

  • Tur, Ḥoshen Mishpat 28; Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 28:11-13, with Rema. The Tur sets Rashi and Maimonides against Rabbeinu Tam on written testimony; the Shulḥan Arukh rules that testimony sent in writing is not testimony, admits signed documents in monetary cases, and lets a witness whose memory a note revives testify.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Edut 3:4. By Torah law testimony is received only from the witnesses' mouths; documentary evidence in monetary cases is a rabbinic enactment and is not used for fines, flogging, or exile.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 5:1. Witnesses in capital cases are examined with seven inquiries into the time and place of the act.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46b, Tosafot s.v. be-muḥzak lekha. Rabbeinu Tam holds that one not known to have been a gentile is believed when he says he is Jewish, adding that most who come forward as Jews are Jews.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Pesaḥim 3b, Tosafot s.v. ve-ana. Hold that the gentile who ate of the paschal offering in Jerusalem was accepted because most there were Jews, so that the case does not prove that anyone who claims to be Jewish is believed.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 11a. Derives the rule of following the majority from "incline after the majority" (Exodus 23:2).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 3a. Treats what each litigant holds as his by the court's common certainty (anan sahadei) and compares it to the testimony of witnesses.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 79a; Bava Metzia 27a; Mishnah Yevamot 120a. Core sources on simanim (identifying marks): determining an animal's species, returning lost property by description, and identifying a deceased person so that his wife may remarry, where the Mishnah requires recognition of the face with the nose and rejects marks on the body or clothing; the Talmud at Yevamot 120a raises whether simanim operate on a biblical or rabbinic level.

  • Mishnah Sotah 6:1, with Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, and Rashash to Sotah 31a. R. Eliezer obliges a husband to divorce his wife "even if he heard it from a bird flying," against R. Yehoshua, who requires common talk; Maimonides reads the bird as evidence from its chirping, and the Rashash as a bird taught to speak.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Edut 9:1-12. Codifies the exclusion of minors, people lacking legal competence, and deaf or mute persons from formal testimony under the classical rules. Halakhah 9:11 refuses the written testimony of one who has become mute, except testimony that frees a woman to remarry.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 159a. Holds that relatives are disqualified as witnesses by "a decree of the King" and not for suspicion of lying, since Moses and Aaron could not testify for their father-in-law.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 7:7, 8:2. The court is commanded to decide on the word of two qualified witnesses although they may have testified falsely.

  • R. Ben-Zion Meir Ḥai Uziel, Mishpetei Uziel 4, Ḥoshen Mishpat 18. Holds that the acceptance of the parties cannot validate the testimony of a shoteh or a ḥeresh, since they "are not within the category of testimony at all."

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 2:2, with Be'er Heitev s.k. 4. On requiring proof of Jewish status from a person of unknown origin; the Be'er Heitev cites the Beit Hillel commentary and reflects established practice.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Even ha-Ezer 17:24, with Rema and Beit Shmuel, s.k. 70. The code requires that a body be identified by the face with the nose and admits only highly distinctive bodily marks, and Isserles adds that even a hundred non-distinctive marks count for nothing; the Beit Shmuel distinguishes inferior, intermediate, and highly distinctive marks and infers from the biblical force of the last that recognition by sight (tevius ayin) is biblical.

  • Netivot ha-Mishpat, Beurim, Ḥoshen Mishpat 46:8. Holds that money is not taken by intermediate marks but is taken by highly distinctive marks, which are biblical by all opinions, and that a defendant identified only by name and place is not executed without recognition by sight.

  • R. Yitsḥak Elḥanan Spektor, Be'er Yitsḥak, Even ha-Ezer 6, anafim 6 and 8. Holds that an intermediate mark does not take money even if simanim are biblical and that a highly distinctive mark equals recognition by sight, and in anaf 8 discusses the Shakh's view that money may be taken by simanim.

  • R. Yitsḥak Elḥanan Spektor, Ein Yitsḥak 1, Even ha-Ezer 31. Permits an agunah to remarry on several grounds, among them the likeness between a photograph of her husband taken in his lifetime and the photograph the London police kept of a drowned man.

  • R. Mordechai Leib Winkler, Levushei Mordekhai, Even ha-Ezer, Mahadura Tinyana 5. Holds that photographic likeness is more reliable than comparison of handwriting and perhaps a distinctive mark, in permitting the wife of a soldier found dead in a trench during the World War.

  • R. Ovadiah Yosef, Yabia Omer 6, Even ha-Ezer 3. Relies on photographs taken within three days of death, compared with photographs from life or recognized by relatives, to identify soldiers killed in the Yom Kippur War, citing Ḥavatzelet ha-Sharon, Even ha-Ezer 54, to the same effect.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 24a; R. Yaakov Ḥagiz, Halakhot Ketanot 2:82; R. Ḥayyim Yosef David Azulai, Birkei Yosef, Ḥoshen Mishpat 35:11. Witnesses who saw the new moon in water or through glass may not testify; R. Ḥagiz asks whether witnesses who saw a transgression reflected in a mirror may testify, and the Ḥida, citing him as 2:83, leaves open that such sight counts where error is impossible.

Secondary Sources

Halakhic Analysis of AI, Identification, and Evidence

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. Facial-recognition evidence for Jewish lineage analyzed through rov, simanim, and tevius ayin. Also reports R. Yosef Shalom Elyashiv's ruling, as cited by Farbstein in Teḥumin 12, that an individual may rely on a statistical majority to treat a person as Jewish for a specific purpose such as completing a minyan at an airport, whereas a court or appointed official may not (48).

  • David, Ariel. "Using Artificial Intelligence as Evidence in the Rabbinical Court" [Hebrew: שימוש בבינה מלאכותית כראיה בבית הדין]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 272-284. Holds that an AI system cannot be a witness but may serve the court's fact-finding as umdena in monetary cases or as evidence the parties accept, and that recordings open to forgery need basic verification.

Jewish Law, Privacy, and Digital Evidence

  • Bamberger, Kenneth A., and Ariel Evan Mayse. "Pre-modern Insights for Post-modern Privacy: Jewish Law Lessons for the Big Data Age." Journal of Law and Religion 36, no. 3 (2021): 495-532. Jewish-law perspectives on personal information at scale.

Statistical and Digital Evidence in General Legal Theory

  • Munch, Lauritz Aastrup. "Privacy Rights and 'Naked' Statistical Evidence." Philosophical Studies 178, no. 11 (2021): 3777-3795. Argues that privacy rights can restrict what may be inferred about a person from statistical evidence, as they restrict direct observation.

  • Chesney, Robert, and Danielle Keats Citron. "Deep Fakes: A Looming Challenge for Privacy, Democracy, and National Security." California Law Review 107, no. 6 (2019): 1753. Synthetic media and the reliability of recordings as evidence.

  • Grother, Patrick, Mei Ngan, and Kayee Hanaoka. Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects. NISTIR 8280. Gaithersburg, MD: National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2019. Finds that the false-positive rates of face-recognition algorithms often vary across demographic groups by factors of ten to more than one hundred.

  • Diel, Alexander, Tania Josan Lalgi, Isabel Carolin Schröter, Karl Fredric MacDorman, Martin Teufel, and Alexander Bäuerle. "Human Performance in Detecting Deepfakes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 56 Papers." Computers in Human Behavior Reports 16 (2024): 100538. Finds that people's overall accuracy in detecting deepfakes is not significantly above chance.

  • Wixted, John T., and Gary L. Wells. "The Relationship Between Eyewitness Confidence and Identification Accuracy: A New Synthesis." Psychological Science in the Public Interest 18, no. 1 (2017): 10-65. Finds that high-confidence eyewitness identifications are highly accurate under pristine testing conditions and much less reliable under others.
