Primary Sources

  • Mishnah Pe'ah 1:1. Ranks the study of Torah as "equivalent to them all" (talmud Torah ke-neged kulam); the foundational statement that study is not one commandment among others.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:3. Codifies the supremacy of study over all other commandments, "for study brings to deed", codifying the conclusion of Kiddushin 40b.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 81a; Bava Metzia 85a-b. The land was lost "because they did not bless on the Torah first," read by the Ran (citing Rabbeinu Yonah) and by Rashi as showing that the Torah was not precious in their eyes.

  • Jeremiah 9:11-12. The prophet asks why the land was lost, and God answers "because they abandoned My Torah."

  • Ran to Nedarim 81a, s.v. davar zeh, citing Rabbeinu Yonah's Megillat Setarim; Rashi to Bava Metzia 85b. The generation studied constantly but did not bless, because it did not study for the Torah's sake and so did not value it as a precious gift.

  • Baḥ to Tur, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 47. Reads the failure to bless as study conducted without the aim of attachment to the holiness of the Torah and its Giver. It also explains the Ashkenazi wording la'asok be-divrei Torah as referring to toil, the object of the divine promise.

  • Taz to Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 47:1; Mishnah Berurah 47:2. The Taz reads the blessing as referring to study pursued with toil, and the Mishnah Berurah describes the condemned generation as studying Torah like any other discipline.

  • Sifra, Beḥukotai 1 (on Leviticus 26:3). "If you walk in My statutes" is read as "that you be toiling in Torah."

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 47:2-4; Mishnah Berurah 47:5. The blessing over Torah is required for speaking or writing words of Torah but not for thinking them, and one who studies from a book is advised to say some of it aloud.

  • Maharal, Introduction to Tiferet Yisrael. Identifies the failure to bless as the root of the generation's sins; Torah studied in detachment from its Giver is a tree severed at the root, and cleaving to the Giver is the condition of the Torah's endurance.

  • Beit ha-Levi on Exodus 24:7 (Parashat Mishpatim). Distinguishes study as preparation for practice from study as a commandment in itself, compares purely instrumental study to tefillin made by a hired craftsman, and reads Menaḥot 99b as evidence of the second.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Menaḥot 42b. A blessing is recited over a commandment whose performance completes it, and not over its preliminary acts.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 40b. The debate of R. Tarfon and R. Akiva at Lod, concluding "study is greater, for study brings to deed"; with the diverging readings of Rashi and Tosafot at Bava Kamma 17a.

  • Tosafot to Kiddushin 40b; She'iltot as cited in Tosafot to Bava Kamma 17a. An opinion in Tosafot holds that one who has not yet learned must study first, while for one already learned deed is better; the She'iltot is cited with Rabbeinu Tam for the priority of study.

  • Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv ha-Torah, ch. 5; cf. Derush al ha-Torah. The Torah is intellect and the cause that brings deed into actuality; study's greatness is the greatness of cause over effect, against Tosafot's instrumental reading of Kiddushin 40b. The same chapter blames the printing of Tosafot beside the Gemara for students' studying Tosafot before the Talmud itself.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 30b, with the Vilna Gaon's commentary on Proverbs 16:26 and Ma'alot ha-Torah. The fetus is taught the whole Torah in the womb and an angel causes it to forget at birth. The Gaon reads this against yagati u-matsati: knowledge that arrives without toil is withdrawn, because the point of study is the labor that forms the student.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Introduction to Sifra di-Tsni'uta. Reports that maggidim offered to reveal Torah secrets to the Vilna Gaon and that he refused, wanting no understanding of the Torah that he had not labored for.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35b. R. Yishmael's "conduct yourself with them in the way of the world" against R. Shimon bar Yoḥai's insistence that study displace labor entirely; "many acted according to R. Yishmael and succeeded." The base text for how much of life Torah study is supposed to occupy.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Menaḥot 99b. Whether "you shall meditate on it day and night" requires a chapter morning and evening or constant study, and R. Yishmael's answer to Ben Dama about Greek wisdom.

  • Joshua 1:8. "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 30a. Words of Torah are to be "sharp in your mouth," and one's study is to be divided among Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud.

  • Ran to Nedarim 8a. Distinguishes the obligation of constant study from the obligation to know the Torah, which the Shema does not satisfy.

  • R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Shulḥan Arukh ha-Rav, Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:6. Now that the Oral Torah is written, a father need only have his son taught to understand the Talmud well enough to study and rule on his own.

  • Maimonides, Shemonah Perakim, ch. 6. The sages' preference for one who overcomes his desire over one who never had it holds for the commandments known from tradition, while for evils recognized by reason the one who does not desire them is greater.

  • Kohelet Rabbah 1:13; Vayikra Rabbah 19:2. Forgetting keeps a person studying, and the learner, like a worker filling a perforated basket, is paid for the toil.

  • Mishnah Shabbat 16:1 (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 115a, 116b). Ketuvim are not read during the hours of the beit midrash, which the Talmud places on Shabbat afternoon, so as not to draw people away from it.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 6b. "I toiled and I found, believe it", a rule the Talmud limits to sharpness of understanding as distinct from the retention of learning.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88b-89a. Moses answers the ministering angels that the Torah was not given to them, for they have no bodily needs and no evil inclination, so that the Torah is addressed to embodied beings.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7b. Attendance upon Torah scholars (shimush) is greater than study itself; formation through apprenticeship rather than text alone.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Horayot 13b. The plot to unseat Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel through tractate Uktzin, and the readmission of the plotters because the beit midrash needed their knowledge.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 64a; Horayot 14a. The contrast of "Sinai" and "uprooter of mountains," resolved in favor of mastery of sources; invoked in the contemporary literature on models that reason fluently from unreliable knowledge.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 14b. R. Yoḥanan's dictum that "the writers of halakhot are as those who burn the Torah, and one who learns from them receives no reward," which withholds the reward without saying that nothing is learned.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 19a-b. Rava: reasoning may be gathered from many teachers, but fixed text is better learned from one, "so that the formulations not diverge."

  • Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 60a-b; Eruvin 54a. The writing of the Oral Torah under et la'asot la-Shem, and the forgetting of Torah occasioned by the shattered Tablets; the classical precedents for media shifts and for loss as a condition of renewal.

  • Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed I:71. The prohibition on writing the Oral Torah had prevented the multiplication of opinions and disputes that followed its writing.

  • Mishnah Avot 5:22. "Turn it and turn it, for everything is in it." Study as an unbounded return to the same material rather than as the extraction of its content.

  • Mishnah Avot 3:8. Forgetting one's learning as mortal fault; retention as religious labor.

  • Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah 2:4. Even what a seasoned student (talmid vatik) will one day expound before his teacher was already said to Moses at Sinai. R. Hillel Shimon Shimanowitz, writing on AI-generated Torah, reads it in two directions: as conditioning the status "said at Sinai" on the student who will in fact innovate, which machine output lacks, or as encompassing every conceivable ḥiddush, so that a machine merely reveals what was already Torah.

  • R. Simḥah Zissel Ziv, Ḥokhmah u-Musar, vol. 1, no. 11. In the name of R. Yisrael Salanter: since the Torah is not decided in heaven but entrusted to the sages of each generation, a judge who has not first perfected his character produces no Torah even when his conclusion is correct.

  • R. Yom Tov Lipmann Heller, Introduction to Tosafot Yom Tov. God "showed" Moses the refinements of future generations without transmitting them to him.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 59a, with the glosses of R. Jacob Emden. The Gentile who engages in Torah, and the language of theft, which Emden explains as expounding what Israel was to have said; the classical form of the question whose intellectual products count as Torah.

  • Ra'ah, Ḥiddushim to Berakhot 11b. Midrash requires no blessing over Torah because it is subject to dispute.

  • Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayyim 206:5. No blessing is recited over food or drink until it is brought before the person.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim, Sha'ar 4. Torah study as attachment to the divine word and as the sustaining act of the created order; 4:12 on the cosmic significance of ḥiddush.

  • R. Ḥayyim of Volozhin, Nefesh ha-Ḥayyim 1:3. Man is created in the image of God in that his deeds, speech, and thoughts sustain or destroy the upper worlds and powers.

  • R. Abraham Isaac Kook, Orot ha-Torah 2:1. The light renewed through the Torah's connection to one soul differs from that born of its connection to another, so that each person has a share in Torah to innovate.

  • Maimonides, Introduction to the Mishneh Torah. Traces the transmission of the Oral Torah from Moses through a chain of named teachers and courts.

  • Judah Halevi, Kuzari 2:72. "From the mouths of scribes and not from the mouths of books"; living instruction ranked above book-knowledge.

  • Leḥem Mishneh to Hilkhot Talmud Torah 5:4. Reports the view that in an age of written Torah "the books are the teachers."

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, no. 419. Gives the root of the commandment as knowledge: through study a person knows the ways of God.

  • R. Paltoi Gaon, Ḥemdah Genuzah, no. 110. Objects to studying abridged codes in place of the Talmud, which diminishes the Torah and causes it to be forgotten; cf. Sefer ha-Eshkol, Hilkhot Sefer Torah, p. 50.

  • R. Hai Gaon, as cited in J. N. Epstein, Mevo'ot le-Sifrut ha-Amora'im, p. 143. Writing down halakhot is proper once memory has declined and readers need written texts to consult.

  • R. Ḥayyim ben Betsalel, Introduction to Vikuaḥ Mayim Ḥayyim. Opposes fixed written codes of halakhah in favor of rulings transmitted from teacher to disciple.

  • Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, vol. 6, no. 61. Gives thanks for the invention of printing while holding that its loss is also very great.

  • R. Yitsḥak Canpanton, Darkhei ha-Talmud, no. 1. The learner is to work out a passage with all his strength before consulting the commentators.

  • R. Yitsḥak Hutner, Paḥad Yitsḥak, Ḥanukkah 3; Shavuot 5, 18. The forgetting of Torah as the condition for the renewal of Torah.

  • R. Shlomo Kluger, glosses to Peri Megadim, Oraḥ Ḥayyim, Eshel Avraham 136. Argues that the Talmud's preference for Sinai over oker harim lapsed with the printing of books.

  • Rivash, Responsa, no. 271; Maharik, Responsa, shoresh 167. The Rivash criticizes dialecticians who reach confident and wrong conclusions, and both hold that Sinai takes precedence over oker harim in later generations as well.

  • Ḥazon Ish, Emunah u-Bitaḥon 3:8-9. Toil in the investigation of the law implants a love of it, which only exacting study over many years can acquire.

  • Leket Yosher, vol. 2, p. 39. R. Israel Isserlein's disapproval of the labor-saving revolving bookstand; a premodern source on effort as aid to retention.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations: The Nature and Status of Torah Study

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. Halakhic Man. Translated by Lawrence Kaplan. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1983. The halakhic personality as creative; the learner as partner in creation (pp. 81, 99).

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "Redemption, Prayer, Talmud Torah." Tradition 17, no. 2 (1978): 55-72. Study as an act of self-recovery in which the learner "returns to his own self."

  • Lamm, Norman. "Knowing vs. Learning: Which Takes Precedence?" In Wisdom from All My Teachers: Challenges and Initiatives in Contemporary Torah Education, edited by Jeffrey Saks and Susan Handelman. Jerusalem: Urim Publications and ATID, 2003. Weighs knowing and learning when they may present competing values in Torah study.

  • Lamm, Norman. Torah Lishmah: Torah for Torah's Sake in the Works of Rabbi Hayyim of Volozhin and His Contemporaries. Hoboken, NJ: Ktav, 1989. The standard monograph on Torah for its own sake.

  • Sinensky, Tzvi. "The Purpose of Talmud Torah." Yeshivat Har Etzion (Israel Koschitzky Virtual Beit Midrash), 2019. Reads R. Soloveitchik's thesis through the mourner's exclusion from study.

  • Shagar (Shimon Gershon Rosenberg). Be-Torato Yehegeh: Limmud Gemara ki-Vakashat Elokim [Hebrew: בתורתו יהגה: לימוד גמרא כבקשת אלוקים]. Edited by Zohar Maor. Makhon Kitvei ha-Rav Shagar, 5769/2008. Essays on Torah study, describing it primarily as a form of intimacy with God (p. 25).

  • Weiss, Asher. "Is Study Greater or Is Deed Greater?". Shiur, Parashat Beḥukkotai 5778. [Hebrew] Surveys the medieval positions on Kiddushin 40b, organizing them around whether deed is the telos of study or study and deed are independent modes of divine service.

Media, Orality, and the History of Jewish Learning

  • Soloveitchik, Haym. "Rupture and Reconstruction: The Transformation of Contemporary Orthodoxy." Tradition 28, no. 4 (1994): 64-130. The displacement of mimetic tradition by text.

  • Halbertal, Moshe. People of the Book: Canon, Meaning, and Authority. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1997. The textualization of the Oral Torah and the authority of the book.

  • Kanarfogel, Ephraim. "Progress and Tradition in Medieval Ashkenaz." Jewish History 14, no. 3 (2000): 287-316. Medieval authorities on whether later scholars may dispute their predecessors.

  • Ong, Walter J. Orality and Literacy: The Technologizing of the Word. London: Methuen, 1982. Oral and literate cultures distinguished.

  • Epstein, J. N. Mevo'ot le-Sifrut ha-Amora'im [Hebrew: מבואות לספרות האמוראים]. Edited by E. Z. Melamed. Jerusalem, 1962. Introduction to amoraic literature, citing geonic responsa on the writing of halakhot (p. 143).

  • Elman, Yakov and Israel Gershoni. Editors, Transmitting Jewish Traditions: Orality, Textuality, and Cultural Diffusion. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2000. Series of studies on the transmission of Jewish religious scholarship and cultural knowledge throughout Jewish history.

AI and Contemporary Applications

  • Kaufman, Meir, et al. "Aleh Binah: Torah Insights Generated by Artificial Intelligence" [Hebrew: עלה בינה: דברי תורה שנתחדשו ע"י בינה מלאכותית והמסתעף]. Shabbos Gilyon (Lakewood), Parashat Pinḥas through Va'etḥanan 5786 (2026). Multi-issue exchange, opened by remarks of R. Aryeh Malkiel Kotler, on whether AI-generated Torah is a ḥefetz shel Torah and whether birkat ha-Torah applies to its study.

  • Cherlow, Yuval. "Artificial Intelligence as a Study Partner (Ḥavruta)" Hebrew: הבינה המלאכותית כחברותא]. Be-Sheva, Tammuz 5785 (2025); reprinted at [Yeshiva.org.il. Proposes treating AI as a study partner that challenges the learner without becoming an authority.

  • Fish, Zach. "Talmud Torah in the Age of AI." Shtark Tank (Substack), May 29, 2025. Distinguishes searching for sources from toil over them and locates the commandment in the toil.

  • Fraenkel, Avinoam. "Torah Genius, Infallibility and Augmented Intelligence." The Seforim Blog, March 11, 2022. Argues that digital databases favor the oker harim over the Sinai as a model of Torah scholarship.

  • Kalman, David Zvi. "Computers Can Write Torah Now. Should We Be Excited or Terrified?" The Forward, May 13, 2021. Examines GPT-3 imitations of Jewish texts and argues that style is much of what makes a text feel sacred.

  • Hollander, Max. "Ameilut in the Age of AI." The Lehrhaus, October 12, 2025. Argues that AI need not be rejected if ameilut ba-Torah is redefined toward physicality, identity and connection, and ḥiddush in a world of instantaneous information.

  • Koppel, Moshe, and Avi Shmidman. "Torah Study and the Digital Revolution: A Glimpse of the Future." The Lehrhaus, January 28, 2020. Explains how machine learning can support vocalization, critical editions, source identification, and thematic research while retaining a need for expert review.

  • Wiederblank, Netanel. "Ten Reasons Why We Cannot Turn to AI for Psak: Understanding the Nature and Philosophy of the Halachic Process." In The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785. New York: Yeshiva University, 2024. Shimush, masora as a chain of persons, and obligatory ḥiddush against machine replacement.

  • Flug, Josh. "The Rabbi & AI." Tradition (Tradition Questions), February 2025. Poses the question of what becomes of ameilut ba-Torah as AI makes information instantaneous, and refers in a note to Norman Lamm's essay on the conflicting values of knowing and learning.

  • Flug, Josh. "Artificial Intelligence and Halacha: Navigating the New Frontier Across the Four Sections of Shulchan Aruch." The Benjamin and Rose Berger Torah To-Go Series, Kislev 5785 (2024): 45-50. Asks whether Torah knowledge supplied by a brain implant would fulfill the commandment of study, drawing on the Vilna Gaon's reading of Niddah 30b.

  • Student, Gil. "Talmud Torah in the Age of AI." Torah Musings, August 11, 2025. Compares AI to the writing down of the Oral Torah and treats it as a supplement to classical study.

  • Wolkenfeld, Sara Tillinger. "Torah, Like Technology, Is a Form of Optimism." Shalom Hartman Institute, May 29, 2025. Presents AI as the latest technology through which Torah reaches learners.

  • Klein, Reuven Chaim. "AI and the New Frontier of Torah Study." The Jewish Press, September 2, 2026. Places AI after the codex, print, and the internet as a medium of Torah study, and holds that it cannot decide between interpretations.

  • Lubin, Shmuel. "AI the Rabbi? Musings on the 'Hot Topic' of the Day." Shmuel's Substack, January 10, 2025. Reads the Talmud's preference for Sinai over oker harim against language models trained to persuade, and proposes treating them as an unreliable ḥavruta rather than a teacher.

  • Koppel, Moshe. "What Artificial Intelligence Has in Store for Judaism." Mosaic / Tikvah Ideas, March 2024. Communal Torah study as an answer to the social isolation of a laborless information environment.

  • Wolkenfeld, Sara. "Who Has Not Made AI a Woman." Guest post on David Zvi Kalman's Substack, August 9, 2026. Contrasts the welcome extended to AI in Torah study with the gatekeeping of women's learning, and argues from Shabbat 88b-89a that Torah was designed for embodied study.

  • Schachter, Hershel. "Can Women Be Rabbis?" TorahWeb, 2004. Argues from God's hiddenness against public religious leadership roles for women.

Primary Sources

  • Genesis 1:26-28; 2:7; 2:15. Divine image, embodied life, and the mandate to cultivate and guard.

  • Genesis 3:22-24; Psalms 90:12; Ecclesiastes 1:4. God bars the human being from the tree of life lest he live forever; the psalmist asks to be taught to number his days; and one generation goes and another comes while the earth endures.

  • Genesis Rabbah 11:6; Midrash Tanḥuma, Tazria 5. R. Hoshaya holds that everything created in the six days requires further work and that "even a human being needs tikkun"; R. Akiva sets loaves beside sheaves to show that human works improve on what God made, and concludes that the commandments were given to refine Israel.

  • Genesis Rabbah 12:1. R. Shimon bar Yoḥai rebukes one who wishes he had three eyes or three legs, since the heavenly court deliberated over each of his limbs.

  • Exodus 21:19; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 85a. Derives from "and he shall surely heal" the physician's permission to heal, the license for medical treatment from which halakhic discussion of enhancement begins.

  • Deuteronomy 4:9, 15; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 32b; Bava Kamma 90b-91b. Verses on guarding oneself, applied to bodily safety in Berakhot, and the Mishnah and Talmud on whether a person may injure himself, which together bound the risks a person may take with his own body.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33b. R. Ḥanina's "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," read as placing human freedom in moral choice and cited against technological moral enhancement.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, De'ot 1:4-7. Good traits are acquired by performing the corresponding acts repeatedly until they become easy and fixed in the soul, a model of moral formation by practice.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:7-14. The levels of charity, the highest being help that makes a poor person self-supporting so that he need not depend on others.

  • Abraham Isaac Kook, Orot, "Orot me-Ofel," Orot ha-Teḥiyah 33. "We have engaged much in the soul and forgotten the holiness of the body... we have holy flesh no less than we have a holy spirit." A call for national physical revival that treats the holiness of the body as a religious value; the passage does not discuss enhancement.

  • Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5; Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58a. Every human being is struck from the seal of the first Adam and none is like another; one who sees a crowd blesses God as "Wise One of secrets" (ḥakham ha-razim), since their minds and faces are not alike.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 46b; Ta'anit 23a. Luz, the city the angel of death may not enter, whose elders leave it to die when weary of life; and Ḥoni ha-Me'agel, who woke after seventy years without companions and prayed for death.

  • R. Moshe Ḥayyim Luzzatto, Derekh Hashem I:3:11. The final perfection is attained neither by the body nor by the soul alone, only by their reunion after the resurrection.

  • Genesis Rabbah 8:11; Babylonian Talmud, Ḥagigah 16a. Humans share four traits with the angels and four with the beasts, and their mortality is tied to sin; Ḥagigah lists six traits, three angelic and three animal.

Secondary Sources

Jewish Engagement with Enhancement

  • Tirosh-Samuelson, Hava. "Transhumanism as a Secularist Faith." Zygon 47, no. 4 (2012): 710-734. Transhumanism as technological eschatology.

  • Tirosh-Samuelson, Hava. "In Pursuit of Perfection: The Misguided Transhumanist Vision." Theology and Science 16, no. 2 (2018): 200-222. A Jewish philosophical critique of radical enhancement.

  • Glick, Shimon M. "Some Jewish Thoughts on Genetic Enhancement." Journal of Medical Ethics 37, no. 7 (2011): 415-419. Holds germline enhancement unethical at present, but suggests that if safety were established, Jewish sources might weigh the benefits of some genetic enhancements above the objections.

  • Loike, John D., and Moshe D. Tendler. "Tampering with the Genetic Code of Life: Comparing Secular and Halakhic Ethical Concerns." Ḥakirah 18 (2014): 41-58. Holds that halakhah would forbid risky gene editing for non-medical enhancement of oneself and any non-medical gene editing of an embryo or child.

  • Soloveitchik, Joseph B. "The Lonely Man of Faith." Tradition 7, no. 2 (Summer 1965): 5-67. Creative mastery and covenantal vulnerability as paired vocations.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "To Cultivate and to Guard: The Universal Duties of Mankind." In By His Light: Character and Values in the Service of God, adapted by Reuven Ziegler. Jersey City: Ktav, 2003. Reads le-ovdah u-le-shomrah as two distinct mandates, one conservative and one creative, and distinguishes the view that man must maintain creation as given from the view that he is empowered to transcend it.

  • Lichtenstein, Aharon. "'Mah Enosh': Reflections on the Relation between Judaism and Humanism." The Torah u-Madda Journal 14 (2006-07): 1-61. Defends a halakhic humanism that values the mundane order and seeks its redemption, and holds that the Halakhah cannot satisfy the radical secular humanist.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. Golems Among Us: How a Jewish Legend Can Help Us Navigate the Biotech Century. Chicago: Ivan R. Dee, 2004. Draws on the golem legend to endorse genetic engineering within limits while criticizing transhumanism.

  • Sherwin, Byron L. "Golems in the Biotech Century." Zygon 42, no. 1 (2007): 133-44. Applies the golem legend to bioengineering, reproductive technology, robotics, and artificial intelligence as a source of prudent guidance.

  • Rubin, Charles T. "The Golem and the Limits of Artifice." The New Atlantis 39 (Summer 2013): 56-72. A critique of Sherwin's golem-based case for biotechnology, citing Genesis Rabbah 12:1 and arguing that the golem literature counsels restraint.

  • Kass, Leon R. "L'Chaim and Its Limits: Why Not Immortality?" First Things 113 (May 2001). Argues from Genesis 3, Psalm 90, and Jewish practice that the affirmation of life does not license the unlimited pursuit of longevity.

  • Rosenfeld, Azriel. "Human Identity: Halakhic Issues." Tradition 16, no. 3 (Spring 1977): 58-74. Treats a person reconstructed from an electronic recording as a new legal individual and the destruction of the original in scanning as murder, and applies the same reasoning to copies of an intelligent computer program.

  • Navon, Mois. "The Moral Status of Artificial Intelligence: A Jewish Ethical Perspective." PhD diss., Bar-Ilan University, 2023. Its appendix (pp. 217-218) raises Jewish objections to AI brain chips for moral enhancement and asks whether uploaded minds fit the doctrine of the world to come.

Enhancement Ethics and Human Limits

  • Kass, Leon R. "Ageless Bodies, Happy Souls: Biotechnology and the Pursuit of Perfection." The New Atlantis 1 (Spring 2003): 9-28. Argues that aging, mortality, and longing give a human life its shape, and that the goods enhancement promises depend on the finitude it proposes to remove.

  • Schneider, Susan. "Should You Add a Microchip to Your Brain?" The New York Times, June 10, 2019. A fictional op-ed in the series "Op-Eds From the Future" on whether a person survives the gradual replacement of brain tissue by microchips.

  • Sotala, Kaj. "Advantages of Artificial Intelligences, Uploads, and Digital Minds." International Journal of Machine Consciousness 4, no. 1 (2012): 275-91. Catalogues the capability advantages a digital mind, whether an upload or an artificial general intelligence, might hold over a biological one.

  • Nussbaum, Martha C. "Human Functioning and Social Justice: In Defense of Aristotelian Essentialism." Political Theory 20, no. 2 (1992): 202-246. Flourishing grounded in embodied capabilities and shared limits.

  • Nussbaum, Martha C. "Transcending Humanity." In Love's Knowledge: Essays on Philosophy and Literature, 365-391. New York: Oxford University Press, 1990. Argues that human limits give human excellence its structure and significance, and that the aspiration to leave the conditions of humanity behind altogether is incoherent.

  • Sandel, Michael J. The Case Against Perfection: Ethics in the Age of Genetic Engineering. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007. Giftedness, humility, and solidarity against enhancement.

  • Bostrom, Nick. "Human Genetic Enhancements: A Transhumanist Perspective." Journal of Value Inquiry 37, no. 4 (2003): 493-506. A representative defense of enhancement.

  • Bostrom, Nick. "In Defense of Posthuman Dignity." Bioethics 19, no. 3 (2005): 202-214. Argues for a concept of dignity inclusive enough to apply to many possible posthuman beings, against bioconservative critics of enhancement.

  • Savulescu, Julian, Ruud ter Meulen, and Guy Kahane, eds. Enhancing Human Capacities. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell, 2011. Interdisciplinary analysis of cognitive, physical, moral, and lifespan enhancement.

  • Savulescu, Julian, and Ingmar Persson. "Moral Enhancement, Freedom, and the God Machine." The Monist 95, no. 3 (2012): 399-421. Tests biomedical moral enhancement against human freedom through a hypothetical machine that intervenes before immoral action.

  • Harris, John. "Moral Enhancement and Freedom." Bioethics 25, no. 2 (2011): 102-111. Holds that the only reliable means of moral enhancement are socialization, education, and parental supervision, or high-technology methods general in their application.

  • Vallor, Shannon. Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. New York: Oxford University Press, 2016. Technomoral virtue as a guide where prediction fails.

Transhumanism and Artificial Intelligence

  • Kurzweil, Ray. The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology. New York: Viking, 2005. Forecasts a merger of human and machine intelligence and defends the patternist view that a person could survive as an uploaded model of the brain.

  • Tegmark, Max. Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. New York: Knopf, 2017. Distinguishes stages of life by their capacity to redesign their own software and hardware, and surveys the futures that artificial general intelligence might bring.

  • Harari, Yuval Noah. Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow. London: Harvill Secker, 2016. Predicts that humanity will turn to the pursuit of immortality, happiness, and godlike powers, and that a "Dataism" centered on data-processing systems may displace humanism.

  • Yudkowsky, Eliezer. "Transhumanism as Simplified Humanism." 2007. Reposted on LessWrong, December 5, 2018. Argues that transhumanism is the common sense of standard humanism applied rigorously to cases outside present experience.

Primary Sources

  • Exodus 23:7. "From a false matter keep far" (mi-devar sheker tirḥak). The unusually strong biblical command, read by the rabbis as extending beyond lying to a general duty of distancing from falsehood and deception (Shevuot 30b-31a).

  • Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1. Gives two explanations of why the seal of the Holy One is emet: R. Bun's, that He is the living God and King of the universe (Jeremiah 10:10), and Resh Lakish's, that alef, mem, and tav stand first, middle, and last in the alphabet.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 104a. The letters of sheker stand on one foot and those of emet on a broad base, "truth stands, falsehood does not"; falsehood is common and truth uncommon.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 30b-31a. A series of baraitot derives from "from a false matter keep far" that a judge may not advocate for his own position, may not seat an ignorant student before him, and may not decide a case he knows to be fraudulent on the strength of the testimony, and that one may not stand silently beside a creditor's single witness to create the appearance of a second.

  • Sefer Yere'im, siman 235. Collects the applications of "from a false matter keep far" and limits the Torah prohibition to falsehood from which harm to others follows, explaining Beit Shammai's objection in the bride case on that ground, since praising a defective bride looks like stealing the husband's mind.

  • Ḥafetz Ḥayyim, Petiḥah, Positive Commandments 13. Counts "from a false matter keep far" as a positive commandment, transgressed when falsehood is mixed into lashon ha-ra or reḥilut.

  • Genesis 18:12-13. God's report to Abraham of Sarah's words substitutes "and I am old" for her "and my husband is old"; cited as the scriptural basis for permitting deviation from strict accuracy for the sake of peace.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a. "The seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth." Classical statement that truth is a divine attribute, said by R. Ḥanina and brought to explain the tav marked on the foreheads of the righteous (Ezekiel 9:4).

  • Meiri, Beit ha-Beḥirah, Shabbat 55a. On the dictum that there is no death without sin: the principles of belief do not depend on proofs drawn from the plain sense of verses and of aggadot, and one does not raise objections from aggadah.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 94a. The locus classicus for geneivat da'at (creating a false impression), prohibiting the manufacture of misleading impressions even absent an explicit lie or monetary loss. Among its cases is carrying into a house of mourning a jug that rattles as though it held wine; Rashi explains that the jug is partly empty and the mourner takes it for full.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ḥullin 94b. Limits geneivat da'at where the mistaken party draws his own inference: a crier may announce that meat has fallen to the soldiers, since "they are the ones who deceive themselves."

  • Ritva on Ḥullin 94a. Reports in the name of the Tosafists that geneivat da'at is a Torah prohibition derived from "you shall not steal" (Leviticus 19:11), and quotes the Tosefta of Bava Kamma that the greatest of thieves is one who steals another's mind.

  • Tosefta Bava Kamma 7:3. "There are seven thieves, the first of them one who steals the mind of others," followed by the cases of Ḥullin 94a, false measures, and false weights; the Ritva's text reads three thieves rather than seven.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b. R. Elazar b. R. Shimon: "a person may alter in a matter of peace," proved from the brothers' message to Joseph (Genesis 50:16-17); R. Natan holds the alteration a commandment, from God's instruction to Samuel (I Samuel 16:2); and the school of R. Yishma'el that God Himself altered Sarah's words. The permission is distinct from mipnei darkei shalom, the enactments for social peace (Gittin 59b-61a).

  • Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 16b-17a. The dispute between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel on how to praise a bride; the House of Hillel permits describing every bride as "beautiful and graceful," against Beit Shammai's objection from "keep far from falsehood," and answers from the practice of praising to a buyer the poor purchase he has already made.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97a. Rava's account of a town called Kushta whose people did not alter their words and where no one died before his time, and of the deaths that followed his own concealment of his wife's presence at home.

  • Rabbeinu Yonah, Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:178-186. Nine classes of liars, among them one who invents a whole narrative without gain to himself or loss to another (3:181), the deceiver whose sin the sages weighed as graver than theft (3:184), and one who praises himself for virtues he does not have (3:185); 3:181 lists the praise of a bride and alteration for peace as the permitted cases.

  • Sefer Ḥasidim §§426, 1060-1061 (Zhitomir 1857 numbering; the Parma edition numbers differently). Limits the permission to alter for peace to a matter already past (426); forbids telling another to ask a sage on the ground that he will rule as the speaker does, since he may not (1060); and holds that one who knows a matter and will not disclose it should keep silent rather than deny knowing (1061).

  • Mishnah Avot 5:7, with Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 4a. Among the marks of the wise, that concerning what he has not heard he says "I have not heard," and he concedes the truth; the Talmud adds the instruction to train one's tongue to say "I do not know," lest one be caught out in a fabrication.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b. R. Shmuel b. Naḥmani: monetary fraud can be restored and wounding speech (ona'at devarim) cannot.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 72b. Rava: a scholar whose inside is not like his outside (tokho ke-varo) is no scholar.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 2a and following. The Mishnaic law of damage caused by one's property and animals, set out as four primary categories, the ox, the pit, maveh, and fire, with the Gemara dividing the ox into foot, tooth, and horn at 2b-3a. Perl (2022) takes the law of damage done by one's livestock as the model for a programmer's liability for an autonomous system.

  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 2:6. Rules that a person must not accustom himself to smooth or deceptive speech and that inner thought and outward expression must correspond, codifies geneivat da'at with the cases of Ḥullin 94a, and holds that even a single word of enticement or of geneivat da'at is forbidden.

  • R. Nissim of Gerona (Ran), Derashot ha-Ran 7. The determination of the law was handed to the sages of each generation, so that where their reasoning inclined to declare the oven of Akhnai impure they were bound to do so although they knew the truth was the reverse. Klark (2026) reads Derashot ha-Ran 11 as holding instead that each question has a single correct answer.

  • Genesis 27:19, with Rashi and Radak ad loc. Jacob says "I am Esau your firstborn." Rashi reparses the words so that no false statement is made ("I am the one bringing to you, and Esau is your firstborn"); Radak grants that the words were untrue but denies that Jacob was a speaker of falsehood, on the grounds that he knew the blessing was rightly his, that he feared his brother, that his mother had commanded him, and that she had prophecy.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 23b-24a, with Rashi ad loc. Scholars alter their words in three matters, tractate, bed, and hospitality, which Rashi explains as humility, modesty, and the protection of a host; the Talmud's point is that outside these three a scholar does not alter his words, which is why lost property is returned to him on his recognition of it alone.

  • Dessler, Eliyahu E. Mikhtav me-Eliyahu, vol. 1, p. 94. Rejects the identification of truth with accurate report: truth is what leads to good and to the will of the Creator, and falsehood is what gives success to the works of the prince of falsehood, the sitra aḥra.

  • Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 89b. One may not keep a false measure in one's house "even as a chamber pot"; the prohibition attaches to possession of the falsifying instrument itself.

  • Sefer ha-Ḥinukh, Mitzvah 74. Treats the prohibition on hearing one litigant without the other as part of the Torah's demand to distance oneself from falsehood, and includes false testimony and harmful speech within its discussion. Notes that the Torah uses the language of distance in no other warning, and grounds the commandment in God as a God of truth, blessing resting on those whose deeds resemble His.

Secondary Sources

Conceptual Foundations: Truth and Deception in Jewish Thought

  • Ha-Levi, Aaron. Sefer HaHinnuch: The Book of Mitzvah Education. Translated by Charles Wengrov. New York: Feldheim, (1523) 1978. English translation of the Ḥinukh, whose authorship is traditionally assigned to Aaron ha-Levi and is disputed; on Mitzvah 74 it grounds the distance from falsehood in God as a God of truth and in the resemblance to Him on which blessing rests.

  • Zimmerman, Binyamin. "Geneivat Daat: Misleading, Misrepresentation and Deception." Torat Har Etzion. Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2016. The scope of geneivat da'at across the codes. Surveys the concept through the Ritva, the Semag, Seforno on Leviticus 25:17, the Semak, Shulḥan Arukh Ḥoshen Mishpat 228, and the dispute between Rashi and the Meiri on Ḥullin 94a.

  • Rosensweig, Michael. "Elu va-Elu Divrei Elokim Ḥayyim: Halakhic Pluralism and Theories of Controversy." Tradition 26, no. 3 (1992): 4-23. Argues that the relation between halakhic pluralism and pesak as an enterprise aimed at a single binding conclusion is complex and double-edged, and that the procedural aspect of halakhic resolution dominates.

  • Avraham, Michael. "Geneivat Da'at and Intellectual Property" [Hebrew: גניבת דעת וקניין רוחני]. Teḥumin 25 (5765/2005): 350-366. Argues that geneivat da'at may rest on theft rather than on falsehood, citing the Ritva's derivation from "you shall not steal" and the Tosefta's list of thieves.

The Ethics of Deception, Manipulation, and Fabricated Evidence

  • Noggle, Robert. "The Ethics of Manipulation." In Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, edited by Edward N. Zalta. Summer 2020 Edition. (first published 2018; substantively revised 2026). Deception, coercion, and manipulation distinguished.

  • Chesney, Robert, and Danielle Keats Citron. "Deep Fakes: A Looming Challenge for Privacy, Democracy, and National Security." California Law Review 107, no. 6 (2019): 1753-1820. Synthetic media as a threat to shared evidence.

  • Rini, Regina. "Deepfakes and the Epistemic Backstop." Philosophers' Imprint 20, no. 24 (2020). Fabricated recordings erode the testimonial backstop.

  • Fallis, Don. "The Epistemic Threat of Deepfakes." Philosophy and Technology 34, no. 4 (2021): 623-643. Argues that deepfakes reduce the quantity of information a recording carries and so the knowledge it can give.

  • Rini, Regina. "Fake News and Partisan Epistemology." Kennedy Institute of Ethics Journal 27, no. 2 suppl. (2017): E-43-E-64. How false information circulates within communities.

  • Susser, Daniel, Beate Roessler, and Helen F. Nissenbaum. "Online Manipulation: Hidden Influences in a Digital World." Georgetown Law Technology Review 4, no. 1 (2019): 1-45. Online manipulation as covert exploitation of decision-making vulnerabilities.

  • Gino, Francesca. "Dazzled by Creativity: Why We Excuse Dishonest Acts." Scientific American, March 14, 2017. On the psychology of dishonesty and the conditions under which deception is excused or overlooked.

  • Hicks, Michael Townsen, James Humphries, and Joe Slater. "ChatGPT Is Bullshit." Ethics and Information Technology 26, no. 2 (2024): article 38. Argues that the falsehoods of large language models are neither lies nor hallucinations, since the models are indifferent to the truth of their outputs.

  • Mata v. Avianca, Inc. 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023). Sanctions against counsel who filed a brief citing non-existent judicial opinions, with fabricated quotations, generated by ChatGPT; cited for the event rather than for argument.

AI Reliability, Deception, and Halakhic Application

  • Student, Gil. "AI-Generated Deep Fakes and Halakhah." Torah Musings, July 28, 2025. Treats deepfakes as wronging both the person depicted, under hotsa'at shem ra, lashon ha-ra by gesture, and ona'at devarim, and the misled public, under geneivat da'at and "keep far from falsehood."

  • Klark, Yisrael. "The Future of Artificial Intelligence as a Halakhic Decisor (A Response to R. Erez Abramov's Article)" [Hebrew: עתידה של בינה מלאכותית כפוסק הלכה (תגובה למאמרו של הרב ארז אברהמוב בתחומין מה)]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 527-537. Holds that no formal halakhic condition bars an AI system from ruling, and sets the Ritva's view that all sides of a question were given at Sinai against the Ran's that each question has one correct answer.

  • David, Ariel. "Using Artificial Intelligence as Evidence in the Rabbinical Court" [Hebrew: שימוש בבינה מלאכותית כראיה בבית הדין]. Teḥumin 46 (5786/2026): 272-284. Argues that presumptions against forgery may lapse where machines can forge perfectly, and that analytic systems able to detect generated material restore a document's standing rather than supplying new evidence.

  • Cherlow, Yuval, and Yaron Moskowitz. "Using Artificial Intelligence Systems to Rule Halacha [Abridged Position Paper]." Tzohar Center for Jewish Ethics, 1 Sivan 5786 (2026). Holds that promoting a system which creates a false perception of halakhic authority is geneivat da'at, and calls for transparency about the sources behind a generated answer.

  • Marcus, Mitch. "ChatGPT Is the Opposite of the Golem." Evolve, June 4, 2023. Argues that truth plays no part in statistical word prediction, and that fluent output invites readers to attribute an intent the system does not have.

  • Perl, Elimelekh Y. "Jewish and Western Ethical Perspectives on Emerging Technologies." Undergraduate honors thesis, Yeshiva College, Yeshiva University, 2022. Takes the law of damage done by one's livestock, rather than programmed ethics, as the model for a programmer's responsibility for an autonomous system.

  • Ji, Ziwei, Nayeon Lee, Rita Frieske, Tiezheng Yu, Dan Su, Yan Xu, Etsuko Ishii, Ye Jin Bang, Andrea Madotto, and Pascale Fung. "Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation." ACM Computing Surveys 55, no. 12 (2023): 1-38. Reviews the definitions, metrics, and mitigations of hallucination across summarization, dialogue, question answering, data-to-text generation, and translation.

  • Walters, William H., and Esther Isabelle Wilder. "Fabrication and Errors in the Bibliographic Citations Generated by ChatGPT." Scientific Reports 13 (2023): 14045. Finds 55 percent of GPT-3.5 and 18 percent of GPT-4 citations in 84 generated literature reviews to be fabricated, with substantive errors in many of the rest.

  • Farquhar, Sebastian, Jannik Kossen, Lorenz Kuhn, and Yarin Gal. "Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy." Nature 630 (2024): 625-630. Estimates a model's uncertainty at the level of meaning rather than wording in order to detect arbitrary and incorrect generations.

  • Kalai, Adam Tauman, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, and Edwin Zhang. "Why Language Models Hallucinate." arXiv:2509.04664, September 4, 2025. Argues that models guess when uncertain because training and evaluation reward guessing over an admission of uncertainty.

  • Bertolini, Andrea. "Human-Robot Interaction and Deception." Osservatorio del Diritto Civile e Commerciale 2 (2018): 645-659. Deception in interaction with human-like machine interfaces.
